pelvic-pain.name: Pelvic pain
pelvic-pain.what: Pain felt low in the abdomen, below the navel and between the hip bones. The pelvis holds the bladder and the lower bowel in everyone, the uterus, ovaries and fallopian tubes in women and anyone with these organs, and the prostate in men and anyone with a prostate, including trans women, all resting on the sling of the pelvic floor muscles. Pain from these organs is often felt in the same place, so its timing (with periods, with passing urine or stool, with sex), whether it is one-sided, and whether a pregnancy is possible do more to point to the cause than the site alone. Pain that lasts six months or more is called chronic pelvic pain; it frequently has more than one contributing cause, including tension in the pelvic floor muscles and sensitised nerves, and is managed differently from a single acute episode.

commonCauses.name: Period pain (primary dysmenorrhoea)
commonCauses.note: Cramping pain in the lower abdomen and back during the first days of a period, caused by the uterus contracting; it usually eases with heat and simple painkillers.

commonCauses.name: Ovulation pain (mittelschmerz)
commonCauses.note: A one-sided ache or sharp twinge around the middle of the cycle, lasting from a few hours to a day or two, as a follicle releases its egg.

commonCauses.name: Urinary tract infection
commonCauses.note: A suprapubic ache with burning on passing urine, frequency and urgency, and cloudy or bloody urine.

commonCauses.name: Constipation and irritable bowel syndrome
commonCauses.note: Cramping, bloating and a change in bowel habit, often relieved by passing stool or wind; irritable bowel syndrome is a common contributor to long-standing pelvic pain.

commonCauses.name: Endometriosis
commonCauses.note: Painful periods that worsen over the years, pain during or after sex, and pain on opening the bowels or passing urine during a period; a common cause of chronic pelvic pain that often takes a long time to diagnose.

commonCauses.name: Pelvic inflammatory disease
commonCauses.note: Infection of the uterus, tubes and ovaries, often following a sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea, although other bacteria spreading up from the vagina or cervix also cause it, with pain, unusual discharge, bleeding after sex or between periods and sometimes fever; untreated, it can scar the tubes.

lessCommon.name: Ectopic pregnancy
lessCommon.note: A pregnancy implanted outside the uterus, most often in a fallopian tube: one-sided pain and light bleeding about six to eight weeks after the last period, with shoulder-tip pain or faintness if the tube ruptures. An emergency.

lessCommon.name: Ovarian cyst torsion or rupture
lessCommon.note: Most ovarian cysts cause no pain, but a cyst that twists on its blood supply or bursts causes sudden, severe one-sided pain, often with vomiting; torsion needs urgent surgery to save the ovary.

lessCommon.name: Appendicitis
lessCommon.note: Pain that starts around the navel and settles in the lower right abdomen, with loss of appetite, nausea and fever; it can be hard to tell from pain in the right ovary or tube.

lessCommon.name: Fibroids
lessCommon.note: Benign growths of the uterine muscle that cause pressure, heaviness and heavy periods, and acute pain if a fibroid outgrows its blood supply or twists.

lessCommon.name: Prostatitis and chronic pelvic pain in men
lessCommon.note: Pain in the perineum, testicles, lower back or penis with urinary symptoms; acute bacterial prostatitis brings fever and feeling very unwell and needs urgent antibiotic treatment, whereas chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men usually has no identified infection.

lessCommon.name: Adhesions and pelvic floor muscle dysfunction
lessCommon.note: Scar tissue after surgery or infection, and pelvic floor muscles that are over-tight or poorly coordinated, can cause persistent deep pain, pain with sex and difficulty emptying the bladder or bowel.

urgent: Pelvic pain with a positive pregnancy test or a missed period, especially with vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, faintness or collapse
Sudden, severe pain on one side, particularly with vomiting, a racing pulse or cold, clammy skin
Pain with a high temperature, shivering or an unusual vaginal discharge
Pain with an inability to pass urine, or with blood in the urine

New and persistent bloating, feeling full quickly or loss of appetite, pelvic or abdominal pain, or passing urine more often or more urgently, when these happen on most days (NICE uses more than about 12 times a month), especially at age 50 or over

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

vaginal-bleeding.name: Unusual vaginal bleeding
vaginal-bleeding.what: Bleeding from the vagina at a time when a period is not due: between periods, after sex, after the menopause (once a year has passed since the last period), or during pregnancy. Cervical screening is offered to people without symptoms and is not the test for unusual bleeding: bleeding needs the cervix to be looked at directly. The blood may come from the lining of the uterus, the cervix, the vaginal wall or the vulva, and is occasionally confused with bleeding from the urethra or rectum. Stage of life narrows the causes. In the reproductive years hormonal and infective causes are the commonest, and a pregnancy test is part of every assessment. After the menopause even a single episode of light bleeding is treated as a warning sign: most post-menopausal bleeding turns out to have a benign cause, most often thinning of the lining of the vagina and of the uterus, but it can be the first sign of cancer of the uterine lining, and NICE guidance treats it as a reason for urgent investigation. Trans men and non-binary people with a uterus usually stop having periods on testosterone; bleeding that starts again needs the same assessment.

commonCauses.name: Hormonal contraception
commonCauses.note: Breakthrough bleeding or spotting is common in the first few months of the pill, patch, implant, injection and hormonal coil, and after missed pills; it usually settles, but bleeding that persists is checked for other causes.

commonCauses.name: Irregular ovulation
commonCauses.note: In the first years after periods start, in the years before the menopause and in polycystic ovary syndrome, cycles are unpredictable and bleeding can be irregular, prolonged or arrive between expected periods.

commonCauses.name: Cervical ectropion and polyps
commonCauses.note: Soft glandular cells on the outer surface of the cervix (common in pregnancy and on the pill) and benign polyps of the cervix or uterine lining bleed easily, typically after sex or as spotting between periods.

commonCauses.name: Infection
commonCauses.note: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea and pelvic inflammatory disease cause bleeding after sex or between periods, often with discharge, pain or fever; swabs for sexually transmitted infections are part of the assessment.

commonCauses.name: Fibroids
commonCauses.note: Benign growths of the uterine muscle cause heavy, prolonged periods and sometimes bleeding between them.

commonCauses.name: Early pregnancy
commonCauses.note: Light spotting around the time of implantation is common, but bleeding in a known or possible pregnancy can signal a threatened or actual miscarriage and always needs assessment.

lessCommon.name: Ectopic pregnancy
lessCommon.note: Light, often dark bleeding with one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain or faintness about six to eight weeks after the last period; a pregnancy outside the uterus can rupture and is an emergency.

lessCommon.name: Cervical cancer
lessCommon.note: Bleeding after sex, between periods or after the menopause, with or without an unusual discharge. Cervical screening is a test for people without symptoms, so bleeding needs the cervix to be examined directly.

lessCommon.name: Cancer of the uterine lining
lessCommon.note: Endometrial cancer most often presents as post-menopausal bleeding and is more likely with obesity, diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome or oestrogen taken without a progestogen; it is investigated with a transvaginal ultrasound of the lining and an endometrial biopsy.

lessCommon.name: Vaginal atrophy and injury
lessCommon.note: Low oestrogen after the menopause, and in trans men on testosterone, thins the vaginal lining so that it bleeds after sex; injury to the vulva or vagina is another cause. Atrophy is settled on as the explanation only once cancer has been excluded.

lessCommon.name: Bleeding disorders and anticoagulant medicines
lessCommon.note: Inherited clotting disorders and anticoagulant medicines make menstrual and other bleeding heavier and more prolonged.

urgent: Heavy bleeding with dizziness, fainting, a racing pulse or breathlessness
Bleeding in pregnancy or when pregnancy is possible, especially with one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain or faintness
Any bleeding after the menopause, even a single episode of spotting, which needs an urgent GP appointment
Bleeding after sex on more than one occasion, or bleeding between periods that continues for more than a few cycles
Bleeding with pelvic pain, fever or an offensive discharge, or bleeding that returns after periods had stopped on testosterone

coronary-artery-disease.name: Coronary artery disease
coronary-artery-disease.definition: Narrowing of the coronary arteries by fatty plaque (atherosclerosis), limiting blood flow to the heart muscle.
coronary-artery-disease.overview: Plaque builds up over decades in the arteries that supply the heart. When a narrowing limits flow during exertion the muscle becomes short of oxygen and signals this as angina; when a plaque ruptures and a clot blocks the artery, the result is a heart attack. It is the leading cause of death worldwide, and largely preventable.
causes: Atherosclerosis: cholesterol-rich plaque forming in the artery wall, driven by inflammation
riskFactors: Family history of early heart disease
signs: Often none between attacks
Signs of risk factors: high blood pressure, xanthelasma, nicotine staining
complications: Myocardial infarction
Heart failure
Arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death
coronary-artery-disease.diagnosis: The story of exertional chest pressure relieved by rest is the key. An ECG may be normal at rest; a stress test, CT coronary angiography or invasive angiography shows the narrowings. Blood tests assess cholesterol, glucose and kidney function.
coronary-artery-disease.treatment: Lifestyle change and medication for everyone: stop smoking, statins to lower LDL, aspirin to prevent clots, blood pressure and diabetes control, and drugs to relieve angina (nitrates, beta blockers). Significant narrowings can be opened with angioplasty and a stent or bypassed with surgery.
coronary-artery-disease.prevention: Not smoking, regular exercise, a diet low in saturated fat and salt, healthy weight, and treating blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes.
coronary-artery-disease.seekCare: Call emergency services for chest pain lasting more than a few minutes, or angina that is new, more frequent or occurs at rest.

myocardial-infarction.name: Heart attack (myocardial infarction)
myocardial-infarction.definition: Death of heart muscle because a coronary artery is suddenly blocked, usually by a clot forming on a ruptured plaque.
myocardial-infarction.overview: Every minute of blockage kills more muscle, so a heart attack is treated as a race to reopen the artery. Survival and the amount of muscle saved depend on how quickly the person calls for help and reaches a hospital able to perform emergency angioplasty.
causes: Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with clot formation
Less often: coronary spasm, spontaneous artery dissection, severe anaemia or oxygen lack with a fixed narrowing
riskFactors: Same as coronary artery disease: smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure, diabetes, family history, age
signs: Pale, sweaty, distressed
Fast or slow pulse, low or high blood pressure
Crackles in the lungs if the heart is failing
complications: Cardiac arrest from ventricular fibrillation
Heart failure
Rupture of the heart wall or a papillary muscle
Arrhythmias and heart block
Pericarditis
myocardial-infarction.diagnosis: An ECG within ten minutes of arrival shows ST elevation (STEMI) when a large artery is fully blocked; troponin in the blood rises over hours and confirms muscle damage in other cases. Echocardiography shows which wall has stopped moving.
myocardial-infarction.treatment: Aspirin immediately, then emergency angioplasty with a stent to reopen the artery (or clot-dissolving drugs if angioplasty is not reachable within about two hours). Afterwards: a second antiplatelet drug, a statin, a beta blocker and an ACE inhibitor, cardiac rehabilitation and risk factor control.
myocardial-infarction.prevention: The measures that prevent coronary artery disease; after a first attack, lifelong medication and rehabilitation halve the risk of another.
myocardial-infarction.seekCare: Call emergency services immediately for crushing chest pain, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, or chest discomfort with sweating, breathlessness or nausea. Do not drive yourself.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a heart attack?
sections.body:
The NHS says to call 999 for chest pain that feels tight or squeezing or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw; other symptoms can include shortness of breath, feeling or being sick, sweating, and pale, blue or grey skin. A heart attack is a medical emergency.

Not everyone has the classic chest pain. NHS 111 Wales notes that women are more likely to have other symptoms such as shortness of breath, feeling or being sick, and back or jaw pain. Symptoms vary from person to person, and some people, including older adults and people with diabetes, may have milder or atypical symptoms.

The NHS advises that, while waiting for the ambulance, a person who is not allergic to aspirin may chew and swallow an aspirin tablet.

sections.heading: What causes a heart attack?
sections.body:
The NHS says a heart attack happens when the blood supply to part of the heart is suddenly cut off, so that the heart muscle begins to die. Coronary heart disease is the leading cause. In coronary heart disease, fatty plaques build up in the coronary arteries, and a plaque can rupture and trigger a clot that blocks the vessel. A shortage of oxygen in the blood, for example from carbon monoxide poisoning or lung problems, is a less common cause.

The NHS lists smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, being overweight and a close relative who has had a heart attack among the risk factors. NHS Inform lists age and ethnicity among the risk factors for coronary heart disease.

A heart attack is a problem with the blood supply to the heart muscle. Cardiac arrest is different: the NHS says that if a large part of the heart is damaged, the heart can stop beating altogether.

sections.heading: How is a heart attack diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says the main tests for finding out whether someone is having a heart attack are an electrocardiogram (ECG) and blood tests.

There are two main types. In a STEMI, the ECG shows a rise in a part of the tracing called the ST segment. In an NSTEMI, the ECG does not show the ST rise seen in a STEMI, and it can look normal or show other changes.

Troponin, a marker of damage to the heart muscle, is measured in blood tests. Troponin is the preferred blood marker for diagnosing a heart attack, and a raised level with an ECG that lacks STEMI changes points to an NSTEMI. A BHF-funded trial in Edinburgh found that a high-sensitivity troponin test doubled the number of women diagnosed with a heart attack.

sections.heading: How is a heart attack treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says the choice of treatment depends on how severe the heart attack is. The NHS lists medicines to treat the blockage, angioplasty with a stent, and coronary artery bypass surgery. In angioplasty, a small plastic tube called a stent is used to open a blocked artery.

For a STEMI, the usual approach is to offer a coronary angiogram, which images the arteries, followed by primary percutaneous coronary intervention (primary PCI), meaning emergency angioplasty, when symptoms began recently enough for it to help. NICE guideline NG185 covers the early management of acute coronary syndromes.

The BHF says most people stay in hospital for about two to five days after a heart attack, and for two or three days after coronary angioplasty or stents.

 The NHS describes rupture of the heart's muscle, walls or valves as an extremely serious but relatively uncommon complication of a heart attack.

sections.heading: What happens after a heart attack?
sections.body:
People are commonly prescribed medicines after a heart attack, such as antiplatelets, beta blockers and statins, to lower the chance of another one. The BHF says antiplatelet drugs such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor are commonly prescribed for a year, and most people are prescribed aspirin for life. Beta blockers and statins are also common, and a glyceryl trinitrate spray can ease chest pain.

The NHS says people are offered cardiac rehabilitation, which can be done in person or remotely. The BHF says cardiac rehabilitation usually starts around a month to six weeks after getting home from hospital, and typically covers topics such as driving, returning to work and holidays.

The NHS says recovery after a heart attack can take several weeks or longer, and hospital guidance says when someone can return to work depends on their job, how severe the heart attack was and how quickly they recover. A GP can provide a fit note if someone is not fit for work.

sections.heading: Feelings, anxiety and sex after a heart attack
sections.body:
The BHF says rehabilitation should include support for wellbeing, including an assessment of anxiety or depression, tips for dealing with stress and information on other sources of help.

Most people can return to having sex after a heart attack, and NHS 111 Wales, citing the BHF, gives about four to six weeks as a usual time.

 Chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw, is a reason to call 999 immediately, as described at the top of this article.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a heart attack and cardiac arrest?
faqs.a: In a heart attack the blood supply to part of the heart muscle is suddenly cut off. In cardiac arrest the heart stops beating. The NHS says that if a large part of the heart is damaged in a heart attack, the heart can stop beating altogether.

faqs.q: Do women have different heart attack symptoms?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales notes women are more likely to have other symptoms too, such as breathlessness, feeling sick, and back or jaw pain.

faqs.q: How long do people stay in hospital?
faqs.a: The BHF says people usually stay in hospital for about two to five days after a heart attack. If they have had coronary angioplasty or stents, the stay is likely to be 2 or 3 days.

faqs.q: Will I need heart medicines for life?
faqs.a: The BHF says antiplatelets such as clopidogrel or ticagrelor are commonly prescribed for a year, and most people are prescribed aspirin for life. Beta blockers and statins are also common.

faqs.q: When can I have sex again after a heart attack?
faqs.a: Most people can return to having sex after a heart attack, and NHS 111 Wales, citing the BHF, gives about four to six weeks as a usual time.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.definition: A syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, or can do so only at raised filling pressures.
heart-failure.overview: Heart failure is the end result of damage from heart attacks, high blood pressure, valve disease or cardiomyopathy. Blood backs up behind the failing ventricle: fluid in the lungs causes breathlessness, fluid in the tissues causes swelling. It is a chronic condition managed with drugs that reduce the heart's workload and, in some cases, devices. Coronary artery disease is the commonest cause, followed by high blood pressure, valve disease and cardiomyopathy; lung disease, congenital heart disease and, rarely, heart tumours also contribute, and obesity, diabetes, smoking, heavy alcohol and cocaine use raise the risk. People notice breathlessness on exertion or at rest, fatigue that worsens with activity, swelling of the feet and ankles that can spread up the legs, and sometimes light-headedness or fainting; some mainly have reduced exercise tolerance, others mainly swelling. There is no cure, but treatment controls symptoms, slows progression and improves quality of life.
causes: Coronary artery disease and previous heart attacks
High blood pressure
Valve disease
Cardiomyopathies (genetic, viral, alcohol, chemotherapy)
Atrial fibrillation
Congenital heart disease
Lung disease
signs: Raised jugular venous pressure
Crackles at the lung bases
Pitting ankle oedema
Enlarged liver
Third heart sound
Weight gain from fluid retention
complications: Pulmonary oedema (acute breathlessness)
Kidney impairment
Arrhythmias and sudden death
Repeated hospital admissions
Acute decompensation triggered by missed medicines or excess salt and fluid
heart-failure.diagnosis: Blood natriuretic peptide (BNP) is raised; echocardiography measures the ejection fraction and finds the cause. ECG, chest X-ray and blood tests for kidney function and anaemia complete the picture. The diagnosis needs both symptoms or signs and objective evidence of heart dysfunction, which is why echocardiography is central: it measures the ejection fraction, separating reduced from preserved ejection fraction, and shows valve disease and the wall-motion abnormalities left by previous infarcts. A 24-hour ECG is used when a rhythm disturbance is suspected, and breathing tests check whether a lung problem is contributing to the breathlessness.
heart-failure.treatment: Diuretics relieve fluid overload; ACE inhibitors or ARNI, beta blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors prolong life in reduced ejection fraction. Salt and fluid moderation, daily weights, vaccination and exercise rehabilitation. Selected patients receive pacemakers, defibrillators or, rarely, transplantation. Treatment depends on the stage. Early on the aim is to prevent progression through risk-factor control and medicines such as statins, beta blockers and renin-angiotensin system inhibitors; later, procedures such as valve repair or an implantable defibrillator are added. Acute deteriorations (decompensation) are often triggered by missed medicines or by exceeding salt and fluid limits, so identifying and treating the trigger is part of each admission, and daily weighing lets fluid gain be caught early. Lifestyle changes, including lower salt intake, run alongside the medicines throughout.
heart-failure.prevention: Treating blood pressure and coronary disease early, limiting alcohol, and controlling diabetes. Because coronary disease causes most heart failure, the measures that prevent heart attacks (not smoking, blood pressure and cholesterol control, physical activity and a healthy weight) prevent most heart failure too.
heart-failure.seekCare: Seek urgent help for breathlessness at rest, waking at night gasping, pink frothy sputum, chest pain, fainting, or rapid weight gain (more than 2 kg in three days).

sections.heading: What does heart failure feel like, and how does it progress?
sections.body:
Heart failure means the heart cannot pump blood properly. The NHS says it does not mean the heart has stopped working or is about to stop. Symptoms the NHS lists include breathlessness during everyday activity or when lying down, unusual tiredness, light-headedness, swelling in the feet, ankles, legs or tummy, sudden weight gain and a cough at night. MedlinePlus adds that the pulse may feel fast or irregular.

The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) says symptoms usually get worse as the heart grows weaker. It adds that weight gain, ankle swelling or increasing breathlessness may mean fluid is building up in the body.

NHS 111 Wales describes heart failure as a long-term condition that usually gets slowly worse over time, although it is very difficult to tell how it will progress in any one person.

sections.heading: What are the types of heart failure?
sections.body:
NHLBI says heart failure can develop suddenly, which is called acute, or over time as the heart gets weaker, which is called chronic. It can affect one or both sides of the heart.

NHLBI describes two forms of left-sided heart failure, named after the ejection fraction. This is the percentage of the blood in the left ventricle that is pumped out with each heartbeat. In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, weakened heart muscle is the usual driver. In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, the ventricle is stiff rather than weak, so it cannot fill with enough blood to pump out to the body.

NHLBI says left-sided heart failure is the main cause of right-sided heart failure, because pressure backs up into the lungs and strains the right side. Other causes of right-sided heart failure include congenital heart defects, abnormal heart valves and lung damage such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

sections.heading: How is heart failure diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says a GP should check the symptoms and offer a blood test to see how well the heart is working. NHS England advises GPs to arrange an NT-proBNP blood test for people with suspected heart failure. NICE says a low result in a person who is not on treatment makes heart failure less likely, while higher results lead to faster referral for specialist assessment and an echocardiogram.

The NHS lists blood tests, an electrocardiogram (ECG), an echocardiogram, breathing tests and a chest X-ray among the tests used. Its main heart failure page also mentions urine tests and MRI scans. An echocardiogram is an ultrasound scan of the heart. NICE says it is used to exclude important valve disease, among other purposes.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for heart failure?
sections.body:
The NHS lists healthy lifestyle changes, medicines, implanted devices and surgery among the treatments for heart failure, and describes medicines as the main one. It says diuretics reduce fluid build-up, ankle swelling and breathlessness, and that beta blockers slow the heart.

Implanted devices can help control or monitor the heart rhythm. They include pacemakers, cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) devices and implantable cardioverter defibrillators. Surgery can repair or replace damaged valves or improve blood flow from blocked arteries. For severe cases, options include a left ventricular assist device and a heart transplant. The NHS says a transplant may be needed when severe heart failure cannot be treated effectively with medicines or other surgery, and that it carries serious risks and is not suitable for everyone.

The NHS says people should be offered an exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme, which often includes education and emotional support.

sections.heading: What is it like living with heart failure?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment will usually need to continue for the rest of life. It describes taking medicines as prescribed, weighing regularly, staying active, eating well and stopping smoking as helpful.

The NHS says people can usually still drink alcohol within the recommended limits, but may be advised to stop completely if their heart failure is directly related to drinking. NHLBI says people may be asked to limit salt and liquids to reduce fluid build-up. The NHS says everyone with heart failure should be offered a flu vaccine every year and a one-off pneumococcal vaccine.

NHLBI says living with heart failure may cause fear, anxiety, depression and stress, and that relaxation techniques, counselling and support groups can help lower stress and anxiety. The NHS says worries can be raised with the GP or care team, and that a heart support group may be useful.

sections.heading: What is the outlook, and when should someone get help?
sections.body:
The NHS says that for most people heart failure is a long-term condition that cannot be cured, but treatment can help keep the symptoms under control, possibly for many years. NHLBI says treatment can help many people have a higher quality of life.

The NHS advises booking a GP appointment for symptoms of heart failure. It advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 for breathlessness when lying down or during everyday activity, coughing up frothy pink phlegm, or sudden weight gain. The NHS says to call 999 for severe breathlessness, such as gasping, choking or being unable to get words out, for pale, blue or grey lips or skin, or if someone has passed out and is not responding normally. It advises people not to drive themselves to A&E.

faqs.q: Does heart failure mean the heart has stopped?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says heart failure means the heart cannot pump blood properly, but it does not mean the heart has stopped working or is about to stop working. For most people it is a long-term condition, and the NHS says treatment can help keep symptoms under control, possibly for many years.

faqs.q: Can heart failure be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says that for most people heart failure is a long-term condition that cannot be cured. Treatment can help keep symptoms under control, possibly for many years. The NHS says treatment will usually need to continue for the rest of life.

faqs.q: Will treatment be needed for life?
faqs.a: The NHS says treatment will usually need to continue for the rest of life. It describes medicines as the main treatment, alongside healthy lifestyle changes. Care teams may suggest daily weighing so that changes in weight are caught quickly, and the NHS lists regular monitoring as part of care.

faqs.q: Who looks after people with heart failure?
faqs.a: A GP usually starts by checking the symptoms and offering a blood test. NICE links a raised NT-proBNP result to referral for specialist assessment and an echocardiogram. The NHS says worries can be raised with the GP or care team, and that a heart support group may be useful. Carers can attend appointments too.

faqs.q: Is exercise part of heart failure care?
faqs.a: The NHS says people with heart failure should be offered an exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme, which often includes education and emotional support. The NHS says everyone with heart failure should be offered a flu vaccine every year and a one-off pneumococcal vaccine.

keyFacts.value: Medicines, with healthy lifestyle changes; implanted devices and surgery are also options.

keyFacts.value: People should be offered an exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme.

atrial-fibrillation.name: Atrial fibrillation
atrial-fibrillation.definition: A common heart rhythm disorder in which the atria quiver chaotically instead of contracting, producing an irregular and often fast pulse.
atrial-fibrillation.overview: In atrial fibrillation the sinoatrial node loses control and hundreds of electrical impulses a minute swirl through the atria; the atrioventricular node lets an irregular selection through. Blood stagnates in the fibrillating left atrium and can clot, which is why AF causes one in five strokes. Many people have no symptoms and the rhythm is found at a routine pulse check or on an ECG done for another reason. When symptoms occur, NHLBI describes fatigue as the commonest, with palpitations felt in the chest, throat or neck, breathlessness on lying down or exercising, chest pain, light-headedness or fainting and low blood pressure. AF is not usually life-threatening in itself, but left untreated it can lead to stroke, heart failure, blood clots, sudden cardiac arrest and cognitive impairment or dementia, which is why detection and treatment matter even when the rhythm is painless.
causes: High blood pressure
Coronary artery disease and heart failure
Valve disease, especially mitral
Overactive thyroid
Alcohol binges
Lung disease and sleep apnoea
Often no single cause in older people
signs: Irregularly irregular pulse
Pulse deficit (heart rate higher than the wrist pulse)
Low blood pressure during a fast episode
complications: Stroke and systemic embolism
Heart failure from a persistently fast rate
Falls and fainting
Sudden cardiac arrest (rare)
Cognitive impairment and dementia
atrial-fibrillation.diagnosis: An ECG shows no P waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm. The clinician asks about symptoms, lifestyle, other conditions and any family history of AF. Brief, paroxysmal episodes are caught with a Holter monitor or patch recording over 24 hours or longer, or increasingly with a wearable. Echocardiography looks for valve disease and atrial size; blood tests check thyroid function, kidney function, electrolytes and a blood count, with clotting studies if an anticoagulant is to be started. A chest X-ray is often done to look at the heart and lungs.
atrial-fibrillation.treatment: Treatment has three goals: preventing clots, controlling the heart rate and, where appropriate, restoring normal rhythm. Rate control uses beta blockers, rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers or digoxin. Rhythm control, with electrical cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs or catheter ablation, is recommended for people who remain symptomatic or are not improving on rate-controlling medicines; surgical approaches are used in selected cases. Stroke prevention with an anticoagulant such as warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant is offered when the stroke risk score (which weighs age, high blood pressure, heart failure, diabetes and previous clots or stroke) justifies it. Underlying problems such as thyroid disease and sleep apnoea are treated, and lifestyle changes include aiming for a healthy weight and limiting alcohol and stimulants that raise the heart rate.
atrial-fibrillation.prevention: Control blood pressure, weight, alcohol and sleep apnoea; keep active. Treating the conditions that provoke AF, including thyroid disease and sleep apnoea, and limiting alcohol and stimulants reduce the chance of episodes.
atrial-fibrillation.seekCare: Urgent care for palpitations with chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness, and emergency services for any stroke symptoms. NHLBI advises emergency care when palpitations are accompanied by dizziness, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain or fainting.

sections.heading: What does atrial fibrillation feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS describes atrial fibrillation (AF) as a common heart rhythm problem. It lists palpitations as the most common sign, along with tiredness, breathlessness, dizziness and chest discomfort.

Sometimes there are no symptoms at all. The NHS says the condition may then be found at a routine check-up or when tests are done for something else. NICE guidance advises a manual pulse check to look for an irregular pulse when AF is suspected.

NHS inform describes atrial fibrillation as generally not dangerous in itself, and says many people live normal, healthy lives with it. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) says there is no cure, but people with AF can lead healthy lives.

sections.heading: What are the different types of atrial fibrillation?
sections.body:
NHS inform sorts atrial fibrillation into types by how long episodes last. Paroxysmal, or intermittent, AF comes and goes, with episodes lasting from minutes to hours. Persistent AF is when episodes last for more than seven days. Long-term persistent AF is continuous for over a year.

The BHF describes permanent AF as continuous, and says people with it may always have symptoms.

NHS inform adds that some people with atrial fibrillation will still need treatment, or be advised to have it, even though the condition is generally not dangerous in itself.

Some people have episodes that come and go. The NHS says a portable ECG recorder can help diagnose paroxysmal AF, because it can be worn for 24 hours or longer.

sections.heading: How is atrial fibrillation diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP if a person thinks they may have symptoms of atrial fibrillation. It also advises contacting the GP if palpitations keep happening or get worse, or if treatment is not controlling the symptoms. A GP may refer a person to a cardiologist, a heart specialist, who checks the heart rate and symptoms.

NICE guidance recommends a manual pulse check to look for an irregular pulse when AF is suspected. It says a 12-lead ECG, a recording of the heart's electrical activity, should be used to confirm the diagnosis. The NHS says an echocardiogram, a chest X-ray or blood tests may also be arranged.

NICE says that when paroxysmal AF is suspected but not found on an ECG, an ambulatory ECG monitor is used, and the choice of monitor depends on how far apart the episodes are.

sections.heading: What treatments are there for atrial fibrillation?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is currently no cure for atrial fibrillation, but treatment should help manage the symptoms and lower the risk of complications such as blood clots, stroke and heart failure. NHLBI says treatment uses lifestyle changes, medicines and procedures, including surgery, to help prevent blood clots, slow the heartbeat or restore the heart's normal rhythm.

NHS sources list beta blockers and anti-arrhythmic drugs among the medicines for controlling heart rate and rhythm. Anticoagulants are blood-thinning medicines. An NHS trust leaflet says they do not treat the symptoms of AF but do reduce the risk of stroke. Local NHS guidance lists direct-acting oral anticoagulants first, with warfarin for people who cannot take them.

NHS inform lists cardioversion, ablation and a pacemaker among the other treatments. NICE says catheter ablation is usually reserved for people in whom antiarrhythmic drugs have failed. NHLBI describes rhythm control as recommended for people who continue to have symptoms or are not improving on medicines that control heart rate.

sections.heading: How can people live with atrial fibrillation?
sections.body:
The BHF says working out what triggers episodes is an important part of self-management. NHS 111 Wales lists caffeine, spicy food, stress, dehydration and lack of sleep as possible triggers.

The BHF says people with permanent AF can generally exercise if they feel well, while people with intermittent AF are advised to exercise only when the heart is in a normal rhythm.

NHLBI says combining weight loss with physical activity and managing other risk factors, such as high blood pressure, diabetes, alcohol use and smoking, can improve symptoms more than weight loss alone. NHLBI suggests discussing activity levels, weight control and alcohol use with a provider. It also notes that blood thinners carry risks, including the possibility of severe bleeding in the brain.

sections.heading: Is atrial fibrillation serious, and when is it an emergency?
sections.body:
NHLBI says atrial fibrillation that goes undiagnosed or is left untreated can cause serious and even life-threatening complications, including stroke and heart failure. It also lists blood clots, cognitive decline and dementia. The Stroke Association says AF raises the risk of stroke, and that strokes linked to AF tend to cause more brain damage. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says AFib causes about 1 in 7 strokes in the United States.

The NHS says to call 999 for a fast or irregular heartbeat together with chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting or dizziness, or stroke-like signs such as weakness on one side, confusion or difficulty speaking. It advises against driving yourself to A&E. The Stroke Association says to call 999 straight away for any sign of stroke. For symptoms that are not an emergency, the NHS advises seeing a GP.

faqs.q: Can atrial fibrillation be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is currently no cure for atrial fibrillation. Treatment should help manage the symptoms and lower the risk of complications. NHLBI says treatment aims to prevent blood clots, slow the heartbeat or restore the heart's normal rhythm. The options include lifestyle changes, medicines and procedures, such as cardioversion or ablation.

faqs.q: Is atrial fibrillation dangerous?
faqs.a: NHS inform describes atrial fibrillation as generally not dangerous in itself, and says many people live normal, healthy lives with it. However, NHLBI says it can cause serious complications if it is undiagnosed or left untreated. The Stroke Association says it raises the risk of stroke.

faqs.q: Can you have atrial fibrillation without symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says sometimes there are no symptoms. The condition may then be found at a routine check-up or when tests are done for something else. NICE guidance advises a manual pulse check to look for an irregular pulse when AF is suspected, and a 12-lead ECG is used to confirm the diagnosis.

faqs.q: What is the difference between paroxysmal and permanent AF?
faqs.a: NHS inform groups atrial fibrillation by how long episodes last. Paroxysmal AF comes and goes, with episodes lasting from minutes to hours. The BHF describes permanent AF as continuous, with people possibly always having symptoms. Persistent AF lasts for more than seven days, and long-term persistent AF is continuous for over a year.

faqs.q: What can people do to help with atrial fibrillation day to day?
faqs.a: NHLBI says combining weight loss with physical activity and managing risk factors such as high blood pressure, diabetes, alcohol use and smoking can improve symptoms more than weight loss alone. The BHF says working out what triggers episodes is an important part of self-management.

faqs.q: When should someone call 999 about a fast or irregular heartbeat?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 for a fast or irregular heartbeat together with chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting or dizziness, or stroke-like signs. It advises against driving yourself to A&E. For palpitations that keep happening or get worse, or if treatment is not controlling symptoms, the NHS advises seeing a GP.

hypertension.name: High blood pressure (hypertension)
hypertension.definition: Persistently raised arterial pressure, usually defined as 140/90 mmHg or more in the clinic (135/85 on home readings).
hypertension.overview: High blood pressure rarely causes symptoms but silently damages arteries, heart, brain, kidneys and eyes over years. It affects around one adult in three and is the single biggest contributor to stroke and heart disease worldwide. Treatment is cheap and effective, yet half of those affected do not know they have it.
causes: Primary (essential) hypertension in over 90%: genes, salt, weight, alcohol, inactivity, age
Secondary causes in the rest: kidney disease, adrenal tumours, narrowed renal arteries, sleep apnoea, some drugs (NSAIDs, steroids, the pill), pregnancy
signs: Usually none; very high pressure can show retinal changes, an enlarged heart or kidney damage
complications: Stroke
Heart attack and heart failure
Chronic kidney disease
Aortic aneurysm and dissection
Retinopathy and vision loss
Vascular dementia
hypertension.diagnosis: Repeated readings in clinic confirmed by home or 24-hour ambulatory monitoring. Blood and urine tests, an ECG and eye examination look for organ damage and secondary causes.
hypertension.treatment: Lifestyle first: less salt, weight loss, exercise, less alcohol. Drugs when readings stay high or risk is raised: ACE inhibitors or ARBs, calcium-channel blockers, thiazide-like diuretics, added stepwise; most people need two or more.
hypertension.prevention: A diet rich in fruit, vegetables and low in salt, regular activity, healthy weight, moderate alcohol and no smoking.
hypertension.seekCare: A reading of 180/120 or higher with headache, chest pain, breathlessness, vision change, confusion, weakness or difficulty speaking needs emergency care: call 999 or go to A&E. A reading this high without symptoms needs urgent medical advice from a GP or NHS 111.

sections.heading: Does high blood pressure cause symptoms?
sections.body:
The NHS says high blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so the only way to find out is to have it measured. Rarely, high blood pressure can cause headaches, blurred vision or chest pain, the NHS says. NHS inform lists headaches, blurred or double vision, regular nosebleeds and shortness of breath as symptoms of very high blood pressure and says to contact a GP practice if they occur.

For urgent advice, the NHS names NHS 111 for frequent headaches, blurred vision, or chest pain that comes and goes. It says to call 999 for chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness, as this could be a heart attack.

sections.heading: What are the types and causes of high blood pressure?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus describes primary, or essential, high blood pressure as the most common type, and says it usually develops gradually with age. Secondary high blood pressure is caused by another medical condition or by the use of certain medicines.

MedlinePlus lists chronic kidney disease, disorders of the adrenal gland and pregnancy among the causes of secondary high blood pressure. An NHLBI news item from the US names antidepressants, decongestants, hormonal birth control pills and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen as medicines linked to high blood pressure.

White coat hypertension is the name for readings that run high in the clinic but stay normal outside it. Home or 24-hour monitoring can show whether this is happening.

sections.heading: How is high blood pressure checked and diagnosed?
sections.body:
A blood pressure test usually takes a couple of minutes, according to the NHS. A cuff on the upper arm inflates and then releases. The test may be done a couple of times to make sure the measurement is accurate. The result has two numbers. The top, or systolic, figure is the pressure as the heart pumps. The bottom, or diastolic, figure is the pressure as it rests between beats.

When a clinic reading is high, NICE recommends 24-hour monitoring to confirm the diagnosis, or home monitoring if 24-hour monitoring is declined or not tolerated. The NHS says a doctor or nurse may give a home monitor for use at home.

NICE says investigations for target organ damage should be started while the diagnosis is being confirmed, and that drug treatment may be considered straight away if damage is found.

The NHS says tests are available at pharmacies, GP surgeries and some workplaces.

sections.heading: How is high blood pressure treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says lifestyle changes come first. If those are not enough, or if the risk of other problems is high, medicines are added. Medicine groups named by the NHS and the British Heart Foundation include ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics and beta-blockers. The NHS says more than one medicine may be needed to keep blood pressure under control.

Which medicine is offered first depends on age, ethnic background and whether the person has type 2 diabetes. The NHS says beta-blockers are now mainly used when other treatments have not worked.

Blood Pressure UK says dizziness and tiredness are the most commonly reported side effects of blood pressure tablets, and that they often improve or go away as the body adjusts. NHS inform says some people have to take medicine to treat high blood pressure for the rest of their life. The NHS says not to stop taking the medicine if side effects occur, and Blood Pressure UK says that stopping it on its own lets blood pressure go back up.

sections.heading: What can help lower blood pressure day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS describes a healthy, balanced diet, regular activity, weight loss for people who are overweight, cutting back on alcohol and caffeine, and not smoking. Several NHS leaflets say that losing weight helps to lower blood pressure. NHS trust leaflets say that cutting down on salt, ready meals and takeaways helps. One NHS trust leaflet says salt substitutes made from potassium chloride are not suitable for everyone, for example people with kidney problems or heart failure, or those who take certain blood pressure medicines.

The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) advises continuing the treatment plan, having regular follow-up, and learning to monitor blood pressure at home. It adds that the clinician may change or add medicines over time.

sections.heading: What are the complications of high blood pressure?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus describes high blood pressure as raising the risk of heart disease and stroke. NHS inform names stroke, heart attack, kidney disease and vascular dementia among the problems that untreated high blood pressure can cause. The British Heart Foundation says high blood pressure can lead to complications such as kidney failure, heart failure and vascular dementia.

MedlinePlus says hypertensive heart disease develops because the heart must work harder against the pressure, which over time thickens the heart muscle. A thickened muscle may not get enough oxygen, which can cause chest pain, and without good blood pressure control the heart muscle can weaken and heart failure may develop.

MedlinePlus says the aim of treatment is to lower blood pressure to reduce the risk of related health problems, and that medicines and lifestyle changes can often control it.

faqs.q: Is high blood pressure for life?
faqs.a: NHS inform says some people have to take medicine to treat high blood pressure for the rest of their life. The NHS describes lifestyle changes as the first step, with medicines added if these are not enough or if the risk of other problems is high.

faqs.q: Can blood pressure tablets be stopped if a person feels well?
faqs.a: Blood Pressure UK says that stopping medicine on its own lets blood pressure go back up, and the US CDC says to talk to the health care team or a pharmacist before stopping blood pressure medicine. The NHS says not to stop taking the medicine if side effects occur.

faqs.q: What is white coat hypertension?
faqs.a: White coat hypertension is the name for readings that run high in the clinic but stay normal outside it. Home or 24-hour monitoring can show whether this is happening. An NHS service specification describes 24-hour monitoring as the most accurate method for confirming a diagnosis of high blood pressure, and says it can reduce unnecessary treatment.

faqs.q: Can blood pressure medicines affect pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says some blood pressure medicines may not be suitable in pregnancy, because they can reduce blood flow through the placenta to the baby or affect the baby in other ways. The US NHLBI says women who have high blood pressure during pregnancy are more likely to have high blood pressure later in life.

faqs.q: When does high blood pressure need urgent help?
faqs.a: The NHS says to contact NHS 111 for frequent headaches or blurred vision, or chest pain that comes and goes. It says to call 999 for chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness.

keyFacts.value: Usually none, so the NHS says the only way to know is to have it measured.

keyFacts.label: Where it is checked
keyFacts.value: GP surgeries, pharmacies and some workplaces, or with a home monitor that a doctor or nurse may provide.

keyFacts.label: First step in treatment
keyFacts.value: Lifestyle changes, with medicines added if these are not enough.

keyFacts.label: Medicine groups
keyFacts.value: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-2 receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics and beta-blockers.

keyFacts.label: Emergency route
keyFacts.value: Call 999 for chest pain that does not go away; NHS 111 for frequent headaches, blurred vision or chest pain that comes and goes.

deep-vein-thrombosis.name: Deep vein thrombosis
deep-vein-thrombosis.definition: A blood clot in a deep vein, most often of the calf or thigh.
deep-vein-thrombosis.overview: Clots form when blood flow slows, the vein wall is injured or the blood clots too easily (Virchow's triad). A leg DVT causes pain and swelling; its danger is that a fragment can break off and lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolism. Most clots start in the deep veins of the calf, where flow is slow; damage to the vein from surgery or injury adds to the risk, and pregnancy, ageing and prolonged immobility after an operation or on a long flight are among the commonest triggers. NHS guidance describes the typical leg: swelling, usually at the back of the leg, a throbbing pain or heavy ache in the calf or thigh, skin that is warm or red, and tender, swollen surface veins. Many DVTs cause no symptoms at all, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis. Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism are together called venous thromboembolism (VTE), a serious but largely preventable condition.
causes: Immobility: surgery, long flights, bed rest, plaster casts
Cancer and chemotherapy
Pregnancy, the combined pill and hormone replacement
Inherited clotting tendencies (factor V Leiden and others)
Injury to the vein
signs: One calf swollen more than 3 cm larger than the other, warm, tender, with dilated surface veins
Warm, red or discoloured skin over the clot
Visibly enlarged surface veins
No abnormal findings in a proportion of cases
complications: Pulmonary embolism
Post-thrombotic syndrome: chronic pain and heaviness, swelling, skin discolouration, new varicose veins and in severe cases leg ulcers
deep-vein-thrombosis.diagnosis: The clinician assesses the probability from the history, risk factors and examination, rules out other causes of a swollen leg such as cellulitis, a Baker's cyst, a muscle or joint injury or lymphoedema, and then tests. A D-dimer blood test is used to rule DVT out in low-probability cases; compression ultrasound of the leg veins confirms it. If a pulmonary embolism is suspected, CT angiography images the lung arteries. Because VTE can occur without obvious signs, a low threshold for testing is kept in people with risk factors.
deep-vein-thrombosis.treatment: Anticoagulation for at least three months, usually with a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban) or warfarin; compression stockings for symptoms; early mobilisation. Large clots occasionally need catheter-directed clot removal. Anticoagulants do not literally thin the blood; they alter clotting proteins so that new clots form less easily and the existing clot stops extending while the body breaks it down. Compression socks can ease pain and swelling. Clot-dissolving drugs (thrombolysis), mechanical clot removal (thrombectomy) and inferior vena cava filters are less common options used alongside anticoagulation in selected cases. Current guidance does not recommend routine compression stockings to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome, though a trial is reasonable when leg swelling is troublesome.
deep-vein-thrombosis.prevention: Move early after surgery, use prescribed stockings and injections in hospital, walk and hydrate on long journeys, stop smoking. In hospital, people judged to be at higher risk are given preventive anticoagulant medicine or compression stockings.
deep-vein-thrombosis.seekCare: Same-day assessment for a swollen painful calf; emergency care if breathlessness or chest pain develops. NHS guidance is to call 999 or go to A&E if leg symptoms are accompanied by breathlessness or chest pain, since this can mean the clot has travelled to the lungs.

sections.heading: How is a DVT assessed in practice?
sections.body:
NICE says that people with a likely DVT should have a leg vein ultrasound scan within 4 hours of it being requested, or within 24 hours if that is not possible.

NHS inform says that if a doctor thinks you have DVT, you will need tests, including a blood test called a D-dimer and/or an ultrasound scan. The doctor first estimates the likelihood of a clot using a points score called the Wells score. In NHS guidance, people with a low Wells score but a positive D-dimer test are recommended to have an ultrasound scan. If the Wells score shows that a DVT is likely, NICE says the person should have a leg vein ultrasound scan.

DVT can occur in an arm as well as a leg. Typical symptoms include throbbing pain, usually in the calf or thigh, and swelling in one leg, often with swollen veins, although a clot can sometimes cause no symptoms. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if leg symptoms come with breathlessness or chest pain.

sections.heading: How is a DVT treated?
sections.body:
Blood-thinning medicines (anticoagulants) are the main treatment. NHS hospital leaflets describe treatment with blood-thinning tablets such as rivaroxaban or apixaban, or with warfarin or heparin injections. The NHS says people usually need to take them for at least three months to reduce the risk of another clot.

 NHS hospital leaflets say that if it is not a first DVT, treatment is normally recommended for life.

Anticoagulants reduce the risk of the clot getting worse and give the body time to break the clot down. The body breaks the clot down over time. The medicine stops the clot growing and reduces the risk of another clot. Clot-busting drugs or surgery are reserved for severe cases.

sections.heading: Living with blood thinners
sections.body:
NHS hospital leaflets list minor bruising or bleeding as the most common side effect of blood-thinning injections such as dalteparin. NHS hospital leaflets list warning signs of bleeding on blood thinners, including blood when vomiting or coughing, black or bloody stools, blood in the urine, prolonged nosebleeds and unexplained or severe bruising, and advise seeking medical advice.

 NHS hospital leaflets say that combined contraceptive pills and HRT containing oestrogen can increase the risk of a DVT or pulmonary embolism.

 Some NHS hospital leaflets say aspirin has not been proven to reduce the risk of clots on long journeys.

sections.heading: What are the long-term effects of a DVT?
sections.body:
The most serious complication is a pulmonary embolism, in which a clot travels to the lungs. It can be life-threatening and needs to be treated quickly.

Post-thrombotic syndrome is a common long-term complication of DVT in the leg. A UCLH leaflet describes post-thrombotic syndrome as causing symptoms that include leg swelling, varicose veins and occasionally leg ulcers. Post-thrombotic syndrome usually appears within about six months to two years of the clot. Estimates of how many people develop post-thrombotic syndrome vary: a UCLH leaflet says 20 to 50 in 100, usually after extensive clots, while another hospital leaflet says about 1 in 4.

A UCLH leaflet says compression stockings may help with these symptoms. A UCLH leaflet says compression stockings should not be worn until the initial leg swelling has settled.

An NHS hospital leaflet advises regular exercise, with walking especially helpful, and regular short walking breaks on long journeys.

sections.heading: Who is at risk of a DVT, and what about pregnancy?
sections.body:
The NHS lists risk factors for DVT including being over 60, obesity, smoking, hormonal contraception or HRT, cancer and a previous DVT. The NHS also lists smoking, being over 60 and taking hormone replacement therapy as risk factors.

 NHS trust guidance says warfarin should not be used in pregnancy and that there is too little research on the newer oral anticoagulants in pregnancy. NHS trust guidance describes low-molecular-weight heparin injections as the usual choice for treating a clot in pregnancy.

faqs.q: Does a blood thinner dissolve the clot?
faqs.a: No. A hospital leaflet says anticoagulants reduce the risk of the clot getting worse and let the body break it down. The medicine stops the clot growing and reduces the risk of another clot. Clot-busting drugs or surgery are kept for severe cases.

faqs.q: How long are blood thinners taken for?
faqs.a: The NHS says people usually need them for at least three months. NHS hospital leaflets say that if it is not a first DVT, treatment is normally recommended for life. People prescribed a blood thinner are advised not to stop it without talking to a doctor.

faqs.q: When does a DVT become an emergency?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if leg symptoms come with breathlessness or chest pain, as this can mean the clot has reached the lungs. If a doctor thinks a leg clot is likely, NICE says an ultrasound scan should be available within 4 hours of it being requested, or within 24 hours if that is not possible.

pulmonary-embolism.name: Pulmonary embolism
pulmonary-embolism.definition: Blockage of a pulmonary artery by a clot that has travelled from a vein, usually in the leg or pelvis.
pulmonary-embolism.overview: A pulmonary embolism cuts off blood flow to part of the lung: the affected segment is ventilated but not perfused, oxygen levels fall and the right ventricle strains against the obstruction. Small emboli cause pleuritic pain and breathlessness; a large one can cause collapse and death within minutes. Symptoms are not specific. Chest pain and breathlessness are the commonest, with dizziness or light-headedness, a fast heartbeat, coughing up blood or collapse also possible, so PE can neither be confirmed nor excluded from symptoms alone, and some emboli cause no symptoms and are found incidentally on a scan. Nearly all cases arise from a deep vein thrombosis in the legs or pelvis. A substantial proportion of cases are 'unprovoked', with no identifiable cause; the rest are 'provoked' by a clear trigger such as surgery, immobility or serious illness, and this distinction shapes how long treatment continues.
causes: Deep vein thrombosis of the leg or pelvis
Rarely fat, air or amniotic fluid emboli
riskFactors: Major surgery, especially gynaecological operations and surgery on the pelvis and legs
signs: Fast breathing and pulse
Low oxygen saturation
Signs of DVT in a leg
Low blood pressure in massive PE
A normal examination does not exclude PE; some emboli are found incidentally on imaging
complications: Collapse and cardiac arrest
Right heart failure
Chronic pulmonary hypertension
Significant bleeding in a small proportion of people on anticoagulant treatment
Recurrent clots, more likely when the first was unprovoked or the risk persists
pulmonary-embolism.diagnosis: Probability scoring and D-dimer, then CT pulmonary angiography to show the clot; ventilation-perfusion scanning in pregnancy or kidney disease. ECG and echocardiography assess strain on the right heart. In someone judged at low clinical probability, a negative D-dimer makes PE very unlikely. A positive result is not conclusive, because D-dimer also rises with inflammation and infection, so people at higher risk or with a positive test proceed to lung imaging for a definitive answer.
pulmonary-embolism.treatment: Immediate anticoagulation (low-molecular-weight heparin, then a direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin for three to six months or longer); clot-dissolving drugs or catheter removal for massive PE with shock; oxygen and support. Anticoagulants do not thin the blood or dissolve the clot; they alter clotting so that the clot cannot grow and new clots do not form while the body clears it. The choice of drug depends on kidney function, body weight and other medicines being taken, and significant bleeding occurs in a small proportion of people treated. Clots provoked by a transient risk factor are treated for a limited period, whereas unprovoked clots or persisting risks such as cancer, chronic immobility or a strong clotting disorder may need long-term treatment to prevent recurrence. Oxygen helps breathlessness and low oxygen levels early on. Untreated PE carries a high death rate; with treatment the outlook is much better.
pulmonary-embolism.prevention: DVT prevention: early mobilisation, prophylactic injections in hospital, compression stockings, keeping moving on long journeys.
pulmonary-embolism.seekCare: Emergency services for sudden breathlessness, chest pain on breathing, coughing blood or collapse, especially with a swollen leg or recent surgery.

Kingston and Richmond NHS: Pulmonary embolism

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a pulmonary embolism?
sections.body:
The NHS lists sudden breathlessness, chest pain that gets worse when breathing in and coughing up blood as the main symptoms, with leg pain or swelling also possible if a DVT is present. The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or passing out.

 Hospital leaflets note that a small pulmonary embolism may cause no symptoms at all. NICE guidance on suspected pulmonary embolism describes using a clinical probability score, followed by tests such as a D-dimer blood test or a scan.

sections.heading: What causes a pulmonary embolism?
sections.body:
NHS hospital leaflets say the clot is usually a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), most often in the leg or pelvis, that has travelled to the lungs. A few come from an arm vein or from a clot in the heart.

 Risk factors include pregnancy and the weeks after birth, oestrogen-containing contraception or hormone replacement therapy, and cancer. Some people have an inherited tendency for their blood to clot (thrombophilia), such as factor V Leiden.

Sometimes a pulmonary embolism happens for no obvious reason. Doctors describe these as unprovoked, and the likely cause is important in deciding how long treatment continues.

sections.heading: How is a pulmonary embolism diagnosed?
sections.body:
NICE guidance describes estimating the clinical probability of pulmonary embolism with a score, then using a D-dimer blood test or imaging depending on the result. A Whittington Health policy says a negative D-dimer test reliably excludes pulmonary embolism in people with a low clinical probability, so further imaging is not needed in that group.

The usual confirming scan is a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA).

NICE guidance says that when a scan cannot be done straight away, people thought likely to have a pulmonary embolism are offered interim anticoagulant treatment until it can be done. Treatment can therefore begin before the scan result is back.

sections.heading: How is a pulmonary embolism treated?
sections.body:
Once the diagnosis is confirmed, treatment usually continues with anticoagulant tablets or injections, depending on what suits the person. Anticoagulants do not dissolve the clot. The body clears it over time. They stop existing clots growing and help prevent new ones forming. Clot-busting drugs (thrombolysis) are considered for people whose circulation is affected by a severe pulmonary embolism.

Hospital leaflets say treatment can last anywhere from three months to the rest of a person's life, depending on the cause and the person's risk of another clot.

Anticoagulants raise the risk of bleeding. Hospital leaflets list black or bloody stools, vomiting or coughing up blood, and heavy bleeding that does not stop as reasons to get urgent medical help, by calling NHS 111 or going to A&E.

sections.heading: What is recovery from a pulmonary embolism like?
sections.body:
The NHS says a full recovery is expected if a pulmonary embolism is spotted and treated early. Hospital leaflets say it is common to feel breathless for a few weeks or months after a pulmonary embolism. Hospital leaflets advise talking to a GP if breathlessness does not improve, and note that a minority of people have symptoms for a prolonged period.

Some people have longer-term problems. One NHS leaflet notes that a minority of people continue to have symptoms for a long time, which may be due to a condition called chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH).

 Questions about long-term treatment, travel or hormone medicines belong with the treating team or GP.

faqs.q: Where do the clots in a pulmonary embolism come from?
faqs.a: NHS hospital leaflets say the clot is usually a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), most often in the leg or pelvis, that has travelled to the lungs. A few come from an arm vein or from the heart.

faqs.q: Can a pulmonary embolism cause no symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. Hospital leaflets note that a small pulmonary embolism may cause no symptoms at all. NICE guidance describes using a clinical probability score and tests such as a D-dimer blood test and a scan to diagnose it.

faqs.q: Why is a D-dimer test not enough on its own?
faqs.a: A negative D-dimer test reliably excludes pulmonary embolism in people with a low clinical probability, according to a Whittington Health policy. NICE guidance recommends imaging, usually a CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA), when a pulmonary embolism is thought likely.

faqs.q: How long does treatment last?
faqs.a: Hospital leaflets say it can last from three months to the rest of a person's life. The length depends on the cause of the clot and the risk of another one, and the treating team makes the decision.

faqs.q: How long does recovery take?
faqs.a: Hospital leaflets say it is common to feel breathless for a few weeks or months after a pulmonary embolism. The NHS says people should make a full recovery if the condition is spotted and treated early, though hospital leaflets say it is common to feel breathless for a few weeks or months.

stroke.name: Stroke
stroke.definition: Sudden loss of brain function because blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted, by a blocked artery (ischaemic, 85%) or a bleed (haemorrhagic).
stroke.overview: Brain tissue dies within minutes of losing its blood supply, and the lost functions map the artery: weakness and numbness of the opposite side, loss of speech, loss of half the visual field, or unsteadiness and double vision from the brainstem. Treatment to reopen the artery works only in the first hours, so stroke is a medical emergency recognised by the FAST test.
causes: Atherosclerosis of the carotid and cerebral arteries
Emboli from the heart in atrial fibrillation
Small vessel disease from high blood pressure and diabetes
Bleeding from high blood pressure, aneurysms or vascular malformations
Arterial dissection in younger people
signs: Facial droop
Arm drift
Slurred or absent speech
Loss of a visual field
Unsteady gait
complications: Permanent disability
Swallowing problems and aspiration pneumonia
Depression
Seizures
Recurrent stroke
stroke.diagnosis: Immediate CT to distinguish a bleed from a blockage, then CT or MR angiography to find the blocked vessel. Blood glucose is checked at once to exclude hypoglycaemia. ECG, echocardiography and carotid ultrasound search for the source.
stroke.treatment: For ischaemic stroke, clot-dissolving thrombolysis within 4.5 hours and mechanical thrombectomy for a large-vessel blockage, as soon as possible (usually within 6 hours of onset, and up to 24 hours in selected people whose scans show brain tissue that can still be saved), then antiplatelet drugs, statins, blood pressure control and anticoagulation if AF is found. Bleeds need blood pressure control, reversal of anticoagulants and sometimes surgery. Rehabilitation by a stroke team drives recovery.
stroke.prevention: Treat blood pressure and atrial fibrillation, stop smoking, control diabetes and cholesterol, exercise, and manage weight and alcohol.
stroke.seekCare: Call emergency services immediately at any sign of Face drooping, Arm weakness or Speech difficulty: Time matters. Call 999 even if the symptoms go away: a TIA is a warning that a stroke may follow and needs urgent specialist assessment.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a stroke?
sections.body:
The NHS uses the FAST test to describe the main signs of a stroke. FAST stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999. The main signs are facial droop, arm weakness and slurred speech. Other signs include weakness or numbness down one side of the body, blurred vision, and confusion and memory loss.

The NHS also lists difficulty speaking or finding words, dizziness, a severe headache, and nausea or vomiting among the symptoms. The NHS describes a stroke as a medical emergency and says to call 999 if a stroke is suspected. It says to call 999 even if the symptoms stop, because an assessment in hospital is still needed. A transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, causes symptoms like those of a stroke, and the Stroke Association says they usually last from a few minutes to a few hours.

sections.heading: What are the types of stroke?
sections.body:
Ischaemic strokes happen when the blood supply is stopped by a blood clot, and NHS inform says this is the cause in most cases. The NHLBI says the blockage is usually caused by a piece of plaque that builds up in the arteries during some cardiovascular diseases. Haemorrhagic strokes happen when a weakened blood vessel supplying the brain bursts. The NHS says bleeding can occur inside the brain tissue or in the space around it.

A TIA is also called a mini-stroke because the symptoms are temporary. The WHO says a TIA usually lasts only a few minutes and does not cause long-term damage. The Stroke Association describes a TIA as a warning sign, and the CDC calls it a sign of a serious condition that will not go away without medical help. The NHS lists high blood pressure, diabetes, atrial fibrillation and high cholesterol among the risk factors for stroke.

sections.heading: How is a stroke diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says a stroke is diagnosed mainly through blood tests, scans and other checks. It lists CT scans, MRI scans and ultrasound scans to check in and around the brain, and an electrocardiogram (ECG) to check the heart. NHS inform says that even when the physical signs of a stroke are obvious, a brain scan is needed.

The scan shows whether a clot or a burst blood vessel caused the stroke, which part of the brain is affected and how severe it is. The Stroke Association says a brain scan should ideally happen soon after arrival at hospital. The CDC says there is no way to know at the start whether symptoms are from a TIA or from a major type of stroke.

sections.heading: How is a stroke treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says treatment depends on the type of stroke. Early treatment may include clot-dissolving medicine, surgery to remove a clot or drain fluid, and a procedure to ease pressure inside the skull. The Stroke Association says thrombolysis uses a clot-busting medicine to break up clots and restore blood flow.

Thrombectomy removes the blood clot to help reduce brain damage by restoring blood flow. NHS inform says it is effective for ischaemic strokes caused by a clot in a large artery in the brain. The NHS says clot-dissolving treatment is most effective when started as soon as possible after the stroke.

The Stroke Association says most people who have an ischaemic stroke are given blood-thinning medication to help prevent clots, and that most will need it for life. NHS inform says a combination of treatments is usually recommended to reduce the risk of another stroke, and long-term prevention can involve anticoagulants or antiplatelets and statins to lower cholesterol.

sections.heading: How long does recovery take, and what does rehabilitation involve?
sections.body:
The NHS says it can take days, weeks, months or years to recover from a stroke. Some people recover within days or weeks, while for others recovery can take months or years and may mean making life changes.

NHS inform describes several kinds of rehabilitation. Physiotherapy often involves exercises to improve muscle strength to overcome walking difficulties. Occupational therapists assess a person’s ability to carry out everyday tasks and can help adapt the home or suggest equipment to make tasks easier. Speech and language therapists help with communication and swallowing problems. NHS inform notes that problems with language can affect speaking, understanding, reading and writing. Rehabilitation usually starts in hospital and can continue at home or in the community.

sections.heading: What problems can follow a stroke, and how do people cope?
sections.body:
The WHO lists trouble swallowing (dysphagia) and aspiration pneumonia, a lung infection, among the complications of stroke. The Stroke Association says being immobile raises the risk of blood clots forming in the leg veins. NHS inform says tiredness can be extreme and can last months or even years, and that bewilderment, anger and frustration are also common.

The Stroke Association says depression is common after a stroke and that at least one third of survivors have some form of it within the first year. NHS inform says medicines and psychological therapies, such as counselling or cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), can help some people. The Stroke Association lists its Stroke Helpline as 0303 3033 100.

faqs.q: What does FAST stand for?
faqs.a: FAST stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999, the NHS says. The main signs are facial droop, arm weakness and slurred speech. The NHS says to call 999 even if the symptoms stop, because an assessment in hospital is still needed.

faqs.q: Is a TIA the same as a stroke?
faqs.a: A TIA, or mini-stroke, has symptoms like those of a stroke, but the Stroke Association says they usually last from a few minutes to a few hours. The CDC says there is no way to know at the start whether symptoms are from a TIA or a major type of stroke. The Stroke Association describes a TIA as a warning sign.

faqs.q: Which scans are used to diagnose a stroke?
faqs.a: The NHS lists CT scans, MRI scans and ultrasound scans to check in and around the brain, along with blood tests and an electrocardiogram (ECG) to check the heart. NHS inform says the scan shows whether a clot or a burst blood vessel caused the stroke, which part of the brain is affected and how severe it is.

faqs.q: How long does it take to recover from a stroke?
faqs.a: The NHS says it can take days, weeks, months or years to recover from a stroke. Some people recover within days or weeks, while for others recovery can take months or years and may mean making life changes. NHS inform describes rehabilitation from physiotherapists, occupational therapists and speech and language therapists.

faqs.q: Can a stroke affect mood?
faqs.a: The Stroke Association says depression is common after a stroke, with at least one third of survivors having some form of it within the first year, and that it can appear at any point or return. NHS inform says anger, frustration and bewilderment are also common, and that medicines and psychological therapies can help some people.
