sections.heading: What does a UTI feel like?
sections.body:
NHS guidance lists pain or a burning feeling when passing urine, needing to go more often than usual, cloudy urine, blood in the urine, and pain in the lower tummy or in the back just under the ribs. Feeling tired or weak and smelly urine can also occur. NIDDK, a US health institute, describes similar bladder infection symptoms, including discomfort in the lower abdomen and cloudy, bloody or strong-smelling urine.

When a bladder infection spreads to one or both kidneys, NIDDK lists fever and chills, nausea or vomiting, and pain in the back, side or groin as warning signs. It says early treatment prevents most complications. MedlinePlus says bladder infection symptoms usually improve within a day or two of starting treatment, while kidney infections can take a week or more to resolve.

sections.heading: How does a UTI show up in older people and children?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says older adults may show only confusion. The NHS says that in older, frail people with memory problems such as dementia, and in people with a urinary catheter, symptoms can include changes in behaviour such as acting agitated or confused, wetting that is worse than usual, or new shivering or shaking.

In babies and young children, fever is the most common sign and may be the only one. Poor feeding and vomiting can also occur. Children who were toilet trained may start having accidents by day or night. MedlinePlus says antibiotics for a child's UTI should start quickly to protect the kidneys, and a child under six months old, or with other complications, should see a specialist right away.

sections.heading: How is a UTI diagnosed?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus describes urinary tract infections as affecting the bladder, kidneys, ureters or urethra, and calls a kidney infection pyelonephritis. A urine culture identifies the bacteria so a clinician can choose an antibiotic. A positive culture, meaning bacteria or yeast grew, likely indicates a UTI, although earlier antibiotic use can produce a falsely negative result.

For older adults, the NICE quality standard recommends diagnosing UTI by full clinical assessment, without a urine dipstick test, because dipstick accuracy varies. A UK hospital study of older patients found that most positive dipstick results did not match the laboratory result. The NHS England and UKHSA toolkit likewise says dipsticks should be avoided in older adults to support an accurate diagnosis.

sections.heading: What treatments are used?
sections.body:
NIDDK says a health professional will likely prescribe antibiotics for a bacterial bladder infection, and the length of treatment depends on how severe the infection is and whether symptoms go away. It advises finishing the whole course, because antibiotic resistance could make an infection harder to treat, and says drinking more liquids, with water best, can speed recovery and ease symptoms.

The NHS says antibiotics are not always needed. A GP may offer self-care advice and a painkiller, a short course of antibiotics, or a prescription to use after waiting 48 hours in case symptoms go away alone.

For kidney infection, the NHS says most people are treated at home with antibiotics. Paracetamol helps with pain and high temperature, and ibuprofen-type painkillers are not normally recommended because they may increase the risk of further kidney problems. Hospital treatment with antibiotics through a drip may be needed for people who are pregnant, have a long-term health condition, are severely dehydrated or cannot keep down fluids or medicines.

sections.heading: Why do some people get UTIs again and again?
sections.body:
Reviews define recurrent UTI as two infections within six months or three within twelve months. NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if a UTI returns after treatment or follows that pattern. Options it lists include a different antibiotic, a low-dose antibiotic taken for up to six months, or, after the menopause, an oestrogen vaginal product. NHS patient information also describes taking antibiotics after sex where sex seems to trigger infections.

NIDDK says vaginal oestrogen increases good bacteria and helps prevent infection, and that diaphragms, unlubricated condoms or spermicide may raise the chance of a bladder infection. It says cranberry products do not treat an existing infection and there is not enough evidence to be sure they prevent one.

sections.heading: Can a UTI become serious, and who should be contacted?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus lists kidney infection and sepsis, a dangerous overreaction to infection, as risks of a UTI, with sepsis risk greatest in young children, very old adults and people with weakened immunity. NHS England says older adults made up almost three fifths of UTI hospital admissions over five years.

NHS 111 Wales advises calling 999 or going to A&E if a person with a suspected UTI, or their child, is confused, drowsy or has difficulty speaking, and not driving themselves. NHS guidance advises urgent help from a GP or NHS 111 for a very high or very low temperature, vomiting, blood in the urine, passing no urine all day, or symptoms that get worse quickly or do not improve within 48 hours. NI Direct says to see a GP if symptoms are very uncomfortable or last more than five days.

faqs.q: Can a UTI get better without antibiotics?
faqs.a: NHS 111 Wales says antibiotics may treat UTIs but are not always needed. A GP may offer self-care advice and a painkiller, a short course of antibiotics, or a prescription to use after waiting 48 hours in case symptoms go away alone. NHS guidance says symptoms that do not improve within 48 hours need review by a GP or NHS 111.

faqs.q: How is a kidney infection different from a bladder infection?
faqs.a: NIDDK says a bladder infection can spread to one or both kidneys, with warning signs of fever and chills, nausea or vomiting, and pain in the back, side or groin. MedlinePlus says kidney infections can take a week or more to resolve. The NHS describes blood poisoning as a medical emergency.

faqs.q: What are the signs of a UTI in babies and children?
faqs.a: Fever is the most common sign in children under one and may be the only one, with poor feeding and vomiting also possible. Children who were toilet trained may start having accidents by day or night. MedlinePlus says a child under six months old, or with other complications, should see a specialist right away.

faqs.q: When should someone see a GP about a UTI?
faqs.a: NI Direct says to see a GP if symptoms are very uncomfortable or last more than five days, or if there is a high temperature, symptoms suddenly worsen, or the person is pregnant or has diabetes. NHS 111 Wales advises calling 999 or going to A&E for confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking.

kidney-stones.name: Kidney stones
kidney-stones.definition: Hard crystals, most commonly calcium oxalate, that form in the kidney and can pass into and block the ureter.
kidney-stones.overview: Stones form when urine is concentrated and rich in stone-forming salts. A stone leaving the kidney scrapes and blocks the ureter, producing renal colic: waves of agonising pain from the loin to the groin with blood in the urine. Most stones under 5 mm pass on their own; larger or infected obstructions need intervention. Stones form when urine carries high concentrations of calcium, oxalate or phosphate, although in many individuals no specific reason is ever found. Many small stones cause no symptoms and are passed unnoticed. Pain that comes in waves and radiates from the back or side towards the groin usually means a stone has moved into the ureter; blood in the urine, nausea and vomiting and pain on passing urine are common, and fever or chills point to infection alongside the stone, which changes the urgency entirely.
causes: Low urine volume
High urinary calcium, oxalate or uric acid
Urinary infection with urease-producing bacteria (struvite stones)
Rare inherited causes (cystinuria)
Metabolic conditions such as hyperparathyroidism that raise urinary calcium
riskFactors: High salt, animal protein and oxalate intake
Vigorous exercise or a hot environment without replacing fluid
A first stone at a young age
signs: Restless, unable to lie still
Loin tenderness
Blood in the urine on dipstick
Fever if infected
complications: Obstruction with infection (an emergency)
Kidney damage
Recurrence in half within ten years
Acute kidney injury with reduced urine output when drainage is blocked
kidney-stones.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT of the urinary tract is the definitive test; ultrasound in pregnancy and children; urine dipstick and culture, kidney function and calcium and urate levels; analysis of the passed stone. Assessment begins with the history, including existing conditions, current medicines, diet and whether relatives have had stones, and with examination. Blood tests check calcium, phosphate, uric acid and electrolytes; urinalysis looks for crystals and red blood cells. Non-contrast CT is the preferred imaging test to confirm a stone and check for obstruction; ultrasound is used first in children and in pregnancy to avoid radiation.
kidney-stones.treatment: Strong analgesia (NSAIDs are most effective), fluids, and drugs to relax the ureter to help small stones pass; shock-wave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy with laser fragmentation or percutaneous surgery for larger stones; urgent drainage with a stent or nephrostomy if obstructed and infected. Stone size is the main determinant of initial treatment, and most small stones pass spontaneously. Alpha blockers and calcium-channel blockers can aid passage by relaxing the ureter. Stones unlikely to pass are candidates for minimally invasive treatment such as shock-wave lithotripsy. For adults with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and high urinary calcium, NICE CKS advises considering a thiazide once salt intake has been reduced; potassium citrate and allopurinol are used for other recurrent stone types.
kidney-stones.prevention: Drink enough to pass 2 to 2.5 litres of urine a day, limit salt and animal protein, keep normal calcium intake, lemon juice for citrate; specific drugs for recurrent formers. Recurrence is common, approaching half of people within ten years, which is why fluid intake, dietary review and, for repeated stones, metabolic assessment with targeted medication are emphasised.
kidney-stones.seekCare: Emergency care for colicky pain with fever or shivering, vomiting preventing fluids, pain not controlled by painkillers, or a single functioning kidney. NHS advice is to ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for severe pain or for fever and chills. Unrelieved pain, reduced urine output, infection or acute kidney failure in the presence of an obstructing stone are medical emergencies.

chronic-kidney-disease.name: Chronic kidney disease
chronic-kidney-disease.definition: Persistent reduction in kidney function (a filtration rate below 60 ml/min) or evidence of kidney damage such as protein in the urine, for more than three months.
chronic-kidney-disease.overview: The kidneys lose nephrons slowly and silently, most often from diabetes and high blood pressure. Symptoms appear only when function is severely reduced, so CKD is found by blood and urine tests in at-risk people. Progression can be slowed for years; a minority reach kidney failure needing dialysis or transplantation. Chronic kidney disease means the kidneys are damaged or structurally abnormal and cannot filter blood as they should, with function declining over months to years. Because early disease causes no symptoms, NHS guidance recommends testing for people with high blood pressure, diabetes or a family history of kidney disease. When symptoms do appear in advanced disease they are non-specific: tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands from fluid retention, shortness of breath, nausea, loss of appetite and blood in the urine, all of which overlap with many less serious conditions. An episode of acute kidney injury can also leave lasting damage that becomes CKD.

Low calcium and high phosphate levels
Loss of appetite and depression
chronic-kidney-disease.diagnosis: Estimated GFR from blood creatinine and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, repeated over three months; the two together both make the diagnosis and set its severity, staged G1 to G5 by filtration rate and A1 to A3 by albuminuria. Albumin is a protein that passes into the urine when the filtering units are damaged, so it is an early marker even while the eGFR is still normal. Testing is the only reliable way to know how well the kidneys are working, which is why at-risk groups are screened rather than waiting for symptoms. Ultrasound of the kidneys shows size, obstruction and cysts, and further tests look for the cause, because the cause changes management.
chronic-kidney-disease.treatment: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, statins, glucose control, salt restriction, stopping smoking, avoiding NSAIDs, dose adjustment of medicines; treating anaemia and bone disease; preparing for dialysis or transplantation as function declines. CKD cannot be cured, but progression can often be slowed for years. NIDDK describes blood pressure control as the most important single step; ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the usual choice because they also reduce protein leak, and loop diuretics manage fluid. Blood glucose and cholesterol are treated alongside. Lifestyle measures include lower-salt food, limiting alcohol, staying physically active and not smoking. Anaemia, bone and mineral disorder and fluid overload are treated as they arise. When function falls far enough (kidney failure), dialysis or a kidney transplant is needed for survival, and preparation begins well in advance.
chronic-kidney-disease.prevention: Control diabetes and blood pressure, keep a healthy weight, do not smoke, avoid regular NSAIDs, stay hydrated during illness, have kidney checks if at risk. People with diabetes, high blood pressure or a family history of kidney disease are offered regular eGFR and urine albumin checks so that damage is found early.
chronic-kidney-disease.seekCare: Urgent care for breathlessness, chest pain, severe drowsiness, or a sudden fall in urine output; routine review for swelling, frothy urine or persistently high blood pressure. CKD is usually found by routine testing rather than symptoms, so people in at-risk groups are advised to ask about kidney checks.

sections.heading: How does chronic kidney disease feel and progress?
sections.body:
Early chronic kidney disease usually causes no symptoms, and it is often found by chance when a blood or urine test is done for another reason. Symptoms can appear at a more advanced stage, including tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands, shortness of breath, feeling sick and blood in the urine. Later kidney failure can also bring itching and muscle cramps.

Doctors describe the condition in stages, and a higher stage means more severe disease. In stage 1 the filtering is normal but there is other evidence of kidney damage, and stage 2 is a slight decrease in function. Stage 3 is split into 3a and 3b, and stage 5 is kidney failure. Only a small proportion of people with the condition go on to kidney failure, which the NHS puts at around 2 in 100 people. When the kidneys do stop working, this usually happens slowly.

sections.heading: How is it checked?
sections.body:
Chronic kidney disease can be diagnosed with blood and urine tests. The blood test is used to estimate how well the kidneys are filtering, and the urine test looks for protein and blood. One abnormal result is not usually enough, and repeated tests are used to confirm the diagnosis. The blood test result, called the eGFR, is used to give a stage from 1 to 5.

In many cases the condition is only found when a routine blood or urine test, done for another problem, shows that the kidneys may not be working normally. NHS guidance lists high blood pressure, diabetes and heart disease as reasons for regular testing. The NHS says most people with the condition can control it with medicine and regular check-ups.

sections.heading: What treatments are used?
sections.body:
There is no cure for chronic kidney disease, but treatment can help relieve the symptoms and stop it getting worse. The NHS describes lifestyle changes to stay as healthy as possible, together with medicines to manage problems such as high blood pressure and high cholesterol. ACE inhibitors are often used for blood pressure in this condition, and statins are prescribed to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, meaning heart and blood vessel problems.

Anaemia, a shortage of red blood cells, can develop in kidney disease, and the NHS says tablets or injections may be given to help the body make more red blood cells. Medical reviews describe anaemia in kidney disease as traditionally treated with iron preparations or erythropoiesis-stimulating agents. Medicines can also be used for other symptoms of kidney failure, such as breathlessness, loss of appetite and itchy skin.

sections.heading: What are dialysis and a kidney transplant?
sections.body:
For a small number of people the kidneys eventually stop working, and dialysis or a transplant is then considered. Dialysis is a way of removing waste products and extra fluid from the blood. NIDDK describes haemodialysis as a machine filtering the blood outside the body, while peritoneal dialysis uses the lining of the abdomen to filter waste and extra fluid.

A kidney transplant is the other main option, and the kidney can come from a living or a deceased donor. NHS Blood and Transplant says living donors account for roughly 30 in 100 kidney transplants, with a much shorter wait than for a kidney from a deceased donor. People with a transplant take anti-rejection medicines, and NIDDK notes these can cause other health problems. Some people choose not to have dialysis or a transplant, and conservative care then continues their care without either, including treatment for symptoms.

sections.heading: Living with chronic kidney disease
sections.body:
A hospital leaflet from an NHS trust says that with good care many people with chronic kidney disease live long and active lives. It favours plenty of fruit and vegetables, including pulses, with smaller amounts of animal protein such as meat, fish and eggs. Kidney Care UK says a diet low in salt and rich in fibre and potassium from fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts, seeds and pulses helps to lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of complications.

Kidney Care UK also notes that studies have shown exercise can improve kidney function. NHS 111 Wales lists some long-term medicines, including NSAIDs and lithium, among the causes of chronic kidney disease. The hospital leaflet says over-the-counter anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are avoided unless a medical professional advises otherwise, because these medicines can harm the kidneys in people with kidney disease.

sections.heading: Complications and outlook
sections.body:
Heart and blood vessel disease is a major concern in chronic kidney disease. One review says cardiovascular complications are the most common cause of death in people with kidney failure on regular dialysis, and that most people with progressive chronic kidney disease die before reaching kidney failure because of the high rate of cardiovascular death.

Many people with stage 3, 4 and 5 disease develop anaemia. Mineral and bone disorder can also develop in advanced kidney disease and is linked to a higher risk of bone fractures, heart and blood vessel events and death. NHS 111 Wales gives the proportion of people with the condition who reach kidney failure as around 1 in 50.

faqs.q: Can chronic kidney disease be cured?
faqs.a: There is no cure for chronic kidney disease, but treatment can help relieve symptoms and stop it getting worse. The NHS says most people can control the condition with medicine and regular check-ups. A hospital leaflet from an NHS trust adds that with good care many people live long and active lives.

faqs.q: Does it always lead to kidney failure?
faqs.a: No, only a small proportion of people do. The NHS says around 2 in 100 people with the condition reach kidney failure, and NHS 111 Wales gives the figure as around 1 in 50. When the kidneys do stop working, this usually happens slowly rather than suddenly.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the two kinds of dialysis?
faqs.a: Dialysis removes waste products and extra fluid from the blood. In haemodialysis, a machine filters the blood outside the body. In peritoneal dialysis, the lining of the abdomen is used to filter waste and extra fluid. NIDDK describes a kidney transplant and conservative management as the other treatment paths for kidney failure.

faqs.q: Does everyone with kidney failure have dialysis or a transplant?
faqs.a: No. NIDDK describes conservative management as continuing a person's care without dialysis or a kidney transplant. The NHS says medicines can be used to treat symptoms of kidney failure such as breathlessness, loss of appetite and itchy skin, as part of supportive care.

faqs.q: Which painkillers can affect the kidneys?
faqs.a: A hospital leaflet from an NHS trust says over-the-counter anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen can harm the kidneys in people with kidney disease and are avoided unless a medical professional advises otherwise. NHS 111 Wales also lists long-term use of some medicines, including NSAIDs and lithium, among the causes of chronic kidney disease.

faqs.q: Does diet matter in chronic kidney disease?
faqs.a: A hospital leaflet from an NHS trust favours plenty of fruit and vegetables, including pulses, with smaller amounts of animal protein such as meat, fish and eggs. Kidney Care UK describes a diet low in salt and rich in fibre and potassium from fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts, seeds and pulses as helping to lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of complications.

anaemia.name: Anaemia
anaemia.definition: A haemoglobin concentration below normal (roughly under 130 g/L in men and 120 g/L in women), reducing the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.
anaemia.overview: Anaemia is a sign, not a diagnosis. Iron deficiency from blood loss or poor intake is the commonest cause worldwide; others include vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, chronic disease, kidney failure, inherited haemoglobin disorders and bone marrow failure. Finding the cause matters because in adults it can be bleeding from a bowel cancer. Haemoglobin inside red cells carries oxygen, so a low concentration leaves tissues short of oxygen and the heart working harder to compensate. How much a person notices depends largely on how quickly the anaemia develops: a slow fall from chronic blood loss may cause few symptoms until it is marked, whereas a rapid fall is felt early. Iron deficiency arises when more blood and iron are lost than the body can replace, when iron is poorly absorbed (as in coeliac disease or Crohn's disease), when the diet is low in iron, or when needs rise, as in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Mild or moderate iron deficiency may produce no symptoms at all and is often picked up on a routine blood count.
causes: Iron deficiency: heavy periods, gut bleeding, poor diet, malabsorption, pregnancy
Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Chronic inflammation or kidney disease
Thalassaemia and sickle cell disease
Haemolysis
Bone marrow disease
Malabsorption from coeliac disease or Crohn's disease
Increased requirement in pregnancy and breastfeeding
signs: Pale conjunctivae and palms
Fast pulse, flow murmur
Spoon nails, sore tongue in iron deficiency
Jaundice in haemolysis
Numb feet and unsteadiness in B12 deficiency
Reported cravings for non-food items (pica), hair loss, headache or tinnitus in iron deficiency
complications: Heart failure in severe anaemia
Poor pregnancy outcomes
Delayed development in children
Missed underlying cancer
anaemia.diagnosis: Full blood count is the starting point: a low haemoglobin with a reduced mean cell volume (MCV) is the usual first finding in iron deficiency, and red cell size separates the main groups of cause. Serum ferritin reflects iron stores and confirms iron deficiency; B12, folate, reticulocytes and a blood film narrow down other causes. Because anaemia is a sign rather than a diagnosis, the search for the cause matters as much as the count: coeliac tests, and endoscopy or colonoscopy to look for a bleeding source in men and in women past the menopause. A bone marrow examination is reserved for cases where the diagnosis remains unclear after these tests. During treatment, blood tests are repeated every few months to confirm that the haemoglobin is rising.
anaemia.treatment: Treat the cause; oral iron for three months after correction (or intravenous iron if not tolerated), B12 injections or folate, erythropoietin in kidney disease, transfusion only for severe or symptomatic anaemia. Oral iron tablets are the standard first step and are usually effective; they commonly cause gastrointestinal side effects, and taking them with meals eases this at the cost of reduced absorption. Treatment continues for about three months after the haemoglobin has returned to normal so that iron stores are replenished, with follow-up blood tests to check the response. Intravenous iron is used when tablets are not tolerated or not absorbed. Correcting the count without finding and treating the cause leaves the problem to recur.
anaemia.prevention: Iron-rich diet with vitamin C, treating heavy periods, iron supplements in pregnancy where advised, avoiding unnecessary NSAIDs. Groups at higher risk, such as women with heavy periods, pregnant women, people on restricted diets and older people, benefit from attention to dietary iron and early testing when symptoms appear.
anaemia.seekCare: Urgent care for breathlessness at rest, chest pain, fainting, or black or bloody stools; routine review for persistent tiredness and pallor. NHS guidance is that anyone with symptoms of anaemia should see their GP, who can usually diagnose it with a simple blood test; untreated iron deficiency can lead to heart problems, complications in pregnancy and delayed development in children.

sections.heading: What does anaemia feel like?
sections.body:
Many people with iron deficiency anaemia have only a few symptoms. How much a person notices depends on how quickly the anaemia develops, and iron deficiency can be mild enough to cause no symptoms. Tiredness and a lack of energy are common, and some people also notice shortness of breath, a pounding heartbeat, paler skin or headaches. Less often there may be ringing in the ears, an altered sense of taste, hair loss, a craving to eat non-food items (called pica) or spoon-shaped nails. Low iron has also been linked with restless legs syndrome, even when anaemia is not fully present.

Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia can cause tiredness, a sore red tongue, pins and needles and mouth ulcers. It can also cause muscle weakness and problems with vision, memory or judgement. Some of these problems, especially those affecting the nervous system, can become permanent without treatment, and long-term B12 deficiency can damage nerves. The NHS says body stores of B12 can last for a few years, so problems may take a long time to appear.

sections.heading: What are the main types of anaemia?
sections.body:
Iron deficiency is the most common type of anaemia, and vitamin B12 and folate deficiency can also cause it. MedlinePlus also lists anaemia of chronic disease, sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia and aplastic anaemia among the types. Anaemia of chronic disease is linked with long-term illnesses. Sickle cell anaemia is inherited and involves abnormal haemoglobin that changes the shape of red blood cells. Thalassaemia is inherited, while aplastic anaemia involves damage to the stem cells in the bone marrow that make blood cells.

In the UK, the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency is pernicious anaemia. In this condition the immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach, so the body cannot absorb B12 from food. Diet can also contribute, particularly for people who eat little or no animal-source food, such as vegans, and some medicines, including anticonvulsants and proton pump inhibitors, can reduce absorption. Folate deficiency can also follow alcohol misuse.

sections.heading: What happens at an appointment, and which tests are used?
sections.body:
A GP usually asks about lifestyle and medical history and then arranges a blood test. This is a full blood count, which checks the red blood cells, and the GP may also test ferritin, a protein that stores iron. A low ferritin suggests that there is not much iron stored in the body. The NHS advises seeing a GP if iron deficiency anaemia is suspected, and diagnosis relies on blood tests.

Finding the cause matters because treatment depends on it. Heavy periods and medicines such as ibuprofen or aspirin, which can cause bleeding in the stomach, are among the causes the GP considers. In men and in women after the menopause, bleeding in the gut is the most common cause of iron deficiency, whereas in women before the menopause it is heavy periods. If the cause is unclear, further tests may follow, such as a gastroscopy or colonoscopy to look for a source of bleeding, and testing for coeliac disease may be suggested.

sections.heading: How is anaemia treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on the type of anaemia and its cause. Iron deficiency anaemia is usually treated with iron tablets and iron-rich foods, while the underlying cause, such as heavy periods or bleeding, is also addressed. Common side effects of iron tablets include constipation or diarrhoea, tummy pain, heartburn, feeling sick and darker than usual poo. Taking tablets with or shortly after food can help, and a GP may adjust the tablets if side effects are troublesome. An iron infusion may be used when a person cannot take tablets or cannot absorb iron through the gut.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is usually treated with hydroxocobalamin injections, followed by tablets or continuing injections depending on the cause. When the deficiency is not caused by diet, injections may be needed long term. Folate deficiency is treated with folic acid tablets, and doctors check B12 first because folic acid can sometimes hide a B12 deficiency. After iron treatment, a follow-up blood test is used to check the response. MedlinePlus says anaemia of chronic disease may improve when the disease causing it is treated.

sections.heading: Living with anaemia and what to expect
sections.body:
Vitamin B12 is found in meat, fish, eggs, dairy products and fortified foods. Good sources of folate include broccoli, brussels sprouts, asparagus, peas, chickpeas and brown rice. NHS 111 Wales notes that an iron overdose in a young child can be fatal, which is why iron tablets are kept out of children's reach.

NHS 111 Wales says most people with iron deficiency anaemia respond to dietary changes and iron tablets. Untreated iron deficiency anaemia may lead to heart problems, complications in pregnancy and delayed development in children. Delays in treating B12 deficiency can cause lasting nerve damage. Vitamin B12 deficiency anaemia most often responds well to treatment. Overall, the outlook depends on the condition causing the anaemia.

faqs.q: Is anaemia the same as iron deficiency?
faqs.a: No, iron deficiency is only the most common type. Anaemia can also come from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, long-term conditions, inherited conditions such as sickle cell disease and thalassaemia, or aplastic anaemia. Treatment depends on the type and cause.

faqs.q: Why do doctors look for the cause of iron deficiency?
faqs.a: Finding the cause matters because treatment depends on it. In men and in women after the menopause, bleeding in the gut is the most common cause. Doctors may arrange a gastroscopy or colonoscopy to look for a source of bleeding, including a cancer, if the reason is unclear.

faqs.q: Do iron tablets have side effects?
faqs.a: They can, and the NHS lists constipation or diarrhoea, tummy pain, heartburn, feeling sick and darker than usual poo. Taking them with or shortly after food can help. A GP may adjust the tablets if the side effects are troublesome. An iron infusion may be used when a person cannot take tablets or cannot absorb iron through the gut.

faqs.q: Why might vitamin B12 be given by injection?
faqs.a: Injections are used when the problem is poor absorption, as in pernicious anaemia, where the immune system attacks healthy stomach cells. The NHS says vitamin B12 injections are called hydroxocobalamin. When low B12 is only due to diet, tablets may be enough.

faqs.q: Does anaemia always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No, many people with iron deficiency anaemia have only a few symptoms. Sources note that iron deficiency can be mild enough to cause no symptoms, so a blood test is the reliable way to confirm it. The NHS advises seeing a GP for anyone who thinks they may have iron deficiency anaemia.

sepsis.name: Sepsis
sepsis.definition: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated body response to infection.
sepsis.overview: Any infection can trigger sepsis, most often pneumonia, urinary infection, abdominal infection or skin infection. The immune response spills over into the whole body: blood vessels leak and dilate, clotting is disturbed, and organs fail. Sepsis kills millions a year; each hour of delay in antibiotics raises mortality, so recognition is everything.
causes: Bacterial infection most often (pneumococcus, E. coli, staphylococci, streptococci, meningococcus)
Viral, fungal or parasitic infections
riskFactors: Weak immune system: chemotherapy, steroids, diabetes, no spleen
Pregnancy and the weeks after birth
signs: Fast breathing (over 22/min), fast pulse, low blood pressure
New confusion or drowsiness
Mottled, cold or clammy skin; non-blanching rash
Passing little urine
Very high or abnormally low temperature
complications: Septic shock and death
Acute kidney injury, lung failure, liver failure
Disseminated clotting and limb loss
Long-term physical and cognitive effects
sepsis.diagnosis: Clinical recognition (NEWS or qSOFA scores), blood cultures and cultures from the likely source before antibiotics, lactate, blood counts, kidney and liver function, clotting; imaging to find the source.
sepsis.treatment: The 'sepsis six' within an hour: oxygen, blood cultures, intravenous antibiotics, intravenous fluids, lactate measurement and urine output monitoring; then source control (drain an abscess, remove an infected line), vasopressors and organ support in intensive care.
sepsis.prevention: Vaccination, hand hygiene, prompt treatment of infections, careful care of wounds and catheters, and knowing the warning signs.
sepsis.seekCare: Call emergency services for an infection with slurred speech or confusion, extreme shivering or muscle pain, passing no urine in a day, severe breathlessness, mottled or discoloured skin, or a feeling of impending doom; for children also fast breathing, a fit, blue or pale skin, a non-fading rash, or unusual drowsiness.

breast-cancer.name: Breast cancer
breast-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour arising from the cells that line the ducts or lobules of the breast. It may remain within the ducts (in situ) or invade the surrounding tissue and spread to the axillary lymph nodes and beyond.
breast-cancer.overview: Breast cancer is the commonest cancer in women worldwide, and most cases occur after 50. Most tumours start in the milk ducts, fewer in the milk-producing lobules; ductal carcinoma in situ stays within the duct, while invasive cancer has broken through it. Every invasive cancer is tested for oestrogen receptors, progesterone receptors and the HER2 protein, which with grade and stage decides treatment. It is rare in men, and anyone with breast tissue can develop it.
causes: Accumulated DNA damage in duct or lobule cells, driven in part by lifetime exposure to oestrogen and progesterone
Inherited faults in BRCA1, BRCA2 and a few other genes, responsible for a minority of cases
Previous radiotherapy to the chest, particularly in youth
No single cause is found in most cases; ageing is the strongest factor
riskFactors: Increasing age: most cases are diagnosed after 50
A close relative with breast or ovarian cancer, or a known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation
Longer lifetime oestrogen exposure: an early first period, a late menopause, no pregnancies or a first pregnancy late in life
Combined hormone replacement therapy and, to a small degree, the combined contraceptive pill: the increase is small, relates to how long they are used, and falls after stopping
Alcohol, and being overweight after the menopause
Dense breast tissue on mammography, a previous breast cancer or some benign breast conditions

In trans women, several years of feminising hormone therapy: the risk is thought to be higher than in cis men but lower than in cis women; in men, conditions that raise oestrogen levels such as obesity, Klinefelter syndrome and cirrhosis
signs: A firm, irregular, usually painless lump in the breast or armpit
Dimpling, puckering or an orange-peel texture of the skin over the breast
A newly inverted nipple, a rash or crusting on the nipple, or blood-stained discharge
A change in the size or outline of one breast
In advanced disease, bone pain, breathlessness or jaundice from spread to bone, lung or liver
complications: Spread to the axillary lymph nodes and to bone, lung, liver or brain (metastatic breast cancer)
Lymphoedema of the arm after axillary surgery or radiotherapy
Bone loss and menopausal symptoms from endocrine therapy; heart effects of some chemotherapy and HER2-targeted drugs
Recurrence in the breast, chest wall or elsewhere, sometimes many years later
Anxiety, altered body image and loss of fertility in younger patients
breast-cancer.diagnosis: A suspicious lump or nipple change is assessed in a one-stop breast clinic by triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (mammography, with ultrasound for younger women and dense breasts) and a core needle biopsy of anything abnormal. The biopsy confirms invasive or in situ disease, grade and receptor status (oestrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2). Ultrasound of the axilla with needle sampling of suspicious nodes, and MRI in selected cases, complete local staging; CT and bone scans are reserved for larger tumours, involved nodes or symptoms suggesting spread. Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 is offered when the age at diagnosis, tumour type or family history suggests an inherited cause. Screening in England invites women, and anyone else registered female with a GP who has breast tissue, for mammography every three years; the first invitation arrives between the ages of 50 and 53, routine invitations stop after 70, and anyone aged 71 or over can still ask their local breast screening service for screening. Trans women who have taken hormones for some years and trans men who have not had chest surgery may need to ask to be included.
breast-cancer.treatment: Early breast cancer is treated with surgery: either wide local excision, removing the tumour with a margin of normal tissue and followed by radiotherapy to the rest of the breast, or mastectomy, in each case with sentinel lymph node biopsy to check the axilla and clearance of the nodes if they are involved. Reconstruction can be immediate or delayed. Treatment given after surgery, or before it to shrink a large tumour, is chosen by receptor status and the risk of recurrence: chemotherapy; endocrine therapy for oestrogen-receptor-positive cancers (tamoxifen, or an aromatase inhibitor after the menopause), taken for years; and trastuzumab or similar antibodies for HER2-positive disease. Metastatic breast cancer is not usually curable but is often controlled for years with endocrine, targeted and chemotherapy, radiotherapy for painful bone deposits and bone-protecting drugs. Care is planned by a multidisciplinary team following NICE guidance.
breast-cancer.prevention: Not all breast cancer can be prevented, but keeping to a healthy weight, being physically active, limiting alcohol and breastfeeding all lower the risk, and hormone replacement therapy is best reviewed regularly and continued only for as long as it is needed. Attending screening finds cancers before they can be felt. People at high risk because of family history or a BRCA mutation can be offered earlier and more frequent imaging, risk-reducing medicines or risk-reducing surgery, planned with a genetics service.
breast-cancer.seekCare: See a GP promptly about any new lump in the breast or armpit, skin dimpling, a change in a nipple or blood-stained nipple discharge, in anyone with breast tissue, at any age and whatever their gender. Chest masculinisation removes most but not all of the breast tissue, so a new lump or change in the chest wall still needs the same assessment. NICE recommends urgent referral to a breast clinic for an unexplained breast lump in anyone aged 30 or over and for discharge, retraction or other changes of one nipple in anyone aged 50 or over. A hot, red, swollen breast with fever suggests infection and should be seen the same day; a red, inflamed breast that does not settle with antibiotics also needs referral.

sections.heading: What do the first signs of breast cancer feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS says the first symptom most women notice is a lump or an area of thickened tissue in the breast. Most breast lumps are not cancer, but the NHS advises having any new lump checked by a doctor.

Other changes can include a different size or shape of the breast, fluid coming from the nipple, a lump or swelling in the armpit, and changes to the skin or nipple.

Breast pain is not usually a symptom of breast cancer. Pain linked to the menstrual cycle usually affects both breasts and tends to begin up to two weeks before a period, then eases when the period ends.

The NHS advises contacting a GP urgently if breast pain comes with a very high temperature, if any part of the breast is red, hot or swollen, or if there is a hard lump that does not move.

sections.heading: What are the types, grades and stages of breast cancer?
sections.body:
Ductal and lobular carcinoma are the two most common types of invasive breast cancer. Inflammatory breast cancer is rarer.

Staging describes how far a cancer has grown and spread. Stage 0 is ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), where the cells are inside the breast ducts and have not spread into the surrounding breast tissue. Stages 1 to 3 describe invasive cancer of increasing size and spread. Stage 4 means the cancer has spread to distant parts of the body.

Cancer Research UK explains that breast cancer is also graded from 1 to 3. Grade 1 cancers tend to grow more slowly, while grade 3 cancers grow faster and are more likely to spread.

Breast cancer cells are also usually tested for oestrogen receptors, progesterone receptors and a protein called HER2. These results help to plan treatment.

sections.heading: What happens at a breast clinic appointment?
sections.body:
NHS England guidance says people with suspected breast cancer should be seen in a one-stop clinic with same-day access to clinical examination, mammography, ultrasound and biopsy. Combining a clinical examination, imaging and a biopsy is called triple assessment.

A mammogram is an x-ray of the breast. One London cancer centre describes a mammogram as the usual scan for patients over 40, and another NHS trust says women under 40 have an ultrasound scan if a scan is needed.

A biopsy takes a small sample of breast cells or tissue with a needle.

All the results are discussed at a multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting. The team includes breast surgeons, specialist nurses and radiologists.

sections.heading: How is breast cancer treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says surgery is usually the first type of treatment, although chemotherapy or hormone therapy is sometimes given first. After breast-conserving surgery, which removes the cancer but not the whole breast, people are usually offered radiotherapy to destroy any remaining cancer cells. The NHS describes this combination as being as successful as removing the whole breast for early-stage breast cancer.

A sentinel lymph node biopsy removes the first lymph nodes in the armpit to check whether cancer has spread there. Chemotherapy may be given before surgery to make the cancer smaller.

Hormone therapy is used for hormone-sensitive breast cancers and has no effect if the cancer is not sensitive to hormones. In most cases it is taken for five years or more. It may be the only treatment if general health prevents surgery, chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

Cancer Research UK says radiotherapy can cause skin problems that usually start to improve three to four weeks after treatment. Hot flushes are a frequent effect of hormone therapy.

sections.heading: Living with breast cancer after treatment
sections.body:
The Royal Marsden says people can feel more tired than usual for several months after treatment ends. NHS Scotland guidance says exercise is safe after breast cancer treatment and can help with fatigue and lymphoedema.

Lymphoedema is swelling caused by a build-up of fluid. NHS Scotland says it typically begins within the first four years after breast cancer treatment. Macmillan advises having any swelling in the hand, arm, chest or breast checked by the cancer doctor or specialist nurse. People with lymphoedema can be referred to a specialist, who can advise on exercise, massage and skin care.

Breast Cancer Now says treatment can affect intimacy through pain, discomfort or loss of sensitivity. A hospital follow-up leaflet lists intimacy and relationship issues among the topics that can be discussed at follow-up.

sections.heading: What is secondary breast cancer?
sections.body:
Secondary breast cancer, also called metastatic or stage 4 breast cancer, is breast cancer that has spread to another part of the body. The most common places are the bones, liver, lungs and brain.

Breast Cancer Now says metastatic breast cancer can be treated but cannot be cured. Cancer Research UK says treatment can hold the cancer back for some time and help to relieve symptoms. Breast Cancer Now describes the aims as slowing the spread, controlling the cancer, relieving symptoms and maintaining health and wellbeing. Chemotherapy, hormone therapy and targeted drugs are the usual options.

Breast Cancer Now says that as treatments have improved, more and more people are living longer after a diagnosis. Supportive care can help with symptoms such as pain and fatigue at any stage, alongside treatment for the cancer.

faqs.q: Are most breast lumps cancer?
faqs.a: The NHS says most breast lumps are not cancer, but it advises having any new lump checked by a doctor. The NHS says the first symptom most women notice is a lump or an area of thickened tissue in the breast.

faqs.q: Does breast pain mean breast cancer?
faqs.a: The NHS says breast pain is not usually a symptom of breast cancer. Pain linked to the menstrual cycle usually affects both breasts and eases when a period ends. The NHS advises contacting a GP urgently if pain comes with a very high temperature, or if any part of the breast is red, hot or swollen, or if there is a hard lump that does not move.

faqs.q: Is surgery always the first treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS says surgery is usually the first type of treatment for breast cancer, but chemotherapy or hormone therapy will sometimes be the first treatment. Chemotherapy may be given before surgery to make the cancer smaller. Hormone therapy may be the only treatment if a person's general health prevents surgery, chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

faqs.q: Can secondary breast cancer be treated?
faqs.a: Secondary breast cancer is cancer that has spread to another part of the body. Breast Cancer Now says it can be treated but cannot be cured. Treatment aims to control and slow the spread, relieve symptoms and maintain health and wellbeing. Breast Cancer Now adds that more people are living longer as treatments improve, and that each person's situation is different.

keyFacts.value: Ductal and lobular carcinoma are the two most common invasive types; inflammatory breast cancer is rarer

keyFacts.value: 0 to 4; stage 0 is DCIS and stage 4 means spread to distant parts of the body

cervical-cancer.name: Cervical cancer
aliases: squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
cervical-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour of the cervix, the neck of the uterus, that develops almost always from persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV) after years of precancerous change.
cervical-cancer.overview: Cervical cancer arises at the transformation zone, where the lining of the cervical canal meets that of the outer cervix. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV, mainly types 16 and 18, turns the cells there abnormal (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, CIN). Most infections clear and most CIN regresses, but some progresses to invasive cancer over years, which is why screening can find and treat the change first. It affects anyone with a cervix, including trans men and non-binary people.
causes: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, mainly types 16 and 18, passed on by skin-to-skin sexual contact
Viral proteins that disable the cell's tumour-suppressor controls, so that abnormal cells (CIN) accumulate further mutations over years
A very small number of cervical cancers are not associated with HPV
riskFactors: Not being vaccinated against HPV and not attending cervical screening
Smoking, which makes it more likely that an HPV infection persists and progresses
A weakened immune system: HIV infection, organ transplant or long-term immunosuppressive medicines
Earlier first sexual intercourse and a greater number of sexual partners, because these increase exposure to HPV
Long-term use of the combined contraceptive pill (a small increase that falls after stopping)
A previous high-grade abnormality (CIN) or another HPV-related cancer
signs: Often none: precancer and early cancer are usually found only by screening
Bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause, or periods that become heavier
A persistent, unusual or smelly vaginal discharge, and pain or discomfort during sex
On examination, an abnormal-looking cervix that bleeds on contact; a hard, irregular mass in advanced disease
In advanced disease, swelling of a leg, blood in the urine or symptoms of kidney obstruction where the tumour blocks a ureter
complications: Spread to the vagina, parametrium, bladder, rectum and pelvic lymph nodes, and later to lung, liver and bone
Blockage of one or both ureters causing hydronephrosis and kidney failure
Fistulas between the bladder or rectum and the vagina, from tumour or from radiotherapy
Loss of fertility after radical surgery or chemoradiotherapy, and early menopause where the ovaries are removed or damaged by radiotherapy; a higher chance of preterm birth after cone biopsy or LLETZ
Long-term bowel, bladder and sexual effects of pelvic radiotherapy
cervical-cancer.diagnosis: Screening detects HPV and abnormal cells before cancer develops: a sample of cells from the transformation zone is tested first for high-risk HPV and, if positive, examined under the microscope, and abnormal results lead to colposcopy. Symptoms such as unusual bleeding are investigated by speculum examination of the cervix and referral for colposcopy, not by a screening test. At colposcopy the cervix is examined under magnification after acetic acid is applied, and a biopsy or a loop excision (LLETZ) provides tissue for the pathologist. If cancer is confirmed, staging uses examination, MRI of the pelvis, CT of the chest and abdomen and sometimes PET-CT, with blood tests including kidney function; the extent of spread (the FIGO stage) determines treatment.
cervical-cancer.treatment: Precancerous change (CIN) is treated by removing or destroying the transformation zone, usually with a large loop excision (LLETZ) under local anaesthetic or with a cone biopsy, after which HPV testing continues as a test of cure. Very early cancers can be removed by cone biopsy or, for those who wish to preserve fertility, by trachelectomy, which removes the cervix and upper vagina and leaves the uterus in place. Most early-stage cancers are treated by radical hysterectomy with removal of the pelvic lymph nodes, or by radiotherapy where surgery is unsuitable. Locally advanced disease is treated with chemoradiotherapy: external beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy to the cervix, with weekly platinum chemotherapy to sensitise the tumour. Cancer that has spread or returned is treated with chemotherapy, sometimes with targeted or immunotherapy drugs, and with palliative care to control symptoms.
cervical-cancer.prevention: Two measures prevent most cervical cancer. HPV vaccination, offered in the UK to all children aged 12 to 13 and to some adults at higher risk, protects against the types that cause the great majority of cases and works best before exposure to the virus. It does not protect against every high-risk type, so everyone with a cervix still needs cervical screening even if they have been vaccinated. Cervical screening is offered in England to everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64, including trans men and non-binary people (who may need to ask their GP practice if they are registered as male), at intervals that depend on age and the HPV result; it finds and treats precancer before it becomes cancer. Not smoking, and using condoms, which reduce but do not remove HPV transmission, also help. The WHO strategy for eliminating cervical cancer combines high coverage of vaccination, screening and treatment of precancer and cancer.
cervical-cancer.seekCare: See a GP about bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause, a persistent unusual discharge, or pelvic pain. These are usually not cancer, but they need an examination and cannot be assessed by a screening test. Any bleeding after the menopause needs prompt assessment. NICE advises an urgent suspected cancer referral for post-menopausal bleeding in anyone aged 55 or over, mainly to rule out cancer of the womb lining, and bleeding below that age is still investigated. NICE also advises considering an urgent suspected cancer referral when the appearance of the cervix on examination is consistent with cervical cancer. Attend screening when invited, and ask to be included if you have a cervix but have not been invited.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of cervical cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS lists unusual vaginal bleeding, including bleeding after sex or between periods, as a symptom of cervical cancer. Other symptoms are changes in vaginal discharge, pain during sex, and pelvic or lower back pain.

Early cervical cancer often causes no symptoms, so the NHS says that symptoms appearing between regular screening appointments should not wait for the next one. A GP appointment is the route to getting symptoms checked, rather than waiting for the next screening appointment.

These symptoms can have other causes, so they do not by themselves mean cancer.

sections.heading: What causes cervical cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says nearly all cervical cancers are linked to infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV).

 All children aged 12 to 13 are offered the HPV vaccine, and everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 is invited for regular cervical screening. This includes women and anyone else who has a cervix. Screening looks for HPV and abnormal cells before cancer develops.

 Cervical screening is not a test for cancer.

sections.heading: How is cervical cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
Diagnosis often begins with an abnormal screening result. Colposcopy is usually offered after an abnormal screening result: the cervix is looked at closely through a magnifying instrument, and a small tissue sample (biopsy) may be taken from anywhere that looks unusual. A loop excision (LLETZ) or cone biopsy can also give tissue to examine. Colposcopy does not establish a diagnosis of cancer on its own. A biopsy does.

Most findings at colposcopy are cell changes that are not cancer, and the NHS says cancer is found only in rare cases.

If cancer is found, tests such as an MRI scan, a PET-CT scan or a chest X-ray may be used to see how far it has spread. Doctors describe this as the stage, using the FIGO system, which has four stages numbered 1 to 4 based on the size of the cancer and whether it has spread.

sections.heading: How is cervical cancer treated?
sections.body:
Treatment usually includes surgery, chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and depends on the size and type of the cancer and where it is. Surgery is the main treatment for early disease, and the types include LLETZ, cone biopsy, hysterectomy and trachelectomy. Radiotherapy is mainly used for more advanced cancer or when surgery is not suitable, and chemotherapy or radiotherapy may be given after surgery.

Cancer Research UK says chemotherapy can be given at the same time as radiotherapy, called chemoradiotherapy, for stage 1B2 to stage 4A cervical cancer, and that cisplatin is the most common drug. For stage 2B, chemoradiotherapy is the most likely treatment, and for some larger stage 2A cancers it may be suggested instead of surgery. In stage 4A a few people may be offered a pelvic exenteration, a major operation.

For cervical cancer that is persistent, has come back or has spread, NICE recommends the immunotherapy drug pembrolizumab with chemotherapy, with or without the targeted drug bevacizumab, for some adults. Small cell cancer of the cervix is rare and is treated differently.

sections.heading: Fertility and support
sections.body:
People are usually referred to a fertility specialist before treatment starts, so that options such as storing eggs, embryos or ovarian tissue can be discussed. Options such as storing eggs or embryos before treatment can be discussed. Trachelectomy is one operation designed for people who wish to keep the option of pregnancy.

 Outlook is generally better when cervical cancer is found before it has spread outside the cervix, which is one reason early diagnosis matters.

faqs.q: Does an abnormal screening result mean cancer?
faqs.a: No. An abnormal result leads to colposcopy, a closer look at the cervix. Most findings at colposcopy are cell changes that are not cancer, and the NHS says cancer is found only in rare cases. Most abnormal findings at colposcopy are cell changes rather than cancer.

faqs.q: What happens at colposcopy?
faqs.a: The cervix is looked at closely, and a small tissue sample (biopsy) may be taken from anywhere that looks unusual. Tissue can also be taken with a loop excision (LLETZ) or cone biopsy. Colposcopy is usually the first step after an abnormal screening result.

faqs.q: Does bleeding after sex mean cervical cancer?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. These symptoms can have other causes, so they do not by themselves mean cancer. The NHS advises that symptoms between screening appointments should not wait for the next appointment, and that a GP can check them.

faqs.q: Can I still have children after treatment?
faqs.a: It depends on the treatment. People are usually referred to a fertility specialist before treatment starts, so that options such as storing eggs, embryos or ovarian tissue can be discussed. Egg or embryo storage before treatment can be discussed, and for some people with early cancer a trachelectomy can remove the cancer while keeping the womb.

faqs.q: Who is invited for cervical screening?
faqs.a: The NHS says everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 is invited for regular screening. All children aged 12 to 13 are offered the HPV vaccine.

ectopic-pregnancy.name: Ectopic pregnancy
ectopic-pregnancy.definition: A pregnancy in which the fertilised egg implants and begins to grow outside the cavity of the uterus, most often in a fallopian tube, where it cannot develop normally and can rupture the tissue around it.
ectopic-pregnancy.overview: After fertilisation in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, the embryo normally travels into the uterus and implants in the endometrium about a week later. In an ectopic pregnancy it implants elsewhere: most often in the tube itself, less commonly in the interstitial part of the tube where it enters the uterus, in the cervix, an ovary, a previous caesarean scar or the abdominal cavity. The NHS estimates that around 1 in every 90 pregnancies in the UK is ectopic. Symptoms usually appear between about the fourth and twelfth week of pregnancy, often in the first weeks after a missed period and sometimes before the pregnancy is known. The tube cannot stretch or support a placenta, so as the pregnancy grows it bleeds and can tear through the tubal wall, causing heavy bleeding into the abdomen. An ectopic pregnancy cannot be moved into the uterus and cannot survive, and a ruptured ectopic pregnancy is a life-threatening emergency. It can occur in anyone who can become pregnant, including trans men and non-binary people with a uterus and tubes, and should be considered in anyone of reproductive age with pelvic pain or bleeding until pregnancy has been excluded.
causes: Implantation of the fertilised egg outside the uterine cavity, usually because damage or narrowing of the fallopian tube slows or blocks the embryo's passage to the uterus
Scarring of the tube after pelvic inflammatory disease, most often from chlamydia or gonorrhoea
Previous surgery on the tubes, including sterilisation and its reversal, and a previous ectopic pregnancy
Impaired movement of the tube and its cilia, which smoking and hormonal factors are thought to affect
In many cases no cause is found
riskFactors: Pelvic inflammatory disease or a history of sexually transmitted infection
Surgery on the fallopian tubes, including sterilisation, or other pelvic or abdominal surgery

Becoming pregnant with an intrauterine device or system in place, or while taking the progestogen-only pill: these methods make pregnancy itself unlikely, but a pregnancy that does happen is more likely to be ectopic
signs: Tenderness, sometimes with guarding, in one side of the lower abdomen
Tenderness on moving the cervix or beside the uterus on pelvic examination, sometimes with a tender mass
Pain in the tip of the shoulder, from blood in the abdomen irritating the diaphragm, which points to internal bleeding
Pallor, a fast pulse, low blood pressure and collapse when the tube has ruptured
Vaginal bleeding that is often lighter, darker and more watery than a period
complications: Rupture of the tube with heavy bleeding into the abdomen, shock and, if not treated quickly, death
Loss of the affected fallopian tube, or damage to it after surgery that keeps the tube
Reduced fertility and a higher chance of another ectopic pregnancy in a later pregnancy
Persistent trophoblast tissue after salpingotomy or medical treatment, needing further treatment
Rhesus sensitisation in a rhesus-negative woman if anti-D is not given after surgery
Grief and anxiety about future pregnancies; the loss is a bereavement as well as an emergency
ectopic-pregnancy.diagnosis: Ectopic pregnancy is suspected in anyone who could be pregnant and has lower abdominal or pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding or unexplained faintness, so a pregnancy test comes first. If it is positive, a transvaginal ultrasound scan in an early pregnancy unit looks for a pregnancy inside the uterus; it may instead show a mass beside the ovary, occasionally with a heartbeat, or free fluid behind the uterus that indicates bleeding. When neither an intrauterine nor an ectopic pregnancy is seen, the situation is called a pregnancy of unknown location: serum hCG is measured and repeated 48 hours later, when a rise of about two thirds or more over 48 hours makes a developing pregnancy in the uterus more likely, though it does not exclude an ectopic and a scan is still arranged; a falling level suggests a pregnancy that is failing, and a slow rise or a plateau raises suspicion of an ectopic. NICE advises interpreting the result alongside the clinical picture rather than on its own. A full blood count and the blood group are checked, and miscarriage, a bleeding or twisted ovarian cyst, appendicitis and urinary infection are considered. Anyone who is shocked or in severe pain is treated as having a rupture without waiting for further tests.
ectopic-pregnancy.treatment: Treatment follows NICE guidance and depends on how unwell the person is, the size of the ectopic pregnancy and the hCG level. Expectant management, with repeated hCG measurements until the level falls to normal, suits a small unruptured ectopic pregnancy with a low and falling hCG in someone who has little or no pain and can return for follow-up. Medical treatment is an injection of methotrexate, which stops the trophoblast cells dividing so that the pregnancy is reabsorbed; blood tests continue until hCG is undetectable, and pregnancy is avoided for some months afterwards as the team advises. Surgery, almost always laparoscopic, is used for significant pain, a larger mass, a high hCG, a visible heartbeat or rupture: salpingectomy removes the affected tube, while salpingotomy keeps a tube when the other one is damaged, at the cost of residual tissue that needs further monitoring. Rupture is an emergency treated with resuscitation, transfusion if needed and immediate surgery, and rhesus-negative women who have surgery are offered anti-D immunoglobulin. The loss is a bereavement as well as an emergency, and most women conceive again, even after a tube has been removed.
ectopic-pregnancy.prevention: Most ectopic pregnancies cannot be prevented, but the risk can be lowered by reducing the chance of tubal damage: using condoms to protect against chlamydia and other sexually transmitted infections, being tested and treated promptly if infection is suspected, and not smoking. Anyone who has had an ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery or pelvic inflammatory disease should tell their GP or midwife as soon as they know they are pregnant so that an early scan can confirm that the pregnancy is in the uterus.
ectopic-pregnancy.seekCare: Anyone who could be pregnant and has one-sided lower abdominal or pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding or brown watery discharge, or pain in the tip of the shoulder should contact a GP, NHS 111 or an early pregnancy unit the same day, even if no period has been missed yet. Call 999 or go to A&E for sudden severe abdominal pain, feeling faint or collapsing, a racing pulse, or looking very pale and feeling sick and sweaty with pain, as these can mean the tube has ruptured and internal bleeding has started.

endometriosis.name: Endometriosis
endometriosis.definition: A chronic condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus (the endometrium) grows outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, the peritoneum and the ligaments of the pelvis, where it responds to the hormones of the menstrual cycle and causes inflammation, pain and scarring.
endometriosis.overview: Endometriosis affects roughly 1 in 10 women of reproductive age worldwide, and anyone with a uterus and ovaries can develop it, including trans men and non-binary people. The misplaced tissue bleeds a little with each period but has no way out, so it provokes inflammation, adhesions and cysts: a deposit on the ovary can grow into a blood-filled endometrioma, often called a chocolate cyst, and deep infiltrating disease can involve the uterosacral ligaments, the space between the rectum and the vagina, the bowel and the bladder. The result is period pain that stops normal life, pain with sex, bowel and bladder symptoms and, for some, difficulty conceiving. The condition depends on oestrogen, so it begins after puberty and symptoms usually improve after the menopause, although they do not always settle, and oestrogen-containing HRT can keep deposits active. Its symptoms overlap with other pelvic conditions and examination and scans are often normal in early disease, and the NHS notes that getting a diagnosis can take a long time.
causes: The cause is not fully understood, and endometriosis probably arises in more than one way
Retrograde menstruation, in which menstrual blood carrying endometrial cells flows back along the fallopian tubes into the pelvis, is the most widely accepted explanation
Transformation of peritoneal cells into endometrial-like tissue, and spread of cells through lymph or blood vessels, may explain deposits at distant sites
Oestrogen drives the deposits to grow and bleed, and an altered immune response fails to clear them
Genetic factors: the condition runs in families
riskFactors: A mother or sister with endometriosis
Early first period, short cycles, and heavy or prolonged periods
Never having given birth, or a late first pregnancy
Anything that obstructs the outflow of menstrual blood, such as a congenital abnormality of the uterus or vagina
Reproductive age: the condition is rare before puberty, and symptoms usually improve after the menopause, although they do not always settle
signs: Tenderness on pelvic examination, particularly behind the uterus and over the uterosacral ligaments
Nodules felt in the posterior vaginal fornix in deep disease
A fixed, retroverted uterus, or an enlarged ovary where an endometrioma has formed
A normal examination, which does not rule endometriosis out
complications: Subfertility and infertility, from adhesions that distort the tubes and ovaries and from inflammation that impairs fertilisation and implantation
Chronic pelvic pain with a large effect on work, education, relationships and mental health
Ovarian endometriomas, which can rupture or twist the ovary (torsion)
Adhesions binding the bowel, bladder and uterus together; rarely bowel obstruction or blockage of a ureter
A small increase in the risk of some types of ovarian cancer, although the overall risk remains low
endometriosis.diagnosis: Diagnosis starts with the pattern of symptoms: pain that follows the menstrual cycle, pain during or after sex, and cyclical bowel or urinary symptoms, together with an abdominal and pelvic examination. Transvaginal ultrasound is the first investigation and can show endometriomas and deep deposits in the bowel or bladder, but it often misses superficial disease on the peritoneum. MRI helps to map deep infiltrating disease before surgery. Laparoscopy, with a biopsy of the deposits seen, is the definitive test, although NICE advises that a normal examination, ultrasound or MRI should not be used to rule the condition out or to withhold treatment. There is no diagnostic blood test. A pregnancy test, urinalysis and a full blood count help to exclude pregnancy, urine infection and anaemia while the cause of pelvic pain is being worked out.
endometriosis.treatment: Treatment depends on symptoms, age and whether pregnancy is wanted. Pain is managed first with paracetamol and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen. Hormonal treatment aims to stop the deposits responding to the cycle: the combined hormonal contraceptive or a progestogen is offered first, and GnRH analogues, which produce a temporary menopause, are reserved for specialist use and are normally given with add-back hormone therapy to protect bone and limit menopausal symptoms. Some of these treatments, such as the combined hormonal contraceptive and contraceptive progestogens, also prevent pregnancy; others, including GnRH analogues, are not contraceptives, so contraception is discussed separately. Hormonal treatment does not have a lasting effect on fertility once it is stopped. Surgery is laparoscopic excision or ablation of the visible deposits, removal of endometriomas and division of adhesions; deep disease involving the bowel, bladder or ureter is managed by a specialist endometriosis centre. Hysterectomy, with or without removal of the ovaries, is a last resort for those who have completed their family; it is normally combined with excision of the deposits, it does not guarantee that pain will end, and hormone replacement therapy is discussed if the ovaries are removed before the menopause. Fertility treatment, pain management services and support groups such as Endometriosis UK are part of long-term care.
endometriosis.prevention: There is no known way to prevent endometriosis. Hormonal contraception that makes periods lighter or stops them may reduce symptoms and slow the growth of deposits. Recognising the symptoms early, and taking period pain that disrupts life seriously rather than accepting it as normal, shortens the delay to diagnosis and treatment.
endometriosis.seekCare: See a GP for period pain that stops normal activities, pain during or after sex, pain when passing urine or opening the bowels during a period, blood in the urine or stool during periods, or difficulty getting pregnant. Seek urgent care for sudden severe pelvic pain, pain with fever or vomiting, fainting, or pain with a positive pregnancy test, which can signal a ruptured or twisted cyst or an ectopic pregnancy.

fibroids.name: Fibroids
fibroids.definition: Benign (non-cancerous) growths of smooth muscle and fibrous tissue that develop in the muscular wall of the uterus, ranging from the size of a pea to a mass that fills the abdomen.
fibroids.overview: Fibroids are the commonest benign (non-cancerous) growth of the uterus: the NHS estimates that around 1 in 3 women develop them at some point, most often between the ages of 30 and 50, and they are more common in Black women. They occur in anyone with a uterus, including trans men and non-binary people. Fibroids depend on oestrogen and progesterone, so they grow during the reproductive years and in pregnancy and usually shrink after the menopause. They are described by position: intramural fibroids sit within the myometrium, subserosal fibroids bulge from the outer surface towards the abdomen, submucosal fibroids push into the cavity and distort the lining, and pedunculated fibroids hang on a stalk inside or outside the uterus. Many cause no symptoms and are found by chance on a scan. When they do cause trouble it is usually heavy periods, pressure on the bladder or bowel, pain or, with submucosal fibroids, difficulty conceiving.
causes: The exact cause is unknown; each fibroid arises from a single smooth muscle cell of the myometrium that multiplies abnormally
Growth is driven by oestrogen and progesterone, which is why fibroids appear after puberty, enlarge in pregnancy and shrink after the menopause
Genetic changes within the fibroid cells and local growth factors sustain the growth
Fibroids are not caused by infection and do not develop from the endometrium
riskFactors: A mother or sister with fibroids
Being overweight, which raises oestrogen levels
Never having given birth; pregnancy appears to lower the risk
signs: An enlarged, firm, irregular uterus felt on abdominal or pelvic examination
A mass in the lower abdomen that can be large enough to resemble pregnancy
Pallor and other signs of iron deficiency anaemia from heavy bleeding
A normal examination when the fibroids are small
complications: Iron deficiency anaemia from heavy or prolonged periods
Pressure effects: frequent urination or difficulty emptying the bladder, constipation, and rarely blockage of a ureter
Subfertility and miscarriage, particularly with submucosal fibroids that distort the cavity
Problems in pregnancy: pain from degeneration of a fibroid, an awkward position of the baby, obstructed labour, caesarean birth and heavier bleeding after delivery
Torsion of a pedunculated fibroid, causing sudden severe pain

Uterine sarcoma (leiomyosarcoma) is a rare cancer that can look like a fibroid on a scan; fibroids themselves are not thought to turn cancerous, but a fibroid that grows quickly, or any growth or bleeding after the menopause, needs prompt assessment
fibroids.diagnosis: Fibroids are often discovered on a scan done for another reason. When symptoms prompt investigation, the history covers the heaviness and pattern of bleeding, pressure symptoms and plans for pregnancy, and the examination feels for an enlarged or irregular uterus. Ultrasound, transvaginal or through the abdomen, is the first imaging and shows the number, size and position of the fibroids; NICE recommends it when the uterus can be felt through the abdomen or a pelvic mass is suspected. MRI maps fibroids more precisely before myomectomy or uterine artery embolisation and helps to distinguish them from adenomyosis. Hysteroscopy is used when submucosal fibroids are suspected and allows small ones to be removed at the same time. A full blood count is offered to anyone with heavy bleeding to check for anaemia; NICE does not recommend testing ferritin routinely, and iron treatment is guided by the blood count and symptoms. A pregnancy test is done in anyone of reproductive age with bleeding or a pelvic mass.
fibroids.treatment: Fibroids that cause no symptoms need no treatment, only review if they are large. For heavy bleeding the options are those for heavy menstrual bleeding generally. For fibroids smaller than about 3 cm, NICE advises the levonorgestrel intrauterine system as the first option where the cavity is not distorted, with tranexamic acid, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen, the combined pill or cyclical progestogens if it is unsuitable, and iron to correct anaemia. Fibroids of 3 cm or more are referred for specialist assessment. GnRH analogues shrink fibroids and stop bleeding by inducing a temporary menopause; they are used for a few months before surgery, with add-back hormone therapy to protect bone. Procedures that keep the uterus are myomectomy (removal of the fibroids through the abdomen, laparoscopically or hysteroscopically), uterine artery embolisation, in which a radiologist blocks the blood supply so that the fibroids shrink, endometrial ablation for small fibroids with heavy bleeding, and MRI-guided focused ultrasound where it is available. The effect of uterine artery embolisation and myomectomy on future pregnancy is uncertain and is discussed before choosing between them; endometrial ablation is not suitable for anyone who may want a pregnancy. Hysterectomy is the definitive treatment for those who have completed their family and whose symptoms are severe.
fibroids.prevention: There is no proven way to prevent fibroids. Keeping to a healthy weight may lower the risk. Treating heavy periods early prevents iron deficiency anaemia, and regular review of known fibroids catches growth or new symptoms before they cause complications.
fibroids.seekCare: See a GP for periods heavy enough to disrupt life, bleeding between periods, tiredness or breathlessness that could mean anaemia, pressure symptoms in the bladder or bowel, a swelling in the lower abdomen, or difficulty conceiving. Seek urgent care for sudden severe abdominal pain, bleeding that soaks a pad every hour for several hours, or faintness. Any bleeding after the menopause, or a fibroid that grows after the menopause, needs prompt assessment.
