blood-glucose.name: Blood glucose
blood-glucose.what: The concentration of glucose in blood, measured from a vein or a fingerprick. Fasting, random and after-a-sugar-drink (oral glucose tolerance) versions answer different questions.

measures.meaning: After 8 hours without food; normal fasting values differ slightly between countries and laboratories, so the report gives the range used, diabetes at 7.0 or above on two occasions.
Any time of day; 11.1 mmol/L or above with symptoms suggests diabetes.
Glucose two hours after a 75 g drink; used in pregnancy and borderline cases.

whyOrdered: Thirst, passing lots of urine, weight loss
Screening for diabetes in people at risk
Confusion, sweating or collapse (hypoglycaemia)
Monitoring insulin and other diabetes treatment
blood-glucose.how: Venous sample in a fluoride tube, or a capillary fingerprick on a meter; continuous glucose monitors sample fluid under the skin.
blood-glucose.preparation: Fasting tests need 8-12 hours without food, water allowed.

interpretation.meaning: Impaired fasting glucose: prediabetes, a chance to change course
Diabetes if repeated or with symptoms

Hypoglycaemia: usually from insulin or a sulfonylurea; mild episodes are treated with fast-acting carbohydrate as set out in the care plan, and confusion, drowsiness or a seizure is an emergency (call 999)

blood-glucose.limitations: A single value is a snapshot; HbA1c gives the three-month average. Stress and illness raise glucose temporarily.

hba1c.name: HbA1c
hba1c.what: The fraction of haemoglobin that has glucose stuck to it. Because red cells live about 120 days, it reports the average blood glucose over the previous two to three months in a single number.

measures.meaning: Reported in mmol/mol (and %). Below 42 (6.0%) normal; 42-47 (6.0-6.4%) prediabetes; 48 (6.5%) or above diabetes.

whyOrdered: Diagnosing type 2 diabetes
Monitoring diabetes control every 3-6 months
Setting and reviewing treatment targets

interpretation.meaning: Diabetes (if no condition affecting red cells)

interpretation.finding: Individualised: commonly 48 or 53 mmol/mol in adults with type 2 diabetes, tighter in the young and newly diagnosed, looser in frail or older people
interpretation.meaning: Individualised: tighter in the young and newly diagnosed, looser in the frail
Treatment and lifestyle changes are working

hba1c.limitations: Unreliable when red cell life is abnormal: anaemia, haemoglobin variants, recent transfusion, pregnancy, kidney failure. Not for diagnosing type 1 diabetes, which moves too fast.

references.title: NHS: Type 2 diabetes – symptoms and diagnosis
NICE NG28: Type 2 diabetes in adults: management

hba1c.specimen: Venous blood in an EDTA tube; fingerprick point-of-care devices in some clinics
hba1c.resultType: Numeric, read against diagnostic and target thresholds

quick.sample: Blood from a vein, no fasting
quick.usedFor: Diagnosing type 2 diabetes, monitoring diabetes control
quick.measures: Glycated haemoglobin, the average blood glucose of the previous two to three months

components.name: HbA1c
components.measures: Percentage of haemoglobin with glucose attached, reported in mmol/mol
components.high: Diabetes, prediabetes; falsely high with iron deficiency and slow red-cell turnover
components.low: Improving control; falsely low with haemolysis, blood loss, transfusion, pregnancy

hba1c.rangeNote: HbA1c is not read against a laboratory reference interval but against internationally agreed diagnostic thresholds and individualised treatment targets. Conditions that change red-cell lifespan make the value unreliable whatever the threshold.

thresholds.name: Diabetes
thresholds.context: Diagnosis of type 2 diabetes; repeated to confirm unless symptoms are present. Not valid in conditions that affect red cells

source.title: NHS: Type 2 diabetes – symptoms and diagnosis

thresholds.name: Non-diabetic hyperglycaemia (prediabetes)
thresholds.context: High risk of type 2 diabetes; lifestyle intervention offered

source.title: NICE PH38: Type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk

thresholds.name: Treatment target (diet or a single drug not causing hypoglycaemia)
thresholds.context: Adults with type 2 diabetes managed by lifestyle or one agent; individualised

source.title: NICE NG28: Type 2 diabetes in adults: management

thresholds.name: Treatment target (a drug that can cause hypoglycaemia)
thresholds.context: Adults with type 2 diabetes on treatment associated with hypoglycaemia; relaxed for older or frail people

source.title: NICE NG28: Type 2 diabetes in adults: management

factors: Anything that shortens or lengthens red-cell life: haemolysis, blood loss, transfusion, iron deficiency, kidney failure, pregnancy
Haemoglobin variants, which interfere with some assay methods
Very recent changes in glucose control, which the value has not yet caught up with
Erythropoietin and iron treatment
cannotTell: Day-to-day swings in glucose or episodes of hypoglycaemia
Type 1 diabetes at presentation, where glucose rises too fast for HbA1c to reflect it
Whether control is good in someone whose red cells turn over abnormally
hba1c.medicinesNote: Glucose-lowering medicines lower it; corticosteroids and some antipsychotics raise it by raising glucose; iron and erythropoietin treatment can shift it independently of glucose.

liver-function-tests.name: Liver function tests
liver-function-tests.what: A panel of enzymes and proteins that together show whether liver cells are injured, whether bile is flowing, and whether the liver is still doing its manufacturing job.

measures.meaning: Enzymes that leak from damaged liver cells (hepatitis, fatty liver, drugs, alcohol).
Rise when bile ducts are blocked or irritated; ALP also comes from bone.
The pigment from broken-down red cells; high levels cause jaundice.
The main blood protein the liver makes; falls in chronic liver disease and malnutrition.
Clotting factors are made in the liver, so slow clotting means poor synthetic function.

whyOrdered: Jaundice, dark urine, pale stools
Abdominal pain, nausea, itching
Heavy alcohol use or viral hepatitis risk
Monitoring statins, methotrexate, antiepileptics and many other drugs
Fatty liver in obesity and diabetes
liver-function-tests.preparation: None, though fasting improves consistency for some labs.

interpretation.finding: ALT and AST much higher than ALP
interpretation.meaning: Hepatocellular injury: viral hepatitis, drugs, fatty liver, alcohol

interpretation.finding: ALP and GGT high with raised bilirubin
interpretation.meaning: Cholestasis: gallstone in the bile duct, pancreatic tumour, some drugs
Loss of synthetic function: cirrhosis or acute liver failure
Often Gilbert syndrome, a harmless inherited variation

liver-function-tests.limitations: Despite the name, they mostly detect damage rather than measure function; a normal panel does not exclude cirrhosis. Muscle injury raises AST, bone growth raises ALP.
liver-function-tests.resultType: A panel of numeric values, each with a laboratory reference interval; the pattern across the panel matters more than any single value

quick.usedFor: Jaundice, abdominal symptoms, alcohol, fatty liver, drug monitoring
quick.measures: Liver enzymes, bilirubin and albumin: injury, bile flow and synthesis

components.name: ALT
components.measures: Enzyme released from injured liver cells
components.high: Hepatitis, fatty liver, alcohol, drugs, congestion

components.name: AST
components.measures: Enzyme from liver, muscle, heart and red cells
components.high: Liver injury (alcohol-related if AST exceeds ALT), muscle injury, haemolysis

components.name: Alkaline phosphatase
components.measures: Enzyme from bile ducts and bone
components.high: Cholestasis, bone disease, growth, pregnancy

components.name: GGT
components.measures: Enzyme induced by cholestasis, alcohol and drugs
components.high: Bile-duct obstruction, alcohol, fatty liver, enzyme-inducing drugs

components.name: Bilirubin
components.measures: Breakdown product of haemoglobin processed by the liver
components.high: Haemolysis, Gilbert syndrome, hepatitis, bile-duct obstruction

components.name: Albumin
components.measures: Main protein made by the liver
components.high: Dehydration
components.low: Cirrhosis, inflammation, malnutrition, kidney or gut protein loss

components.name: Prothrombin time / INR (often added)
components.measures: Clotting factor production by the liver
components.high: Severe liver injury, cirrhosis, vitamin K deficiency, warfarin

liver-function-tests.rangeNote: Each enzyme has its own laboratory reference interval that varies by method, sex and age (alkaline phosphatase is naturally high in growing children). A mild elevation of one enzyme is common and often needs only a repeat; the pattern (hepatocellular versus cholestatic), the size of the rise and the trend guide what happens next.
factors: Alcohol in the preceding days and weeks
Obesity and fatty liver, which cause the commonest mild abnormalities
Strenuous exercise and muscle injury (AST, and to a lesser extent ALT)
Pregnancy (ALP), growth in childhood, fasting (bilirubin in Gilbert syndrome)
Many medicines and herbal supplements
cannotTell: How much scarring (fibrosis) the liver has: a normal panel does not exclude cirrhosis, and fibrosis is assessed with scores such as FIB-4, elastography or biopsy
The cause of liver injury without further tests (viral serology, autoimmune antibodies, iron studies, ultrasound)
True 'function' in most cases: the enzymes show injury, and only albumin and clotting reflect synthesis
liver-function-tests.medicinesNote: Statins, paracetamol in overdose, antibiotics such as flucloxacillin and co-amoxiclav, antiepileptics, methotrexate, antifungals, antituberculous drugs and some herbal products can raise liver enzymes; oral contraceptives and anabolic steroids can cause cholestasis.

kidney-function-tests.name: Kidney function tests
kidney-function-tests.what: Creatinine and urea are waste products the kidneys should clear; how much builds up in blood shows how well they are filtering. Creatinine is converted into an estimated filtration rate (eGFR), the standard measure of kidney function.

measures.meaning: Muscle waste cleared by filtration; rises as kidney function falls. Depends on muscle mass.
Estimated glomerular filtration rate in mL/min/1.73 m²; over 90 normal, under 60 for three months defines chronic kidney disease, under 15 is kidney failure.
Protein waste; rises with poor kidney function but also dehydration, bleeding into the gut and high protein intake.
Usually reported together; potassium climbs dangerously when kidneys fail.

whyOrdered: Screening people with diabetes or high blood pressure
Before contrast scans and many drugs
Swelling, reduced urine, tiredness, nausea
Dehydration, vomiting, diarrhoea
Monitoring ACE inhibitors, diuretics, lithium and NSAIDs
kidney-function-tests.how: Venous blood; usually paired with a urine protein test.
kidney-function-tests.preparation: None; avoid heavy exercise or a large meat meal the day before if possible.

interpretation.finding: Rising creatinine over hours to days
interpretation.meaning: Acute kidney injury: dehydration, sepsis, obstruction, drugs; usually reversible if caught
Chronic kidney disease, staged 3-5 by the value
Dehydration or gut bleeding rather than kidney damage

kidney-function-tests.limitations: eGFR is an estimate; it is inaccurate at extremes of muscle mass, in pregnancy and in rapidly changing illness. Half of kidney function can be lost before creatinine leaves the normal range.

references.title: NICE NG203: Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management

kidney-function-tests.specimen: Venous blood (serum); usually paired with a urine sample
kidney-function-tests.resultType: A panel of numeric values with laboratory reference intervals, plus an eGFR read against staging thresholds

quick.usedFor: Kidney function, dehydration, electrolyte balance, drug monitoring
quick.measures: Urea, creatinine, eGFR, sodium and potassium

components.name: Creatinine
components.measures: Muscle waste product cleared by the kidney
components.high: Reduced filtration, dehydration, high muscle mass

components.name: eGFR
components.measures: Estimated filtration rate
components.high: Normal in the young
components.low: Chronic kidney disease, acute kidney injury

components.name: Urea
components.measures: Protein waste made by the liver, cleared by the kidney
components.high: Kidney impairment, dehydration, gut bleeding, high-protein diet, steroids

components.name: Sodium
components.measures: Main extracellular ion; reflects water balance
components.high: Water loss without replacement
components.low: Excess water, SIADH, thiazides, heart or liver failure

components.name: Potassium
components.measures: Main intracellular ion; sets cardiac excitability
components.high: Kidney impairment, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, haemolysed sample

kidney-function-tests.rangeNote: Urea, creatinine and the electrolytes each have a laboratory reference interval; the eGFR is read against chronic kidney disease staging thresholds (see the creatinine and eGFR page) and requires two results at least three months apart before a diagnosis is made.
factors: Hydration, recent vomiting or diarrhoea and intravenous fluids
Muscle mass, diet (meat), creatine supplements and exercise
Sample handling: a squeezed, delayed or haemolysed sample raises potassium
Medicines: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, lithium
cannotTell: The cause of kidney impairment or whether it is reversible
Protein or blood in the urine, which need urine tests
Total body potassium or sodium, only their blood concentration

lipid-profile.name: Lipid profile
lipid-profile.what: Measures the fats carried in blood: total cholesterol, LDL ('bad', deposited in artery walls), HDL ('good', carried away for disposal) and triglycerides. Used mainly to estimate and manage the risk of heart attack and stroke.

measures.meaning: Ideally below 5 mmol/L for the general population.
The particle that builds atherosclerotic plaque; the main treatment target.
Higher is protective; above 1.0 in men and 1.2 in women.
Fat from food and the liver; very high levels can cause pancreatitis.
Total minus HDL: all the harmful particles together.

whyOrdered: Cardiovascular risk assessment from age 40, earlier with family history
Known heart disease, stroke or peripheral artery disease
Diabetes, kidney disease, high blood pressure
Monitoring statin treatment
Xanthomas or very early heart disease in a family (familial hypercholesterolaemia)
lipid-profile.how: Venous blood, fasting no longer required for most purposes.
lipid-profile.preparation: Usually none; a fasting sample if triglycerides are very high.

interpretation.meaning: Raised risk; combined with age, blood pressure and smoking into a 10-year risk score to decide on statins

interpretation.finding: Total cholesterol above 7.5 with family history
interpretation.meaning: Possible familial hypercholesterolaemia; genetic testing and family screening
Risk of pancreatitis; look for alcohol, diabetes, drugs

lipid-profile.limitations: Cholesterol is one risk factor among several; the numbers matter less than the overall risk. Acute illness lowers cholesterol for weeks.

Acute illness, surgery and heart attack lower cholesterol for weeks
Weight change, pregnancy and the menstrual cycle
Untreated hypothyroidism raises LDL; check thyroid function before treating an unexpectedly high result

Whether arteries already contain plaque (that needs imaging)
Which lipid-lowering treatment is appropriate

electrolytes.name: Electrolytes
electrolytes.what: The dissolved salts that set the water content of the body and the electrical behaviour of nerves, muscle and the heart: sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, calcium, magnesium and phosphate. An electrolyte panel is a blood test that checks for imbalances of these salts, of body water and of acid-base (pH) status. Sodium, which sits mostly in the fluid outside cells, governs how much water the body holds and keeps nerves and muscles working; potassium, which sits mostly inside cells, sets the excitability of the heart and muscle, so even small shifts in the blood level matter; chloride helps maintain blood volume and blood pressure; and bicarbonate is the main buffer against acid. From sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate the laboratory also calculates the anion gap, a derived figure that helps classify an acidosis. The panel is a commonly requested hospital test and is almost always read together with kidney function.

measures.meaning: Governs water balance; low sodium is the commonest electrolyte disorder in hospital. Because most sodium is in the fluid outside cells, the blood level mainly reflects how much water the body is holding relative to salt. Symptoms of a low sodium depend on how fast it falls: a rapid drop causes weakness, tiredness and, when severe, confusion or coma, whereas a slow fall may cause nothing at all.

High or low levels cause dangerous heart rhythms. Most potassium is inside cells, so a small change in the plasma concentration can alter the heart's rhythm and its ability to contract, which is why it is checked so often in kidney disease, heart disease and in people taking diuretics or drugs that act on the kidney.
Helps maintain blood volume and blood pressure. High levels accompany dehydration, kidney disease and metabolic acidosis; low levels are seen with heart failure and lung disease.

The blood's main buffer; low in acidosis, high in alkalosis. Read with the anion gap, it helps separate acidosis caused by acid accumulation (diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, kidney failure) from acidosis caused by bicarbonate loss.
Corrected for albumin; high in parathyroid overactivity and cancer, low after thyroid surgery and in vitamin D deficiency.
Fall with malnutrition, alcohol and refeeding; matter for heart rhythm and muscle. Not every laboratory includes them in the basic panel, so they may need to be requested separately.

whyOrdered: Confusion, weakness, seizures, palpitations
Vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration
Kidney disease and diuretic treatment
Before and after surgery
Endocrine disease (adrenal, parathyroid)
Monitoring treatment with intravenous fluids
High blood pressure, heart failure, liver disease and the medicines used for them
Suspected acid-base disturbance (diabetic ketoacidosis, shock, severe diarrhoea)
electrolytes.how: Venous blood, analysed on an automated chemistry analyser; the panel is commonly run as part of a basic or comprehensive metabolic panel alongside kidney function and glucose. Point-of-care blood gas analysers in emergency departments and intensive care report sodium and potassium within minutes, but their values can differ from the central laboratory's and are confirmed with a laboratory sample when a decision rests on them. Potassium is falsely high if the sample is squeezed, haemolysed or delayed before separation.
electrolytes.preparation: None for a routine panel. The person's medicines, fluid intake and any vomiting or diarrhoea are noted because they strongly affect how the result is read.

interpretation.meaning: Often too much water relative to salt: diuretics, heart or liver failure, SIADH, excess drinking; also sodium loss through vomiting, diarrhoea or the kidneys, or fluid accumulating as oedema. The speed of the fall determines the symptoms
Water deficit from dehydration or inadequate intake, or less commonly a hormone or kidney disorder that wastes water
Kidney failure, ACE inhibitors and spironolactone, tissue breakdown; needs an ECG. A haemolysed or delayed sample is excluded first by repeating it
Vomiting, diarrhoea, loop diuretics, steroid excess
Dehydration, kidney disease or a metabolic acidosis in which bicarbonate has been lost
Heart failure or lung disease

interpretation.finding: Low bicarbonate with a raised anion gap
interpretation.meaning: Acid accumulation: diabetic ketoacidosis, shock or kidney failure
Primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy in most adults

electrolytes.limitations: Blood levels do not always reflect total body stores (potassium is mostly inside cells, so a normal level can hide a large deficit or excess). Haemolysed, squeezed or delayed samples give spurious potassium. Each electrolyte is read against the reference interval of the laboratory that ran it, and intervals differ between laboratories and methods, so results from a blood gas analyser and the central laboratory are not interchangeable. An abnormal result identifies a disturbance but not its cause, which needs the history, medicines, kidney function and sometimes urine electrolytes and hormone tests.

thyroid-function-tests.name: Thyroid function tests
thyroid-function-tests.what: TSH from the pituitary and the thyroid hormones T4 and T3 measured together. Because the pituitary reacts to tiny changes in hormone level, TSH is the most sensitive single indicator of thyroid status.

measures.meaning: Thyroid-stimulating hormone; high when the thyroid is underactive, suppressed when it is overactive.
The main hormone the thyroid releases; low in hypothyroidism, high in hyperthyroidism.
The active hormone; added when TSH is low to detect T3 toxicosis.
TPO antibodies mark autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis; TSH-receptor antibodies mark Graves disease.

whyOrdered: Tiredness, weight change, feeling cold or hot, palpitations, anxiety
A goitre or neck lump
Atrial fibrillation, high cholesterol, depression
Monitoring levothyroxine or antithyroid drugs
Amiodarone or lithium treatment, pregnancy planning
thyroid-function-tests.how: Venous blood, any time of day (take levothyroxine after the sample).
thyroid-function-tests.preparation: None; biotin supplements can interfere and should be paused for two days.

interpretation.meaning: Primary hypothyroidism
Subclinical hypothyroidism: usually confirmed by repeating the test after a few weeks to months; whether to treat depends on the TSH level, age, symptoms, antibodies and pregnancy

interpretation.finding: Low TSH, high T4 or T3
interpretation.meaning: Hyperthyroidism: Graves disease, toxic nodules, thyroiditis
Pituitary (secondary) failure, or recent overtreatment

thyroid-function-tests.limitations: Acute illness and some drugs disturb results ('sick euthyroid'); repeat once recovered. TSH lags six weeks behind a dose change.

references.title: NICE NG145: Thyroid disease: assessment and management

Biotin supplements interfering with the assay
Pregnancy and the first trimester rise in hCG
Amiodarone, lithium, glucocorticoids, dopamine, some antiepileptics
Levothyroxine timing and absorption

Whether a nodule is present or cancerous
Thyroid status reliably during severe non-thyroidal illness

hormone-tests.name: Hormone tests
hormone-tests.what: Blood levels of hormones and related chemicals, interpreted against the time of day, the cycle and the level of the controlling hormone from the pituitary. Includes cortisol, sex hormones, prolactin, growth hormone, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and, by convention on this site, uric acid. Most hormones are released in pulses, follow a daily rhythm or vary with the menstrual cycle, so the laboratory value only makes sense when the time and circumstances of the sample are known. The usual logic is to measure a gland's hormone together with the pituitary hormone that drives it: a low gland hormone with a high pituitary signal points to failure of the gland itself, whereas a low gland hormone with a low or inappropriately normal pituitary signal points to the pituitary or hypothalamus. Where a single level cannot settle the question, dynamic tests are used: the gland is deliberately stimulated (for example with synthetic ACTH, Synacthen, to test the adrenal cortex) or suppressed (for example with dexamethasone to test whether cortisol production can be switched off) and the hormone is measured before and after.

measures.meaning: The stress hormone from the adrenal cortex; highest at 9 am. Low in Addison disease, high in Cushing syndrome. Measured in blood, in a 24-hour urine collection (which averages the day's output and may need repeating because production varies) or in late-night saliva, and often paired with ACTH to work out whether an abnormality arises in the adrenal gland or the pituitary. Severe stress, acute illness and severe depression also raise it.

Sex hormones; measured with LH and FSH from the pituitary to tell gland failure from pituitary failure. In men, testosterone with sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) helps investigate infertility, low libido and erectile dysfunction; prolactin, oestradiol and LH are often measured alongside to see the whole hormonal balance.

Raised by pituitary tumours, stress, many drugs and pregnancy; causes milk production and lost periods. Checked for unexplained milk production, irregular periods, fertility problems and persistent headaches or visual change; in men a raised prolactin often causes a low testosterone, so it is tested when testosterone is found to be low. An underactive thyroid is a common and easily treated cause of a raised prolactin.
Control calcium and bone; a high PTH with high calcium is primary hyperparathyroidism.
The waste product that crystallises in gout; above 360 micromol/L raises risk, targets in gout are below 300-360.

whyOrdered: Suspected adrenal, pituitary or gonadal disease
Osteoporosis and calcium problems
Gout diagnosis and treatment targets
Infertility, missed periods, erectile dysfunction, hair changes
Assessing pituitary function after tumours or surgery
Monitoring gender-affirming hormone therapy (oestradiol or testosterone with the treating team's targets)
Suspected Cushing syndrome (weight gain with thin limbs, a rounded face, easy bruising) or suspected adrenal insufficiency (fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure, low sodium with high potassium)
Unexplained milk production, irregular or absent periods, or headaches with visual change (prolactin)
hormone-tests.how: Venous blood, often at a set time (9 am cortisol, early morning testosterone) or after a stimulation or suppression drug. For a short Synacthen test, blood is taken for cortisol, a synthetic ACTH injection is given into the arm and further samples are drawn at set intervals afterwards to see whether the adrenal glands respond; a morning cortisol is checked first and the dynamic test is reserved for results that are neither clearly normal nor clearly low. A dexamethasone suppression test gives a dose of the synthetic steroid and then measures whether cortisol production has been switched off. Cortisol can also be measured in a 24-hour urine collection or a late-night saliva sample. Hormones are measured by immunoassay, and the laboratory's reference interval for the time of day, sex and, where relevant, phase of the cycle is printed on the report.
hormone-tests.preparation: Depends on the test; some need fasting, timing to the menstrual cycle, and biotin supplements can affect some results; tell the team about every medicine you take, including steroids, and never stop or change one unless the prescriber tells you to. Cortisol is sampled early in the morning because it peaks then, and the person notes any steroid medicines (tablets, inhalers, creams or injections), which suppress the body's own production and invalidate the result. Prolactin is taken when the person is rested, because stress raises it. Medicines are reviewed before a prolactin test because many commonly used drugs increase it.

interpretation.meaning: Adrenal insufficiency; confirmed with a synacthen stimulation test. Low sodium and high potassium on the electrolyte panel support the diagnosis of Addison disease

interpretation.finding: Poor cortisol response to Synacthen with high ACTH
interpretation.meaning: Primary adrenal failure (Addison disease), usually with low aldosterone; a poor response can also follow long-standing lack of ACTH from the pituitary, so further tests and endocrine referral separate the two
Makes primary adrenal failure unlikely but does not exclude recent-onset ACTH deficiency from the pituitary, which needs specialist assessment if suspected

interpretation.finding: High cortisol that does not suppress with dexamethasone
interpretation.meaning: Cushing syndrome from a pituitary or adrenal tumour, or from ACTH produced by a tumour elsewhere in the body; severe stress, illness and depression can mimic it, so results are confirmed with repeat and further tests
Primary hyperparathyroidism, usually a single adenoma
Testicular failure; low LH points to the pituitary instead
Macroprolactin (a harmless large form) is excluded, thyroid function and medicines are reviewed, and an MRI of the pituitary is considered
Supports gout, but can be normal during an attack

hormone-tests.limitations: Hormones pulse and cycle; a single random level is often uninterpretable. Dynamic tests (stimulate or suppress the gland, then measure) are needed to prove most diagnoses, and even these have grey zones: a normal Synacthen response does not exclude early pituitary disease, and a failed response does not by itself say whether the adrenal gland or the pituitary is at fault. Stress, acute illness, depression, pregnancy, the contraceptive pill and many medicines shift the values. Reference intervals depend on time of day, sex, age and cycle phase and differ between laboratories. In a suspected adrenal crisis there is no time for dynamic testing: a blood sample is taken and treatment starts before the result is known.

urinalysis.name: Urinalysis
urinalysis.what: A plastic strip with chemical pads dipped into a fresh urine sample. In sixty seconds it screens for infection, blood, protein, glucose, ketones and how concentrated the urine is, with microscopy for cells and crystals when needed.

measures.meaning: White cells and bacterial nitrite together point to a urinary infection.
Infection, stones, tumours or kidney inflammation; persistent invisible blood needs investigation.
A sign of kidney damage, especially in diabetes and high blood pressure; confirmed with a lab ratio.
Glucose spills over when blood sugar is high; ketones mean fat is being burned (starvation, diabetic ketoacidosis).
How concentrated the urine is and its acidity, useful in dehydration and stone disease.

whyOrdered: Burning, frequency or urgency (suspected infection)
Abdominal or loin pain
Screening in diabetes, high blood pressure and pregnancy
Unexplained fever in children and older adults
Kidney disease monitoring
urinalysis.how: Midstream urine into a clean pot; dipped immediately or sent for microscopy and culture.
urinalysis.preparation: Clean the area and catch the middle of the stream; first-morning samples are most concentrated.

interpretation.meaning: Likely urinary tract infection; a culture confirms the organism
Glomerular disease: needs kidney function tests and specialist review
Check blood glucose for diabetes (or SGLT2 inhibitor treatment)
Possible diabetic ketoacidosis, an emergency

urinalysis.limitations: Dipsticks in older adults often show bacteria without infection (asymptomatic bacteriuria) and should not drive antibiotics on their own. Menstrual blood and vigorous exercise cause false positives for blood.

urinalysis.resultType: Semi-quantitative dipstick pads (negative to 3+), specific gravity and pH, plus microscopy when requested

quick.usedFor: Urinary infection, kidney disease, diabetes screening, pregnancy checks
quick.measures: Chemical pads for leucocytes, nitrite, blood, protein, glucose, ketones, concentration and acidity; cells and crystals on microscopy

Delay before testing (bacteria multiply, cells break down) and exposure of the strip to air
Very dilute or very concentrated urine
Vitamin C can cause false negatives for blood and glucose; some antibiotics and dyes discolour the sample
Vigorous exercise, fever and dehydration cause transient protein or blood
cannotTell: Whether bacteria in the urine are causing illness: older adults often carry bacteria without infection and should not be treated on the dipstick alone
How much protein is leaking (quantified by an albumin-to-creatinine ratio)
The cause of blood in the urine, which needs microscopy, imaging and sometimes cystoscopy

urine-culture.name: Urine culture
urine-culture.what: A urine sample is spread on culture plates and incubated for 24-48 hours to grow any bacteria, identify them and test which antibiotics kill them. It turns a dipstick suspicion into a proven infection with a targeted treatment. The laboratory first examines the urine under the microscope for white blood cells and bacteria, then plates a measured volume on nutrient agar and incubates it overnight; the colonies that grow are counted, identified and exposed to a panel of antibiotics (microscopy, culture and sensitivity, MC&S). Because the urethra and surrounding skin carry their own bacteria, how the sample is collected matters as much as what the laboratory does with it: a clean-catch midstream sample reduces contamination, and a catheter or, rarely, a needle sample through the lower abdomen is used when a clean sample cannot be obtained. Culture is the reference standard for diagnosing urinary tract infection, but it is often unnecessary when the diagnosis is already clear, and in people without symptoms a positive culture usually should not be treated.

measures.meaning: 100,000 or more colony-forming units per mL of a single organism is significant; lower counts count in symptomatic patients and catheter samples. The count is estimated from the number of colonies that grow from the measured volume plated; a low count of a single organism in a symptomatic person can still be a true infection.

E. coli causes most infections; Proteus suggests stones; Staphylococcus saprophyticus in young women; mixed growth usually means contamination. Yeasts are also reported and interpreted with symptoms and risk factors.
Which antibiotics the organism is sensitive or resistant to, so that empirical treatment can be confirmed, narrowed or changed.
White cells and bacteria seen under the microscope support infection and decide whether the sample goes on to culture.

whyOrdered: Infection in men, children, pregnancy and anyone with a catheter or kidney disease
Infections that keep coming back or fail treatment
Suspected kidney infection or sepsis from a urinary source
Before urological surgery
Symptoms of cystitis with a dipstick result suggesting infection, when the result will change treatment
Confirming clearance after treatment in pregnancy or before a urological procedure
urine-culture.how: Midstream sample in a sterile pot (or from a fresh catheter); refrigerate if it cannot reach the lab within hours. For a clean-catch sample the area is cleaned, the first part of the stream is passed into the toilet and the middle portion is caught in the sterile container without touching its inside; kits for collection at home are available. A catheter sample is taken from a freshly placed or freshly changed catheter, and the person may be asked not to pass urine for an hour or so beforehand (or to drink water) so that enough urine is present. Culture results take one to two days; microscopy can be reported sooner. A repeat culture is sometimes taken after treatment to confirm the bacteria have cleared, particularly in pregnancy or before urological procedures.
urine-culture.preparation: Collect before starting antibiotics whenever possible. The laboratory form records symptoms, pregnancy, catheter status and any antibiotics already taken, because these change how the colony count is interpreted.

interpretation.finding: Pure growth of E. coli, sensitive to nitrofurantoin
interpretation.meaning: Confirmed infection; treat with the narrowest effective antibiotic
No bacterial infection detected; if symptoms persist, consider antibiotics taken before sampling, organisms that do not grow on standard culture, or a non-infective cause of the symptoms
Probably contaminated; repeat with careful collection
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: treat only in pregnancy or before urological procedures
The antibiotic already started is changed to one the organism is sensitive to; recurrent resistant infections prompt a review of the urinary tract and of antibiotic use
Reported alongside bacteria; its significance is judged from symptoms and risk factors rather than from the culture alone

urine-culture.limitations: Results take two days, so treatment often starts empirically. Antibiotics taken beforehand can sterilise the sample. Contamination is common, especially in primary care where a large share of samples grow mixed skin or genital flora, which wastes a culture and can lead to treatment of a non-existent infection. Standard culture does not detect anaerobes, mycobacteria or some fastidious organisms, and yeasts may grow but are not always reliably detected, and in a large proportion of people with asymptomatic bacteriuria, including older adults and people with catheters, a positive culture is not an infection to treat. Culture confirms bacteria in the urine but not where in the urinary tract the infection sits or whether it has reached the kidneys or the bloodstream; that needs the clinical picture, blood tests and sometimes imaging.

urine-protein.name: Urine protein
urine-protein.what: Healthy kidney filters hold back almost all protein. Measuring albumin leaking into urine, corrected for how dilute the sample is, detects kidney damage years before blood tests change, particularly in diabetes and high blood pressure. Albumin is the main protein in blood, and healthy kidneys let only a trace of it through. Because early kidney disease usually causes no symptoms, the test is used above all as a screen in people at higher risk: those with diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease or a family history of kidney disease, and smokers and people with obesity. UK guidance recommends the albumin:creatinine ratio in preference to other tests of proteinuria, and reads it alongside the eGFR blood test: the two measure different things, kidney damage and kidney filtration, and together they diagnose and classify chronic kidney disease. A raised ratio matters at any eGFR, because albumin in the urine is an independent marker of risk both for progression to kidney failure and for cardiovascular disease.

measures.meaning: The amount of albumin in a single urine sample divided by the creatinine in the same sample. Creatinine leaves the body at a fairly steady rate, so dividing by it corrects for how concentrated or dilute the urine is, which depends on how much the person has drunk. Below 3 mg/mmol normal; 3-30 moderately raised (formerly microalbuminuria); above 30 severe. Combined with eGFR to stage kidney disease, and used to follow how well treatment is protecting the kidneys.

All proteins, not just albumin, used when large amounts leak (nephrotic range above 300 mg/mmol) and when non-albumin proteins are suspected; the ACR is the more sensitive test for the small leaks of early disease.
The old gold standard; a random or early-morning ACR performs as well and is far more convenient, so timed collections are now rarely needed.

A quick bedside screen that detects only larger amounts of protein; it is not sensitive enough to pick up the moderately raised albumin of early kidney damage, so a negative dipstick does not replace a laboratory ACR in people at risk.

whyOrdered: Yearly in diabetes
High blood pressure, kidney disease, lupus
Frothy urine or unexplained swelling
Pregnancy with high blood pressure (pre-eclampsia)
Staging chronic kidney disease and deciding on ACE inhibitors and SGLT2 inhibitors
Heart disease, a family history of kidney disease, smoking or obesity, where early kidney damage is more likely
Monitoring known kidney disease and checking whether treatment is reducing the leak
Confirming or excluding kidney damage when the eGFR is reduced, or detecting it when the eGFR is still normal
urine-protein.how: A single urine sample is passed into a clean container; the first sample can be collected at any time of day, but an early-morning sample is preferred to confirm a raised result because it is less affected by the day's activity and fluid intake. The laboratory measures albumin, usually by immunoassay, and creatinine on a chemistry analyser, and reports the ratio as a single number. No blood test is needed for the ratio itself, though it is usually requested together with creatinine and eGFR. Semi-quantitative point-of-care devices exist for settings where laboratory testing is hard to access, at the cost of precision.
urine-protein.preparation: Avoid hard exercise the day before; repeat if there is infection or fever. Heavy exertion, fever and infection can raise albumin temporarily, so a raised result is usually repeated, ideally on an early-morning specimen, to show it persists and is not explained by something else.

interpretation.meaning: Kidney damage: the treating team uses the ACR together with blood pressure and diabetes status to decide on kidney-protecting medicines

interpretation.finding: Nephrotic-range protein with low albumin and swelling
interpretation.meaning: Nephrotic syndrome, needs a kidney biopsy in adults
Glomerulonephritis; urgent specialist referral

interpretation.finding: Raised ACR with a normal eGFR
interpretation.meaning: Early kidney damage can be present while filtration is still normal; if the leak persists on repeat testing it is itself enough to diagnose chronic kidney disease, and it raises cardiovascular risk

interpretation.finding: Reduced eGFR with a normal ACR
interpretation.meaning: Kidney disease without albumin leak; the two results are classified together, and risk rises as either worsens
Not diagnostic on its own: repeated to exclude exercise, fever, infection or other temporary causes, and chronic kidney disease is diagnosed only when the abnormality persists over months

interpretation.finding: Negative dipstick in someone at risk
interpretation.meaning: Does not exclude moderately raised albumin; a laboratory ACR is still needed
The more albumin leaks, the greater the risk of progression to kidney failure and of cardiovascular events, independently of eGFR

urine-protein.limitations: Exercise, fever, infection and standing for long periods raise protein transiently; two out of three samples must be positive to confirm. The ratio shows that the kidney is leaking albumin but not why, so the cause is sought from the history, blood pressure, glucose, blood tests, imaging and sometimes a biopsy. It measures albumin only, so a protein:creatinine ratio is needed when other proteins may be leaking. A dipstick is not a substitute for the laboratory ratio because it misses small leaks. Laboratories in different countries report the ratio in different units, so a result is read against the units and reference information of the laboratory that produced it.

National Kidney Foundation: Urine albumin-creatinine ratio (uACR)

NHS Scotland Right Decision Service: Chronic Kidney Disease, Adult: Diagnosis and Management

pregnancy-test.name: Pregnancy test
pregnancy-test.what: Detects human chorionic gonadotropin, a hormone made by the placenta from about a week after implantation. Urine tests give a yes/no answer; a blood test gives a number that should double every two days in a healthy early pregnancy. hCG appears in blood and urine within days of the embryo implanting and rises steeply through early pregnancy, which is why home tests become reliable from around the first day of a missed period and some sensitive tests can turn positive a little earlier. The urine test is a widely used point-of-care test: a strip or stick is dipped into urine or held in the stream and shows a line, symbol or word when hCG is present. In hospital, a urine test is done routinely in women of reproductive age with abdominal pain, bleeding or collapse, and before X-rays, operations and certain medicines, because an unrecognised pregnancy, and above all an ectopic pregnancy, changes what happens next.

measures.meaning: Positive from around the first missed period; modern tests detect 20-25 IU/L. A qualitative result: it says whether hCG is present above the test's detection limit, not how much. First-morning urine is the most concentrated and gives the clearest result when testing early, although most tests work at any time of day once the period is late.

Quantitative; used to track ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage and molar pregnancy, and some tumours. A laboratory blood test can be qualitative (present or absent) or quantitative (the concentration), and serial quantitative results show whether a pregnancy is progressing normally, failing or abnormally sited; results take from a few hours to more than a day.

whyOrdered: A missed period, nausea, breast tenderness
Abdominal pain or bleeding in any woman of reproductive age (to exclude ectopic pregnancy)
Before X-rays, CT, surgery and many drugs
Monitoring after ectopic pregnancy or molar pregnancy treatment
Confirming pregnancy before booking antenatal care
Investigating a late period when the date of the expected period is uncertain
pregnancy-test.how: A drop of urine on a test strip, ideally first-morning; or a venous blood sample. For a home test the strip is dipped into a collected sample or passed through the urine stream, and read within the time stated in the instructions. The instructions matter: reading too early or too late, using too little urine or testing before the period is due are the usual reasons for a misleading result. A blood sample for quantitative hCG is sent to the laboratory and is usually repeated after an interval so the trend can be judged.
pregnancy-test.preparation: None; testing before the missed period risks a false negative. If the date of the expected period is unknown, NHS advice is to wait at least three weeks after the last unprotected sex before testing. Drinking large volumes beforehand dilutes the urine and can push an early positive below the detection limit.

interpretation.meaning: Pregnant, almost always, provided the instructions were followed; an ultrasound from 6 weeks locates the pregnancy

interpretation.finding: Negative urine test with a period still overdue
interpretation.meaning: Possibly tested too early or with dilute urine; repeat after a few days, and seek advice if a second test is negative and the period has still not started

interpretation.finding: Positive test with pain or bleeding
interpretation.meaning: Ectopic pregnancy must be excluded urgently
Failing or ectopic pregnancy

interpretation.finding: Serum hCG unusually high for dates
interpretation.meaning: Twins or a higher multiple, a molar pregnancy or wrong dates; ultrasound clarifies
Resolution of a miscarriage, ectopic or molar pregnancy; followed until it is undetectable

pregnancy-test.limitations: False negatives when tested too early or with very dilute urine; rare false positives from fertility drugs, some tumours and recent pregnancy loss. A positive result is more reliable than a negative one. Very rarely, extremely high hCG levels, as in a molar pregnancy or a multiple pregnancy, overwhelm a urine test and give a false negative. Some medicines can affect the result. The test confirms that hCG is present but cannot say where the pregnancy is or whether it is viable; that needs ultrasound and, where there is doubt, serial blood hCG.

ecg.name: Electrocardiogram
ecg.what: Ten sticky electrodes on the chest and limbs record the heart's electrical activity from twelve angles over ten seconds. The tracing shows rhythm, rate, the direction of electrical spread and signs of muscle strain, damage or blocked blood supply.

measures.meaning: Normal sinus rhythm 60-100 per minute; irregular with no P waves in atrial fibrillation.
Atrial activation and the delay at the AV node; a long PR is heart block.
Ventricular activation; wide when conduction is blocked in a bundle branch.
Repolarisation; ST elevation is the signature of an acute heart attack, ST depression of ischaemia or strain.
Total activation time; prolonged by drugs and electrolyte problems, risking dangerous rhythms.

whyOrdered: Chest pain (within 10 minutes of arrival)
Palpitations, blackouts, breathlessness
Screening before surgery or in athletes
Electrolyte problems and drug monitoring
Suspected pulmonary embolism, pericarditis, heart failure
ecg.how: Lie still for a minute while the machine prints; painless, no electricity goes into the body.
ecg.preparation: None; chest hair may be shaved for contact.

interpretation.finding: ST elevation in two adjacent leads
interpretation.meaning: STEMI: an artery is blocked, needs emergency angioplasty

interpretation.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves
interpretation.meaning: Atrial fibrillation
High potassium, needs immediate treatment
Reassuring but does not exclude a heart attack or intermittent rhythm problems

ecg.limitations: A ten-second snapshot: intermittent arrhythmias need longer monitoring, and a third of heart attacks have a normal first ECG.
ecg.specimen: None: a recording of the heart's electrical activity from skin electrodes
ecg.resultType: A tracing read for rate, rhythm, intervals and waveform changes, with an automated interpretation checked by a clinician

quick.sample: No sample; ten electrodes on the chest and limbs
quick.usedFor: Chest pain, palpitations, blackouts, rhythm problems, screening
quick.measures: The heart's electrical rhythm and conduction from twelve angles over ten seconds

components.name: Rate and rhythm
components.measures: How fast and how regularly the heart beats
components.high: Sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or flutter, supraventricular and ventricular tachycardias
components.low: Sinus bradycardia, heart block, sick sinus syndrome

components.name: P wave and PR interval
components.measures: Atrial activation and conduction through the AV node
components.high: Long PR: first-degree heart block

components.name: QRS complex
components.measures: Ventricular activation
components.high: Wide QRS: bundle branch block, ventricular rhythms, high potassium; tall complexes: hypertrophy; Q waves: old infarction
components.low: Small complexes: obesity, pericardial fluid, lung disease

components.name: ST segment and T wave
components.measures: Ventricular recovery; the part most changed by ischaemia
components.high: ST elevation: acute infarction (STEMI) or pericarditis; tall T waves: high potassium
components.low: ST depression and T inversion: ischaemia, strain, digoxin, low potassium

components.name: QT interval
components.measures: Total time for ventricular activation and recovery, corrected for heart rate
components.high: Long QT: inherited syndromes, many medicines, low potassium, magnesium or calcium; risk of dangerous rhythms
components.low: Short QT: rare inherited syndromes, high calcium

ecg.rangeNote: An ECG is interpreted against standard interval limits and waveform criteria rather than a laboratory range; the automated report on the machine is a starting point that a clinician confirms or overrules, ideally by comparison with a previous tracing.
factors: Electrode placement, movement, shivering and electrical interference
Body shape, lung disease and pericardial fluid change voltages
Electrolyte levels (potassium, calcium, magnesium) and many medicines
Heart rate, which changes the corrected QT
Timing: a tracing between episodes of an intermittent arrhythmia is often normal
cannotTell: Whether a heart attack has occurred when the first tracing is normal (a third of infarctions are); serial ECGs and troponin are needed
How well the heart pumps or whether the valves work (echocardiography)
Whether the coronary arteries are narrowed when the person is at rest (stress testing or angiography)
Intermittent rhythm problems that were not happening during the ten seconds recorded
ecg.medicinesNote: Many medicines prolong the QT interval (some antibiotics including macrolides, antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiemetics); digoxin, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers slow conduction; sodium channel blockers widen the QRS.

echocardiogram.name: Echocardiogram
echocardiogram.what: An ultrasound of the beating heart. It shows the size and thickness of the chambers, how strongly the ventricles pump, whether the valves open and close properly, and the pressures inside, all in real time and without radiation.

measures.meaning: The fraction of blood the left ventricle ejects each beat; 55% or more is normal, below 40% is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction.
Narrowing (stenosis) or leaking (regurgitation), graded by Doppler flow.
A segment that does not move marks scar from a previous heart attack.
Dilated in heart failure, thickened in high blood pressure and cardiomyopathy.
Fluid around the heart (effusion) and whether it compresses the chambers.

whyOrdered: Breathlessness or raised BNP (heart failure)
A murmur or suspected valve disease
After a heart attack
Atrial fibrillation, stroke (looking for a source of clots)
Suspected endocarditis, pericardial fluid, congenital heart disease
echocardiogram.how: Lying on the left side, a probe with gel is moved over the chest for 20-40 minutes. A transoesophageal echo passes a probe down the gullet for clearer views, with sedation.
echocardiogram.preparation: None for the standard test; fasting for the transoesophageal version.

interpretation.meaning: Significantly reduced pumping; start heart-failure treatment
Valve replacement when symptoms appear
Coronary disease with previous infarction
Makes reduced pumping function and significant valve disease unlikely at rest; if symptoms persist, further tests such as stress imaging or blood tests may be considered

echocardiogram.limitations: Image quality falls with obesity and lung disease. Coronary arteries themselves are not seen; a stress echo or angiogram is needed for that.

references.title: NICE NG106: Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management

echocardiogram.specimen: None: ultrasound images of the beating heart
echocardiogram.resultType: Measurements (ejection fraction, chamber sizes, wall thickness, valve gradients) with a structured report

quick.sample: No sample; a probe with gel on the chest, 20-40 minutes
quick.usedFor: Heart failure, murmurs and valve disease, after a heart attack, stroke work-up
quick.measures: Heart structure, pumping function, valve function and pressures in real time

components.name: Left ventricular ejection fraction
components.measures: Percentage of blood the left ventricle ejects each beat
components.high: Hyperdynamic states (sepsis, anaemia, thyrotoxicosis)
components.low: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, previous infarction, cardiomyopathy

components.name: Wall motion
components.measures: Whether each segment of muscle contracts normally
components.high: Not applicable
components.low: Regional abnormality: infarction or ischaemia in a coronary territory

components.name: Chamber size and wall thickness
components.measures: Dilatation or hypertrophy of the atria and ventricles
components.high: Dilated: heart failure, valve leaks, atrial fibrillation; thick walls: hypertension, aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

components.name: Valve function
components.measures: Narrowing (stenosis) or leaking (regurgitation) of each valve, graded by Doppler
components.high: Severe stenosis or regurgitation may need repair or replacement

components.name: Diastolic function and filling pressures
components.measures: How the ventricle relaxes and fills
components.high: Raised filling pressures: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, hypertension, older age

components.name: Pericardium and estimated pulmonary pressure
components.measures: Fluid around the heart; right-heart pressures
components.high: Pericardial effusion; pulmonary hypertension from lung disease, clots or left-heart disease

echocardiogram.rangeNote: Measurements are compared with published reference values adjusted for body size, age and sex, and graded (mild, moderate, severe) using society criteria; the report is a clinical interpretation, not a laboratory range.
factors: Image quality: obesity, lung disease and chest-wall shape limit the acoustic window (a transoesophageal echo or contrast may be needed)
Heart rate and rhythm at the time (atrial fibrillation makes measurements variable)
Blood pressure and fluid status on the day
Operator experience and machine settings
cannotTell: Whether the coronary arteries are narrowed (stress echo, CT or angiography)
The heart's electrical rhythm over time (ECG and monitoring)
The cause of breathlessness when the heart is normal
echocardiogram.medicinesNote: Heart-failure medicines can improve ejection fraction over months; beta blockers and rate control change measurements in atrial fibrillation; some chemotherapy (anthracyclines, trastuzumab) is monitored with serial echocardiograms.

stress-test.name: Cardiac stress test
stress-test.what: The heart is made to work hard, by treadmill or bicycle exercise or by a drug that mimics exercise, while its electrical activity, images or blood flow are recorded. A narrowed coronary artery that copes at rest fails under load, revealing itself as ECG change, a segment of muscle that stops moving, or a patch that does not take up tracer. The exercise ECG (exercise tolerance test) is the simplest version: it shows whether the heart muscle receives enough blood through the coronary arteries during physical activity and is used to investigate chest pain, palpitations, dizziness and breathlessness on exertion, to judge prognosis after a heart attack or angioplasty and to set a safe exercise level for cardiac rehabilitation. When a person cannot exercise adequately, a drug such as dobutamine or adenosine stresses the heart instead, and imaging with echocardiography, a radioactive tracer or MRI is added when a more accurate answer is needed than the ECG alone can give.

measures.meaning: ST depression, arrhythmia or a fall in blood pressure signal ischaemia. The ECG is watched continuously during exercise and for a recovery period afterwards, because changes can appear only as the heart rate comes down.

Minutes achieved and heart rate reached; a strong predictor of prognosis in itself. The test aims for a target heart rate calculated from age, and whether that target is reached determines how much a negative test can be trusted.
Chest pain, breathlessness, leg fatigue and the way blood pressure rises or falls with increasing work are recorded at each stage; a falling blood pressure with exertion is a warning sign.
A segment that moves at rest but not under stress marks a significant narrowing.
Reduced tracer uptake under stress that recovers at rest = reversible ischaemia; fixed defect = scar.

whyOrdered: Chest pain on exertion with an intermediate probability of coronary disease
Assessing how much a known narrowing matters
After a heart attack or angioplasty, before cardiac rehabilitation
Exercise-induced palpitations or blackouts
Setting a safe exercise level during cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack or heart surgery
Checking blood flow to the heart after coronary angioplasty
stress-test.how: Electrodes and blood pressure cuff on; the treadmill speeds up every three minutes until target heart rate, symptoms or ECG change. Imaging versions add ultrasound or a radioactive tracer. Electrodes are attached to the chest and shoulders and a resting ECG and blood pressure are taken first. The person then walks on the treadmill or pedals a static bicycle while the speed, incline or pedal resistance increases in stages; the blood pressure cuff inflates every few minutes and feels tight. Staff stop the test when the target heart rate is reached, if chest pain, worrying blood pressure changes or ECG signs of the heart muscle lacking oxygen appear, or if the person is too tired or has symptoms such as leg pain. The exercise itself usually lasts around a quarter of an hour; monitoring continues during recovery until the heart rate has returned towards baseline, and the whole appointment takes about an hour. The test is supervised by trained staff, and serious complications are rare, the most frequent being transient extra beats.
stress-test.preparation: Light meal only; comfortable shoes; some heart drugs (beta blockers) are paused on instruction. Loose clothing and trainers are worn, a heavy meal and caffeine are avoided for a few hours beforehand, and the person brings a list of their medicines; beta blockers may be stopped for a day or two before the test only if the doctor has said so, because they blunt the heart-rate response. Anyone who has taken a medicine for erectile dysfunction (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) in the previous day or two tells the team beforehand.

interpretation.finding: Marked ST depression early in exercise
interpretation.meaning: High-risk coronary disease; proceed to angiography

interpretation.finding: Good exercise capacity with no changes
interpretation.meaning: Low risk; significant disease unlikely

interpretation.finding: Test stopped before target heart rate without ECG change
interpretation.meaning: Inconclusive rather than negative; a pharmacological or imaging stress test, or CT coronary angiography, is considered
Supports angina as the cause of the person's exertional symptoms and guides anti-anginal treatment and further imaging

interpretation.finding: Fall in blood pressure or sustained arrhythmia with exercise
interpretation.meaning: A high-risk response; the test is stopped and early specialist assessment follows
Viable muscle with restricted supply, likely to benefit from revascularisation

stress-test.limitations: Exercise ECG alone misses a fifth of disease and gives false positives, especially in women and with abnormal resting ECGs; CT coronary angiography is now the first test in many guidelines. Its sensitivity and specificity are only moderate, so it works best in people with an intermediate likelihood of coronary disease: in those at low risk a positive result is more often false than true, and in those at high risk a negative result does not exclude disease. People who cannot walk or cycle hard enough to reach the target heart rate, because of arthritis, lung disease, frailty or beta blockers, produce inconclusive tests and need pharmacological stress instead. Heart size and abnormalities on the resting ECG also reduce the accuracy of the ECG changes. The test shows the functional consequence of narrowing, not the anatomy of the arteries, which needs CT or invasive angiography.

East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust: Exercise ECG test

holter-monitor.name: Ambulatory ECG monitoring
holter-monitor.what: A portable recorder worn for 24 hours to two weeks (or an implanted loop recorder for up to three years) that captures the heart's rhythm during normal life, catching the intermittent arrhythmias a ten-second ECG misses. Holter and event monitors are small, battery-powered electrocardiogram devices that record the heart's electrical activity continuously, or when triggered, while the person goes about their usual activities. The recording is used to diagnose an arrhythmia (an irregular heartbeat), to match symptoms such as palpitations, dizziness or blackouts to what the heart was doing at that moment, and to check whether treatment for a rhythm problem is working. A Holter monitor records every beat for one or more days; an event monitor is worn for longer and records when the wearer presses a button or when the device detects an abnormal rhythm; a loop recorder keeps overwriting its memory and saves the stretch around an event; and an implantable loop recorder sits under the skin of the chest for long-term monitoring.

measures.meaning: Every beat is recorded and analysed; runs of atrial fibrillation, pauses and extra beats are counted and timed, and the report tabulates how often each abnormality occurred over the whole recording.

The wearer presses a button or keeps a diary of activities and symptoms so that each symptom can be matched to the tracing at that moment; a symptom with a normal tracing is as informative as one with an arrhythmia.
Slowest and fastest rates, including during sleep and exercise, and how quickly the rate responds to activity.
Whether a rate-controlling drug, an ablation or a pacemaker is keeping the rhythm as intended, judged by how much arrhythmia remains on the recording.

whyOrdered: Palpitations that come and go
Unexplained blackouts or falls
Looking for atrial fibrillation after a stroke
Checking a pacemaker or drug treatment is controlling a rhythm
Suspected heart block
Matching intermittent symptoms such as dizziness or breathlessness to the heart rhythm at that moment
Measuring how much of the day a known arrhythmia is present (its burden) before and after treatment
holter-monitor.how: Three to five chest electrodes lead to a small recorder on a belt, or a single adhesive patch; normal activities continue except bathing. Small sticky electrode patches are placed on the chest and connected by thin wires to a battery-powered recorder worn in a pocket or in a pouch around the neck or waist. The wearer keeps a diary of what they were doing and how they felt, and presses the event button when symptoms occur. At the end of the period the device is returned to the clinic, where clinical staff analyse the recording, tabulate the rhythm findings and correlate any irregular activity with the diary entries. Event monitors and patch monitors are worn for days to weeks and send or store recordings when triggered. Implantable loop recorders are injected under the skin of the chest.
holter-monitor.preparation: None; keep a symptom diary of activities and how the person felt, and keep the recorder dry.

interpretation.meaning: Diagnosis made; consider anticoagulation and rate or rhythm control

interpretation.finding: Pause of more than 3 seconds with dizziness
interpretation.meaning: Symptomatic bradycardia; likely pacemaker
Palpitations are not due to an arrhythmia; reassuring
Silent atrial fibrillation or frequent extra beats found incidentally; significance depends on the burden and the person's other risks, and after a stroke it changes treatment

interpretation.finding: No symptoms and no arrhythmia during the recording
interpretation.meaning: Non-diagnostic rather than normal; if symptoms are infrequent a longer event or patch monitor, or an implantable recorder, is considered
The drug, ablation or device is not controlling the rhythm as intended; treatment is adjusted

holter-monitor.limitations: Only useful if symptoms occur during the recording; rare events need longer monitoring or an implanted device. A one- or two-day Holter recording detects only a small proportion of the intermittent atrial fibrillation that longer monitoring eventually finds, which is why extended event, patch or implantable monitoring is used after an unexplained stroke. With a conventional Holter recorder the analysis is retrospective, so the device itself does not warn the wearer or the clinic of a dangerous rhythm as it happens. Electrodes can irritate the skin and come loose, movement produces artefact that mimics arrhythmia, and the recorder must be kept dry, which limits bathing and swimming. The recording shows rhythm only: it does not measure blood pressure, oxygen or how the heart muscle is pumping.

spirometry.name: Spirometry
spirometry.what: A forced breath out into a tube measures how much air the lungs can move and how fast. It is the test that diagnoses and grades asthma and COPD by separating airways that are narrowed (obstruction) from lungs that are stiff or small (restriction). The spirometer records the volume of air exhaled against time, starting from a maximal breath in, and draws two curves from it: volume against time and flow against volume. From these come the volume blown out in the first second (FEV1), the total volume blown out (FVC) and their ratio, each compared with the value predicted for a person of the same age, sex, height and ethnic background. A result is compared with the normal range for that person: many laboratories use the lower limit of normal, while UK COPD guidance uses a fixed post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.7. Spirometry is also repeated after an inhaled bronchodilator to see whether the obstruction reverses, which helps separate asthma from COPD, and it is used to follow a known lung disease over time. The manoeuvre is standardised by the American Thoracic Society and European Respiratory Society, and the test is only as good as the effort and technique that go into it.

measures.meaning: The volume blown out in the first second; reduced when airways are narrowed. It is the main measure used to grade the severity of obstruction and to follow change over time.
Forced vital capacity, the total volume blown out; reduced when lungs are small or stiff, or when air is trapped behind narrowed airways.

In UK COPD guidance a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7, with typical symptoms, confirms airflow obstruction; many laboratories also report a lower limit of normal. A low ratio means air leaves the lungs slowly relative to their size; a normal or high ratio with a low FVC suggests restriction.

FEV1 rising by at least 12% and 200 mL after a bronchodilator supports asthma but is also seen in COPD; it is read with the history and other tests. The test is repeated after inhaling a bronchodilator and the change in FEV1 is measured.
The fastest flow, measured at home on a hand-held meter to track asthma control.
The shape of the curve of flow against volume helps distinguish an obstructive pattern from a restrictive one.

whyOrdered: Breathlessness, wheeze or chronic cough
Smokers over 35 with symptoms (COPD screening)
Asthma diagnosis and monitoring
Before lung or major surgery
Occupational lung disease surveillance
Measuring how well treatment is controlling a known lung disease, and detecting decline over time
Confirming or excluding an obstructive pattern before a COPD or asthma diagnosis is recorded
spirometry.how: Take the deepest breath possible and blast it out as hard and long as possible through a mouthpiece, repeated three times; 15-30 minutes with a bronchodilator test. The person sits upright with a nose clip on, seals their lips around the mouthpiece, fills the lungs completely and then empties them as forcefully and completely as they can while the operator coaches them to keep going. The manoeuvre is repeated until at least three technically acceptable blows have been obtained whose best values agree closely with each other, within a limited number of attempts, so that the result reflects the lungs rather than a poor effort. If reversibility is being tested, a bronchodilator is inhaled and the blows are repeated after a short wait. Results are reported as measured values, as a percentage of predicted and against the lower limit of normal, and they are interpreted with the clinical picture, never in isolation; depending on the findings, a chest X-ray, CT scan or a fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) test may follow.
spirometry.preparation: Avoid inhalers, big meals, alcohol and vigorous exercise before the test as instructed. The department advises which inhalers to withhold and for how long so that reversibility can be assessed, and the person's height, age and sex are recorded accurately because the predicted values depend on them.

interpretation.meaning: COPD; severity graded by FEV1 as % predicted
Supports asthma
Restrictive pattern: fibrosis, chest wall or muscle disease, obesity; full lung function tests next
Does not exclude asthma, which varies over time; peak-flow diary, FeNO or repeat testing when symptomatic is used instead
The result cannot be interpreted; the test is repeated with coaching or referred to a specialist laboratory
Progression of the lung disease or poor control; prompts a review of treatment

spirometry.limitations: Depends on effort and technique; normal spirometry between attacks does not exclude asthma. Not safe soon after a heart attack, eye surgery or pneumothorax. Results are compared with reference values derived from populations, so the choice of reference equations and the handling of ethnicity affect who is labelled abnormal, and predicted values are less reliable at the extremes of age and height. Spirometry cannot measure the air left in the lungs after a full breath out or how well gas crosses into the blood, so a restrictive pattern needs full lung function tests to confirm, and it cannot by itself establish the cause of an obstructive pattern. Poor-quality tests are common when operators are not trained and quality-assured, and over-reading them leads to misdiagnosis in both directions.

references.title: NCBI PMC: Pulmonary function tests – easy interpretation in three steps

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

pulmonary-function-tests.name: Full pulmonary function tests
pulmonary-function-tests.what: Spirometry plus measurements it cannot make: the total volume of the lungs including the air that cannot be blown out, and how easily gas crosses from the air sacs into blood (gas transfer, DLCO). Together they classify almost any lung disease. Spirometry shows how much air can be moved and how fast, but it cannot see the air left in the chest after a full breath out, and it says nothing about whether oxygen is getting from the alveoli into the blood. Full pulmonary function tests add a lung-volume measurement, by body plethysmography in a sealed cabin or by breathing a harmless tracer gas that is diluted by the air in the lungs, and a gas-transfer test in which a very low concentration of carbon monoxide is inhaled, held for a few seconds and exhaled so the amount taken up by the blood can be calculated. The results are compared with values predicted for the person's age, sex and height, and the pattern across all three parts (airflow, volumes and transfer) distinguishes airway disease from disease of the lung tissue, the blood vessels, the chest wall or the breathing muscles.

measures.item: Total lung capacity and residual volume
measures.meaning: Measured in a sealed booth (plethysmography) or by gas dilution; high in emphysema (air trapping), low in fibrosis. Total lung capacity is the volume in the lungs after the fullest possible breath in; residual volume is what remains after the fullest breath out and can only be measured indirectly, which is why spirometry alone cannot confirm a restrictive defect.

How much of a trace of carbon monoxide crosses into blood in one breath; reduced in emphysema, fibrosis and pulmonary vascular disease, raised in lung bleeding. Carbon monoxide is used because it diffuses rapidly and binds tightly to haemoglobin, so the amount that disappears from the exhaled breath reflects the surface area and thickness of the alveolar-capillary membrane and the blood available to take it up.
The shape reveals upper airway obstruction and the site of narrowing.
For suspected neuromuscular weakness.
A six-minute walk test or similar measures how far the person can walk and how their oxygen saturation and breathlessness change with effort, adding a functional measure to the laboratory numbers.

whyOrdered: Unexplained breathlessness with normal spirometry
Interstitial lung disease and sarcoidosis
Assessing fitness for lung resection or chemotherapy (bleomycin)
Neuromuscular disease affecting breathing
Grading emphysema
Separating airway disease from disease of the lung tissue, chest wall or breathing muscles when spirometry shows a restrictive pattern
Monitoring the response of a lung disease to treatment over time
pulmonary-function-tests.how: Sitting in a clear booth breathing through a mouthpiece with a nose clip through a series of manoeuvres, about an hour. For lung volumes by plethysmography the person sits in a sealed, transparent cabin resembling a telephone box and breathes against a mouthpiece; as the chest moves, the pressure changes in the cabin and at the mouth are used to calculate the volume of gas in the chest. The dilution alternative has the person breathe a known quantity of an inert tracer gas from the machine until it mixes evenly with the air in the lungs. For gas transfer the person breathes out fully, takes a single deep breath of the test gas containing a very low concentration of carbon monoxide, holds it for a few seconds and breathes out; the exhaled gas is analysed and compared with what was inhaled. Spirometry, often with a bronchodilator, is repeated in the same session, and the operator coaches each manoeuvre and repeats it until the results are consistent.
pulmonary-function-tests.preparation: As for spirometry; avoid smoking for 24 hours because carbon monoxide affects gas transfer. Inhalers, a heavy meal, alcohol and vigorous exercise are avoided beforehand as instructed, and a recent haemoglobin result is helpful because anaemia lowers gas transfer.

interpretation.finding: Obstruction with high residual volume and low DLCO
interpretation.meaning: Emphysema
Asthma or chronic bronchitis without emphysema; the airways are narrowed but the gas-exchanging tissue is intact
Pulmonary fibrosis or other interstitial disease
Chest wall, obesity or muscle weakness rather than lung parenchyma
Pulmonary vascular disease, early fibrosis, anaemia

interpretation.finding: Normal full lung function with persistent breathlessness
interpretation.meaning: Points away from the lungs towards the heart, deconditioning, anaemia or other causes; exercise testing may follow

pulmonary-function-tests.limitations: Anaemia lowers DLCO; results are compared with predicted values that depend on age, sex, height and ethnicity. Lung function results alone cannot name the disease: they describe a pattern (obstructive, restrictive, mixed, impaired transfer) that must be combined with the history, examination and imaging. All the manoeuvres depend on the person's understanding, effort and ability to hold their breath, so frail or very breathless people and young children may not produce valid results. Smoking shortly before the test, carbon monoxide exposure and a recent lung bleed alter gas transfer. Full tests need a hospital laboratory and take considerably longer than spirometry.

Asthma + Lung UK: Lung volume test (body plethysmography)
Royal Brompton and Harefield Hospitals (Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust): Lung function tests
