pulse-oximetry.name: Pulse oximetry and blood gases
pulse-oximetry.what: A clip on the fingertip shines red and infrared light through the tissue and reads the colour of pulsing blood to estimate how saturated haemoglobin is with oxygen. When more precision or a carbon dioxide level is needed, an arterial blood gas takes blood directly from an artery. Pulse oximetry is painless, takes seconds and can be done anywhere: in a GP surgery, clinic, ambulance, hospital ward or at home, which made it useful for remote monitoring during the COVID-19 pandemic. It is part of routine observations in hospital, and it is used to decide whether a person needs oxygen, to check that oxygen therapy or a lung medicine is working, to monitor breathing before, during and after surgery and sedation, and overnight to screen for sleep apnoea. The reading, SpO2, is an estimate of arterial oxygen saturation; it is not the same as the oxygen content of the blood or the adequacy of breathing, and it does not measure carbon dioxide.

measures.meaning: 95-100% normal in healthy adults; 88-92% is the target in people with COPD who retain carbon dioxide. The percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen, estimated from the ratio of red to infrared light absorbed by pulsing arterial blood. People with long-term lung disease may run a lower baseline even when well, so their usual reading, agreed with their clinician, is the comparison that matters. Oxygen can be low without any feeling of breathlessness.
The pressure of dissolved oxygen; below 8 kPa on air defines respiratory failure.
High when ventilation is inadequate (type 2 respiratory failure); low with hyperventilation.
Acid-base status: respiratory or metabolic acidosis and alkalosis.
Rises when tissues are starved of oxygen; a key sepsis marker.
The oximeter also displays the pulse detected at the fingertip; a steady, clearly detected pulse signal is a check that the saturation reading can be trusted.

whyOrdered: Any breathless or unwell patient (oximetry is a vital sign)
Pneumonia, COVID-19, asthma attacks, COPD flares
Monitoring oxygen therapy and ventilation
Suspected sepsis, diabetic ketoacidosis, poisoning (blood gas)
Sleep apnoea screening overnight
Home monitoring of people with COVID-19 or other acute respiratory illness who are well enough to stay at home
Checking that a lung medicine or oxygen therapy is delivering the intended effect
Before, during and after surgery and sedation
pulse-oximetry.how: The probe reads within seconds; a blood gas needs a needle in the radial artery at the wrist, which stings briefly, with pressure afterwards. For an accurate oximetry reading the person rests for a few minutes beforehand, sits with the hand warm and relaxed, and the clip is placed on a finger free of nail varnish or false nails; the number is recorded once it has stopped changing for several seconds. Home monitoring programmes ask people to take readings at set times and to write them down with their pulse and how they feel, with clear instructions on which readings should prompt a call for help. Devices sold for home use should carry a CE, UKCA or CE UKNI mark.
pulse-oximetry.preparation: Warm hands and remove nail varnish or false nails for oximetry; rest for at least five minutes before taking a home reading.

interpretation.meaning: Low oxygen saturation: needs urgent assessment; clinicians give oxygen to a target range, which is lower (88 to 92%) for people at risk of carbon dioxide retention

interpretation.finding: Reading lower than the person's usual baseline
interpretation.meaning: Deterioration in someone with chronic lung disease even if the absolute number is one others would tolerate; compared with the target range agreed with their clinician
Collapse, confusion, new drowsiness or marked breathlessness need urgent care regardless of the number; the oximeter does not measure carbon dioxide or how hard the person is working to breathe

interpretation.finding: Erratic reading with a poor pulse signal
interpretation.meaning: Cold hands, movement, poor circulation or a loose probe; warm the hand, keep still and repeat before acting on the value
Acute type 2 respiratory failure; may need ventilatory support

interpretation.finding: Low pH, low bicarbonate, high lactate
interpretation.meaning: Metabolic acidosis from sepsis or poor perfusion

pulse-oximetry.limitations: Oximetry misreads with cold hands, poor circulation, nail varnish, movement, carbon monoxide poisoning and, to a degree, darker skin; it says nothing about carbon dioxide. A normal saturation does not mean breathing is adequate: a person can maintain their oxygen level by breathing hard until they tire, and someone retaining carbon dioxide may have a reassuring saturation while becoming drowsy. A weak pulse signal corrupts the reading, and the device estimates saturation rather than measuring oxygen directly, so when the result will change management or a carbon dioxide level is needed, an arterial blood gas is taken. Home readings are only as good as the technique and the device, which is why rest, warm hands, no nail varnish and a certified oximeter are stressed.

endoscopy.name: Endoscopy (as a test)
endoscopy.what: A flexible or rigid tube with a light and camera passed into a body cavity through a natural opening or a small cut, so the lining can be seen directly and sampled. Each region has its own scope: the gullet and stomach (gastroscopy), the large bowel (colonoscopy and the shorter sigmoidoscopy), the airways (bronchoscopy), the bladder and urethra (cystoscopy, with ureteroscopy for the ureters), joints (arthroscopy), the abdomen and pelvis (laparoscopy), the womb (hysteroscopy), the cervix (colposcopy) and the nose and sinuses (nasal endoscopy). As a test, endoscopy is used to find the cause of symptoms such as stomach pain, indigestion, difficulty swallowing or bleeding, to take tissue samples and, at the same sitting, to treat what is found, for example by stopping bleeding or removing small growths. It is almost always a day-case procedure in a dedicated endoscopy unit.

measures.meaning: Inflammation, ulcers, bleeding, polyps, narrowings and tumours are seen and photographed; the operator records the site, size and appearance of each finding so it can be followed up or compared later.

Tiny samples taken painlessly from the lining with forceps passed through the scope, sent for microscopy; biopsies can bleed a little, which usually stops on its own and otherwise is treated through the scope.
Polyps removed, bleeding stopped, narrowings stretched, stones retrieved at the same sitting, avoiding a separate operation in many cases.

whyOrdered: Difficulty swallowing, persistent indigestion, vomiting blood, weight loss (gastroscopy)
Bleeding from the bowel, change in bowel habit, positive stool screening test, anaemia (colonoscopy)
Coughing blood, a shadow on a chest scan (bronchoscopy)
Blood in the urine (cystoscopy)
Surveillance of Barrett oesophagus, ulcerative colitis, polyps
Taking tissue samples from the lining to confirm or exclude cancer or inflammatory disease
Treating a problem already found: stopping bleeding, removing polyps or stretching a narrowing
endoscopy.how: Usually a day case with throat spray or sedation; 10-45 minutes depending on the scope, and a transnasal gastroscopy with a very thin scope can take only a few minutes. Sedation makes the person drowsy and relaxed but not unconscious, so they can still hear what is happening; a trained endoscopy nurse monitors breathing, heart rate and blood pressure throughout because sedatives can depress them briefly. Afterwards the person rests in a recovery area for an hour or two until the sedation wears off before going home. A sore throat or nose, bloating, wind and mild abdominal discomfort are common for a day and settle on their own. Full details of each examination are on its procedure page.
endoscopy.preparation: Fasting for upper scopes, because food in the stomach obscures the view and can be inhaled under sedation; the unit's instructions on when to stop eating and drinking must be followed or the test may be cancelled. Bowel preparation laxatives and a low-residue diet for colonoscopy and capsule endoscopy. The team is told about all medicines, including over-the-counter products and supplements, and about allergies; anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs may need to be paused on the unit's instructions, never stopped without advice. Consent is taken after the risks have been explained.

interpretation.meaning: No structural cause found in the part examined; symptoms are then attributed to functional disorders, reflux without visible damage or disease outside the reach of the scope, and other tests may follow
Biopsies establish the cause (acid, infection, inflammatory bowel disease); an ulcer with a visible vessel has a high re-bleeding risk and is treated endoscopically
Surveillance interval set by number and size of the polyps
Staging scans and multidisciplinary team planning
Benign scarring or a tumour; biopsied and, if appropriate, stretched or stented at the same or a later sitting

endoscopy.limitations: Invasive, with small risks of bleeding and perforation (a tear in the wall) that are much lower than for open surgery but can need admission or an operation; sedation can transiently affect breathing and blood pressure, which is why monitoring is continuous. The small bowel is mostly out of reach of standard scopes (capsule endoscopy and enteroscopy cover it), and the view depends on preparation: a poorly cleared bowel or a stomach containing food can hide lesions and force a repeat. Endoscopy shows the surface of the lining; disease in the wall or outside the organ needs imaging. Abdominal pain, black or dark stools, vomiting or fever after the procedure are reasons to contact the unit promptly.

references.title: University Hospitals of Morecambe Bay NHS Foundation Trust: Endoscopy – having a gastroscopy

biopsy.name: Biopsy
biopsy.what: Removal of a small piece of tissue or a few cells so a pathologist can examine them under the microscope. It is the only way to prove most cancers and many inflammatory diseases, and it grades and types a tumour so that treatment can be planned. A biopsy is usually arranged when imaging, blood tests or a screening test have found something that cannot be explained without looking at the tissue itself: a lump, a shadow, abnormal cells or an inflamed organ. It is almost always done in hospital, most often as a day case under local anaesthetic, and the sample goes to a pathology laboratory where it is processed and examined under the microscope by a pathologist.

measures.meaning: The architecture of the tissue: normal, inflamed, precancerous or malignant, and which type. A normal result means the tissue looks healthy; an abnormal result means the cells or tissue have an unusual structure, shape, size or condition, which may be cancer or another disease depending on the site and the question asked.
How abnormal the cells look compared with the normal tissue they came from, which predicts how aggressively a cancer is likely to behave and helps decide how intensively it is treated.

Protein and gene tests on the sample (HER2, EGFR, PD-L1) that decide targeted treatment. A core or surgical sample gives more tissue for these tests than a fine-needle aspirate, which can show that cells are malignant but may not be able to name the exact type or subtype.
For excision biopsies, whether abnormal tissue reaches the edge of what was removed; a clear margin suggests the lesion has been taken out completely.
Whether enough representative tissue was obtained. A fine-needle sample sometimes contains too few cells to answer the question, and the report says so rather than guessing.

whyOrdered: A lump, mass or shadow on imaging
Abnormal cells on a screening test
Unexplained organ inflammation (liver, kidney, muscle, skin)
Staging lymph nodes
Monitoring transplant rejection
Working out what is causing a symptom when imaging and blood tests cannot explain it
Confirming or excluding infection such as tuberculosis in tissue or the lining of the lung
biopsy.how: Depends on the site. Needle biopsies pass a hollow needle through the skin into the area, usually with ultrasound, CT or MRI guidance so the needle lands exactly on the target: a fine-needle aspiration uses a thin needle on a syringe to draw off a small number of cells from organs or lumps under the skin, while a core biopsy uses a wider spring-loaded needle to cut out slivers of tissue, which gives the pathologist more to work with. Skin lesions are sampled with a punch or shave that removes the top layers. During an endoscopy, small cutting forceps passed through the scope take samples from the lining of the gut, airway or bladder. An excision biopsy removes a whole lump or area surgically. Most biopsies are done awake under local anaesthetic, sometimes with sedation; some, particularly in children or deep organs, use a general anaesthetic. The procedure itself is often well under an hour. People commonly feel the sting of the anaesthetic injection, pressure as the sample is taken and a loud click from a spring-loaded needle. After sedation or general anaesthetic a period of observation follows, but most people go home the same day. Soreness and bruising at the site are common and settle within about a week. The sample is examined by a pathologist under the microscope, with extra stains or molecular tests as needed; results commonly take from several days to a few weeks depending on the hospital and the tests required, and are discussed with the person by the team that requested them.
biopsy.preparation: The team explains which regular medicines to continue. Blood tests may be taken beforehand to check bleeding risk, and anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs may need to be paused for several days; clotting is checked before liver and kidney biopsies. Fasting for a few hours is often requested, particularly if sedation or a general anaesthetic is planned, although clear fluids are usually allowed. A consent form is signed after the risks have been explained. Afterwards the dressing is kept clean and dry and strenuous exercise is avoided for a day or so.

interpretation.meaning: No cancer; the tissue may still explain the symptoms by showing inflammation, infection or a non-cancerous growth, and the report usually names the specific benign process
Precancerous change in the cells; treated or kept under surveillance depending on its degree and the site
Cancer confirmed; the type, grade and marker results feed into staging with imaging and a multidisciplinary team discussion that plans treatment
Cells or tissue with an unusual structure, shape or size that point to a disease other than cancer, such as an inflammatory, infective or metabolic process; the meaning depends on the organ sampled
Too little tissue or too few cells to answer the question, most often after a fine-needle sample; repeated with a wider needle, an image-guided core or a surgical biopsy

biopsy.limitations: A biopsy samples a tiny fraction of an organ and can miss a lesion that lies a few millimetres away, so a benign result from a needle sample is weighed against how suspicious the imaging looks and may be followed by repeat or surgical sampling. Fine-needle aspirates can confirm malignancy but may not identify the exact cancer type, which matters for planning treatment. Results take time, because tissue must be processed before it can be read, and further marker tests add to the wait. The main risks are infection at the site and bleeding, which is why clotting is checked and blood thinners are paused for deep organs; a lung biopsy carries a small risk of a collapsed lung (pneumothorax).

genetic-testing.name: Genetic testing
genetic-testing.what: Reading part or all of a person's DNA (from blood or saliva) or a tumour's DNA (from a biopsy) to find variants that cause disease, raise risk, or predict which drug will work. Modern sequencing panels test hundreds of genes at once. In the NHS, genetic (or genomic) testing is used mainly to find gene changes behind rare inherited conditions and some cancers: to diagnose a rare condition in a child, to show whether someone has a higher risk of certain conditions, and to guide the choice of treatment or medicine. Tests range from a chromosome study that checks the number and structure of whole chromosomes, through a single-gene test when a particular disorder is suspected, to whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing when it is unclear which gene might be responsible. Testing is free on the NHS when it is requested by a hospital specialist, and it is offered with genetic counselling because the result can affect relatives as well as the person tested.

measures.meaning: Confirms a suspected inherited condition (cystic fibrosis, Huntington disease, familial hypercholesterolaemia). A single gene is sequenced when the diagnosis is clear from the symptoms; a panel or whole-genome test is used when several genes could be responsible.

Finds high-risk variants before disease appears (BRCA1/2 for breast and ovarian cancer, Lynch syndrome for bowel cancer). A positive predictive result shows raised risk but usually cannot say exactly how likely, or when, the disease will develop.
Mutations in the cancer itself (EGFR, ALK, KRAS in lung cancer) that match targeted drugs. These are acquired changes in the tumour, not inherited ones, and are tested on the existing biopsy.
Variants that change how drugs are handled (DPYD before fluorouracil, HLA-B*57:01 before abacavir), so that a dose can be adjusted or a drug avoided.

Carrier testing shows whether a healthy person carries a variant that could be passed to children; prenatal testing looks for genetic conditions in a fetus; newborn screening picks up treatable inherited conditions soon after birth.

whyOrdered: A family history of cancer at young ages or in several relatives
A child with developmental problems or an unexplained syndrome
Choosing targeted cancer treatment
Planning a pregnancy in carriers of recessive conditions
Sudden cardiac death in a young relative
Checking whether a healthy person carries a variant that could be passed on (carrier testing), and newborn screening for treatable inherited conditions
Confirming a genetic cause when a condition is already suspected clinically, so that the right screening and treatment can be planned
genetic-testing.how: A routine blood sample is usual; saliva or a cheek swab (buccal smear), hair, skin, amniotic fluid or other tissue can also be used, and tumour testing uses the existing biopsy. The laboratory looks for specific changes in chromosomes, DNA or proteins according to the question asked: sequencing reads the letters of a gene or of the whole genome, chromosome tests look for large gains, losses or rearrangements, and protein or enzyme tests infer a gene change from its effect. Because many thousands of variants must be interpreted, results take weeks and sometimes months; NHS laboratories quote a range of several weeks to a few months for most tests, with longer waits for complex genome analyses. The written report goes to the referring clinician, who explains it to the person; stored data can be reanalysed later if new gene-disease links are discovered. Direct-to-consumer kits that use a saliva sample are also sold; a worrying result from one of these is usually discussed with a doctor or genetic counsellor, who may arrange confirmatory testing.
genetic-testing.preparation: Counselling before predictive tests, because results affect relatives and insurance in some countries. A genetic counsellor or clinician explains what the test can and cannot show, the chance of an uncertain result, how the information will be shared with family members and that the result may affect life or medical insurance; a consent form records the decision. No fasting or other physical preparation is needed for a blood or saliva sample.

interpretation.finding: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant found
interpretation.meaning: Diagnosis confirmed or high risk established; usually, though not always, this explains the condition. Cascade testing is offered to relatives and the result may guide screening, treatment or family planning
A DNA change not yet known to cause or not cause disease; cannot be used for diagnosis or to change management, but may be reclassified as evidence accumulates
Lowers but does not abolish the chance of a genetic cause; the test only reads the genes on the panel, and other genomic tests or reanalysis may be possible in future. Relatives may still carry risk

interpretation.finding: Positive predictive result in a healthy person
interpretation.meaning: Raised lifetime risk of the condition, but the test usually cannot give the exact risk or the age at which disease might start; surveillance or risk-reducing options are discussed
The person is healthy but could pass the variant on; testing of a partner and reproductive options are discussed

genetic-testing.limitations: Most common diseases are polygenic and environmental, so a single gene test says little; incidental findings and implications for family members need careful counselling. Everyone carries many harmless gene changes, so the difficulty lies in interpretation: variants of uncertain significance are common and cannot be acted on, a negative result does not exclude a genetic cause because only the genes tested are read, and even a confirmed diagnosis may say little about how severe the condition will be. Results take weeks to months. In some countries a result can affect insurance, and knowledge of risk cannot be undone, which is why counselling precedes predictive testing.

microbiology-tests.name: Microbiology tests
microbiology-tests.what: Tests that find the organism causing an infection: growing it on culture, detecting its genes by PCR, its proteins by antigen tests, or the antibodies the body makes against it. Culture also reports which antibiotics work. A culture test takes a sample from the site of suspected infection (blood, urine, sputum, a wound or throat swab, stool, spinal fluid or tissue) and places it in or on a nutrient medium that lets bacteria multiply until there are enough to identify. Once an organism grows, it is identified and exposed to a panel of antibiotics to see which stop it (susceptibility or sensitivity testing), which is what turns an empirical antibiotic choice into a targeted one. Molecular and antigen tests detect the organism directly, in hours rather than days, and serology shows the immune response to it. Microbiology results are read alongside the clinical picture, inflammatory markers and imaging, because the same organism may be a harmless coloniser in one person and the cause of sepsis in another.

measures.meaning: Two bottles from separate sites before antibiotics; growth is the first sign of possible bloodstream infection; the organism, growth in more than one set and the clinical picture decide whether it is real. The skin is cleaned with an antiseptic such as chlorhexidine before the needle goes in, because skin bacteria that fall into the bottle produce a false-positive result. Bacteria may be present in the blood only intermittently, so more than one set is often taken.
Throat, wound, genital and sputum samples cultured or tested by PCR; a Gram stain of the sample under the microscope gives an early clue to the type of bacteria before culture results are back.

Fast detection of viruses (COVID-19, influenza) and hard-to-grow bacteria; molecular panels can also identify the organism and some resistance genes directly from a positive blood-culture bottle within hours, well before conventional identification is complete.
Antibodies show past or current infection (hepatitis, HIV, glandular fever) and immunity after vaccination.
Bacteria, parasites and C. difficile toxin; faecal immunochemical test screens for bowel cancer.
For each organism grown, which antibiotics it is sensitive or resistant to, so that treatment can be narrowed to the most effective, least broad agent.

whyOrdered: Fever with no obvious source, rigors, suspected sepsis
Pneumonia, urinary infection, wound infection, meningitis
Diarrhoea lasting more than a few days or after travel
Screening for HIV, hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections
Outbreak control and infection prevention (MRSA screening)
Choosing or narrowing an antibiotic once the organism and its sensitivities are known
Checking that an infection has cleared after treatment
microbiology-tests.how: Samples taken with sterile technique, ideally before antibiotics; results from hours (PCR) to days (culture) or weeks (TB). In the laboratory the sample is placed in a dish or bottle containing a nutrient medium and incubated; most disease-causing bacteria grow enough to be tested within one to two days, but some species take much longer. After growth is detected, identifying the species and running antibiotic susceptibility tests adds a day or more, so a culture report usually arrives in stages: a Gram stain or early positive first, then the organism, then its sensitivities. Rapid molecular tests on positive blood-culture broth shorten this to hours in some laboratories. PCR and antigen tests are run on swabs or fluids and reported the same day.
microbiology-tests.preparation: None for most; clean-catch technique for urine, deep cough for sputum. Blood cultures are drawn with careful skin antisepsis, and the laboratory is told which antibiotics, if any, have already been given because they can stop organisms growing.

interpretation.finding: Two blood cultures grow the same organism
interpretation.meaning: True bacteraemia; find the source and treat for the right duration

interpretation.finding: Skin organism in one bottle only
interpretation.meaning: Probably contamination introduced at the time of sampling rather than infection
Antiviral treatment if early and at risk; isolation
Antibiotic changed to a sensitive agent; infection control alerted

Does not exclude infection, especially if antibiotics were given first, the organism is slow-growing or hard to culture, or the sample came from the wrong site; the clinical picture decides whether to continue treatment

interpretation.finding: Growth of a usual coloniser from a non-sterile site
interpretation.meaning: Skin, throat or gut flora on a swab may simply reflect normal carriage; treated only if the clinical picture indicates infection

microbiology-tests.limitations: Cultures are negative in a third of sepsis cases, especially after antibiotics; a positive result can mean colonisation rather than infection, and contamination of blood cultures by skin bacteria is a recognised problem that leads to unnecessary treatment unless the pattern of growth is read carefully. Conventional culture is slow, so initial treatment is almost always empirical and adjusted when results arrive. Some organisms (anaerobes, fungi, mycobacteria, many viruses) grow poorly or not at all in standard culture and need special media, prolonged incubation or molecular tests.

troponin.name: Troponin test
troponin.what: A blood test for cardiac troponin, a protein released when heart muscle cells are injured. It is the test that rules a heart attack in or out: with modern high-sensitivity assays, a value above the assay's upper limit and a rise or fall between two samples taken a few hours apart, read alongside the symptoms and the ECG, defines acute myocardial injury.

measures.meaning: Starts rising 1-3 hours after heart muscle injury, peaks at about 24 hours and can stay raised for one to two weeks. A change between serial samples separates an acute event from a stable, chronically raised level.

whyOrdered: Chest pain or other symptoms of a possible heart attack (on arrival and again after 1-3 hours)
Suspected myocarditis or pericarditis
Assessing heart injury in pulmonary embolism, sepsis and critical illness
After cardiac procedures, to detect procedure-related injury
Risk stratification in acute coronary syndromes
troponin.how: A venous blood sample; a second sample is timed from symptom onset or from arrival so that a rise or fall can be seen. Results are usually available within an hour in emergency departments.

interpretation.finding: Troponin above the assay's 99th percentile with a rise or fall between samples
interpretation.meaning: Acute myocardial injury; with symptoms of ischaemia, ECG change or imaging evidence it is classified as a myocardial infarction

interpretation.finding: Chronically raised, flat troponin on repeat samples
interpretation.meaning: Injury without an acute event: chronic kidney disease, heart failure, structural heart disease, older age

interpretation.finding: Very low or undetectable troponin hours after symptom onset
interpretation.meaning: Acute infarction is very unlikely; other causes of the symptoms are considered

interpretation.finding: Raised troponin with a clear non-cardiac illness
interpretation.meaning: Pulmonary embolism, sepsis, kidney failure, a very fast rhythm or extreme exertion can all release troponin

troponin.limitations: Troponin says that heart muscle was injured, not why: many conditions other than a blocked coronary artery raise it. A single sample taken too early can be normal, so the timing of the second sample matters. Each assay has its own reference limit, and results from different hospitals are not directly comparable.
troponin.resultType: Numeric, compared with the assay's 99th-percentile upper reference limit and with the previous sample

quick.sample: Blood from a vein, two samples a few hours apart
quick.usedFor: Suspected heart attack, heart muscle injury
quick.measures: Cardiac troponin I or T released from injured heart muscle

components.name: High-sensitivity troponin
components.measures: Cardiac troponin I or T in blood
components.high: Acute injury (rise or fall pattern) or chronic injury (stable level): infarction, myocarditis, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, kidney disease
components.low: A low level is expected; it makes acute infarction unlikely when the timing is right

troponin.rangeNote: There is no 'normal range' in the usual sense: each assay has its own 99th-percentile upper reference limit, often different for women and men, and the diagnosis rests on a change between samples rather than on a single number.

thresholds.name: Myocardial injury
thresholds.value: above the assay's 99th percentile upper reference limit
thresholds.context: Acute injury requires a rise and/or fall on serial samples; with evidence of ischaemia it is a myocardial infarction

factors: Time since symptom onset: sampling too early can miss the rise
Kidney function, which slows clearance
The assay used and its sex-specific limits
Very rarely, interfering antibodies in the sample
Recent strenuous exercise, cardioversion or cardiac procedures
cannotTell: Whether the injury was caused by a blocked coronary artery or by something else
Whether the heart's pumping function is reduced (that needs an echocardiogram)
Whether chest pain that started minutes ago is a heart attack, until the second sample
troponin.medicinesNote: Few medicines change troponin directly; cardiotoxic chemotherapy and some drugs that cause myocarditis can raise it.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

bnp.name: BNP and NT-proBNP test
bnp.what: A blood test for the natriuretic peptides the heart's ventricles release when they are stretched by high pressure or extra volume. It is the first test for suspected heart failure: a normal level makes heart failure unlikely, while a raised level in a breathless person calls for an echocardiogram and specialist assessment within a set time.

measures.meaning: Laboratories measure one or the other; they are not interchangeable and have separate thresholds. Both rise with ventricular wall stress from heart failure, valve disease, atrial fibrillation and pulmonary embolism.

whyOrdered: Breathlessness, ankle swelling or fatigue where heart failure is possible
Deciding how urgently a person needs echocardiography
Prognosis and monitoring of known heart failure
Assessing the heart in pulmonary embolism and sepsis
bnp.how: A venous blood sample; no special timing.

interpretation.finding: NT-proBNP below 400 ng/L (or BNP below 100 ng/L) in an untreated person
interpretation.meaning: Heart failure is unlikely; another cause of the symptoms is looked for
Heart failure possible: referral for echocardiography and specialist assessment within six weeks in UK guidance
High likelihood and worse prognosis: urgent referral within two weeks

interpretation.meaning: Obesity lowers natriuretic peptides and treatment changes them, so results are read with these in mind

bnp.limitations: Natriuretic peptides show that the heart is under strain, not why: kidney disease, older age, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism and sepsis all raise them, and obesity can lower them enough to mask heart failure. The test cannot describe the structure or pumping function of the heart; that is the echocardiogram's job.

crp.name: CRP test
crp.what: A blood test for C-reactive protein, a protein the liver releases within hours of significant inflammation, infection or tissue injury. It measures the size and course of an inflammatory response and how it changes with treatment, but not its cause. CRP is a general marker: it is often the first laboratory evidence that something inflammatory is happening, with the level rising before pain, fever or other signs are obvious, and its concentration can climb many hundred-fold during a severe infection. Because it falls quickly once the trigger settles, repeated measurements are more informative than a single value, and clinicians read it alongside the symptoms, the examination and other tests.

measures.meaning: Rises within about 6 hours of a trigger, peaks at about 48 hours and falls quickly once the trigger resolves. Levels in the hundreds suggest bacterial infection or major inflammation; mild elevations are common and non-specific. The protein is made by the liver as part of the acute-phase response, so it reflects the whole-body inflammatory signal rather than any one organ. It is also raised after a heart attack, after surgery and in sepsis, and a high-sensitivity version of the assay (hs-CRP) picks up the very low-grade inflammation linked to cardiovascular risk. Laboratories report in different units, so the reference limit printed on the report is the one to use.

whyOrdered: Suspected infection or sepsis, and monitoring the response to antibiotics
Distinguishing inflammatory joint disease from wear-and-tear pain
Unexplained fever, weight loss or fatigue
Monitoring rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, polymyalgia and vasculitis
After surgery, where a rising level can signal a complication
Deciding whether a respiratory infection in primary care is likely to need antibiotics (point-of-care CRP)
Estimating cardiovascular risk with a high-sensitivity assay in selected people
crp.how: A venous blood sample, measured in the laboratory by an immunoassay such as nephelometry or turbidimetry. Point-of-care fingerprick CRP, read on a small device in the consulting room, is used in some primary-care settings to help decide whether an infection is likely to be bacterial and whether antibiotics are needed.

interpretation.meaning: Significant bacterial infection or major inflammation until proven otherwise; the source is sought with examination, imaging and cultures
Minor inflammation, viral illness, obesity, smoking or recent exertion; interpreted with the clinical picture and often repeated rather than acted on

interpretation.finding: Normal CRP with a high ESR
interpretation.meaning: Consider conditions that raise ESR without much CRP: myeloma, lupus, anaemia, pregnancy
The inflammation is settling or the antibiotic is working; a persistently rising value after surgery prompts a search for infection or a leak

interpretation.finding: Raised CRP in a long-term inflammatory disease
interpretation.meaning: A flare of rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis, lupus or inflammatory bowel disease, or an intercurrent infection; a fall after a change of treatment shows the anti-inflammatory therapy is taking effect

interpretation.finding: Normal CRP very early in an illness
interpretation.meaning: Does not exclude infection, because the level takes hours to rise; a repeat sample the next day is often more informative

crp.limitations: Non-specific: it cannot say where the inflammation is or what is causing it, and it is not diagnostic of any single disease. A normal CRP early in an illness does not exclude infection, and some infections (viral, some fungal) and lupus flares barely raise it. Steroids and immunosuppressants blunt the rise. Although CRP is often used to help separate bacterial from viral infection, the overlap between the two is considerable, so it supports rather than replaces clinical judgement. Different laboratories and point-of-care devices use different methods and units, so results from different sources are not directly interchangeable.

esr.name: ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate)
esr.what: An old but still useful test that measures how far red blood cells settle in a narrow tube in one hour. Inflammatory proteins such as fibrinogen and immunoglobulins make red cells stack and sink faster, so the ESR rises with inflammation, infection and some blood disorders, more slowly and less specifically than CRP. The mechanism is physical rather than chemical: changes in the composition of plasma reduce the electrical charge that normally keeps red cells apart, so they aggregate into stacks (rouleaux) that are heavier than single cells and fall faster through the plasma. The classical Westergren method, in which anticoagulated blood stands in an upright graduated tube, remains the reference standard, and modern automated analysers are calibrated against it. The ESR is a non-specific indicator: it shows that inflammation is probably present and how it is changing over weeks, but it cannot say which disease is responsible, so it is always read alongside the history, examination, CRP and other tests.

measures.meaning: The distance in millimetres the red cells fall in an hour. Rises over days with inflammation and falls over weeks after it resolves; also raised by anaemia, pregnancy, older age and high immunoglobulin levels. Because the result reflects plasma protein composition and the red cells themselves, reference limits differ between women and men and increase with age, and each laboratory publishes its own.

whyOrdered: Suspected temporal (giant cell) arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica, where it is part of the diagnostic picture
Monitoring rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and other long-term inflammatory diseases
Suspected myeloma and other conditions that raise immunoglobulins
Unexplained symptoms where inflammation is one possibility, alongside CRP
Monitoring vasculitis and other long-term inflammatory conditions over months, alongside CRP and symptoms
esr.how: A venous blood sample in an anticoagulant tube, tested within a few hours of collection because standing blood changes the result. In the Westergren method the blood is drawn up a long, narrow graduated tube that is left upright and undisturbed for one hour, and the height of clear plasma above the settled red cells is read in millimetres. Most laboratories now use automated analysers that reproduce the method on smaller volumes and report in the same units; these are validated against the manual Westergren test. The tube must be vertical and undisturbed, because tilting or vibration speeds settling and falsely raises the value.

interpretation.meaning: Giant cell arteritis, myeloma, serious infection or widespread cancer are among the causes considered
Active inflammation or infection; the CRP will have risen first and will fall first as the problem settles
Anaemia, pregnancy, kidney disease, lupus, myeloma or simply older age
Makes active inflammatory disease less likely but does not exclude it; the ESR is slow to rise and can be held down by red-cell abnormalities

interpretation.finding: ESR falling over weeks of treatment
interpretation.meaning: The inflammatory disease is coming under control; used to track rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis and other long-term conditions alongside symptoms
Polycythaemia, abnormally shaped red cells such as sickle cells, or a very high white-cell count interfere with settling and can mask inflammation

esr.limitations: The ESR is influenced by many things other than inflammation, including anaemia, red-cell shape, pregnancy, age, sex and immunoglobulin levels, and it changes slowly, lagging days behind the onset of inflammation and weeks behind its resolution. It is not specific to any disease: it indicates that an inflammatory process is probably present but cannot identify the cause, so an isolated raised ESR in a well person is a prompt for a careful history and examination rather than a diagnosis. Technical factors such as tube angle, temperature and delay before testing alter the result. CRP is preferred for tracking acute infection because it rises and falls faster; the ESR keeps a place in a few conditions and in long-term monitoring.

tsh.name: TSH test
tsh.what: The single most sensitive blood test of thyroid function: TSH from the pituitary rises when the thyroid is underactive and falls when it is overactive, often before the thyroid hormones themselves leave their reference range. It is the first-line screening test and the value used to adjust levothyroxine.

measures.meaning: The pituitary's signal to the thyroid. High TSH means the pituitary is pushing a failing thyroid (hypothyroidism); very low TSH means it is being suppressed by excess thyroid hormone (hyperthyroidism). Laboratories add free T4 automatically when TSH is abnormal.

whyOrdered: Tiredness, weight change, feeling cold or hot, palpitations, anxiety, constipation or low mood
A goitre, neck lump or family history of thyroid disease
Atrial fibrillation, high cholesterol, depression, infertility or menstrual change
Monitoring levothyroxine (6-8 weeks after a dose change, then yearly) or antithyroid drugs
Before and during pregnancy in women with thyroid disease; on amiodarone or lithium
tsh.how: A venous blood sample at any time of day; people on levothyroxine usually take the dose after the sample.
tsh.preparation: None; tell the laboratory about biotin supplements, which can interfere with the assay and are paused for two days before the test.

interpretation.finding: High TSH with low free T4
interpretation.meaning: Primary hypothyroidism (the thyroid itself is failing)

interpretation.finding: High TSH with normal free T4
interpretation.meaning: Subclinical hypothyroidism: often repeated after three months; treatment considered if TSH stays above 10 mU/L or with symptoms, pregnancy or planning pregnancy

interpretation.finding: Low TSH with high free T4 or T3
interpretation.meaning: Hyperthyroidism: Graves disease, toxic nodules or thyroiditis

interpretation.finding: Low TSH with low free T4
interpretation.meaning: Pituitary (secondary) hypothyroidism, severe non-thyroidal illness or recent over-treatment; TSH alone cannot be trusted here

tsh.limitations: TSH is unreliable when the pituitary is diseased, during and shortly after severe illness ('sick euthyroid'), in the first trimester of pregnancy and with some medicines; it takes about six weeks to settle after a levothyroxine dose change, so testing sooner misleads. A normal TSH does not exclude thyroid problems that involve antibodies or nodules.

ferritin.name: Ferritin test
ferritin.what: A blood test that estimates the body's iron stores by measuring ferritin, the protein that holds iron inside cells. It is the best single test for iron deficiency, the commonest cause of anaemia, and it also detects iron overload; because ferritin rises with inflammation, it is often read alongside CRP.

measures.meaning: Mirrors stored iron: low when stores are exhausted, high with iron overload but also with inflammation, infection, liver disease, alcohol and cancer.

whyOrdered: Anaemia, especially with small red cells (low MCV)
Tiredness, restless legs, hair loss or brittle nails where iron deficiency is suspected
Heavy periods, pregnancy, vegetarian or vegan diets, coeliac disease, after gastric surgery
Suspected haemochromatosis or iron overload from repeated transfusions
Monitoring iron treatment and, in chronic kidney disease and heart failure, iron status before intravenous iron
ferritin.how: A venous blood sample, often with a full blood count and sometimes transferrin saturation.
ferritin.preparation: None; a recent iron infusion or blood transfusion should be mentioned.

interpretation.meaning: Iron stores are depleted (iron deficiency), whether or not anaemia is present yet; the cause, often blood loss, is then looked for

interpretation.finding: Normal ferritin with raised CRP and anaemia
interpretation.meaning: Inflammation may be masking iron deficiency; transferrin saturation or a trial of iron helps decide
Iron overload (haemochromatosis, transfusions) or severe inflammation, liver disease, cancer or a haemophagocytic syndrome
Stores are being replenished; treatment usually continues for months after haemoglobin normalises

ferritin.limitations: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein: any inflammation, infection, liver disease or alcohol excess raises it and can hide a deficiency. It does not show why iron is low; in adults iron deficiency is a reason to look for a source of blood loss, particularly in the gut.

creatinine-egfr.name: Creatinine and eGFR
creatinine-egfr.what: The everyday measure of how well the kidneys filter. Creatinine, a waste product of muscle, builds up in blood as filtration falls; the laboratory converts it, with age and sex, into an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), the number used to stage chronic kidney disease, detect acute kidney injury and adjust the doses of many medicines.

measures.meaning: Produced steadily by muscle and cleared by the glomeruli; rises when filtration falls, but only after a substantial loss of function
Millilitres of blood filtered per minute, estimated from creatinine by the CKD-EPI equation and adjusted to a standard body size; below 60 for three months defines chronic kidney disease

whyOrdered: Screening people with diabetes, high blood pressure or cardiovascular disease
Before starting or adjusting medicines cleared by the kidney (metformin, DOACs, many antibiotics) and before contrast scans
Swelling, reduced urine, tiredness, nausea or confusion
Acute illness, dehydration, vomiting or diarrhoea, particularly in people on ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics or NSAIDs
Monitoring chronic kidney disease, lithium and nephrotoxic drugs
creatinine-egfr.how: A venous blood sample; usually reported together with urea and electrolytes, and paired with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio when kidney disease is being assessed.
creatinine-egfr.preparation: None; avoid a large meat meal and strenuous exercise the day before if the result matters for staging, and mention creatine supplements.

interpretation.finding: Creatinine rising over hours to days
interpretation.meaning: Acute kidney injury: dehydration, sepsis, obstruction or drugs; the eGFR is unreliable while the value is changing

interpretation.finding: eGFR below 60 on two tests at least 90 days apart
interpretation.meaning: Chronic kidney disease, staged G3a to G5 by the value and combined with the urine albumin category

interpretation.finding: eGFR 60-89 with no markers of kidney damage
interpretation.meaning: Not chronic kidney disease on its own; common with age

interpretation.finding: Small creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
interpretation.meaning: Expected; a rise above about 30% prompts review of the dose and a search for renal artery narrowing

creatinine-egfr.limitations: Creatinine depends on muscle mass, so eGFR overestimates function in frail people and underestimates it in the very muscular; the equation assumes a steady state and is inaccurate in pregnancy, at extremes of body size and in rapidly changing illness. About half of kidney function can be lost before creatinine leaves the reference interval. Cystatin C offers a second estimate when the creatinine-based one is doubtful.

prothrombin-time-inr.name: Prothrombin time and INR
prothrombin-time-inr.canonicalName: Prothrombin time and international normalised ratio
prothrombin-time-inr.what: The prothrombin time measures how many seconds plasma takes to clot once the tissue-factor pathway is triggered; the INR expresses that time as a ratio standardised across laboratories. It is the test that tunes the dose of warfarin and one of the quickest measures of how well the liver is making clotting factors.

measures.meaning: Seconds to clot after tissue factor and calcium are added to citrated plasma; depends on factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen, the factors warfarin and liver disease reduce.
The PT expressed as a standardised ratio so that a result means the same whichever laboratory or reagent produced it; the number used to dose warfarin.

Assessing the liver's synthetic function in liver disease
Unexplained bleeding or bruising, and before surgery or a biopsy
Suspected vitamin K deficiency or disseminated intravascular coagulation

prothrombin-time-inr.preparation: None. Tell the laboratory or clinic about all medicines, supplements and any recent change in diet, illness or alcohol intake, which change the result.

Anticoagulation is weaker than intended; a missed dose, a new medicine or a change in diet is looked for

prothrombin-time-inr.rangeNote: For someone taking warfarin the INR is read against the individual target range their prescriber has set, not against a population reference interval. In people not on anticoagulants the prothrombin time is read against the laboratory's own reference interval, which depends on the reagent used.

Vitamin K intake (green leafy vegetables) and supplements
Antibiotics, antifungals, amiodarone, some antiepileptics and many other interacting medicines
Acute illness, diarrhoea, alcohol binges and liver disease

Whether bleeding will happen at a given INR, which also depends on age, other medicines and the reason for anticoagulation

iron-studies.name: Iron studies
iron-studies.what: A group of blood tests that together describe how much iron the body has stored, how much is circulating and how much of the transport protein transferrin is carrying it. Ferritin reflects the stores, serum iron and transferrin saturation the supply in transit, and the pattern across them separates iron deficiency from the anaemia of chronic disease and from iron overload.

components.name: Transferrin saturation
components.measures: The percentage of transferrin's iron-binding sites occupied, calculated from serum iron and TIBC
components.high: Iron overload including haemochromatosis

whyOrdered: Anaemia, especially with small red cells (a low MCV)
Tiredness, restless legs, hair loss or brittle nails when iron deficiency is suspected
Suspected iron overload or haemochromatosis
Monitoring iron treatment or blood transfusions
Assessing iron status in kidney disease, heart failure and before surgery
iron-studies.how: A venous blood sample, ideally in the morning because serum iron varies through the day.
iron-studies.preparation: Fasting is sometimes requested. Iron tablets taken in the previous 24 hours raise the serum iron, so the laboratory may ask for them to be paused; say if you have had an iron infusion or transfusion recently.

interpretation.meaning: Iron deficiency; the cause (blood loss, poor intake or absorption, pregnancy) is then looked for

interpretation.finding: Low serum iron and transferrin saturation with normal or high ferritin
interpretation.meaning: Usually the anaemia of inflammation or chronic disease, in which iron is present but locked away; ferritin alone can mislead here

interpretation.finding: High transferrin saturation and high ferritin
interpretation.meaning: Possible iron overload; genetic testing for haemochromatosis may follow
Iron is not the explanation; B12, folate, kidney function, thalassaemia and other causes are considered

iron-studies.rangeNote: Each component is read against the interval supplied by the laboratory that ran the test. Ferritin behaves as an acute-phase protein, so a value in the reference interval does not exclude iron deficiency when inflammation is present.
factors: Inflammation, infection and liver disease, which raise ferritin whatever the iron stores
Time of day and recent meals or iron tablets, which change serum iron
Pregnancy and oestrogen-containing medicines, which raise transferrin
Recent transfusion or intravenous iron
cannotTell: The cause of iron deficiency: bleeding from the gut, heavy periods, diet and malabsorption need their own investigation
Whether anaemia is present, which is a haemoglobin question
Iron status with certainty during active inflammation, when ferritin is unreliable
iron-studies.limitations: No single component is definitive: ferritin rises with inflammation, serum iron swings through the day and with meals, and the pattern across the panel is what the clinician reads. Soluble transferrin receptor is used in some laboratories to separate iron deficiency from inflammation.
iron-studies.medicinesNote: Oral and intravenous iron raise the results; proton-pump inhibitors reduce iron absorption over time; oestrogens raise transferrin.

quick.sample: Blood from a vein, ideally in the morning
quick.usedFor: Investigating anaemia and iron deficiency, suspected iron overload, monitoring iron treatment
quick.measures: Ferritin, serum iron, total iron-binding capacity and transferrin saturation

iron-studies.resultType: Numeric panel read as a pattern

vitamin-b12-folate.name: Vitamin B12 and folate
vitamin-b12-folate.what: Two blood tests, usually ordered together, for the vitamins the bone marrow needs to make normal red cells and the nervous system needs to keep nerves working. Deficiency of either causes anaemia with large red cells; vitamin B12 deficiency can also damage nerves, sometimes before the blood count changes.

measures.meaning: The vitamin absorbed in the last part of the small intestine with the help of intrinsic factor from the stomach; low in pernicious anaemia, after gut surgery, in strict vegan diets and with some medicines.
The B vitamin from green vegetables and fortified foods; low with poor diet, alcohol excess, pregnancy, malabsorption and some medicines.

whyOrdered: Anaemia with large red cells (a high MCV)
Numbness, tingling, balance problems or memory change that could be B12 deficiency
Tiredness, a sore tongue or mouth ulcers
Long-term metformin or acid-suppressing treatment, which can lower B12
Before and during pregnancy planning, for folate
vitamin-b12-folate.preparation: None usually; the laboratory may ask for a fasting sample. Say if you take B12 or folic acid supplements, or have had a B12 injection, which mask deficiency.

interpretation.meaning: Deficiency, whose cause (pernicious anaemia, diet, absorption, medicines) is then sought; further tests such as intrinsic-factor antibodies may follow
An indeterminate zone in which symptoms, the blood count and sometimes additional markers decide whether treatment is given
Deficiency from diet, alcohol, malabsorption, pregnancy or a medicine; treated after B12 status is known, because folic acid alone can worsen the nerve damage of untreated B12 deficiency

interpretation.finding: Both normal with a high MCV
interpretation.meaning: Other causes of large red cells are considered: alcohol, liver disease, thyroid disease, some medicines, bone-marrow disorders

vitamin-b12-folate.rangeNote: Both vitamins are read against the interval supplied by the laboratory that ran the test; assays differ, and a borderline B12 result is interpreted with symptoms and the blood count rather than as a fixed cut-off.
factors: Supplements, injections and fortified foods, which raise the results
Metformin, proton-pump inhibitors and H2 blockers, which lower B12 over years
Pregnancy and oral contraceptives, which lower measured B12
Recent meals, which raise serum folate
Liver disease and some blood disorders, which raise B12 without reflecting stores
cannotTell: Whether nerve damage from B12 deficiency will recover
The cause of a low result without further tests
Tissue B12 status precisely: the blood level is an imperfect proxy
vitamin-b12-folate.limitations: Serum B12 has a wide indeterminate range and can be falsely normal in people with intrinsic-factor antibodies; serum folate reflects recent intake more than stores. Treatment is often started on clinical grounds when a result is borderline.
vitamin-b12-folate.medicinesNote: Metformin, proton-pump inhibitors, H2 blockers and colchicine can lower B12; methotrexate, some antiepileptics and trimethoprim interfere with folate.

quick.usedFor: Investigating anaemia with large red cells, nerve symptoms, and monitoring people on long-term metformin
quick.measures: The blood levels of vitamin B12 and folate

vitamin-b12-folate.resultType: Numeric, read against the laboratory's intervals with a borderline zone for B12

references.title: NHS: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia

components.name: Vitamin B12
components.measures: Serum cobalamin
components.high: Supplements, liver disease

components.name: Folate
components.measures: Serum (or red cell) folate
components.high: Supplements, recent meal

vitamin-d.name: Vitamin D test
vitamin-d.what: Measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the storage form the liver makes from vitamin D obtained from sunlight on skin and from food or supplements. It is the best single measure of vitamin D status and is used when bone pain, muscle weakness, osteoporosis, malabsorption or a low calcium make deficiency likely.

measures.meaning: The circulating storage form, reflecting weeks of sun exposure and intake; the kidney converts it to the active hormone that raises calcium absorption.

whyOrdered: Bone pain, muscle weakness or unexplained fatigue when deficiency is suspected
Osteoporosis, fractures and before starting bone treatments
Low calcium or a raised alkaline phosphatase or parathyroid hormone
Conditions that impair absorption: coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, after bariatric surgery
Chronic kidney disease and some other long-term conditions

interpretation.meaning: Levels at which bone softening (rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults) becomes likely; treatment with vitamin D is usually given
Below the level considered adequate for bone health; supplementation is often advised, particularly in groups at risk
Sufficient for bone health in most people
Usually from excess supplements; can cause a high calcium and is reviewed

vitamin-d.rangeNote: Vitamin D is read against widely used cut-offs for deficiency, insufficiency and adequacy that differ between countries and professional bodies, so the report states the ones used, not against a population reference interval. The laboratory reports the cut-offs it applies, and the assay method affects the value.
factors: Season and latitude: levels fall in winter and in people who cover their skin or stay indoors
Skin pigmentation, age and body weight
Supplements and fortified foods
Liver and kidney disease, which affect the conversion of vitamin D
The assay method, which changes results between laboratories
cannotTell: Bone density, which needs a DXA scan
Whether symptoms are caused by the deficiency, which is common and often coincidental
The active hormone level (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), a separate test used only in specific disorders
vitamin-d.limitations: Population screening is not recommended; the test is for people with symptoms or risk factors. Assays vary and the value moves with the seasons, so a single result is interpreted with the time of year and the person's circumstances.
vitamin-d.medicinesNote: Vitamin D supplements raise it; some antiepileptics, glucocorticoids, orlistat and cholestyramine lower it.

quick.usedFor: Suspected vitamin D deficiency, bone disease, malabsorption, before bone treatments
quick.measures: 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the storage form of vitamin D

vitamin-d.resultType: Numeric, read against deficiency and adequacy cut-offs

references.title: NICE TA464: Bisphosphonates for treating osteoporosis

components.name: 25-hydroxyvitamin D
components.measures: The storage form of vitamin D
components.high: Excess supplements
components.low: Little sunlight, low intake, malabsorption, kidney or liver disease

hepatitis-b-serology.name: Hepatitis B tests
hepatitis-b-serology.what: A set of blood tests that shows whether someone has hepatitis B now, had it in the past, is immune from vaccination, or carries the virus long term. Each marker answers a different question: the surface antigen shows current infection, the antibodies show immunity or past exposure, and the viral DNA measures how actively the virus is multiplying.

measures.meaning: Part of the virus's outer coat; present in acute and chronic infection. Persisting beyond six months defines chronic hepatitis B.
The protective antibody; present after vaccination or recovered infection.
Marks exposure to the virus at some time; absent after vaccination alone. The IgM form points to recent infection.

measures.item: e antigen and e antibody (HBeAg, anti-HBe)
measures.meaning: Indicate how actively the virus is replicating in chronic infection.
The amount of virus in the blood, measured by PCR; guides the decision to treat and shows whether treatment is working.

whyOrdered: Abnormal liver tests or symptoms of hepatitis
Screening in pregnancy, before immunosuppressive treatment, and in people at higher risk
After a possible exposure, such as a needlestick injury
Checking immunity after vaccination
Monitoring chronic hepatitis B and its treatment
hepatitis-b-serology.how: A venous blood sample; the laboratory runs the markers as a panel and adds viral DNA when the surface antigen is positive.

interpretation.meaning: Current infection, acute or chronic; further markers and liver assessment follow, and specialist care is arranged
Immunity from vaccination

interpretation.finding: anti-HBs and anti-HBc positive, HBsAg negative
interpretation.meaning: Past infection that has resolved, with immunity

interpretation.finding: HBsAg positive for more than six months
interpretation.meaning: Chronic hepatitis B; the viral load, e-antigen status and liver tests decide on monitoring and antiviral treatment
Never infected and not immune; vaccination is considered

hepatitis-b-serology.rangeNote: Antigen and antibody results are reported as positive or negative (with a level for anti-HBs after vaccination); the viral load is a number whose meaning depends on the clinical context and the treatment guidelines in use, not on a reference interval.
factors: Timing after exposure: markers appear in sequence over weeks
Recent vaccination, which produces anti-HBs only
Immunosuppression, which can reactivate a resolved infection
Very early or 'window period' infection, when only anti-HBc IgM may be positive
cannotTell: How much liver damage has occurred, which needs liver tests, elastography or biopsy
Whether hepatitis C, D or other liver diseases are also present without their own tests
Exactly when the infection was acquired
hepatitis-b-serology.limitations: The markers must be read as a pattern; a single result can mislead in the window period, after vaccination or in people with weak immunity. Chronic infection needs long-term specialist monitoring even when the person feels well.
hepatitis-b-serology.medicinesNote: Antiviral treatment for hepatitis B lowers the viral load; the test monitors that treatment. Immunosuppressive medicines can reactivate the virus, so screening is done before they are started.

quick.usedFor: Diagnosing and monitoring hepatitis B, checking immunity, screening in pregnancy and before immunosuppression
quick.measures: Hepatitis B antigens, antibodies and viral DNA

hepatitis-b-serology.resultType: Positive or negative markers read as a pattern, plus a viral load

hiv-test.name: HIV test
hiv-test.what: A blood test that looks for the human immunodeficiency virus, usually by detecting both a viral protein (p24 antigen) and the antibodies the immune system makes against the virus. Modern combined tests become positive within a few weeks of infection; a positive screening result is always confirmed with a second test before a diagnosis is given.

measures.item: HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies with p24 antigen
measures.meaning: The standard fourth-generation laboratory screen, reliable from about 45 days after exposure; antigen detection shortens the window.
Fingerprick or saliva tests with results in minutes; a reactive result must be confirmed by a laboratory.

measures.item: HIV RNA (viral load) and CD4 count
measures.meaning: After diagnosis: the amount of virus and the number of CD4 immune cells, used to plan and monitor treatment rather than to screen.

whyOrdered: Routine screening: HIV testing is offered widely because early treatment protects health and prevents transmission

After a possible exposure, at the right interval; after a possible high-risk exposure, seek urgent advice (sexual health clinic, A&E or NHS 111) about post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), which must start within 72 hours
Symptoms of seroconversion or of an immune system under attack
Pregnancy screening, before some treatments and in people diagnosed with other sexually transmitted infections
hiv-test.how: A venous blood sample in a laboratory, a fingerprick rapid test in a clinic or pharmacy, or a home self-test kit.
hiv-test.preparation: None. The window period matters: a test taken too soon after exposure can be negative, so a repeat at the recommended interval may be advised.

interpretation.meaning: HIV infection is very unlikely; repeat testing is advised after any further exposure
Possible infection; a confirmatory laboratory test on a new sample is done before any diagnosis
HIV infection; referral to specialist care, where viral load and CD4 count guide antiretroviral treatment that keeps the virus suppressed
Inconclusive; the test is repeated at the interval recommended for the type of test used

hiv-test.rangeNote: Screening results are reported as negative or reactive, and confirmed positive or negative; no numeric reference interval applies. Viral load and CD4 count after diagnosis are numbers interpreted against treatment guidelines.
factors: The interval since exposure (window period), which depends on the test type
Post-exposure or pre-exposure prophylaxis medicines, which can delay antibody development
Rare false-reactive screening results, which is why confirmation is required
cannotTell: Whether infection occurred within the last few weeks, before markers appear
The stage of infection or the state of the immune system, which need the viral load and CD4 count
Other sexually transmitted infections, which have their own tests
hiv-test.limitations: No test detects infection immediately after exposure; results are only interpreted in relation to the timing of exposure, and a screening result is never a diagnosis on its own. Self-tests and rapid tests that detect only antibodies have a longer window period (about 90 days in UK guidance), so an early negative needs repeating; a reactive result needs laboratory confirmation.
hiv-test.medicinesNote: Antiretroviral prophylaxis can delay or blunt antibody responses; antiretroviral treatment lowers the viral load, which the monitoring tests track.

quick.type: Blood test (serology; rapid and self-tests available)
quick.sample: Blood from a vein, a fingerprick, or saliva for self-tests
quick.usedFor: Screening for HIV, testing after exposure, monitoring treatment once diagnosed
quick.measures: HIV antibodies and p24 antigen; viral load and CD4 count after diagnosis

hiv-test.specimen: Venous blood (serum) in the laboratory; capillary blood or oral fluid for rapid and self-tests
hiv-test.resultType: Negative, reactive or confirmed positive; numeric viral load and CD4 count in monitoring

blood-pressure-measurement.name: Blood pressure measurement
blood-pressure-measurement.what: The pressure of blood against the artery walls, recorded as two numbers: the systolic pressure when the heart contracts and the diastolic pressure between beats. Measured with a cuff on the upper arm, it is the most frequently taken measurement in medicine because raised blood pressure usually causes no symptoms yet drives heart attacks, strokes and kidney disease.

measures.meaning: The peak pressure as the left ventricle ejects blood, in mmHg.
The lowest pressure, while the heart refills, in mmHg.
Readings taken automatically over 24 hours by a worn cuff; the daytime average is the reference measurement for diagnosing hypertension.
Twice-daily readings taken by the person over several days with a validated arm cuff, averaged.

whyOrdered: Routine health checks and screening for hypertension
Confirming a raised clinic reading with ambulatory or home monitoring
Monitoring blood-pressure treatment
Dizziness on standing, when lying and standing readings are compared
In pregnancy, kidney disease, diabetes and after a stroke or heart attack
blood-pressure-measurement.how: Seated and rested for a few minutes, arm supported at heart level, a correctly sized cuff on the upper arm; readings are repeated and the average used. Ambulatory monitoring uses an automatic cuff worn for 24 hours; home monitoring uses a validated upper-arm device morning and evening for several days.
blood-pressure-measurement.preparation: Avoid caffeine, smoking and exercise for 30 minutes before; empty the bladder; sit quietly with the back supported and legs uncrossed; do not talk during the reading.

interpretation.meaning: Hypertension is suspected but not diagnosed: ambulatory or home monitoring confirms it, because clinic readings are often higher than usual (white-coat effect)

interpretation.finding: Ambulatory or home average above the diagnostic threshold
interpretation.meaning: Hypertension; the stage, cardiovascular risk and any organ damage guide lifestyle advice and treatment
Severe hypertension or an emergency; assessed the same day
Postural (orthostatic) hypotension, a common cause of dizziness and falls, often from medicines or dehydration

blood-pressure-measurement.rangeNote: Blood pressure is read against guideline thresholds for diagnosis and treatment targets, which differ between clinic, ambulatory and home readings and between countries' guidelines; it is not read against a laboratory reference interval.

thresholds.name: Clinic blood pressure suggesting hypertension
thresholds.context: A clinic reading at or above this prompts ambulatory (or home) monitoring to confirm the diagnosis

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management
source.section: 1.2 Measuring blood pressure and 1.3 Diagnosing hypertension

thresholds.name: Ambulatory or home average confirming stage 1 hypertension
thresholds.context: Diagnosis of stage 1 hypertension when the clinic reading is 140/90 or higher

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

thresholds.name: Stage 2 hypertension
thresholds.context: Treatment is offered to adults of any age with stage 2 hypertension

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

factors: Cuff size, arm position, talking, a full bladder and recent caffeine, smoking or exercise
The clinic setting itself (white-coat effect) and, conversely, masked hypertension that is normal in clinic but raised at home
Pain, anxiety, cold and the time of day
Medicines: decongestants, NSAIDs, steroids, oral contraceptives and stimulants raise it; antihypertensives, some antidepressants and alcohol change it
cannotTell: Whether arteries or organs have been damaged, which needs blood tests, urine tests, an ECG and sometimes imaging
The cause of high blood pressure, which is usually not identifiable and occasionally due to kidney, adrenal or other disease
Blood pressure inside the heart or lungs, which needs catheter studies
blood-pressure-measurement.limitations: A single reading is a poor guide: blood pressure varies minute to minute, and diagnosis rests on averaged out-of-clinic readings. Wrist and finger devices are less reliable than validated upper-arm cuffs, and irregular rhythms such as atrial fibrillation make automatic devices inaccurate.
blood-pressure-measurement.medicinesNote: Antihypertensive medicines are what the measurement monitors; NSAIDs, decongestants, corticosteroids and some antidepressants can raise it.

quick.sample: None: a cuff on the upper arm
quick.usedFor: Screening for and diagnosing hypertension, monitoring treatment, assessing dizziness on standing
quick.measures: Systolic and diastolic arterial pressure in mmHg

blood-pressure-measurement.resultType: Two numbers in mmHg, read against guideline thresholds; averaged home or ambulatory readings for diagnosis

cervical-screening.name: Cervical screening (smear test)
cervical-screening.what: A sample of cells brushed from the transformation zone of the cervix, the band where the columnar lining of the cervical canal has been replaced by squamous cells and where nearly all cervical cell changes begin, taken with a small soft brush passed through a speculum. In England the sample is tested first for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), the virus behind almost all cervical cancer, and the cells are examined under the microscope only if that virus is found. Screening looks for the risk of cancer developing rather than for cancer itself, and it is offered to everyone with a cervix, including trans men and non-binary people.

measures.meaning: The virus types that cause cervical cancer, chiefly types 16 and 18. A negative result means the chance of cancer developing before the next screen is very low.
Looked at only when high-risk HPV is found. Cells are reported as normal, borderline, or as low-grade or high-grade dyskaryosis, according to how abnormal they appear.
A sample with too few cells, or obscured by blood or inflammation, is reported as inadequate and has to be repeated.

whyOrdered: Routine screening for everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64 in England, at intervals that depend on age, the previous result and the programme (the four UK nations differ)
A repeat a year after a high-risk HPV result with normal cells, to see whether the infection has cleared
Follow-up after treatment of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), as a test of cure
Trans men and non-binary people who have a cervix: those registered with a GP as male are not sent automatic invitations and need to ask for screening
Not for investigating symptoms: bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause needs an examination of the cervix and referral, not a screening test
cervical-screening.how: A speculum is passed into the vagina so that the cervix can be seen, and a small soft brush is rotated in the opening of the cervix for a few seconds. The tip of the brush is put into a pot of preservative liquid and sent to the laboratory (liquid-based cytology). The appointment takes a few minutes and is usually done by a practice nurse.
cervical-screening.preparation: None is needed, although it is better not to book during a period because blood makes the sample harder to read, and vaginal medicines, lubricants and spermicides are avoided for a couple of days beforehand. A test that falls due in pregnancy is usually put off, and screening is normally taken up again about twelve weeks after giving birth; anyone who is pregnant and has been invited should say so when booking. Discomfort and anxiety can be reduced by asking for a smaller speculum, a different position or a longer appointment, and a course of vaginal oestrogen is sometimes prescribed first when the tissues are thin after the menopause or on testosterone.

interpretation.meaning: Routine recall; the chance of cervical cancer developing before the next invitation is very low
Screening is repeated in a year, because most infections clear on their own

interpretation.finding: High-risk HPV found with abnormal cells
interpretation.meaning: Referral for colposcopy: the cervix is examined under magnification and a biopsy or loop excision may be taken

interpretation.finding: High-risk HPV still present on repeat testing
interpretation.meaning: Screening is repeated after a further year; high-risk HPV that is still present at that second repeat leads to colposcopy even when the cells look normal, because it is persistent infection that leads to cancer
Repeated after about three months; repeated inadequate samples lead to colposcopy

cervical-screening.limitations: Screening lowers the risk of cervical cancer a great deal but does not remove it. HPV vaccination protects against the commonest high-risk types but not all of them, so screening invitations still apply to people who have been vaccinated. A sample can miss an abnormal area, and adenocarcinoma arising high in the cervical canal is harder to detect than squamous disease. A positive HPV result is common, says nothing about when or from whom the virus was acquired, and in most people clears without treatment within about two years. The test says nothing about the ovaries, the lining of the uterus or other infections, and it cannot be used to investigate bleeding or pain, which need an examination. Kits for taking a sample at home are being introduced in some programmes for people who do not attend.
