sections.heading: What is fexofenadine used for?
sections.body:
Fexofenadine is an antihistamine medicine that relieves the symptoms of allergies. The NHS lists hay fever, conjunctivitis, eczema, hives, insect bite and sting reactions and some food allergies among the problems it is used for. MedlinePlus describes it as treating allergy symptoms such as a runny nose, sneezing, and red, itchy or watery eyes, as well as itching and redness caused by hives.

The NHS says tablets for treating hives are available from pharmacies. MedlinePlus has a separate page for products that combine fexofenadine with pseudoephedrine, which are different products from fexofenadine on its own.

sections.heading: How does fexofenadine work?
sections.body:
Fexofenadine blocks histamine, a substance in the body that drives allergy symptoms. The NHS says that by blocking the effects of histamine it reduces the symptoms, and that people should start to feel better within 1 to 2 hours. A 2024 clinical review describes it as a non-sedating, second-generation H1 antihistamine.

The NHS classes fexofenadine as non-drowsy and says it seems less likely to cause sleepiness than other non-drowsy antihistamines. It also says fexofenadine is unlikely to cause harm when used for a long time, though it is best taken only for as long as it is needed.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of fexofenadine?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headaches, feeling sleepy, feeling sick and feeling dizzy as the common side effects. Fexofenadine is classed as a non-drowsy antihistamine, but some people still feel quite sleepy. The NHS advises not driving, cycling or using tools or machinery while feeling sleepy or dizzy. Leaflets say fexofenadine is unlikely to affect the ability to drive or use machinery, but advise checking first that the tablets do not cause sleepiness or dizziness.

Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat with difficulty breathing can be a sign of a serious allergic reaction. The leaflets say to stop the medicine and tell a doctor immediately. In an emergency, call 999.

sections.heading: Fexofenadine with food, drink and other medicines
sections.body:
The NHS says grapefruit, orange and apple juice can reduce how well fexofenadine works. MedlinePlus likewise advises taking it with water rather than with fruit juices such as orange, grapefruit or apple juice. The NHS also says it is best not to drink alcohol while taking fexofenadine, as it can make you feel sleepy.

Leaflets say that indigestion remedies containing aluminium and magnesium can lower how much fexofenadine is absorbed, and advise leaving a gap between the two. A leaflet states that apalutamide, a prostate cancer medicine, may decrease the effect of fexofenadine. The NHS says fexofenadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.

sections.heading: Who can take fexofenadine, and who needs extra care?
sections.body:
The NHS says tablets for adults and children aged 12 and over can be bought from pharmacies and supermarkets, while tablets for children under 12 are only available on prescription from a doctor. The NHS lists liver or kidney problems and heart problems among the reasons fexofenadine may not be suitable, and leaflets advise talking to a doctor or pharmacist first about liver or kidney problems, heart disease or older age. One leaflet says antihistamines such as fexofenadine may cause a fast or irregular heartbeat.

The NHS lists pregnancy, trying to get pregnant and breastfeeding among the situations where fexofenadine may not be suitable. UK leaflets advise against use in pregnancy unless necessary and say it is not recommended while breastfeeding. The NHS also says anyone due an allergy test should check first, because the medicine can affect the results. The NHS lists having ever had an allergic reaction to fexofenadine or any other medicine among the reasons it may not be suitable. Leaflets differ in wording between products, so the leaflet that comes with a particular product applies to it.

faqs.q: Is fexofenadine a non-drowsy antihistamine?
faqs.a: The NHS classes fexofenadine as non-drowsy and says it seems less likely to cause sleepiness than other non-drowsy antihistamines. Even so, some people feel quite sleepy or dizzy, and the NHS advises not driving, cycling or using tools or machinery if that happens.

faqs.q: Can fruit juice be drunk with fexofenadine?
faqs.a: The NHS says grapefruit, orange and apple juice can reduce how well fexofenadine works. MedlinePlus advises taking it with water rather than fruit juice. The NHS also says it is best not to drink alcohol while taking fexofenadine.

faqs.q: How quickly does fexofenadine work?
faqs.a: The NHS says people should start to feel better within 1 to 2 hours. It says fexofenadine is unlikely to cause harm when used for a long time, but it is best taken only for as long as it is needed.

faqs.q: Can fexofenadine be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: The NHS says tablets for adults and children aged 12 and over can be bought from pharmacies and supermarkets. Tablets for children under 12 are only available with a prescription from a doctor.

faqs.q: Does fexofenadine affect contraception?
faqs.a: The NHS says fexofenadine does not affect any type of contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.

faqs.q: Can fexofenadine be used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS lists pregnancy, trying to get pregnant and breastfeeding among the situations where fexofenadine may not be suitable. UK leaflets advise against use in pregnancy unless necessary and say it is not recommended while breastfeeding. A GP or pharmacist can advise on an individual situation.

codeine.name: Codeine and co-codamol
codeine.summary: Codeine is an opioid painkiller used for pain such as pain after an operation or injury, and co-codamol is codeine combined with paracetamol for aches and pains. The NHS lists constipation, drowsiness and sickness as common effects, and says it is possible to become addicted to codeine. Co-codamol contains paracetamol, so taking other paracetamol-containing medicines as well can lead to too much paracetamol, which can harm the liver.
codeine.class: Opioid analgesic (codeine, alone or combined with paracetamol)
usedFor: Codeine is used to treat pain, for example after an operation or injury.
Co-codamol is used for aches and pains such as period pain, muscle pain and toothache.
Co-codamol is often used when other painkillers, such as paracetamol on its own, have not worked.
codeine.howItWorks: Codeine is an opioid that acts on the central nervous system and the brain to block pain signals to the rest of the body. It also slows digestion, which is why it can cause constipation. Co-codamol adds paracetamol, another painkiller, to the codeine.
codeine.onset: The NHS says co-codamol can take up to an hour to start working.

common: Constipation, feeling sick or being sick, and feeling sleepy or tired.
serious: The NHS describes a serious allergic reaction, slow or shallow breathing, an irregular heartbeat and low blood pressure as rare serious side effects of codeine, and says to get emergency help (999) for breathing difficulty, a fit or allergic symptoms such as throat swelling.
The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to codeine, and a prescriber or pharmacist can be asked about any concern.
The NHS advises against stopping codeine suddenly after regular use, and says the doctor reduces the dose gradually over weeks or months.

cautions: Codeine is not suitable for everyone: the NHS lists a lung problem, a head injury, adrenal gland problems, a condition that causes fits, an addiction to alcohol, an underactive thyroid, and kidney or liver problems among the reasons, as well as a previous reaction to codeine.
The NHS says not to give codeine to children under 12, and that people aged 12 to 18 are given it only if everyday painkillers have not worked.
The NHS says codeine should not be given to anyone under 18 who has had their tonsils or adenoids removed because of obstructive sleep apnoea.

The NHS says codeine can be used during pregnancy, but long-term use is not advised, and use at the end of pregnancy can leave the baby with withdrawal symptoms and needing extra time in hospital for observation.
The NHS says not to take codeine while breastfeeding, because small amounts pass into breast milk and can cause breathing problems and drowsiness in the baby.
The NHS says drinking alcohol with codeine may make a person sleepier and can raise the risk of serious side effects.
The NHS says recreational drugs such as cannabis, cocaine or heroin raise the risk of serious side effects of codeine, including breathing difficulties.
Co-codamol leaflets say not to drive or use machinery if it causes dizziness or drowsiness.
The NHS advises against taking co-codamol with other paracetamol-containing medicines unless a doctor says so, and the leaflets include cold and flu remedies among them.
codeine.monitoring: The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to codeine, advises following the prescriber's guidance on how long to take it, and says the doctor reduces the dose gradually before stopping.

regulatory.note: The NHS says the lowest strength can be bought from a pharmacy.
The NHS says higher strengths need a prescription.

regimenNote: Codeine tablets; co-codamol tablets, capsules and effervescent tablets.

sections.heading: What are codeine and co-codamol used for?
sections.body:
Codeine is an opioid painkiller that the NHS describes as a medicine for pain, for example after an operation or injury.

Co-codamol is a combination of two painkillers, paracetamol and codeine. It is used for aches and pains, including period pain, muscle pain and toothache. The NHS says it is used when everyday painkillers such as ibuprofen, aspirin or paracetamol on their own have not worked.

The NHS says codeine is not suitable for everyone. It should not be given to children under 12, and young people aged 12 to 18 are given it only if everyday painkillers have not worked.

Product leaflets show that co-codamol comes in different strengths. The NHS says the lowest strength can be bought from a pharmacy, while higher strengths need a prescription.

sections.heading: How do codeine and co-codamol work?
sections.body:
Codeine is an opioid. The NHS says it acts on pain receptors in the central nervous system and the brain to block pain signals to the rest of the body. It also slows digestion, which is why it can cause constipation.

In co-codamol the codeine is combined with paracetamol. The NHS says co-codamol can take up to an hour to start working.

sections.heading: Side effects, constipation and dependence
sections.body:
The NHS lists constipation, feeling or being sick, and feeling sleepy as common side effects of codeine and co-codamol.

Because codeine slows digestion, the NHS suggests eating more fibre and drinking plenty of fluids for constipation. If that does not help, a laxative can be used after checking with a pharmacist or doctor, and the NHS says lactulose is usually the best choice.

The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to codeine, and advises talking to a doctor if there is a worry. It advises against stopping suddenly after regular use, and says the doctor reduces the dose gradually over weeks or months.

The NHS describes a serious allergic reaction, slow or shallow breathing, an irregular heartbeat and low blood pressure as rare serious side effects. It says to call 999 or go to A&E for breathing difficulty, a fit or allergic symptoms such as swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue.

sections.heading: Paracetamol in co-codamol and other medicines
sections.body:
Co-codamol contains paracetamol. The NHS advises against combining it with other paracetamol-containing medicines unless a doctor has said to, because of the risk of too much paracetamol. The product leaflets say cold and flu remedies are among the products to check.

The NHS says taking too much co-codamol can be harmful, and the leaflets say too much paracetamol can cause delayed, serious liver damage.

The leaflets say to get medical advice if too much has been taken, even when feeling well. A North Tees and Hartlepool NHS leaflet gives NHS 111 as the number to call, and says to call 999 or go to A&E in an emergency.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about pregnancy, driving and alcohol?
sections.body:
The NHS lists a lung problem, a head injury, adrenal gland problems, a condition that causes fits, an addiction to alcohol, an underactive thyroid, and kidney or liver problems among the reasons codeine may not be suitable. It also says codeine should not be given to anyone under 18 who has had their tonsils or adenoids removed because of obstructive sleep apnoea. A pharmacist or doctor can say whether it suits a particular person.

The NHS says codeine can be used during pregnancy, but long-term use is not advised. Codeine used near the end of pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in the baby, who may need extra time in hospital for observation.

The NHS says not to take codeine while breastfeeding, because small amounts reach breast milk and can cause breathing problems and drowsiness in the baby. The Specialist Pharmacy Service says the MHRA gives the same advice. A doctor or pharmacist can recommend a more suitable painkiller.

Co-codamol leaflets say it can cause dizziness or drowsiness, and not to drive or use machinery if affected. The NHS says alcohol may make a person sleepier and can raise the risk of serious side effects, and that recreational drugs such as cannabis, cocaine or heroin also raise the risk of serious side effects, including breathing difficulties.

faqs.q: Can you become addicted to codeine?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to codeine and to talk to a doctor about any worry. The NHS advises against stopping suddenly after regular use, and says the doctor reduces the dose gradually.

faqs.q: Why does codeine cause constipation?
faqs.a: The NHS says codeine slows down digestion, which is why it can cause constipation. The NHS suggests more fibre and fluids, and a laxative after checking with a pharmacist or doctor.

faqs.q: Can co-codamol be taken with other paracetamol medicines?
faqs.a: Co-codamol already contains paracetamol, and the NHS and product leaflets advise against taking other paracetamol-containing medicines with it. Cold and flu remedies are among those to check, because too much paracetamol can cause liver damage.

faqs.q: Is codeine used while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS advises against it, because small amounts of codeine pass into breast milk and can cause breathing problems and drowsiness in the baby. A doctor or pharmacist can recommend a more suitable painkiller.

faqs.q: Can you drink alcohol with co-codamol?
faqs.a: The NHS says drinking alcohol with codeine may make a person sleepier and can raise the risk of serious side effects. Co-codamol leaflets say not to drive or use machinery if drowsy or dizzy.

simvastatin.name: Simvastatin
simvastatin.summary: Simvastatin is a statin, a medicine that lowers cholesterol by reducing how much the liver makes, and it is used to treat high cholesterol and to help prevent heart disease, including heart attacks and strokes. The NHS describes serious side effects as rare, but advises seeking help from a doctor for unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, and a GP or NHS 111 is the route for prompt advice. Grapefruit juice, some antibiotics such as clarithromycin and several other medicines can raise simvastatin levels and the risk of muscle damage.
usedFor: Lowering cholesterol in people who have been diagnosed with high blood cholesterol
Helping to prevent heart disease, including heart attacks and strokes
A doctor may prescribe it when there is a family history of heart disease or a long-term condition such as rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes or type 2 diabetes
simvastatin.howItWorks: Simvastatin stops the liver from making cholesterol, which lowers the level of cholesterol in the blood. It belongs to the group of medicines called statins, also known as HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors.
simvastatin.onset: The NHS says treatment is usually long term, and it takes some weeks for cholesterol levels to fall.

common: Headache, dizziness, feeling sick, digestive problems, muscle aches and sleep problems are listed by the NHS as common side effects.
The NHS says unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness should be reported to a doctor.
serious: The NHS lists muscle damage, inflammation of the liver and inflammation of the pancreas among the serious side effects, which it describes as rare; unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps need prompt advice from a GP or NHS 111.
Yellowing of the skin or eyes can point to liver problems, and a GP or NHS 111 should be contacted promptly.
A serious allergic reaction, with breathing or swallowing problems or a swollen face or throat, is an emergency, and the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E.

cautions: Grapefruit juice raises the level of simvastatin in the blood and makes side effects more likely, and the NHS advises avoiding it.
NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance lists clarithromycin as contraindicated with simvastatin and says that, if the antibiotic is essential, simvastatin is stopped for the course.

The NHS lists other medicines that raise the risk of muscle damage, including the antibiotics clarithromycin, rifampicin and fusidic acid, the antifungals fluconazole and ketoconazole, some HIV medicines, hepatitis C treatments, warfarin, ciclosporin and danazol.
If one of those medicines is needed, the NHS says the doctor may lower the simvastatin dose, switch to a different statin or pause simvastatin for a while.
The NHS says drinking a lot of alcohol may increase the chance of muscle and liver side effects.
The NHS lists liver or kidney problems, lung disease, an underactive thyroid, a muscle disorder and myasthenia gravis as reasons to check with a doctor before taking simvastatin.
The NHS says simvastatin is not recommended in pregnancy because it can affect how the baby develops, and it gives separate advice for people planning a pregnancy.

On breastfeeding, the NHS says simvastatin might be suitable but a person may be told to stop until they are no longer breastfeeding, and NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance prefers rosuvastatin, pravastatin or atorvastatin.
The NHS advises talking to a GP or pharmacist before stopping simvastatin, because stopping can make cholesterol rise again and the risk of heart attacks and strokes may go up.
simvastatin.monitoring: The NHS says that during the first 12 months of treatment a couple of routine tests are offered to check that the liver is working properly.
regimenNote: Tablets and an oral liquid (suspension) that are swallowed.

sections.heading: What is simvastatin used for?
sections.body:
Simvastatin is a type of medicine called a statin. The NHS says it is used to lower cholesterol in people who have been diagnosed with high blood cholesterol. It is also used to help prevent heart disease, including heart attacks and strokes. A doctor may prescribe it when there is a family history of heart disease or a long-term condition such as rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes or type 2 diabetes.

Most adults can take simvastatin, and the NHS says it is sometimes prescribed to children aged 10 and over. It comes as tablets and as a liquid that is swallowed. In the UK, many simvastatin products are sold under the generic name, and the brand name Zocor also appears in the electronic Medicines Compendium. The NHS says it is available on prescription, and describes treatment as usually long term.

sections.heading: How does simvastatin work?
sections.body:
Simvastatin stops the liver from making cholesterol, which lowers the level of cholesterol in the blood. It belongs to the group of medicines also known as HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors. MedlinePlus says it is used to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke in people at high risk, and to decrease cholesterol.

The NHS says it takes some weeks for cholesterol levels to fall.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of simvastatin?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headache, dizziness, feeling sick, digestive problems, muscle aches and sleep problems as common side effects. It describes the serious side effects as rare.

The NHS lists muscle damage, inflammation of the liver and inflammation of the pancreas among the serious side effects. The NHS advises seeking help from a doctor for unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps. A GP or NHS 111 is the route for prompt advice.

Yellowing of the skin or eyes can point to liver problems, and a GP or NHS 111 should be contacted promptly. For breathing or swallowing problems, or a swollen face or throat, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E.

sections.heading: Taking simvastatin with other medicines, grapefruit or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says grapefruit juice increases the level of simvastatin in the blood and makes side effects more likely, so it advises avoiding it. Some medicines also raise the risk of serious side effects such as muscle damage. The NHS lists the antibiotics clarithromycin, rifampicin and fusidic acid, the antifungals fluconazole and ketoconazole, some HIV medicines, hepatitis C treatments, warfarin, ciclosporin and danazol.

NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance lists clarithromycin as contraindicated with simvastatin. Where such a medicine is needed, the NHS says the doctor may lower the simvastatin dose, switch to a different statin or pause simvastatin for a while.

The NHS says drinking a lot of alcohol may increase the chance of muscle and liver side effects. A pharmacist or doctor can check any new medicine against simvastatin.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about pregnancy?
sections.body:
The NHS lists liver or kidney problems, lung disease, an underactive thyroid, a muscle disorder and myasthenia gravis as reasons to check with a doctor before taking simvastatin.

The NHS says simvastatin is not recommended in pregnancy because it can affect how the baby develops, and it gives separate advice for people planning a pregnancy. On breastfeeding, the NHS says simvastatin might be suitable but a person may be told to stop until they are no longer breastfeeding. NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance prefers rosuvastatin, pravastatin or atorvastatin.

The NHS says that during the first 12 months of treatment a couple of routine tests are offered to check that the liver is working properly. It advises talking to a GP or pharmacist before stopping simvastatin, because stopping can make cholesterol rise again and the risk of heart attacks and strokes may go up.

faqs.q: Can I drink grapefruit juice while taking simvastatin?
faqs.a: The NHS says grapefruit juice increases the level of simvastatin in the blood, which makes side effects more likely. It therefore advises avoiding grapefruit juice with simvastatin. A pharmacist or doctor can say how this applies to an individual.

faqs.q: Can I take clarithromycin with simvastatin?
faqs.a: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance lists clarithromycin as contraindicated with simvastatin. If the antibiotic is essential, the guidance is that simvastatin is stopped for the course. The prescriber decides what happens in each case, so the doctor or pharmacist should be told about any antibiotic.

faqs.q: What should I do about muscle pain on simvastatin?
faqs.a: The NHS advises seeking help from a doctor for unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps. A GP appointment or NHS 111 is the route. The NHS advises talking to a GP or pharmacist before stopping simvastatin.

faqs.q: Can simvastatin be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says simvastatin is not recommended in pregnancy because it can affect how the baby develops. It gives separate advice for people planning a pregnancy. On breastfeeding, the NHS says simvastatin might be suitable but a person may be told to stop, and a doctor may suggest a different statin.

faqs.q: Are blood tests needed with simvastatin?
faqs.a: The NHS says that during the first 12 months of treatment a couple of routine tests are offered to check that the liver is working properly. Yellowing of the skin or eyes can point to liver problems and should be reported to a GP or NHS 111 promptly.

sumatriptan.name: Sumatriptan
sumatriptan.summary: Sumatriptan is a medicine used to treat migraines and cluster headaches once an attack has begun, and it does not stop migraines from starting. The NHS lists heart problems among the reasons it may not suit someone, and says a heart attack is a rare serious side effect that needs a 999 call.
usedFor: Treating migraine attacks.
Treating cluster headaches.
sumatriptan.howItWorks: Migraine symptoms may be caused by a temporary widening of blood vessels in the head. The NHS says sumatriptan narrows the blood vessels in the brain that are thought to widen during an attack. It treats an attack that has begun and does not prevent migraines from starting. Sumatriptan belongs to the triptan group of migraine medicines.

common: The NHS lists feeling or being sick, dizziness, feeling sleepy and flushing among the common side effects.
The NHS says many people have no side effects or only minor ones.
The nasal spray can cause nosebleeds and throat irritation, and the injection can cause bruising where it goes in.
The NHS says that if sumatriptan makes someone feel very dizzy or tired, they should avoid driving until they feel better.
serious: Anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction) and a heart attack are listed by the NHS among serious side effects, and the NHS says to call 999 for an ambulance in these emergencies.
The NHS says to call 999 if you think you might be having a heart attack while taking sumatriptan.
The NHS says confusion, muscle twitching, a high temperature or a fast heartbeat can be signs of serotonin syndrome, which needs a doctor to review it straight away.
For other serious side effects the NHS advises calling NHS 111.

cautions: The NHS lists heart problems, including a previous heart attack, among the reasons sumatriptan may not be suitable.
Circulation problems in the legs, a past stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA), liver disease and seizures are also listed by the NHS as reasons for caution.
Most adults up to the age of 65 can take sumatriptan, and older adults sometimes can if a doctor prescribes it.
NHS pages differ on children: one says a specialist may sometimes prescribe sumatriptan for a child aged 6 or over, and another says the nasal spray is sometimes prescribed from age 12.
The NHS says taking too much can narrow blood vessels and lead to heart problems such as chest pain, an abnormal heart rhythm or a heart attack.
The NHS asks people to tell the prescriber about other migraine or headache medicines such as ergotamine or other triptans, and about antidepressants.
Using it with some antidepressants can cause serotonin syndrome, and a UK leaflet states that taking it with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) antidepressant is not allowed.
St John's wort can raise the risk of serotonin syndrome, and the NHS advises against taking it with sumatriptan.
The NHS says there is not enough information to know how other herbal remedies, vitamins and supplements affect sumatriptan.
A UK leaflet says using sumatriptan too often may cause or worsen headaches, including when other painkillers are also needed regularly for migraine.
The NHS pregnancy page says sumatriptan is not thought to harm a developing baby, but the research is not conclusive, so other NHS pages advise asking a doctor first.
NHS pages give different advice on breastfeeding, so it is worth asking a pharmacist or doctor.
sumatriptan.monitoring: The sources used for this page do not describe routine blood tests for sumatriptan. The NHS says using sumatriptan too often can cause medication overuse headaches, and to see a doctor if you are worried about this.

sections.heading: What is sumatriptan used for?
sections.body: Sumatriptan is used to treat migraines and cluster headaches. It does not prevent migraines from starting, so it is a treatment for an attack that has begun. Triptans are generally taken once the headache has begun rather than during an aura, a trust leaflet says, because studies show they do not work as well if taken too early.

sections.heading: How does sumatriptan work?
sections.body: Migraine symptoms may be caused by a temporary widening of blood vessels in the head. The NHS says sumatriptan narrows the blood vessels thought to widen during an attack. It is available in different forms: the NHS describes tablets, a nasal spray and an injection.

sections.heading: Side effects and when to get help
sections.body: The NHS lists feeling or being sick, dizziness, feeling sleepy and flushing as common side effects. The NHS says many people have no side effects or only minor ones. A heart attack and anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, are rare serious side effects, and the NHS says to call 999 and ask for an ambulance if either is suspected. The NHS says to call 999 if you think you might be having a heart attack while taking sumatriptan. Other serious side effects are a reason to call NHS 111, according to the NHS.

sections.heading: Sumatriptan with other medicines and who needs extra care
sections.body: The NHS asks people to tell their prescriber about ergotamine, other triptans and antidepressants. Some antidepressants can cause serotonin syndrome when used with sumatriptan, and the NHS advises against St John's wort. Heart problems, a past stroke or TIA, circulation problems in the legs, liver disease and seizures are among the conditions the NHS lists as reasons it may not be suitable. The NHS pregnancy page says it is not thought to harm a developing baby, but the research is not conclusive; ask a doctor before using it in pregnancy.

faqs.q: Does sumatriptan stop migraines from happening?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says sumatriptan does not prevent migraines from starting. It is used to treat an attack that has already started.

faqs.q: Can sumatriptan be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: Most sumatriptan is prescription only, but packs of tablets can be bought from a pharmacy by adults who have previously been diagnosed with migraine. The Imigran nasal spray is a prescription-only medicine, according to its UK product information.

faqs.q: Can children or older people use sumatriptan?
faqs.a: Most adults up to the age of 65 can take it, and older adults sometimes can if a doctor prescribes it. NHS pages differ on children: one says a specialist may sometimes prescribe sumatriptan for a child aged 6 or over, and another says the nasal spray is sometimes prescribed from age 12.

faqs.q: What can happen if sumatriptan is used too often?
faqs.a: A UK leaflet says using it too often may cause or worsen headaches. The NHS says taking too much can narrow blood vessels and cause heart problems.

ondansetron.name: Ondansetron
ondansetron.summary: Ondansetron is an anti-sickness medicine used to prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery. It belongs to the 5-HT3 receptor antagonist group, and the main cautions are an effect on the heart rhythm (QT prolongation) and use in early pregnancy.
usedFor: Preventing nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy or radiotherapy, with age limits that differ between the two uses.
Preventing nausea and vomiting after surgery.
ondansetron.howItWorks: Ondansetron belongs to a group called serotonin 5-HT3 receptor antagonists, which interfere with serotonin, a natural substance that can cause nausea and vomiting.

common: Headache is very common with ondansetron, according to a UK leaflet.
Constipation and flushing or a feeling of warmth are also listed as common.
Hiccups and low blood pressure are listed as uncommon effects.
serious: Allergic reactions and sudden chest pain or chest tightness are among the serious effects listed in a UK leaflet.
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.

cautions: A UK leaflet says ondansetron must not be used with apomorphine (a Parkinson's disease medicine) or by anyone allergic to it.
The solution leaflet rules out use in the first three months of pregnancy.
The MHRA has warned of a small increased risk of cleft lip or palate after use in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy, and says women should be counselled on the benefits and risks if it is offered.

An NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service page says ondansetron can be used with caution during breastfeeding, with monitoring of the baby. UK manufacturer leaflets, by contrast, advise against breastfeeding during treatment.
Leaflets advise caution in people with a bowel blockage or severe constipation, heart failure, heart rhythm problems, liver problems or abnormal blood levels of potassium, sodium or magnesium.

An NHS prescribing sheet says ondansetron lengthens the QT interval (a measure of the heart's electrical cycle) in a dose-related way, and that torsade de pointes, a dangerous heart rhythm, has been reported.

The same sheet advises avoiding it in congenital long QT syndrome, and caution with heart failure, slow heart rates, other QT-prolonging medicines, and low potassium or magnesium, which are corrected before use.
The sheet also warns of serotonin syndrome when ondansetron is combined with serotonergic medicines such as SSRIs and SNRIs.
ondansetron.monitoring: An NHS prescribing sheet says low potassium and magnesium are corrected before use. A prescriber considers heart rhythm risk when other QT-prolonging medicines are used.

sections.heading: What is ondansetron used for?
sections.body: A UK tablet leaflet lists two licensed uses for ondansetron: preventing nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and preventing it after surgery. MedlinePlus gives the same two groups of uses for adults taking the tablets. Great Ormond Street Hospital describes it as a medicine that stops a child feeling sick and being sick. It may be given by mouth as a tablet, melt or syrup, or as an injection into a vein.

sections.heading: How does ondansetron work?
sections.body: Serotonin is a natural substance that can trigger nausea and vomiting. Ondansetron interferes with serotonin, which can trigger nausea and vomiting, by acting on 5-HT3 receptors. Medicines in this group are called 5-HT3 receptor antagonists. Great Ormond Street Hospital notes that some medicines can react with ondansetron and change how well it works, so a doctor or pharmacist is asked about other medicines first.

sections.heading: Side effects and when to get help
sections.body: Headache is listed as very common, and constipation and flushing as common. Allergic reactions and sudden chest pain or chest tightness are among the serious effects listed in a UK leaflet. These effects need prompt medical assessment: the route to care is 999 for an emergency, or NHS 111 for urgent advice that is not an emergency.

sections.heading: Heart rhythm, pregnancy and other cautions
sections.body: Ondansetron lengthens the QT interval in a dose-related way, according to an NHS prescribing sheet. The sheet advises avoiding it in congenital long QT syndrome and taking care with low potassium or magnesium, heart failure, slow heart rates and other QT-prolonging medicines. The MHRA has reported a small increased risk of cleft lip or palate with use in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy. Apomorphine must not be used with ondansetron, according to a UK leaflet.

faqs.q: Is ondansetron available without a prescription?
faqs.a: No. Ondansetron is a prescription-only medicine in the UK; the emc lists its oral solution as POM.

faqs.q: Can ondansetron affect the heart?
faqs.a: Yes. An NHS prescribing sheet says it lengthens the QT interval in a dose-related way. Torsade de pointes, a dangerous heart rhythm, has been reported after the medicine came into use.

faqs.q: Can ondansetron be used while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: An NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service page says it can be used with caution during breastfeeding, with monitoring of the baby. UK manufacturer leaflets, by contrast, advise against breastfeeding during treatment.

metoclopramide.name: Metoclopramide
metoclopramide.summary: Metoclopramide is an anti-sickness medicine used to stop nausea (feeling sick) and vomiting (being sick), including the sickness that can come with a migraine. The MHRA has restricted its dose and duration to reduce the risk of serious neurological side effects, so it is prescribed for short-term use only.
usedFor: Stopping nausea and vomiting.
Treating the sickness that can happen during a migraine.

In children aged 1 to 18 the MHRA says it is used only as a second-line option, for preventing delayed nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy and for treating established nausea and vomiting after surgery.
metoclopramide.howItWorks: NHS formularies list metoclopramide together with domperidone, which the MHRA describes as a dopamine antagonist with anti-sickness properties. The retrieved NHS and regulator pages do not describe its mechanism in more detail.

common: The NHS says the most common side effects are feeling sleepy (drowsy) and diarrhoea.
The NHS also lists low mood or depression among the common side effects.
Leaflets say it may affect vision and the ability to drive or use machines.
serious: The NHS says the most common serious side effect is uncontrollable movements, such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms.
The MHRA says the risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults.
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.

cautions: The NHS says metoclopramide suits most adults and children aged 1 year or over.
Epilepsy, Parkinson's disease and a past allergic reaction to it are listed by the NHS as reasons it may not suit someone.
Formularies list gastrointestinal obstruction, perforation or bleeding as reasons not to use it, and say it is not used in children under 1 year.

The NHS asks people taking medicines for Parkinson's disease such as levodopa, medicines that cause drowsiness such as diazepam or amitriptyline, or other anti-sickness medicines to speak to a doctor or pharmacist first.
The NHS says some herbal remedies and supplements can make the side effects of metoclopramide worse.
The NHS does not recommend drinking alcohol with it because this increases the risk of side effects.
metoclopramide.monitoring: The NHS says treatment is usually for a short time because longer use can cause side effects. The MHRA limits its use to short-term treatment.

sections.heading: What is metoclopramide used for?
sections.body: The NHS describes metoclopramide as a prescription-only medicine that stops nausea and vomiting. It is also prescribed for the sickness that can happen during a migraine. The NHS says it suits most adults and children aged 1 year or over. NHS formularies list gastrointestinal obstruction, perforation or bleeding as reasons not to use it.

sections.heading: The MHRA restriction on short-term use
sections.body: The MHRA reviewed the neurological risks of metoclopramide and restricted its dose and duration of use, to reduce the risk of serious neurological side effects. The review confirmed known risks such as short-term movement disorders (extrapyramidal disorders) and tardive dyskinesia, a movement disorder that can persist. As a result it is prescribed only for short-term use, and the NHS says it is usually prescribed for a short time because side effects can occur with longer use. The risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults, and the MHRA says it is not used in children under 1 year.

sections.heading: Side effects and when to get help
sections.body: The NHS lists drowsiness and diarrhoea as the most common side effects. The most common serious effect is uncontrollable movement such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms. The NHS advises getting medical help straight away, from a doctor or NHS 111, if muscles or eyes start moving in an unusual or uncontrolled way; in an emergency the route is 999 or A&E.

sections.heading: Other medicines and who needs extra care
sections.body: The NHS asks people to check with a doctor or pharmacist before combining metoclopramide with Parkinson's disease medicines, medicines that cause drowsiness or other anti-sickness medicines. Alcohol is not recommended with it because it increases the risk of side effects. Epilepsy and Parkinson's disease are listed by the NHS as conditions where it may not be suitable.

faqs.q: How long can metoclopramide be taken?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is usually prescribed for a short time because it can cause side effects with longer use, and the MHRA restricts it to short-term use.

faqs.q: Is metoclopramide used in children?
faqs.a: The MHRA says that in children aged 1 to 18 it is only a second-line option for two uses, and it is not used under 1 year.

faqs.q: Can metoclopramide be used for migraine?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is also prescribed for the sickness that can happen during a migraine.

loperamide.name: Loperamide
loperamide.summary: Loperamide is a medicine for diarrhoea that slows the activity of the bowel so that stools firm up. It can help with short-term diarrhoea and, in adults with a doctor's diagnosis, irritable bowel syndrome, and it is not suitable for everyone. The NHS says to contact 111 straight away if you take more than the recommended amount and get a fast or irregular heartbeat, because higher amounts can cause serious heart problems.
usedFor: Treating short-term diarrhoea.
Helping with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in adults whose doctor has diagnosed it.
Treating longer-lasting diarrhoea from conditions such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, on prescription.
loperamide.howItWorks: The NHS says loperamide works by slowing the activity of the bowel. Product information for UK loperamide medicines says it lengthens the time contents spend in the gut and increases absorption of water and electrolytes, so stools become firmer. UK and US product information describes loperamide as an opioid (mu) receptor agonist that acts on the gut wall to reduce propulsive movement of the bowel.

common: The NHS lists constipation, headache and feeling sick as side effects of loperamide; dizziness is also listed in NHS common questions.
The NHS says loperamide can cause dizziness, tiredness and drowsiness, and that drinking alcohol makes these more likely.
The NHS advises against driving or using machinery if affected.
serious: The NHS says swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or very fast or struggling breathing, may be a serious allergic reaction, and to call 999.
MedlinePlus says taking more than the recommended amount of loperamide can cause serious heart problems that may be fatal.
The NHS says to contact 111 or a doctor straight away for fainting, stomach pain or tenderness with a high temperature, severe constipation or difficulty passing urine.
The US FDA says that at much higher than recommended amounts loperamide can cause severe heart rhythm problems and death.

cautions: Over the counter, the NHS says loperamide is for anyone aged 12 or over with short-term diarrhoea, and for adults with IBS only if a doctor has diagnosed it.
Children aged 11 or under and adults with long-lasting diarrhoea need a prescription, according to the NHS.

The NHS lists severe diarrhoea after antibiotics, a flare-up of ulcerative colitis or another inflammatory bowel condition, constipation or a swollen stomach, and blood in the stool with a high temperature among the situations where it is not suitable.
The NHS says loperamide is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough evidence about it, and that anyone pregnant should speak to a doctor first.
The NHS says breastfeeding is considered acceptable because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk and no side effects are expected in the baby.
The NHS says some medicines can affect how loperamide works, including clozapine, ritonavir, quinidine, itraconazole, gemfibrozil, desmopressin and other anti-diarrhoea or bowel medicines.
The NHS says loperamide can be taken alongside paracetamol or ibuprofen and does not stop contraceptive pills working, although severe diarrhoea can make the pill less reliable.
loperamide.monitoring: The NHS says children aged 11 or under and adults with long-lasting diarrhoea need a prescription.

sections.heading: What is loperamide used for?
sections.body: The NHS describes loperamide as a medicine to treat diarrhoea. It can help with short-term diarrhoea and with irritable bowel syndrome that a doctor has diagnosed in an adult. For longer-lasting diarrhoea, such as that from Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, it is available on prescription.

sections.heading: How does loperamide work?
sections.body: Loperamide slows the activity of the bowel, so the contents move more slowly and stay in the intestine for longer. Product information for UK loperamide medicines says it lengthens the time contents spend in the gut and increases absorption of water and electrolytes, so stools become firmer. The NHS says it usually starts to improve diarrhoea within 1 hour.

sections.heading: Side effects and when to get help
sections.body: The NHS lists constipation, headache and feeling sick as side effects of loperamide. Dizziness, tiredness and drowsiness are more likely with alcohol. A fast or irregular heartbeat after taking more than the recommended amount can be a sign of serious heart problems, and the NHS says to contact 111 straight away. Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or very fast or struggling breathing, may be a serious allergic reaction: call 999. Fainting, stomach pain with a high temperature, severe constipation or difficulty passing urine need medical advice straight away: contact NHS 111 or a doctor.

sections.heading: Who should not use loperamide, and other medicines
sections.body: The NHS lists severe diarrhoea after antibiotics, a flare-up of ulcerative colitis or similar conditions, constipation or a swollen stomach, and blood in the stool with a high temperature as situations where it is not suitable. Pregnancy is a situation where the NHS says loperamide is not usually recommended and a doctor should be consulted first. Several medicines can change how loperamide works, including clozapine, ritonavir, quinidine, itraconazole, gemfibrozil and desmopressin.

faqs.q: Can loperamide be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: Yes, for people aged 12 or over with short-term diarrhoea, according to the NHS.

faqs.q: Can too much loperamide be harmful?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus says taking more than the recommended amount can cause serious heart problems that may be fatal. The NHS says to contact 111 straight away if you have a fast or irregular heartbeat after taking more than the recommended amount.

faqs.q: Is loperamide suitable in pregnancy and breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is not usually recommended in pregnancy, and that breastfeeding is considered acceptable.

loperamide.onset: The NHS says loperamide usually starts to make diarrhoea better within 1 hour.

lactulose.name: Lactulose
lactulose.summary: Lactulose is a laxative used to treat constipation, and it is also used for hepatic encephalopathy, a condition caused by severe liver disease. The NHS says it draws water into the bowel to make poo softer, and that it takes at least 2 days to work.
usedFor: Treating constipation.
Treating hepatic encephalopathy, a condition caused by severe liver disease.
lactulose.howItWorks: The NHS says lactulose relieves constipation by drawing water into the bowel, which makes poo softer. The NHS says osmotic laxatives such as lactulose and macrogol draw water into the bowel to soften poo and make it easier to pass.

common: The NHS says diarrhoea, particularly with high amounts, is a very common side effect.
Bloating and wind are also common, and these effects are usually mild and do not last long.
serious: The NHS says serious side effects are rare, and that anaphylaxis, a serious allergic reaction, is possible in rare cases.
Long-term use can lead to prolonged diarrhoea and an imbalance of body salts (electrolytes).
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.

cautions: The NHS says most people aged 14 and over can use lactulose, and that children under 14 need a doctor to prescribe it.
The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to lactulose or a similar medicine and galactosaemia as reasons it may not be suitable.
Irritable bowel syndrome, diverticular disease, Crohn's disease and a bowel blockage that is not caused by constipation are conditions where the NHS advises checking first.
The NHS says lactulose increases gas and bloating, which can make IBS worse.

The NHS says normal amounts of lactulose for constipation should have little or no effect on blood sugar, but long-term high amounts, such as those used for liver-related brain problems, may affect it.
The NHS says lactulose can be taken during pregnancy and is not harmful to the baby, and that breastfeeding is fine if a doctor or midwife says the baby is healthy.
The NHS says contraceptive pills may not protect against pregnancy if lactulose makes someone vomit or causes severe diarrhoea.
lactulose.monitoring: The NHS advises talking to a doctor or pharmacist if constipation does not improve. The NHS says that for hepatic encephalopathy a doctor may recommend taking lactulose for many months.

sections.heading: What is lactulose used for?
sections.body: The NHS lists two uses for lactulose: constipation and hepatic encephalopathy. The NHS describes hepatic encephalopathy as a condition caused by severe liver disease, and says lactulose helps the body clear toxins that build up when the liver is failing. The NHS says lactulose is available on prescription and can also be bought from pharmacies. Babies and children under 14 need a doctor to prescribe it, according to the NHS.

sections.heading: How does lactulose work, and how long does it take?
sections.body: Lactulose draws water into the bowel, which makes poo softer. It is slow-acting and takes at least 2 days to work. The NHS advises talking to a doctor or pharmacist if constipation does not improve. The NHS says osmotic laxatives such as lactulose and macrogol draw water into the bowel to soften poo and make it easier to pass.

sections.heading: Side effects and when to get help
sections.body: Diarrhoea, bloating and wind are the common side effects. They are usually mild and do not last long. Serious side effects are rare, but long-term use can cause prolonged diarrhoea and an imbalance of electrolytes. A serious allergic reaction is an emergency: call 999. For other worries, NHS 111 or a GP can advise.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with lactulose?
sections.body: Children under 14 need a doctor to prescribe it, according to the NHS. The NHS lists a past allergic reaction and galactosaemia as reasons lactulose may not be suitable. The NHS says people with irritable bowel syndrome, diverticular disease or Crohn's disease should check with a doctor or pharmacist first, and that lactulose increases gas and bloating, which can make IBS worse. The NHS says it can be taken during pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can lactulose be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says it is available on prescription and can be bought from pharmacies.

faqs.q: Does lactulose affect blood sugar?
faqs.a: The NHS says normal amounts of lactulose for constipation should have little or no effect on blood sugar, but long-term high amounts, such as those used for liver-related brain problems, may affect it.

faqs.q: Can lactulose be used for liver problems?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS lists hepatic encephalopathy, a liver disease that causes confusion, as one of its uses.

lactulose.onset: The NHS says lactulose is slow-acting and takes at least 2 days to work; if constipation does not improve, it advises talking to a doctor or pharmacist.

diazepam.name: Diazepam
diazepam.summary: Diazepam is a benzodiazepine, a type of medicine used to treat anxiety, muscle spasms and seizures. The NHS says it should only be used for the short term, and that longer use can cause addiction and withdrawal symptoms. It is a controlled drug in the UK, and the NHS advises against driving, cycling or using machinery while it affects alertness.
usedFor: Treating anxiety.
Treating muscle spasms.
Treating seizures.
diazepam.howItWorks: NHS Inform describes benzodiazepines as depressant drugs that slow down the central nervous system. The sources used for this page do not describe the mechanism in more detail.

common: The NHS lists feeling less alert, increased anxiety and depression, drowsiness, tiredness and low blood pressure as common side effects.
The NHS advises against alcohol and grapefruit juice while taking diazepam because they can increase the risk of side effects.
The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using tools or machinery while affected.
serious: Rare serious side effects listed by the NHS include a severe allergic reaction, slowed breathing and yellowing of the skin or eyes.
NHS Inform says stopping benzodiazepines suddenly can cause withdrawal effects that could be life-threatening.
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.

cautions: The NHS says taking diazepam for longer than the short term can cause addiction and withdrawal symptoms.
NHS Inform says tolerance can develop quickly and there is a risk of psychological and physical dependence.
The MHRA says dependence can occur with therapeutic doses of benzodiazepines and can become established within weeks.
NHS Inform says benzodiazepines slow the central nervous system, which increases the risk of overdose, particularly when combined with alcohol, gabapentinoids or opioids.

The NHS lists long-term kidney, liver, heart or breathing problems, certain mental health conditions, a history of alcohol or recreational drug misuse and a past allergic reaction to diazepam or any other medicine as reasons diazepam may not be suitable.

The NHS says diazepam should not be taken in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it. The manufacturer's patient leaflet says that if it is taken regularly during pregnancy, the baby may develop withdrawal symptoms.
The NHS says diazepam passes into breast milk in small amounts, and advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor before use while breastfeeding.
diazepam.monitoring: The NHS says diazepam should only be used for the short term, because longer use can cause addiction and withdrawal symptoms. Reducing use gradually is the approach NHS Inform describes after longer use, rather than stopping suddenly.

sections.heading: What is diazepam used for?
sections.body: The NHS says diazepam is a benzodiazepine used to treat anxiety, muscle spasms and seizures. It is available only on prescription. NHS Inform describes benzodiazepines as depressant drugs that slow down the central nervous system.

sections.heading: Dependence, withdrawal and stopping
sections.body: The NHS says diazepam should only be used for the short term, and that taking it for longer can cause addiction and withdrawal symptoms. NHS Inform says tolerance can develop quickly, with a risk of psychological and physical dependence. The MHRA says dependence can occur at therapeutic doses and can become established within weeks. If benzodiazepines are stopped suddenly, withdrawal effects can occur, and NHS Inform says these could be life-threatening. Because of this, reduction after longer use is gradual and planned with the prescriber; a GP appointment is the route, and NHS 111 or 999 if withdrawal symptoms are severe.

sections.heading: Driving, alcohol and side effects
sections.body: The NHS lists feeling less alert, drowsiness, tiredness and low blood pressure among common side effects. The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using tools or machinery while affected. Alcohol and grapefruit juice can increase the risk of side effects, according to the NHS. Rare serious side effects include a severe allergic reaction, slowed breathing and yellowing of the skin or eyes.

sections.heading: Controlled drug status and who needs extra care
sections.body: Diazepam is a Class C drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 and is in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001. The NHS lists long-term kidney, liver, heart or breathing problems, certain mental health conditions and a history of alcohol or drug misuse among the reasons for care. It is not advised in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist recommends it, and the manufacturer's patient leaflet says that regular use during pregnancy may cause withdrawal symptoms in the baby. NHS Inform warns that combining benzodiazepines with alcohol, gabapentinoids or opioids raises the risk of overdose.

faqs.q: How long can diazepam be taken?
faqs.a: The NHS says it should only be used for the short term, because longer use can cause addiction and withdrawal symptoms.

faqs.q: Is diazepam a controlled drug?
faqs.a: Yes. It is Class C under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 and in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001.

faqs.q: Can diazepam be drunk with alcohol?
faqs.a: The NHS advises against alcohol with diazepam because it can increase the risk of side effects.

zopiclone.name: Zopiclone
zopiclone.summary: Zopiclone is a medicine used to treat insomnia, usually prescribed for just 2 to 4 weeks. The NHS says the body gets used to it quickly and that dependence is possible with longer use, and it advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery for 12 hours after taking it. It is a controlled drug in the UK (Schedule 4 Part 1, Class C).
usedFor: Short-term treatment of insomnia in adults.
NICE says sleeping medicines such as zopiclone should be considered only for severe insomnia that interferes with daily life, and only for short periods.
zopiclone.howItWorks: The NHS says zopiclone boosts the effect of GABA, a calming chemical in the brain, which helps with sleep. The NHS says caffeine has the opposite effect to zopiclone in the body and stops it working.

common: The NHS lists a metallic or bitter taste, a dry mouth and daytime sleepiness as common side effects.
Some people have sleepwalked or made phone calls while asleep without remembering it afterwards, the NHS says.
The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery for 12 hours after taking zopiclone.
serious: The NHS says a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is a rare possible side effect of zopiclone.
The summary of product characteristics says treatment should stop immediately if a complex sleep behaviour such as sleepwalking occurs.
In an emergency the route to care is 999 or A&E; for an urgent concern that is not an emergency it is NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment, and for routine questions a GP appointment or a pharmacist.

cautions: The NHS says alcohol with zopiclone can cause very deep sleep, so that breathing is not normal and waking is very difficult.
The NHS says combining it with opioid painkillers or other sedating medicines can cause problems, and that cannabis, heroin or methadone can intensify its sedative effects.

The NHS says most adults over 18 can take zopiclone, and lists a past allergic reaction, liver or kidney problems, myasthenia gravis, breathing problems or sleep apnoea, a history of mental health problems and past alcohol or drug misuse as reasons for care.
A UK leaflet and the summary of product characteristics say it should not be used by anyone who has previously had complex sleep behaviours with it.
The NHS says taking it in pregnancy may cause drowsiness or withdrawal symptoms such as agitation or shaking in the newborn.
The NHS says zopiclone can be taken while breastfeeding if a doctor or health visitor confirms the baby is healthy, and that it is important not to share a bed with the baby while taking it.
The NHS says stopping suddenly can bring back insomnia, with anxiety and restlessness, although withdrawal symptoms are unlikely after less than a month of use.
zopiclone.monitoring: The NHS says zopiclone is usually prescribed for only 2 to 4 weeks, because the body gets used to it quickly. The summary of product characteristics says long-term use of zopiclone is not recommended, as with all sleeping medicines.

sections.heading: What is zopiclone used for?
sections.body: The NHS describes zopiclone as a medicine used to treat insomnia. The summary of product characteristics gives short-term treatment of insomnia in adults as its licensed use. The NHS says it is usually prescribed for only 2 to 4 weeks, because the body gets used to it quickly.

sections.heading: Dependence and stopping
sections.body: The NHS says someone taking zopiclone for up to 4 weeks is unlikely to become addicted, and may become dependent if it is taken for longer. The NHS says it should not be stopped suddenly without speaking to a doctor. Withdrawal can bring back insomnia, with anxiety and restlessness, but symptoms are unlikely in people who have taken it for less than a month. A GP appointment is the route for questions about stopping, and NHS 111 or 999 if symptoms are severe.

sections.heading: Driving, alcohol and sleep behaviours
sections.body: The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery for 12 hours after taking zopiclone. Alcohol with zopiclone can cause very deep sleep, with breathing that is not normal and great difficulty waking. Some people have sleepwalked or made phone calls while asleep, and the summary of product characteristics says treatment should stop immediately if a complex sleep behaviour happens. Caffeine has the opposite effect to zopiclone and can stop it working, the NHS says.

sections.heading: Side effects and who needs extra care
sections.body: Common side effects listed by the NHS are a metallic taste, a dry mouth and daytime sleepiness. The NHS says a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is a rare possible side effect of zopiclone. Liver or kidney problems, myasthenia gravis, breathing problems or sleep apnoea, a history of mental health problems and past alcohol or drug misuse are listed by the NHS as reasons for care. Zopiclone is a Class C drug in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations.

faqs.q: Is zopiclone addictive?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to zopiclone, and that people taking it for up to 4 weeks are unlikely to become addicted.

faqs.q: Is zopiclone a controlled drug?
faqs.a: Yes. It is Class C and in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations, from June 2014.

faqs.q: Can zopiclone be taken with alcohol?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol with zopiclone can cause very deep sleep with breathing problems and difficulty waking.

doxycycline.name: Doxycycline
doxycycline.summary: Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic, available on prescription, that is used to treat or prevent certain bacterial infections and to treat rosacea. The NHS says its most common side effects are headaches and feeling or being sick, that it can make skin sensitive to the sun, and that it is not recommended during pregnancy because it can affect a baby's tooth and bone development.
usedFor: Chest infections, dental infections and skin infections caused by bacteria
Sexually transmitted infections and some rarer infections
Rosacea, a long-term skin condition
Acne, where MedlinePlus says it acts on bacteria in the pores and reduces skin oil
Prevention of malaria in people travelling abroad
doxycycline.howItWorks: Doxycycline belongs to the tetracycline group of antibiotics. The NHS explains that it stops bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive. For rosacea, MedlinePlus describes a different effect, a reduction in inflammation of the skin.
doxycycline.onset: With most infections the NHS says people usually feel better within a few days, while rosacea responds more slowly.

common: Headaches
Feeling sick or being sick

Skin that is more sensitive to the sun; NHS advice is to cover up, wear a hat and sunglasses and use a high-factor sunscreen, and NHS England pharmacy guidance also describes avoiding direct sunlight and sunbeds
serious: A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is rare; the NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell or breathing becomes difficult

Pain or difficulty swallowing, a sore throat, heartburn or chest pain that gets worse with eating, which the NHS lists as possible signs of an inflamed or ulcerated food pipe; the NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected
A fingernail starting to come away from its base, which the NHS links to a reaction to sunlight

Rare effects listed by the NHS include inflammation of the bowel, changes in blood cells, liver problems, pancreatitis and raised pressure around the brain; the NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected

cautions: The NHS says doxycycline is usually taken by adults and children over 12; for some infections younger children can take it, and it can discolour teeth because it binds to calcium in growing bone and teeth

Previous allergic reaction to doxycycline or other medicines, kidney or liver problems, an inflamed food pipe (oesophagitis), lupus and myasthenia gravis are listed by the NHS among reasons doxycycline may not be suitable
It is not recommended during pregnancy because it can affect a baby's tooth and bone development, although a doctor may still advise it when the benefits outweigh the risks.

For breastfeeding, one NHS page says a short course may be possible once a doctor or health visitor has confirmed the baby is healthy, while another NHS page lists breastfeeding among reasons it may not be suitable; emc product information lists pregnancy and lactation as contraindications
Anticoagulants such as warfarin, antacids, acne medicines, and iron or zinc supplements are among the medicines the NHS says may not mix well with doxycycline
The NHS also lists products containing aluminium, bismuth, calcium or magnesium among those to mention to the prescriber, and local NHS leaflets differ on how far apart to space them from doxycycline
Emc product information says systemic retinoids such as isotretinoin should be avoided with doxycycline, because the combination raises the risk of raised pressure inside the skull
The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with doxycycline because it can stop it working properly
The NHS says doxycycline does not stop contraception working, but being sick or severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours may reduce the protection of contraceptive pills
doxycycline.monitoring: For rosacea the NHS says a doctor usually reviews progress after some weeks. With warfarin, emc product information for a doxycycline dispersible tablet reports a longer prothrombin time.

sections.heading: What is doxycycline used for?
sections.body:
Doxycycline is an antibiotic, a medicine that treats or prevents certain infections caused by bacteria. In the UK it is available only with a prescription. The NHS lists chest infections, dental infections and skin infections among the problems it treats, together with rosacea, sexually transmitted infections and some rarer infections. It can also be used to prevent malaria in people travelling abroad, and people taking it for that reason are not expected to feel any different.

MedlinePlus adds that it is used for acne, where it acts on the bacteria in the pores and lowers the amount of oil on the skin.

sections.heading: How does doxycycline work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
Doxycycline belongs to the tetracycline group of antibiotics. The NHS explains that it stops bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive. In rosacea, MedlinePlus describes a different benefit, a reduction in inflammation of the skin. With most infections people usually start to feel better within a few days, while rosacea responds more slowly and is normally reviewed by a doctor after some weeks.

Doxycycline comes as capsules, tablets and dispersible tablets, which are dissolved in water before they are taken. The NHS describes swallowing capsules and standard tablets whole with water and staying upright for a while afterwards. The NHS says taking it after a meal or snack, or with a drink of milk, may ease feeling sick. The NHS stresses that finishing the whole course matters, even when symptoms have eased.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of doxycycline?
sections.body:
The NHS says the most common side effects are headaches and feeling or being sick. Doxycycline can also make the skin sensitive to the sun. The NHS advises covering up, wearing a hat and sunglasses and using a high-factor sunscreen. NHS England pharmacy guidance also describes avoiding direct sunlight and ultraviolet light, including sunbeds and sun lamps. A fingernail that starts to come away from its base is listed among the serious effects and is linked to a reaction to sunlight.

The NHS lists pain or difficulty swallowing, a sore throat, heartburn and chest pain that worsens with eating as possible signs of an inflamed or ulcerated food pipe. The NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected. Serious allergic reactions are rare, and the NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell or breathing becomes difficult. Other rare effects include inflammation of the bowel, changes in blood cells, liver problems, pancreatitis and raised pressure around the brain.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with doxycycline?
sections.body:
The NHS says doxycycline is usually taken by adults and children over 12, and that younger children can take it for some infections. It can discolour teeth because it binds to calcium in growing bone and teeth. A previous allergic reaction to doxycycline or another medicine, kidney or liver problems, an inflamed food pipe (oesophagitis), lupus and myasthenia gravis are listed as reasons it may not be suitable. The NHS says a penicillin allergy is not a barrier, because doxycycline belongs to a different class of antibiotic.

The NHS does not recommend doxycycline during pregnancy because it can affect a baby's tooth and bone development, although a doctor may still advise it when the benefits outweigh the risks. For breastfeeding, one NHS page says a short course may be possible once a doctor or health visitor has confirmed the baby is healthy, while another NHS page lists breastfeeding among reasons it may not be suitable. Emc product information is stricter and lists pregnancy and lactation as contraindications. The NHS says doxycycline does not stop any type of contraception from working, but being sick or severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours may reduce the protection of contraceptive pills.

sections.heading: Doxycycline with other medicines and alcohol
sections.body: The NHS says anticoagulants such as warfarin, antacids, acne medicines, and iron or zinc supplements may not mix well with doxycycline. The NHS also lists products containing aluminium, bismuth, calcium or magnesium among those to mention to the prescriber, and local NHS leaflets differ on how far apart they should be spaced from doxycycline. Emc product information says systemic retinoids such as isotretinoin should be avoided with doxycycline, because the combination raises the risk of raised pressure inside the skull. With warfarin, emc product information for a doxycycline dispersible tablet reports a longer prothrombin time, a measure of how quickly blood clots. The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with doxycycline because it can stop it working properly. Apart from alcohol, the NHS says people can eat and drink normally while taking it.

faqs.q: Does doxycycline stop contraception from working?
faqs.a: The NHS says doxycycline does not stop any type of contraception from working. The exception is being sick or having severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours, which may mean contraceptive pills do not protect against pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can people drink alcohol while taking doxycycline?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with doxycycline, because alcohol can stop it working properly. Apart from that, it says people can eat and drink normally while taking it.

faqs.q: Does doxycycline make skin more sensitive to the sun?
faqs.a: Yes, the NHS says doxycycline can make the skin sensitive to the sun and advises covering up and using a high-factor sunscreen. NHS England pharmacy guidance also describes avoiding direct sunlight and sunbeds.

faqs.q: Can doxycycline be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS does not recommend it during pregnancy because it can affect a baby's tooth and bone development, though a doctor may still advise it when the benefits outweigh the risks. For breastfeeding, one NHS page says a short course may be possible once a doctor or health visitor has confirmed the baby is healthy, while another lists breastfeeding as a reason it may not be suitable.

faqs.q: How quickly does doxycycline start to work?
faqs.a: For most infections the NHS says people usually feel better within a few days, though the full course still matters. Rosacea responds more slowly and is usually reviewed by a doctor after some weeks, and people taking it to prevent malaria are not expected to feel any different.

faqs.q: Can people with a penicillin allergy take doxycycline?
faqs.a: The NHS says people allergic to penicillin can take doxycycline, because it belongs to a different class of antibiotic. A previous allergic reaction to doxycycline itself is a reason it may not be suitable.

flucloxacillin.name: Flucloxacillin
flucloxacillin.summary: A penicillin-type antibiotic, available on prescription, used for infections of the skin and wounds, bone infections and ear infections. It is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to a penicillin, and a serious allergic reaction is an emergency that needs a 999 call. Rarely it can affect the liver, sometimes after the course has ended.
usedFor: Skin and wound infections
Bone infections (osteomyelitis)
Ear infections
Impetigo and infected insect bites, which community pharmacists in England can supply it for under NHS patient group directions
flucloxacillin.howItWorks: Flucloxacillin kills the bacteria that cause the infection. As a penicillin, it works by damaging the cell wall that bacteria need to survive, which human cells do not have.
flucloxacillin.onset: The NHS says most infections should improve within a few days.

common: Feeling sick and diarrhoea are the main common effects, with bloating and indigestion; the NHS says these affect more than 1 in 100 people.
Simple meals and small sips of fluid are suggested by the NHS to help with an upset stomach and to avoid dehydration.
Being sick or having severe diarrhoea can make the combined pill or the progestogen-only pill less reliable, according to the NHS.
serious: Rarely, anaphylaxis (swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, severe breathing difficulty or fainting) is an emergency that needs a 999 call.
Yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes with pale stools and dark urine can signal liver problems; the NHS says to contact a GP or NHS 111 promptly.
Diarrhoea with blood or mucus, blistering or peeling skin, or unusual bruising also needs a GP or NHS 111 contact.
Some of these serious effects, including liver effects, can appear for up to two months after treatment has finished.

cautions: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to flucloxacillin, another penicillin-type antibiotic or any other medicine as a reason to check with a doctor or pharmacist first.
People with liver or kidney problems, and people who have recently had or are due a vaccination, are also listed for checking first.
Liver injury such as jaundice or hepatitis is a recognised risk; the NHS formulary says it is higher with longer courses and increasing age.
It can make the oral typhoid vaccine less effective.
Medicines to check about include methotrexate, warfarin, gout medicines such as probenecid, voriconazole and other antibiotics.
There is not enough information to say herbal remedies and supplements are free of interaction with it.
Very rarely, taking it with paracetamol has been linked to a blood and fluid imbalance (high anion gap metabolic acidosis).
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking it.
flucloxacillin.monitoring: NHS England pharmacy directions say people taking warfarin or similar anticoagulants should be advised to have their INR monitored during treatment, because rises in INR have been reported.
