sections.heading: What is the combined pill?
sections.body:
The combined pill is a hormonal contraceptive, often just called the pill. It contains two hormones, oestrogen and a progestogen. The emc lists UK brands as ethinylestradiol, an oestrogen, combined with a progestogen. Microgynon and Logynon contain levonorgestrel, Marvelon contains desogestrel, and Yasmin contains drospirenone.

The same two kinds of hormone are also given as a skin patch or a vaginal ring. The NHS says the pill is available from sexual health clinics, GP surgeries and young people's services. Some pharmacies can also supply it, without a prescription and free of charge, after a consultation with a pharmacist.

sections.heading: How does it work, and how well?
sections.body:
The pill mainly works by stopping the ovaries releasing an egg each month. It also makes the mucus from the cervix thicker, which makes it harder for sperm to pass. The NHS says the combined pill is more than 99% effective at preventing pregnancy when always used perfectly. Missed pills, vomiting or severe diarrhoea can make it less effective.

Some medicines and herbal remedies can also stop the pill working properly. The pill does not protect against sexually transmitted infections, so condoms are still needed for that.

sections.heading: What are the benefits and side effects?
sections.body:
The NHS says the pill usually makes periods regular, lighter and less painful, and that it may help with premenstrual syndrome and endometriosis. Bleeding between periods or changes to periods are common in the first few months. Headaches, mood changes, nausea and sore breasts are also listed.

The NHS says there is no evidence that the pill causes weight gain or changes sex drive. Taking the pill can cause high blood pressure in a small number of people. The NHS says the pill can slightly increase the risk of breast and cervical cancer and can lower the risk of womb, ovarian and bowel cancer. If side effects are still a problem after about three months, the NHS says to speak to a pharmacist or doctor, and a different pill may suit better.

sections.heading: Blood clots: what to know and where to go
sections.body:
The NHS lists the possible risks as a blood clot in the leg or lung, a clot causing a heart attack, or a clot causing a stroke. It describes the risk as very small, and a clinician checks risk factors before prescribing. The UK medicines regulator found that pills containing drospirenone, gestodene or desogestrel carry a higher relative risk than those containing levonorgestrel, norethisterone or norgestimate.

For a possible clot in the lung, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or fainting. Chest pain that is worse on breathing in, and coughing up blood, are also listed as symptoms. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for coughing up more than a few spots or streaks of blood, or coughing up blood with breathing difficulty or chest pain. A clot in the leg can cause throbbing pain, usually in the calf or thigh, and swelling in one leg. The NHS advises getting medical help as soon as possible, for example through an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

sections.heading: Who may not be able to use it?
sections.body:
The NHS says the combined pill is not suitable for everyone. Its list of conditions that may make it unsuitable includes a history of blood clots, migraine with aura, breast cancer, liver cancer or severe cirrhosis, complications of diabetes and heart problems. It also lists obesity, and smoking at older ages.

Some medicines can make the pill less effective, including some used for TB, epilepsy or HIV, and St John's wort. The NHS names the antibiotics rifampicin and rifabutin.

faqs.q: Does the combined pill protect against sexually transmitted infections?
faqs.a: No, the NHS says the combined pill does not protect against sexually transmitted infections, so condoms are still needed for that. Sexually transmitted infections, or STIs, are infections that pass from person to person through sexual contact.

faqs.q: Can the combined pill be obtained without seeing a GP?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is available from sexual health clinics, GP surgeries and young people's services. Some pharmacies can supply it without a prescription and free of charge after a consultation with a pharmacist, though not every pharmacy offers this.

faqs.q: What are the warning signs of a blood clot?
faqs.a: A clot in the lung can cause sudden difficulty breathing, chest pain that is worse on breathing in, and coughing up blood. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or fainting. A clot in the leg can cause throbbing pain, usually in the calf or thigh, and swelling in one leg, and the NHS advises getting medical help as soon as possible, for example through an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

faqs.q: Does the combined pill cause weight gain?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no evidence that taking the pill makes a person put on weight or changes sex drive. Headaches, mood changes, nausea and sore breasts are among the listed side effects. If side effects are still a problem after about three months, the NHS says to speak to a pharmacist or doctor, and changing pill may help.

faqs.q: Which medicines can stop the combined pill working?
faqs.a: The NHS says some antibiotics, such as rifampicin and rifabutin, can reduce its effectiveness. Medicines used for TB, epilepsy or HIV, and St John's wort, are also named as able to make the pill less effective.

faqs.q: Does the combined pill change the risk of cancer?
faqs.a: The NHS says the pill can slightly increase the risk of breast cancer and cervical cancer, and can lower the risk of womb, ovarian and bowel cancers. The NHS says the breast and cervical cancer risk goes back to normal about 10 years after stopping the pill.

aciclovir.name: Aciclovir
aciclovir.summary: Aciclovir is an antiviral medicine used for infections such as cold sores, shingles, chickenpox and genital herpes. The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely.
usedFor: Cold sores
Shingles
Chickenpox
Genital herpes
Herpes simplex eye infections
Preventing these infections in some people with a weakened immune system
aciclovir.howItWorks: Aciclovir is an antiviral medicine. The NHS says aciclovir stops the herpes virus growing and spreading, which helps the immune system deal with the infection. MedlinePlus describes aciclovir as a synthetic nucleoside analogue antiviral that works by stopping the spread of the herpes virus in the body. The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely.
aciclovir.onset: The NHS says people should start to feel better after taking or using aciclovir for a few days, and advises starting as soon as the first signs of infection appear.

common: The NHS lists headache, dizziness or feeling faint, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, stomach ache, rash, itching, tiredness, a high temperature and a skin reaction after exposure to light as common side effects, which are usually mild.
The NHS says creams are less likely to cause side effects, though some people get mild burning or stinging that usually goes away quickly.
For a side effect that bothers someone or does not go away, the NHS suggests speaking to a pharmacist or doctor.
serious: A serious allergic reaction, with signs such as sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or struggling to breathe, needs a 999 call, according to the NHS.

Liver problems, kidney problems and changes to blood cells are also listed as serious side effects; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 if someone using or recently using aciclovir thinks they may be having these.

cautions: The NHS advises telling a doctor before use about kidney problems, being over 65, being pregnant or trying to get pregnant, or breastfeeding.
UK product information lists allergy to aciclovir or valaciclovir as a reason the medicine is not used.
UK patient leaflets say the doctor may adjust treatment for children, people over 65 and people with kidney problems.
For people with a weakened immune system, such as HIV or AIDS or a bone marrow transplant, the NHS advises talking to a doctor about the best type of aciclovir.
UK product information says cimetidine and probenecid can raise aciclovir levels in the blood, and that aciclovir may raise theophylline levels.

The NHS says there is not enough information to show that herbal remedies or supplements are safe to take with aciclovir, and that they are not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking aciclovir.
aciclovir.monitoring: Aciclovir is cleared through the kidneys, so the prescriber may adjust treatment for people with kidney problems.
regimenNote: The NHS describes tablets, a liquid to swallow, an eye ointment, a cold sore cream and a genital herpes cream; injections are usually given only in hospital. Cold sore cream can be bought at most pharmacies and shops without a prescription.

sections.heading: What is aciclovir used for?
sections.body: Aciclovir is an antiviral medicine. The NHS says it is used to treat infections such as cold sores, shingles, chickenpox and genital herpes, as well as herpes simplex infections of the eye. It is sometimes used to prevent these infections in people with a weakened immune system. The NHS describes tablets, a liquid to swallow, an eye ointment, a cold sore cream and a genital herpes cream; injections are usually given only in hospital. The NHS says cold sore cream can be bought at most pharmacies and shops without a prescription. Children can usually use the cream or ointment, and may be prescribed tablets for chickenpox and shingles.

sections.heading: How does aciclovir work?
sections.body: The NHS says aciclovir stops the herpes virus growing and spreading, which helps the immune system deal with the infection. MedlinePlus describes aciclovir as a synthetic nucleoside analogue antiviral that works by stopping the spread of the herpes virus in the body. The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely. MedlinePlus says acyclovir does not cure cold sores or genital herpes, does not prevent outbreaks of them and does not stop their spread to other people. The NHS says people should start to feel better after taking or using aciclovir for a few days, and advises starting as soon as the first signs of infection appear. The NHS advises avoiding kissing and oral sex while a person or their partner has a cold sore, until the sores have healed, to reduce the risk of passing on the infection.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of aciclovir?
sections.body: The NHS lists headache, dizziness or feeling faint, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, stomach ache, rash, itching, tiredness, a high temperature and a skin reaction after exposure to light as common side effects, which are usually mild. The NHS says creams are less likely to cause side effects, though some people get mild burning or stinging that usually goes away quickly. For a side effect that bothers someone or does not go away, the NHS suggests speaking to a pharmacist or doctor. A serious allergic reaction, with signs such as sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or struggling to breathe, needs a 999 call, according to the NHS. Liver problems, kidney problems and changes to blood cells are also listed as serious side effects; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 if someone using or recently using aciclovir thinks they may be having these.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with aciclovir?
sections.body: The NHS advises telling a doctor before use about kidney problems, being over 65, being pregnant or trying to get pregnant, or breastfeeding. UK product information lists allergy to aciclovir or valaciclovir as a reason the medicine is not used. UK patient leaflets say the doctor may adjust treatment for children, people over 65 and people with kidney problems. For people with a weakened immune system, such as HIV or AIDS or a bone marrow transplant, the NHS advises talking to a doctor about the best type of aciclovir. Aciclovir is cleared through the kidneys, so the prescriber may adjust treatment for people with kidney problems.

sections.heading: Aciclovir with other medicines and alcohol
sections.body: UK product information says cimetidine and probenecid can raise aciclovir levels in the blood, and that aciclovir may raise theophylline levels. The NHS says there is not enough information to show that herbal remedies or supplements are safe to take with aciclovir, and that they are not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking aciclovir.

faqs.q: Does aciclovir cure cold sores or herpes?
faqs.a: The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely. MedlinePlus says acyclovir does not cure cold sores or genital herpes, does not prevent outbreaks of them and does not stop their spread to other people. The NHS says aciclovir stops the herpes virus growing and spreading, which helps the immune system deal with the infection.

faqs.q: How soon does aciclovir start to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says people should start to feel better after taking or using aciclovir for a few days, and advises starting as soon as the first signs of infection appear.

faqs.q: Can aciclovir cream be bought without a prescription?
faqs.a: The NHS says aciclovir cold sore cream can be bought at most pharmacies and shops without a prescription. A pharmacist can advise whether it suits the infection in question.

faqs.q: Can people drink alcohol while using aciclovir?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking aciclovir. A pharmacist or GP can answer questions about an individual situation.

faqs.q: Which medicines can affect aciclovir?
faqs.a: UK product information says cimetidine and probenecid can raise aciclovir levels in the blood, and that aciclovir may raise theophylline levels. The NHS says there is not enough information to show that herbal remedies or supplements are safe to take with aciclovir, and that they are not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines.

fluconazole.name: Fluconazole

The NHS says fluconazole kills the fungus causing the infection by making holes in the fungus's cell membrane so that the contents leak out. MedlinePlus describes fluconazole as slowing the growth of the fungi that cause infection. Azole antifungals block a step in the making of ergosterol, a main part of fungal cell membranes.
fluconazole.onset: The NHS says symptoms of vaginal thrush, balanitis or oral thrush should be better within a week, and that a serious fungal infection can take longer, 1 to 2 weeks, to work fully.

common: The NHS lists stomach pain or discomfort, diarrhoea, headache, feeling or being sick and rash as common side effects, with nausea and diarrhoea the most common.
Dizziness is uncommon; the NHS advises not driving or cycling until the feeling goes away.
The NHS says fluconazole is not likely to affect contraception, but vomiting or severe diarrhoea can mean contraceptive pills do not protect against pregnancy.
serious: A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), another hypersensitivity reaction or a severe skin reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome needs a 999 call, according to the NHS.

The NHS advises contraception for anyone who could become pregnant while taking fluconazole and for a short time after stopping, because the medicine could harm a baby or increase the chance of miscarriage.

For vaginal thrush or balanitis, the NHS says most adults and children aged 16 or over can take fluconazole, while younger children, and people 16 or over who need it for other conditions, can take it if a doctor prescribes it.

The NHS names pimozide, quetiapine, amisulpride, haloperidol, lithium, risperidone, escitalopram, venlafaxine, warfarin, dabigatran, clopidogrel and statins among medicines to discuss with a doctor before starting fluconazole.

sections.heading: What is fluconazole used for?
sections.body: Fluconazole is an antifungal medicine. The NHS says it is used to treat infections caused by different kinds of fungus. These include thrush in men and women, such as vaginal thrush, balanitis (inflammation of the head of the penis) and oral thrush, and a fungal brain infection called cryptococcal meningitis. It is also used to prevent fungal infections in people at high risk, such as those with HIV or a weakened immune system. The NHS says fluconazole is available on prescription and can also be bought from a pharmacy for vaginal thrush or balanitis. The NHS says pharmacy purchase covers vaginal thrush or balanitis; the brand names it gives include Azocan and Canesten Thrush Oral Capsules.

sections.heading: How does fluconazole work?
sections.body: The NHS says fluconazole kills the fungus causing the infection by making holes in the fungus's cell membrane so that the contents leak out. MedlinePlus describes fluconazole as slowing the growth of the fungi that cause infection. Azole antifungals block a step in the making of ergosterol, a main part of fungal cell membranes. The NHS says symptoms of vaginal thrush, balanitis or oral thrush should be better within a week, and that a serious fungal infection can take longer, 1 to 2 weeks, to work fully. The NHS advises seeing a doctor if symptoms of thrush are not better within the expected time. The NHS describes capsules or a liquid to swallow, and says the length of treatment depends on the kind of infection.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of fluconazole?

The NHS says fluconazole is not likely to affect contraception, but vomiting or severe diarrhoea can mean contraceptive pills do not protect against pregnancy. A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), another hypersensitivity reaction or a severe skin reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome needs a 999 call, according to the NHS. Liver problems can show as itching, darker urine, pale stools or yellowing of the skin or eyes, which may be harder to see on black or brown skin; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 for any other serious side effect.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with fluconazole?
sections.body: The NHS lists an allergic reaction or serious side effect from fluconazole or another antifungal, liver or kidney problems, heart problems including rhythm problems, abnormal potassium, calcium or magnesium levels, and porphyria (a rare blood condition) as reasons fluconazole may not be suitable. For vaginal thrush or balanitis, the NHS says most adults and children aged 16 or over can take fluconazole, while younger children, and people 16 or over who need it for other conditions, can take it if a doctor prescribes it. The NHS says fluconazole is not usually recommended in pregnancy but may be used if the benefits outweigh the risks. The NHS advises contraception for anyone who could become pregnant while taking fluconazole and for a short time after stopping, because the medicine could harm a baby or increase the chance of miscarriage. UK product information says prothrombin time, a blood clotting test, should be carefully monitored in people taking warfarin-type anticoagulants with fluconazole.

sections.heading: Fluconazole with other medicines and alcohol
sections.body: The NHS names pimozide, quetiapine, amisulpride, haloperidol, lithium, risperidone, escitalopram, venlafaxine, warfarin, dabigatran, clopidogrel and statins among medicines to discuss with a doctor before starting fluconazole. A pharmacist or doctor can say whether a particular combination causes problems. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking fluconazole.

faqs.q: Can fluconazole be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says fluconazole is not usually recommended in pregnancy but may be used if the benefits outweigh the risks. Anyone who is pregnant or might be pregnant is asked to speak to a pharmacist or doctor first.

faqs.q: Can fluconazole be bought from a pharmacy?
faqs.a: The NHS says fluconazole is available on prescription and can also be bought from a pharmacy for vaginal thrush or balanitis. For vaginal thrush or balanitis, the NHS says most adults and children aged 16 or over can take fluconazole, while younger children, and people 16 or over who need it for other conditions, can take it if a doctor prescribes it.

faqs.q: How long does fluconazole take to work for thrush?
faqs.a: The NHS says symptoms of vaginal thrush, balanitis or oral thrush should be better within a week, and that a serious fungal infection can take longer, 1 to 2 weeks, to work fully.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk during fluconazole treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking fluconazole. Dizziness is uncommon; the NHS advises not driving or cycling until the feeling goes away.

hydroxychloroquine.name: Hydroxychloroquine
hydroxychloroquine.summary: Hydroxychloroquine is a medicine used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and some skin conditions. With long-term use it can cause changes in the retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, and the Royal College of Ophthalmologists says this is more common than previously reported. NRAS advises contacting the GP or specialist team about any change in vision while taking it.
usedFor: Rheumatoid arthritis
Lupus
Some skin conditions
hydroxychloroquine.howItWorks: The NHS describes it as a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) that works by blocking the effects of chemicals released when the immune system attacks the body. Reviews describe it building up inside small compartments of cells called lysosomes, which disrupts how immune cells process and present antigens, and one review notes that its exact mechanism has not been fully worked out.
hydroxychloroquine.onset: The NHS says it may take several weeks before improvement is noticed, and Versus Arthritis describes it as slow-acting.

common: The NHS lists stomach ache, feeling or being sick, loss of appetite, diarrhoea, headache, an itchy rash and mood changes among the possible side effects.
Blurred vision can occur when treatment starts, and the NHS says to avoid driving, cycling or using machinery until vision is back to normal.
serious: The NHS says most serious side effects are rare.
The NHS says to contact a doctor or call NHS 111 straight away about eye problems, such as constant blurred vision, sensitivity to light or changes in how colours look.

The NHS also lists severe skin reactions such as blistering or peeling, liver problems such as yellow skin or dark urine, unusual infections or bruising, symptoms of low blood sugar, and mood changes including thoughts of self-harm, and says to call NHS 111 about them.
The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if breathing becomes very fast or difficult.

cautions: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to hydroxychloroquine or similar medicines, such as quinine, as a reason it may not be suitable.
The NHS lists liver, kidney, blood or heart problems, maculopathy or other eye problems, diabetes and psoriasis as conditions that may make it unsuitable or need care.
Versus Arthritis says it is not usually prescribed to people with maculopathy, a problem with the central part of the retina.
The NHS says it is not considered an immunosuppressant but may lower white blood cell numbers, which can make infections more likely.
The NHS pregnancy page says it is recommended to keep taking hydroxychloroquine during pregnancy, because inflammatory conditions that are not well treated can affect the baby.

The NHS says that if the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, hydroxychloroquine can be taken while breastfeeding; it passes into breast milk in very small amounts and has not been known to cause side effects in breastfed babies.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking hydroxychloroquine.

The NHS has a page on taking it with other medicines and herbal supplements; it says antacids can affect how well it is absorbed and that there is not enough information on herbal remedies and supplements.
Versus Arthritis says to report new eye symptoms to a doctor straight away.
hydroxychloroquine.monitoring: Long-term use is monitored, which can include blood counts and eye examinations. The Royal College of Ophthalmologists no longer recommends a routine baseline eye test for people starting treatment. The guidance recommends regular eye monitoring after several years of treatment.

sections.heading: What is hydroxychloroquine used for and how does it work?
sections.body: Hydroxychloroquine is a medicine used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and some skin conditions. It is available only on prescription. MedlinePlus places it in a group of medicines called antimalarials and also describes it as an antirheumatic drug. The NHS describes it as a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) that works by blocking the effects of chemicals released when the immune system attacks the body. Versus Arthritis says it is not a painkiller. Reviews describe it building up inside small compartments of cells called lysosomes, which disrupts how immune cells process and present antigens, and one review notes that its exact mechanism has not been fully worked out. The NHS says it may take several weeks before improvement is noticed, and Versus Arthritis describes it as slow-acting. The NHS advises that feeling better is not on its own a reason to stop treatment.

sections.heading: What are the side effects?
sections.body:
The NHS lists stomach ache, feeling or being sick, loss of appetite, diarrhoea, headache, an itchy rash and mood changes among the possible side effects. Blurred vision can occur when treatment starts, and the NHS says to avoid driving, cycling or using machinery until vision is back to normal.

The NHS says most serious side effects are rare. The NHS says to contact a doctor or call NHS 111 straight away about eye problems, such as constant blurred vision, sensitivity to light or changes in how colours look. The NHS also lists severe skin reactions such as blistering or peeling, liver problems such as yellow skin or dark urine, unusual infections or bruising, symptoms of low blood sugar, and mood changes including thoughts of self-harm, and says to call NHS 111 about them. The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if breathing becomes very fast or difficult.

sections.heading: Why are regular eye checks needed?
sections.body:
With long-term use it can cause changes in the retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, and the Royal College of Ophthalmologists says this is more common than previously reported. A review says early damage to the retina often comes before changes in vision, so eye checks are used to look for it, and it can result in permanent loss of vision. The Royal College of Ophthalmologists describes the retinal changes as largely irreversible, and they can continue to progress after the medicine is stopped.

The Royal College says extra risk factors, such as tamoxifen use, reduced kidney function or a higher daily dose, can justify eye monitoring from the start of treatment, as decided by the prescriber. Its guidance describes monitoring with retinal imaging such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans. The Royal College of Ophthalmologists no longer recommends a routine baseline eye test for people starting treatment. The guidance recommends regular eye monitoring after several years of treatment. A 2026 summary from the Royal College says retinopathy is more common than previously reported. Versus Arthritis advises telling an optician about hydroxychloroquine and having regular eye check-ups. NRAS advises contacting the GP or specialist team about any change in vision while taking it. Versus Arthritis says to report new eye symptoms to a doctor straight away.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about pregnancy or other medicines?
sections.body:
The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to hydroxychloroquine or similar medicines, such as quinine, as a reason it may not be suitable. The NHS lists liver, kidney, blood or heart problems, maculopathy or other eye problems, diabetes and psoriasis as conditions that may make it unsuitable or need care. Versus Arthritis says it is not usually prescribed to people with maculopathy, a problem with the central part of the retina. The NHS says it is not considered an immunosuppressant but may lower white blood cell numbers, which can make infections more likely.

The NHS pregnancy page says it is recommended to keep taking hydroxychloroquine during pregnancy, because inflammatory conditions that are not well treated can affect the baby. The NHS says that if the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, hydroxychloroquine can be taken while breastfeeding; it passes into breast milk in very small amounts and has not been known to cause side effects in breastfed babies. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking hydroxychloroquine. The NHS has a page on taking it with other medicines and herbal supplements; it says antacids can affect how well it is absorbed and that there is not enough information on herbal remedies and supplements.

faqs.q: Does hydroxychloroquine affect the eyes?
faqs.a: With long-term use it can cause changes in the retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, and the Royal College of Ophthalmologists says this is more common than previously reported. The Royal College of Ophthalmologists describes the retinal changes as largely irreversible, and they can continue to progress after the medicine is stopped. Versus Arthritis advises telling an optician about hydroxychloroquine and having regular eye check-ups. The NHS says to contact a doctor or call NHS 111 straight away about eye problems, such as constant blurred vision, sensitivity to light or changes in how colours look. Versus Arthritis says to report new eye symptoms to a doctor straight away.

faqs.q: How long does hydroxychloroquine take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says it may take several weeks before improvement is noticed, and Versus Arthritis describes it as slow-acting. The NHS advises that feeling better is not on its own a reason to stop treatment. Versus Arthritis says it is not a painkiller.

faqs.q: Can hydroxychloroquine be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS pregnancy page says it is recommended to keep taking hydroxychloroquine during pregnancy, because inflammatory conditions that are not well treated can affect the baby. The NHS says that if the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, hydroxychloroquine can be taken while breastfeeding; it passes into breast milk in very small amounts and has not been known to cause side effects in breastfed babies.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk, and what about other medicines?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking hydroxychloroquine. The NHS has a page on taking it with other medicines and herbal supplements; it says antacids can affect how well it is absorbed and that there is not enough information on herbal remedies and supplements. The NHS says it is not considered an immunosuppressant but may lower white blood cell numbers, which can make infections more likely.

methotrexate.name: Methotrexate
methotrexate.summary: Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant used for inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and Crohn's disease, and sometimes for cancer. When it is used for autoimmune conditions such as these, it is taken once a week, not every day. Taking it daily by mistake instead of weekly has caused overdoses that were sometimes fatal. The NHS says to contact NHS 111 right away if more methotrexate than prescribed has been taken, including taking it daily instead of weekly.
usedFor: Rheumatoid arthritis
Psoriasis
Crohn's disease
Some cancers
methotrexate.howItWorks: The NHS says it calms the immune system and helps reduce inflammation. Methotrexate blocks an enzyme called dihydrofolate reductase, which the body uses to make tetrahydrofolate, a form of folate needed to build DNA and RNA. In inflammatory conditions, how low-dose methotrexate works is less clear.
methotrexate.onset: The NHS says it can take a few months to notice any benefit, and that the medicine is likely to be working during that time.

common: The NHS says the skin may become very sensitive to sunlight. Hospital leaflets list nausea or stomach upset, loss of appetite, diarrhoea, headache and tiredness among the more common side effects.
Hair loss can happen and is not likely to be permanent, according to the NHS.
Versus Arthritis says folic acid tablets are usually prescribed to help reduce unpleasant effects of methotrexate.
serious: The NHS says serious side effects are rare.

The NHS says to contact a doctor or NHS 111 straight away about yellow skin or eyes, which can be a sign of liver problems, or a new cough, chest pain or breathlessness, which can be a sign of lung inflammation.
The same NHS list includes signs of infection, such as a high temperature or sore throat, and signs of a blood problem, such as bleeding gums, blood in the urine or unexplained bruising.
The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell or breathing becomes fast or difficult.
Versus Arthritis says methotrexate can affect the liver and lower the number of blood cells made, which is why regular blood tests are done.
The NHS says to contact NHS 111 right away if more methotrexate than prescribed has been taken, including taking it daily instead of weekly.

cautions: When it is used for autoimmune conditions such as these, it is taken once a week, not every day.
Taking it daily by mistake instead of weekly has caused overdoses that were sometimes fatal.

The MHRA says oral methotrexate products used once weekly now come with a patient card that prompts weekly dosing, records the chosen weekday, and is carried to show clinicians who do not know the person's treatment.

The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to methotrexate, severe liver or kidney disease, a blood disorder, an active infection, mouth or stomach ulcers, pregnancy and breastfeeding among reasons it may not be suitable.
The NHS says methotrexate may lower the number of white cells in the blood, which can make infections more likely.
The NHS says to ask a doctor for urgent advice after contact with someone who has chickenpox or shingles.
The NHS says methotrexate is not recommended in pregnancy because it can cause birth defects, and advises speaking to a doctor before trying to get pregnant.
The NHS pregnancy page says methotrexate may affect sperm in men and egg production in women.
NHS hospital guidance advises effective contraception during treatment and for some months afterwards, and the length of time differs between sources.
The NHS says tiny amounts of methotrexate pass into breast milk, and lists breastfeeding among situations where it may not be suitable.
The NHS says it is usually fine to drink alcohol with a low weekly amount of methotrexate, and to ask a doctor if taking a higher amount.
Live vaccines are not recommended during treatment.
NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can increase the risk of methotrexate toxicity, so they are used only on specialist advice.
Trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole are advised against because of the risk of severe bone marrow suppression.
methotrexate.monitoring: Versus Arthritis says blood tests of the blood count, kidney function and liver function are needed before starting, are more frequent at first and become less frequent once treatment is steady. The NHS says a chest X-ray and breathing test may be done before starting. The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service monitoring page lists hepatitis B among the checks before starting.
regimenNote: Methotrexate is available as tablets, an oral liquid and pre-filled injection pens, and for autoimmune conditions it is taken once a week, not daily.

sections.heading: What is methotrexate used for, and how does it work?
sections.body:
Methotrexate is an immunosuppressant used for inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and Crohn's disease, and sometimes for cancer. It is available only on prescription. The NHS says it calms the immune system and helps reduce inflammation. It is not a painkiller, although there may be less pain as symptoms improve. The NHS says it can take a few months to notice any benefit, and that the medicine is likely to be working during that time.

Methotrexate blocks an enzyme called dihydrofolate reductase, which the body uses to make tetrahydrofolate, a form of folate needed to build DNA and RNA. In inflammatory conditions, how low-dose methotrexate works is less clear. Proposed explanations include effects on adenosine release, inflammatory signals and the growth of lymphocytes.

sections.heading: Why is weekly dosing so important?
sections.body: When it is used for autoimmune conditions such as these, it is taken once a week, not every day. Taking it daily by mistake instead of weekly has caused overdoses that were sometimes fatal. In 2020 the MHRA introduced new measures to reduce the risk of fatal overdose from accidental daily dosing. The MHRA says oral methotrexate products used once weekly now come with a patient card that prompts weekly dosing, records the chosen weekday, and is carried to show clinicians who do not know the person's treatment. Prescribers are asked to write the weekday in full on the prescription. The NHS says to contact NHS 111 right away if more methotrexate than prescribed has been taken, including taking it daily instead of weekly.

sections.heading: What are the side effects?
sections.body:
The NHS says the skin may become very sensitive to sunlight. Hospital leaflets list nausea or stomach upset, loss of appetite, diarrhoea, headache and tiredness among the more common side effects. Hair loss can happen and is not likely to be permanent, according to the NHS. Versus Arthritis says folic acid tablets are usually prescribed to help reduce unpleasant effects of methotrexate.

The NHS says serious side effects are rare. The NHS says to contact a doctor or NHS 111 straight away about yellow skin or eyes, which can be a sign of liver problems, or a new cough, chest pain or breathlessness, which can be a sign of lung inflammation. The same NHS list includes signs of infection, such as a high temperature or sore throat, and signs of a blood problem, such as bleeding gums, blood in the urine or unexplained bruising. The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell or breathing becomes fast or difficult. Versus Arthritis says methotrexate can affect the liver and lower the number of blood cells made, which is why regular blood tests are done.

sections.heading: Which tests are needed?
sections.body:
Versus Arthritis says blood tests of the blood count, kidney function and liver function are needed before starting, are more frequent at first and become less frequent once treatment is steady. The NHS says a chest X-ray and breathing test may be done before starting. The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service monitoring page lists hepatitis B among the checks before starting.

The NHS says methotrexate may lower the number of white cells in the blood, which can make infections more likely. The NHS says to ask a doctor for urgent advice after contact with someone who has chickenpox or shingles.

sections.heading: What about pregnancy and contraception?
sections.body: The NHS says methotrexate is not recommended in pregnancy because it can cause birth defects, and advises speaking to a doctor before trying to get pregnant. The NHS pregnancy page says methotrexate may affect sperm in men and egg production in women. NHS hospital guidance advises effective contraception during treatment and for some months afterwards, and the length of time differs between sources. The NHS says tiny amounts of methotrexate pass into breast milk, and lists breastfeeding among situations where it may not be suitable.

sections.heading: Taking methotrexate with other medicines, alcohol and vaccines
sections.body: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to methotrexate, severe liver or kidney disease, a blood disorder, an active infection, mouth or stomach ulcers, pregnancy and breastfeeding among reasons it may not be suitable. The NHS says it is usually fine to drink alcohol with a low weekly amount of methotrexate, and to ask a doctor if taking a higher amount. Live vaccines are not recommended during treatment. NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can increase the risk of methotrexate toxicity, so they are used only on specialist advice. Trimethoprim and co-trimoxazole are advised against because of the risk of severe bone marrow suppression.

faqs.q: Why does methotrexate need to be taken weekly rather than daily?
faqs.a: When it is used for autoimmune conditions such as these, it is taken once a week, not every day. Taking it daily by mistake instead of weekly has caused overdoses that were sometimes fatal. The NHS says to contact NHS 111 right away if more methotrexate than prescribed has been taken, including taking it daily instead of weekly.

faqs.q: Is methotrexate suitable in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says methotrexate is not recommended in pregnancy because it can cause birth defects, and advises speaking to a doctor before trying to get pregnant. The NHS pregnancy page says methotrexate may affect sperm in men and egg production in women. NHS hospital guidance advises effective contraception during treatment and for some months afterwards, and the length of time differs between sources.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk with methotrexate?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is usually fine to drink alcohol with a low weekly amount of methotrexate, and to ask a doctor if taking a higher amount.

faqs.q: Why are regular blood tests needed?
faqs.a: Versus Arthritis says blood tests of the blood count, kidney function and liver function are needed before starting, are more frequent at first and become less frequent once treatment is steady. Versus Arthritis says methotrexate can affect the liver and lower the number of blood cells made, which is why regular blood tests are done.

faqs.q: What should be done about chickenpox or shingles contact?
faqs.a: The NHS says methotrexate may lower the number of white cells in the blood, which can make infections more likely. The NHS says to ask a doctor for urgent advice after contact with someone who has chickenpox or shingles.

montelukast.name: Montelukast
montelukast.summary: Montelukast is a prescription medicine that helps prevent asthma symptoms. The MHRA warns that montelukast can cause neuropsychiatric reactions, including sleep disorders, hallucinations and changes in behaviour and mood. The MHRA advises patients to speak to their prescriber immediately, or seek urgent medical attention, if these reactions occur.

StatPearls describes it as blocking leukotriene effects such as airway swelling and smooth muscle contraction, without any stimulating action of its own. StatPearls says eosinophils are the main source of cysteinyl leukotrienes, which are important in recruiting more eosinophils.

The NHS gives self-care advice for these, such as fluids and rest, and says a pharmacist can advise.
Asthma and Lung UK says montelukast has been linked to depression and anxiety and describes mental health side effects as rare but serious.
serious: The NHS lists mood changes, hallucinations, sleep problems, speech changes such as stuttering and shaking or trembling among serious side effects.
An unusual or fast heartbeat, and yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, which can be a sign of liver problems, are also listed.

The NHS says to call 999 for swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or difficulty breathing, which can signal a serious allergic reaction.

Asthma and Lung UK advises talking to a GP or asthma nurse as soon as possible if montelukast affects sleep or mood.
For thoughts of suicide or self-harm, the usual routes are 999 if in immediate danger, NHS 111 (mental health option) or Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time.

sections.heading: What is montelukast and how does it work?
sections.body:
Montelukast is a prescription medicine that helps prevent asthma symptoms. Asthma and Lung UK describes montelukast as an add-on taken alongside the regular preventer inhaler, and the NHS says it is usually prescribed when asthma is mild. The NHS says montelukast is not a rescue treatment and a reliever inhaler is used for an asthma attack. The NHS advises speaking to a doctor before stopping montelukast, because symptoms may return. The NHS and Asthma and Lung UK say it is also used when exercise or seasonal allergies trigger breathing difficulties. Asthma and Lung UK says it can improve symptoms of seasonal allergies such as hay fever. The NHS says most adults and children aged 6 months and over can take montelukast. The NHS describes tablets, chewable tablets and granules taken by mouth.

Asthma and Lung UK describes montelukast as working in a different way from steroid preventer inhalers. Montelukast blocks cysteinyl leukotriene type 1 receptors, which respond to leukotrienes. StatPearls describes it as blocking leukotriene effects such as airway swelling and smooth muscle contraction, without any stimulating action of its own. StatPearls says eosinophils are the main source of cysteinyl leukotrienes, which are important in recruiting more eosinophils.

sections.heading: Side effects
sections.body: Common side effects listed by the NHS include diarrhoea, a raised temperature, headaches, stomach pain, feeling or being sick and a mild rash. The NHS gives self-care advice for these, such as fluids and rest, and says a pharmacist can advise. Asthma and Lung UK says montelukast has been linked to depression and anxiety and describes mental health side effects as rare but serious. The NHS lists mood changes, hallucinations, sleep problems, speech changes such as stuttering and shaking or trembling among serious side effects. An unusual or fast heartbeat, and yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes, which can be a sign of liver problems, are also listed. For mood changes such as becoming anxious, depressed or aggressive, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 immediately. The NHS says to call 999 for swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or difficulty breathing, which can signal a serious allergic reaction.

sections.heading: Mood, behaviour and sleep: the MHRA warning
sections.body:
The MHRA warns that montelukast can cause neuropsychiatric reactions, including sleep disorders, hallucinations and changes in behaviour and mood. After a review, the MHRA said the risk is unchanged but is probably not well known to healthcare professionals, patients and carers, judging by Yellow Card reports. It said more prominent warnings would be added to the leaflet supplied with every pack, and its April 2024 Drug Safety Update says the warnings in the patient leaflet and product information have been strengthened and highlighted with a black box. The MHRA advises patients to speak to their prescriber immediately, or seek urgent medical attention, if these reactions occur. Prescribers are advised to stop montelukast if new or worsening neuropsychiatric symptoms appear. The MHRA encourages patients, carers and healthcare professionals to report suspected side effects to the Yellow Card scheme.

Asthma and Lung UK advises talking to a GP or asthma nurse as soon as possible if montelukast affects sleep or mood. Asthma and Lung UK lists thoughts of suicide or self-harm as a very rare side effect. For thoughts of suicide or self-harm, the usual routes are 999 if in immediate danger, NHS 111 (mental health option) or Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, other medicines and who needs care
sections.body: The NHS says montelukast can be taken in pregnancy, that it is important asthma is well controlled, and that a doctor should be told if pregnancy happens, as they may review the medicine. The NHS says breastfeeding is possible if a doctor, health visitor or midwife says the baby is healthy; montelukast passes into breast milk in tiny amounts and has not been known to cause side effects in breastfed babies. The NHS asks anyone who has had an allergic reaction to montelukast or another medicine to tell the doctor. The NHS lists epilepsy medicines such as phenobarbital or phenytoin, rifampicin and gemfibrozil as medicines to mention to a doctor or pharmacist before taking montelukast. UK product information says some of these can change montelukast levels.

faqs.q: Can montelukast affect mood and behaviour?
faqs.a: The MHRA warns that montelukast can cause neuropsychiatric reactions, including sleep disorders, hallucinations and changes in behaviour and mood. After a review, the MHRA said the risk is unchanged but is probably not well known to healthcare professionals, patients and carers, judging by Yellow Card reports. The MHRA advises patients to speak to their prescriber immediately, or seek urgent medical attention, if these reactions occur.

faqs.q: Can montelukast be used for an asthma attack?
faqs.a: The NHS says montelukast is not a rescue treatment and a reliever inhaler is used for an asthma attack. The NHS advises speaking to a doctor before stopping montelukast, because symptoms may return.

faqs.q: Can montelukast be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says montelukast can be taken in pregnancy, that it is important asthma is well controlled, and that a doctor should be told if pregnancy happens, as they may review the medicine. The NHS says breastfeeding is possible if a doctor, health visitor or midwife says the baby is healthy; montelukast passes into breast milk in tiny amounts and has not been known to cause side effects in breastfed babies.

faqs.q: What is montelukast used for?
faqs.a: Montelukast is a prescription medicine that helps prevent asthma symptoms. The NHS and Asthma and Lung UK say it is also used when exercise or seasonal allergies trigger breathing difficulties. Asthma and Lung UK says it can improve symptoms of seasonal allergies such as hay fever.

faqs.q: What happens if mood or sleep changes appear?
faqs.a: The MHRA advises patients to speak to their prescriber immediately, or seek urgent medical attention, if these reactions occur. For mood changes such as becoming anxious, depressed or aggressive, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 immediately. Asthma and Lung UK advises talking to a GP or asthma nurse as soon as possible if montelukast affects sleep or mood. The MHRA encourages patients, carers and healthcare professionals to report suspected side effects to the Yellow Card scheme.

meta.name: Drug classes
meta.about: Drug classes: how a family of medicines works, what it targets in the body, which conditions it treats and which medications on this site belong to it. Educational, not prescribing advice.

calcium-channel-blockers.name: Calcium channel blockers
calcium-channel-blockers.summary: Medicines that relax the muscle in artery walls (and, for some members, slow the heart) by blocking the calcium channels those muscles need to contract. Used mainly for high blood pressure and angina.
calcium-channel-blockers.mechanism: Muscle cells contract when calcium enters through L-type channels in their membrane. Blocking the channel leaves arterial smooth muscle relaxed, so arteries widen, resistance falls and blood pressure drops; coronary arteries widen too, improving supply in angina. The dihydropyridines (amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine) act almost only on vessels. Verapamil and diltiazem also block the channels in the heart's conduction tissue and muscle, slowing the rate and reducing force, which makes them useful for fast rhythms but hazardous with beta blockers or in heart failure.
calcium-channel-blockers.target: L-type voltage-gated calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle and cardiac conducting tissue
classEffects: Ankle swelling, flushing and headache from vessel widening (dihydropyridines)
Slow heart rate, constipation and heart block risk (verapamil, diltiazem)
Gum overgrowth with long use
cautions: Verapamil and diltiazem should not be combined with beta blockers or used in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Grapefruit juice raises levels of several members
Severe aortic stenosis and unstable angina need specialist advice

classWarnings.text: Dihydropyridines cause dose-related ankle swelling, flushing and headache from vasodilation; verapamil and diltiazem slow the heart and can cause heart block and heart failure, and are not combined with beta blockers.

Contraindications differ by member: dihydropyridines (such as amlodipine) are not used in cardiogenic shock or significant aortic stenosis, and some also not in unstable angina; verapamil and diltiazem are not used in heart block, sick sinus syndrome, a very slow heart rate or heart failure. The leaflet or BNF entry for the individual medicine lists them.

classInteractions.effect: Amlodipine, diltiazem and verapamil raise simvastatin levels and the risk of myopathy; the simvastatin dose is limited (20 mg with amlodipine).

classInteractions.with: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, some HIV medicines) and grapefruit
classInteractions.effect: Raise calcium channel blocker levels, increasing hypotension and oedema.
Additive slowing of the heart and negative inotropy: bradycardia, heart block, heart failure; the combination is avoided.

ace-inhibitors.name: ACE inhibitors
ace-inhibitors.summary: Medicines ending in -pril that block the enzyme which makes angiotensin II, lowering blood pressure, unloading a failing heart and protecting the kidneys in diabetes.
ace-inhibitors.mechanism: The kidneys release renin when pressure or salt falls; renin makes angiotensin I, and angiotensin-converting enzyme in the lungs and vessels turns it into angiotensin II, which constricts arteries, releases aldosterone (salt and water retention) and thickens heart muscle. Blocking the enzyme removes all of these effects, and the pressure inside the kidney's filters falls, which slows the leak of protein in diabetic kidney disease. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, so it accumulates and causes the characteristic dry cough.
ace-inhibitors.target: Angiotensin-converting enzyme in the lung and vessel endothelium
classEffects: Dry cough in 10-15%
First-dose dizziness
Raised potassium and a small rise in creatinine
cautions: Never in pregnancy
Angio-oedema (swelling of the lips, tongue, face or throat) is an emergency needing immediate help (call 999); an ACE inhibitor is not restarted afterwards and the prescriber chooses an alternative
Pause during vomiting, diarrhoea or dehydration to protect the kidneys
Avoid with potassium supplements and most NSAIDs

classWarnings.text: Kidney function and potassium must be checked before starting, 1-2 weeks after starting and after each dose change; angioedema is a rare class effect that can occur at any time.
Contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal toxicity) and after angioedema with an ACE inhibitor; not combined with an ARB or, in diabetes, with aliskiren.

classInteractions.effect: Reduced blood-pressure effect and increased risk of acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia, especially with a diuretic as well (the 'triple whammy').

classInteractions.with: Potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, salt substitutes
classInteractions.effect: Hyperkalaemia.
Dual renin-angiotensin blockade: more hypotension, kidney injury and hyperkalaemia without extra benefit; not recommended.

source.title: NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

classInteractions.effect: Reduced lithium excretion and toxicity; levels are monitored.
Contraindicated: greatly increased angioedema risk; a 36-hour washout is required.

duplicationRule.text: Two ACE inhibitors together, or an ACE inhibitor with an ARB, duplicate renin-angiotensin blockade and increase the risk of kidney injury, hyperkalaemia and hypotension without extra benefit.

angiotensin-receptor-blockers.name: Angiotensin receptor blockers
angiotensin-receptor-blockers.summary: Medicines ending in -sartan that block the receptor angiotensin II acts on. They do the same job as ACE inhibitors without the cough, and are the usual alternative when an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated.
angiotensin-receptor-blockers.mechanism: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by binding AT1 receptors on arterial muscle, the adrenal cortex and heart muscle. ARBs occupy those receptors so the hormone cannot act: arteries relax, aldosterone falls and the heart and kidneys are spared its growth-promoting effects. Because ACE is untouched, bradykinin is not raised and cough and angio-oedema are rare.

Raised potassium, small rise in creatinine
Rarely angio-oedema
cautions: Never in pregnancy
Not combined with an ACE inhibitor
Sick-day rules as for ACE inhibitors
Monitor kidney function and potassium after starting and after dose changes

classWarnings.text: Kidney function and potassium are monitored as for ACE inhibitors; contraindicated in pregnancy; not combined with an ACE inhibitor or, in diabetes, with aliskiren.

beta-blockers.name: Beta blockers
beta-blockers.summary: Medicines ending in -olol that shield the heart from adrenaline, slowing it and reducing its oxygen demand. Core treatment for angina, after heart attacks, in heart failure and for controlling fast rhythms. Selective (cardioselective) agents such as bisoprolol, atenolol and metoprolol are used mainly for heart problems, while non-selective ones such as propranolol also treat the physical symptoms of anxiety, tremor, migraine and an overactive thyroid, and eye-drop forms lower pressure in glaucoma. For high blood pressure on its own they are now reserved for people in whom other medicines have not worked. They are prescription-only, tiredness is their commonest drawback, and once started they are reduced gradually rather than stopped abruptly.
beta-blockers.mechanism: Adrenaline and noradrenaline speed and strengthen the heart through beta-1 receptors. Beta blockers occupy the receptors so the heart beats more slowly and less forcefully, uses less oxygen and lets fewer atrial impulses through the AV node. Cardioselective members (bisoprolol, metoprolol, atenolol) mostly spare the beta-2 receptors in the airways; non-selective ones (propranolol) block both and can provoke asthma. In heart failure, protecting the heart from chronic adrenaline drive improves survival when started low and increased slowly. Blocking beta-1 receptors lowers contractility, heart rate and the speed of conduction through the nodes; metoprolol, for example, flattens the slow depolarisation of pacemaker cells so they fire less often. Blood pressure falls through several routes, including less renin release from the kidney. Propranolol has additional membrane-stabilising properties that contribute to its antiarrhythmic effect, and because it is non-selective it also blunts the tremor, palpitations and sweating driven by adrenaline in anxiety and thyrotoxicosis. Beyond the heart the class is used for essential tremor, portal hypertension, aortic dissection, long QT syndrome and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; short-acting intravenous agents such as esmolol are used in intensive care for fast rhythms, and labetalol mainly for hypertensive emergencies. The same receptor blockade explains the drawbacks: beta-2 blockade can tighten airways and peripheral vessels, and by damping the adrenaline response the drugs can hide the shaking and racing heart that warn of hypoglycaemia in people with diabetes.
beta-blockers.target: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors on cardiac muscle and conduction tissue (and beta-2 in airways and vessels for non-selective agents)

Vivid dreams, erectile dysfunction

Dizziness, insomnia and nightmares; breathlessness in some people

cautions: Never stop suddenly: rebound angina and fast rhythms
Asthma is a relative contraindication, especially for non-selective agents
Not combined with verapamil or diltiazem
Second- or third-degree heart block
Stopping suddenly increases heart rate and the force of contraction, which can bring on angina or let the underlying condition worsen; doses are reduced gradually

Not used in people with a history of asthma or bronchospasm unless there is no alternative and under specialist advice (cardioselective beta blockers carry the least risk), nor with marked bradycardia, second- or third-degree heart block, cardiogenic shock or unstable heart failure.

statins.name: Statins
statins.summary: The main cholesterol-lowering medicines. They cut LDL cholesterol by 30-55% and reduce heart attacks and strokes in anyone at raised cardiovascular risk.
statins.mechanism: Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme that controls how much cholesterol the liver makes. The liver compensates by displaying more LDL receptors, pulling LDL out of the blood. Lower LDL means less cholesterol deposited in artery walls, and statins also stabilise existing plaques so they are less likely to rupture and cause a clot. High-intensity statins (atorvastatin 40-80 mg, rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) are used after heart attacks and strokes.
classEffects: Muscle aches in a minority
Headache, digestive upset
Small rise in blood glucose
cautions: Interactions with clarithromycin, some antifungals and ciclosporin; grapefruit with simvastatin
Unexplained muscle pain with dark urine needs a same-day creatine kinase test
Not in pregnancy or active liver disease

loop-diuretics.name: Loop diuretics
loop-diuretics.summary: Powerful diuretics that make the kidneys excrete salt and water within an hour. Used to clear fluid in heart failure, kidney and liver disease. Furosemide, bumetanide and torasemide are the 'high-ceiling' diuretics whose effect keeps growing with the dose, so they are chosen when fluid must be shifted quickly or in large amounts. Their power is also their hazard: the same salt and water loss can cause dehydration, low blood pressure and disturbed potassium, sodium and magnesium, so kidney function and electrolytes are checked after starting and the medicine may be paused during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever.
loop-diuretics.mechanism: They block the sodium-potassium-chloride co-transporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, the segment that normally reabsorbs a quarter of filtered sodium. Furosemide competes with chloride for its binding site on the transporter, and because less salt is reabsorbed the medullary interstitium becomes less concentrated, so the kidney also loses much of its ability to reclaim free water. Salt that stays in the tubule carries water with it, so urine output rises several-fold. Potassium, magnesium and calcium are lost through the same blockade, and the resulting hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, metabolic alkalosis and raised uric acid are the predictable laboratory consequences, with hyponatraemia and dehydration when intake does not keep pace. Loop diuretics also reach the inner ear, where they alter the fluid of the stria vascularis and lower the electrical potential the cochlea depends on; the hearing loss this causes is usually temporary, but it can be permanent in severe kidney failure or when combined with other ototoxic drugs such as aminoglycoside antibiotics, whose blood levels furosemide can also raise. Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics (bendroflumethiazide; indapamide) act further along the nephron and are the gentler class used for blood pressure.

anticoagulants.name: Anticoagulants
anticoagulants.summary: Medicines that slow the clotting cascade to prevent and treat clots in veins and the heart: strokes in atrial fibrillation, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. The class spans the direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran), the vitamin K antagonist warfarin and the injectable heparins. UK guidance now favours a direct oral anticoagulant for most people with atrial fibrillation who need stroke prevention, keeping warfarin for those in whom the newer drugs are contraindicated, not tolerated or unsuitable; warfarin also remains the recommended choice for mechanical heart valves. Every member trades a lower risk of harmful clots for a higher risk of bleeding, so the decision to start, to pause for a procedure or to stop is always a balance made with the prescriber.
anticoagulants.mechanism: Direct oral anticoagulants block a single clotting enzyme: factor Xa (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or thrombin (dabigatran), with a predictable effect that needs no blood-level monitoring. Warfarin instead starves the liver of usable vitamin K, so factors II, VII, IX and X are made in inactive form; its effect builds over days and varies with diet and other drugs, so the INR test tunes the dose. Heparins, given by injection, activate antithrombin and are used in hospital and pregnancy. Unfractionated heparin is a mixture of sulphated sugar chains whose negative charges bind antithrombin and change its shape, turning it from a slow inhibitor of thrombin and factor Xa into a very fast one; the shorter low-molecular-weight heparins (enoxaparin, dalteparin) carry the key pentasaccharide sequence and act mainly on factor Xa. Warfarin's block of vitamin K epoxide reductase also affects the natural anticoagulants protein C and protein S, and because warfarin is cleared through several cytochrome P450 enzymes its effect shifts with many other medicines. The factor Xa inhibitors act on Xa within the prothrombinase complex, so prothrombin is no longer converted to thrombin; dabigatran binds thrombin itself. The laboratory reflects these differences: heparin is followed with the aPTT or an anti-Xa level, warfarin with the prothrombin time expressed as the INR, while DOACs are given at fixed doses without routine blood-level checks. Reversal is likewise drug-specific: vitamin K for warfarin, protamine for heparin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, and andexanet alfa for apixaban or rivaroxaban, which NICE recommends only for life-threatening or uncontrolled gastrointestinal bleeding.

antiplatelets.name: Antiplatelet drugs
antiplatelets.summary: Medicines that stop platelets clumping into the clots that block arteries. The backbone of treatment after heart attacks, strokes and stents.
antiplatelets.mechanism: Platelets plug damaged vessels by sticking to each other; in a diseased artery the plug becomes the clot that causes a heart attack or stroke. Low-dose aspirin permanently disables COX-1 in platelets so they cannot make thromboxane; clopidogrel, ticagrelor and prasugrel block the P2Y12 receptor that responds to ADP. After a stent both are used together for months, because a clot on the stent is a catastrophe.

nitrates.name: Nitrates
nitrates.summary: Vasodilators that relieve angina within minutes by relaxing veins and coronary arteries. Available as a spray for attacks and as long-acting tablets for prevention. Glyceryl trinitrate under the tongue works within a few minutes and is used both to treat an attack and before exertion that is known to bring one on; isosorbide mononitrate and dinitrate are the longer-acting tablets for prevention, and intravenous infusions are used in hospital. Nitrates relieve the symptom rather than the underlying coronary disease, and their chief practical limits are headache, a fall in blood pressure and the tolerance that develops with round-the-clock exposure.
nitrates.mechanism: Nitrates release nitric oxide inside vascular smooth muscle, which raises cyclic GMP and relaxes the vessel. Veins dilate most, so less blood returns to the heart and its workload and oxygen demand fall; coronary arteries and collaterals widen, improving supply to ischaemic muscle. Continuous exposure causes tolerance, so long-acting preparations are timed to leave a nitrate-free interval each day. Nitrates are converted in the body to nitric oxide, which activates guanylyl cyclase to turn GTP into cyclic GMP; the pooling of blood in dilated veins is the main therapeutic effect, since it lowers the volume returning to the heart (preload) and so the work the ventricle must do. Taken under the tongue the drug acts within minutes, which suits an attack; swallowed long-acting forms are built for steady prevention. Tolerance develops within about a day of continuous exposure and the clinical effect fades, so long-acting regimens leave a daily nitrate-free or low-nitrate period, and continuous intravenous infusions in hospital face the same problem; proposed explanations include oxidative stress in the vessel wall and increased breakdown of cyclic GMP. The interaction with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, vardenafil, tadalafil) follows directly from the chemistry: these drugs stop cyclic GMP being broken down, so the two together cause a profound fall in blood pressure and fainting, and the combination is absolutely contraindicated.
nitrates.target: Guanylate cyclase in vascular smooth muscle via nitric oxide

nsaids.name: NSAIDs
nsaids.summary: Painkillers that also reduce inflammation and fever: ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac and the COX-2 selective coxibs. Excellent for short-term musculoskeletal pain, hazardous when used long term without care. Heartburn, indigestion, stomach pain and feeling or being sick are the common effects; ulcers and bleeding can occur without warning and may be fatal, and NSAIDs account for a large share of all reported adverse drug reactions. Clinicians therefore use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, give oral forms with or just after food, never combine two NSAIDs (including over-the-counter products) and avoid the class altogether in late pregnancy, in people with previous NSAID-related asthma, hives or anaphylaxis, and around heart bypass surgery. Topical gels deliver far lower systemic exposure and are preferred for localised joint and soft-tissue pain.
nsaids.mechanism: NSAIDs block the cyclo-oxygenase enzymes COX-1 and COX-2, cutting production of prostaglandins, the local messengers that sensitise pain nerves, dilate vessels in inflamed tissue and reset the brain's thermostat in fever. The same prostaglandins protect the stomach lining and keep blood flowing through the kidney, so ulcers, kidney injury, fluid retention and raised blood pressure are the class hazards. COX-2 selective agents spare the stomach somewhat but carry more cardiovascular risk. The two isoforms behave differently. COX-1 is present all the time and supports the stomach lining, kidney function and platelet aggregation, so gastric irritation and bleeding are largely COX-1 effects; COX-2 is mostly induced at sites of inflammation and is the main source of the prostaglandins that drive pain, swelling and fever. Most NSAIDs inhibit both isoforms; aspirin inhibits COX-1 more than COX-2, while celecoxib is COX-2 selective. In the kidney, prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, so blocking them reduces glomerular filtration, blunts the natriuresis produced by diuretics and weakens the benefit of ACE inhibitors; the same sodium retention raises blood pressure. The cardiovascular hazard is explained by suppression of COX-dependent prostacyclin, the vessel wall's natural antithrombotic signal, and the thrombotic risk of a given drug depends on how selective it is for COX-2 over COX-1. Hypersensitivity reactions, from an asthma attack or urticaria to anaphylaxis, are linked to COX-1 inhibition with IgE- and T-cell-mediated components, and a person who has reacted to one NSAID is assumed to react to the others.

non-opioid-analgesics.name: Non-opioid analgesics
non-opioid-analgesics.summary: First-line painkillers without opioid or anti-inflammatory action: paracetamol (acetaminophen) above all, safe at normal doses for most people and most types of mild to moderate pain. NHS information describes paracetamol as a common painkiller and fever reducer that very rarely causes side effects when taken correctly; it can take up to an hour to work and keeps working for about five hours, and regular use over many years is regarded as safe provided the recommended dose is never exceeded. Unlike the NSAIDs it has no peripheral anti-inflammatory action and causes far fewer stomach problems, which is why it sits at the first step of most pain ladders and is combined with, rather than replaced by, other painkillers when pain is more severe.
non-opioid-analgesics.mechanism: Paracetamol acts mainly in the central nervous system, weakly inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase in the brain and spinal cord and, through its metabolite AM404, engaging cannabinoid and TRPV1 pathways that raise the pain threshold and lower the fever set-point. It has almost no effect on inflammation or the stomach lining. Its danger is the liver: in overdose a toxic metabolite overwhelms the liver's glutathione and destroys hepatocytes. The exact mechanism is still debated. StatPearls notes that paracetamol is historically grouped with the NSAIDs because it inhibits the cyclo-oxygenase pathway, yet it appears to do so in the central nervous system rather than in peripheral tissues, so reduced prostaglandin synthesis in the brain and spinal cord accounts for the analgesic and antipyretic effect without the anti-inflammatory, gastric and platelet effects of the NSAIDs. Most of a dose is handled by the liver through phase II glucuronidation and sulphation; only a small fraction passes through cytochrome P450 enzymes, chiefly CYP2E1, forming the reactive intermediate NAPQI. At therapeutic doses NAPQI is swiftly conjugated with hepatic glutathione into harmless cysteine and mercaptate compounds that leave in the urine. In overdose the conjugation pathways are saturated, more drug is diverted through CYP450, the limited glutathione stores are exhausted and NAPQI binds covalently to cysteine groups on liver proteins, particularly mitochondrial proteins, causing oxidative injury, failure of mitochondrial ATP synthesis and necrosis of the centrilobular (zone 3) hepatocytes. N-acetylcysteine, which restores glutathione, is the only approved antidote and is close to fully protective when started early after ingestion, which is why hospitals treat on the basis of the dose and timing rather than waiting for symptoms.

opioids.name: Opioids
opioids.summary: Strong painkillers that act on the body's own endorphin receptors: morphine, codeine, tramadol, oxycodone, fentanyl. Essential for severe acute pain and cancer pain; harmful when used long term for chronic non-cancer pain.
opioids.mechanism: Opioids bind mu-opioid receptors in the spinal cord, brainstem and brain, closing the gate on pain signals entering the cord and dampening the emotional response to pain. The same receptors in the brainstem slow breathing, in the gut cause constipation, and in the reward pathways produce euphoria and, with repeated use, tolerance and dependence. Naloxone displaces opioids from the receptors and reverses overdose within minutes.

biguanides.name: Biguanides
biguanides.summary: Metformin is the only biguanide in routine use and the first-line tablet for type 2 diabetes: it lowers glucose without causing hypoglycaemia or weight gain.
biguanides.mechanism: Metformin reduces the glucose the liver pours into the blood by dampening gluconeogenesis, makes muscle and fat more sensitive to insulin so they take up more glucose, and slightly reduces glucose absorption from the gut. It does not stimulate insulin release, which is why it does not cause low blood sugar on its own. HbA1c falls by about 11 mmol/mol (1%).

insulins.name: Insulins
insulins.summary: Injected replacements for the hormone the pancreas no longer makes or cannot make enough of: essential in type 1 diabetes and used in type 2 diabetes when tablets are not enough. Regimens are built from insulins of different speeds: rapid-acting analogues taken with meals, intermediate and long-acting insulins taken once or twice daily as background, and ready-mixed (biphasic) insulins taken before meals; a once-weekly basal insulin (icodec) now also exists. Insulin is given by pen, syringe or pump into the fat under the skin, and the dose is adjusted continually against glucose readings, food, activity and illness. Hypoglycaemia is the price of effective treatment, so recognising and treating a 'hypo' is part of every insulin user's education.
insulins.mechanism: Insulin binds receptors on muscle, fat and liver cells, moving glucose transporters to the cell surface so glucose leaves the blood, switching the liver from making glucose to storing glycogen, and stopping fat breakdown and ketone production. Modern analogues are engineered to act fast at meals (aspart, lispro, glulisine) or flat over 24 hours or more as background (glargine, detemir, degludec); mixed and pump regimens mimic the natural pattern of a basal trickle with mealtime bursts. Rapid-acting analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) are absorbed quickly after injection and lower glucose mainly by increasing uptake into skeletal muscle and fat. Glargine takes the opposite approach: it is soluble in the acidic solution of the pen but precipitates at the neutral pH of tissue, forming a depot that releases insulin slowly over about a day; detemir and degludec achieve a similarly flat profile by other means. In type 1 diabetes the usual pattern is a basal insulin once or twice daily plus a rapid-acting insulin before meals, the basal dose controlling the glucose the liver releases between meals and overnight; in type 2 diabetes treatment may start with a basal insulin alone, add mealtime doses later, or use a mixed insulin before meals. Insulin is injected into the abdomen, outer thighs or buttocks with a fresh needle each time, moving each injection at least a centimetre from the last, because repeated injection into one spot causes fatty lumps (lipohypertrophy) from which absorption is unreliable.
