thyroid-hormones.name: Thyroid hormones
thyroid-hormones.summary: Synthetic thyroxine (levothyroxine) replaces what an underactive thyroid cannot make, restoring metabolic rate; the dose is tuned by the TSH blood test. Because the tablet replaces a hormone the body lacks rather than adding a foreign drug, it rarely causes side effects at the right dose: the symptoms that do appear (insomnia, headache, anxiety, sweating, hair loss, loose stools, shaky hands) are the signs of too much, and many years of over-replacement can contribute to osteoporosis and heart trouble. Treatment is usually lifelong; doctors start low, adjust the dose on blood tests, and warn that some people feel better within weeks while others take months. Most adults and children can take it, it is continued through pregnancy with closer blood-test monitoring, and it is usually compatible with breastfeeding.
thyroid-hormones.mechanism: Levothyroxine is identical to the thyroid's own T4. Tissues convert it to active T3, which enters cell nuclei and switches on genes controlling metabolic rate, heat production, heart rate, gut motility, growth and brain development. As levels normalise, the pituitary's TSH falls back into range, which is how the dose is checked. Liothyronine (T3) is used rarely, on specialist advice. The thyroid itself releases mostly T4 and only a minority of the body's T3; the rest is made in the tissues by deiodinase enzymes, especially type 2, and in someone whose thyroid has been removed these enzymes are the only source of T3. T3 enters the nucleus and alters the transcription of genes that set the pace of metabolism, which is why the effect on symptoms lags weeks behind a dose change. The TSH test is the preferred monitor because the pituitary is so sensitive to small shifts in free T4 that TSH moves out of range before free T4 does; a normal TSH is taken as evidence the dose is right. A small group of people have persistent symptoms despite a normal TSH, and a normal TSH does not guarantee a normal T3 in every patient, perhaps because peripheral conversion is impaired; this is the rationale for the specialist-only use of liothyronine (synthetic T3), which in the NHS is started by endocrinologists under shared-care arrangements. Absorption from the gut is incomplete and is reduced by food, coffee, calcium and iron, so the tablet is taken on an empty stomach at the same time each day, and the dose is reviewed when any interacting medicine starts or stops.

bronchodilators.name: Bronchodilators
bronchodilators.summary: Inhaled medicines that relax the muscle around the airways within minutes (salbutamol, terbutaline) or for about 12 hours (salmeterol, formoterol) to 24 hours (the antimuscarinic tiotropium); ipratropium is short-acting. They relieve wheeze but do not treat the inflammation behind asthma.
bronchodilators.mechanism: Beta-2 agonists stimulate beta-2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, raising cyclic AMP so the muscle relaxes and the airway widens. Antimuscarinic bronchodilators block the vagal acetylcholine signal that tightens airways and drives mucus, and are especially useful in COPD. Long-acting beta agonists must be paired with an inhaled steroid in asthma, because used alone they mask worsening inflammation and have been linked to asthma deaths.
bronchodilators.target: Beta-2 adrenergic receptors (agonists) and M3 muscarinic receptors (antimuscarinics) on airway smooth muscle

corticosteroids.name: Corticosteroids
corticosteroids.summary: Synthetic versions of cortisol that switch off inflammation of any cause: inhaled for asthma, as tablets or injections for flares of many diseases, and as creams, drops and joint injections for local use. Short courses are generally well tolerated, but with high doses, long courses or several steroid products used together the hazards mount: bone loss, raised blood sugar, infection, eye and mood changes, and suppression of the body's own cortisol. In the UK, people on longer or higher-dose treatment carry a blue steroid card, and those judged at risk of adrenal insufficiency carry a red emergency card, so that any clinician treating them knows to continue the medicine and cover illness or surgery rather than let the dose lapse.
corticosteroids.mechanism: Glucocorticoids enter cells and bind receptors that move to the nucleus, where they switch off genes for inflammatory cytokines and switch on anti-inflammatory ones, shrinking the whole inflammatory response regardless of its trigger. The same receptors in liver, bone, skin, eye and brain produce the side effects of systemic use, and prolonged dosing suppresses the pituitary-adrenal axis, so the body stops making its own cortisol. Inhaled and topical forms deliver tiny doses where they are needed and largely avoid these effects. Alongside this slow genomic route, a faster non-genomic effect appears within minutes of a dose, including inhibition of phospholipase A2, which starves the inflammatory cascade of arachidonic acid. The synthetic agents (prednisolone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone, betamethasone) tend to produce more Cushingoid change and more suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis than hydrocortisone; dose and duration are surprisingly poor predictors of who will be suppressed, and even inhaled and topical preparations can do it. Suppression may persist for up to a year after stopping, which is why doses are tapered and why hydrocortisone, whose short action lets the axis recover between doses, is the replacement used if adrenal insufficiency develops. Recovery of the axis is assessed with a morning cortisol and, where needed, a short Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test. The symptoms of steroid-induced adrenal insufficiency are non-specific and overlap with both the disease being treated and the withdrawal syndrome itself, so clinicians keep a low threshold for suspecting it.

proton-pump-inhibitors.name: Proton pump inhibitors
proton-pump-inhibitors.summary: The strongest acid-reducing medicines (omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole), which heal ulcers and reflux by shutting down the acid pumps in the stomach lining. They are used for heartburn and acid reflux, indigestion, stomach and duodenal ulcers, and alongside antibiotics to clear Helicobacter pylori. Relief begins within a few days but full effect can take weeks. Most adults can take them, and children can when prescribed; low-dose products are sold over the counter for short courses in adults, with persisting symptoms a reason to see a doctor. Because the serious risks (low magnesium, weakened bones and fractures, gut infections, vitamin B12 deficiency) rise with duration, long-term use is reviewed regularly and stopped or stepped down when it is no longer needed.
proton-pump-inhibitors.mechanism: PPIs irreversibly block the hydrogen-potassium ATPase, the proton pump in parietal cells that secretes acid as the final common step of every stimulus. Acid output falls by over 90% and recovers only as new pumps are made, so the effect outlasts the drug. Taken 30-60 minutes before breakfast when the pumps are most active. H2 blockers (famotidine) are the milder alternative. PPIs are prodrugs: absorbed in the proximal small bowel and carried in the blood to the parietal cells, they are activated only by acid-catalysed cleavage inside the acidic secretory canaliculi, which is why they act so selectively on the pump that makes acid. They are metabolised in the liver mainly by CYP2C19, the route behind their interactions and the variation in exposure between individuals. Suppressing acid has consequences beyond the ulcer: stomach acid normally kills swallowed microbes, so profound suppression allows microbial overgrowth and a higher susceptibility to gut and respiratory infections, including Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea. Absorption of some nutrients also depends on acid, which accounts for the vitamin B12 and iron deficiency seen with long use; hypomagnesaemia is rare, is most likely in people also taking a diuretic, and appears to reflect reduced intestinal absorption rather than renal loss. Acute interstitial nephritis is a recognised but uncommon reaction. Many of the other long-term associations reported, such as kidney, liver and cardiovascular disease and dementia, rest on observational data of low grade, so the practical response is the smallest effective dose for the shortest time rather than avoidance of a very effective class.

penicillins.name: Penicillins
penicillins.summary: The oldest family of antibiotics and still the first choice for many chest, ear, throat, skin and dental infections: amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav, flucloxacillin and benzylpenicillin.
penicillins.mechanism: Penicillins bind the enzymes bacteria use to cross-link the peptidoglycan of their cell wall; growing bacteria with a weakened wall burst. Human cells have no cell wall, which makes the class remarkably selective. Bacteria resist by making beta-lactamase enzymes that destroy the drug; clavulanic acid in co-amoxiclav blocks the enzyme, and flucloxacillin is built to withstand the staphylococcal version. They are useless against viruses.

antihistamines.name: Antihistamines
antihistamines.summary: Medicines that block histamine's H1 receptors to relieve hay fever, hives and itching. Newer members (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) cause little drowsiness; older ones (chlorphenamine, promethazine) sedate. Second-generation agents are recommended first for allergic rhinitis and urticaria because they work as well with far fewer effects on the brain. The sedating first-generation drugs (chlorphenamine, promethazine, hydroxyzine, diphenhydramine) still have a place when itching or a streaming nose stops sleep, and some are used for nausea and travel sickness, but their anticholinergic actions make them a poor choice for older people.
antihistamines.mechanism: When mast cells release histamine in an allergic reaction, it makes capillaries leak (swelling, runny nose), stimulates itch nerves and constricts airways. Antihistamines occupy the H1 receptors so these effects are muted. Second-generation drugs cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, which is why they are much less sedating. They are adjuncts only in anaphylaxis, where adrenaline is the treatment. The difference between the generations is largely physical chemistry: the first-generation drugs are lipophilic enough to enter the brain, where blocking H1 receptors produces sedation and slows psychomotor function, and they also block muscarinic receptors, causing dry mouth, blurred vision and difficulty passing urine. Second-generation drugs act mainly on peripheral H1 receptors and penetrate the brain poorly, so they relieve sneezing, itch, hives and watery eyes with little sleepiness, although drowsiness can still appear, particularly at higher-than-usual doses. Because of this profile, current guidelines favour second-generation agents as first-line treatment for allergic rhinitis and urticaria, and they are also preferred when an antihistamine is needed during breastfeeding. Alcohol, sleeping tablets and some antidepressants add to the sedation of the older drugs, and in older adults the first-generation agents are linked to confusion, falls and fractures.

ssris.name: SSRIs
ssris.summary: The most widely used antidepressants (sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine), also first-line for anxiety disorders, panic, OCD and PTSD. The NHS describes them as the usual first choice when an antidepressant is needed, mainly for depression that is persistent or severe, and usually alongside a talking therapy such as cognitive behavioural therapy rather than instead of it. Early side effects (nausea, agitation, sleep change) are common but mostly settle over the first weeks, while sexual problems can persist for as long as the medicine is taken. The medicines are not addictive in the sense of craving or tolerance, but stopping suddenly produces a discontinuation syndrome, so courses are ended by gradual reduction.
ssris.mechanism: SSRIs block the transporter that pumps serotonin back into nerve endings after release, so more remains in the synapse. The clinical benefit arrives over weeks as receptors adapt and neuroplasticity in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex increases; the immediate rise in serotonin mostly produces the early side effects. They are less dangerous in overdose than the older tricyclic antidepressants, although an overdose (especially of citalopram or escitalopram) can still cause serious heart-rhythm effects and seizures and needs emergency care; sertraline has the best evidence of safety after a heart attack. Serotonin released into the synapse is normally pulled back into the nerve ending by the serotonin transporter; SSRIs occupy that transporter, so each burst of serotonin lingers and acts for longer. Too much serotonin signalling produces serotonin syndrome, which StatPearls describes as a triad of altered mental state, autonomic overactivity and neuromuscular signs: agitation, fast heart rate, high blood pressure, fever, brisk reflexes, tremor, nausea, vomiting and clonus; it almost always follows combining an SSRI with another serotonergic medicine or St John's wort, and treatment is to stop the offending drugs with supportive care and benzodiazepines for agitation. Other class effects have their own mechanisms. Serotonin is needed for platelets to aggregate, which explains easy bruising and the bleeding risk, especially with NSAIDs, aspirin and anticoagulants. Citalopram blocks a cardiac potassium channel and so prolongs the QT interval in a dose-dependent way, with the risk of torsades de pointes. Hyponatraemia arises mostly in older people, and the risk is higher with other sodium-lowering drugs, low body weight, female sex, a low baseline sodium and severe illness. Discontinuation symptoms (dizziness, lethargy, sleep disturbance, sensory and gut symptoms, then low mood or anxiety within days) are thought to reflect a sudden fall in synaptic serotonin while receptors remain down-regulated; they are more frequent with short-half-life drugs such as paroxetine and least with fluoxetine, whose long half-life gives a built-in taper.

xanthine-oxidase-inhibitors.name: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors
xanthine-oxidase-inhibitors.summary: Medicines that lower uric acid by blocking the enzyme that makes it, dissolving the crystals that cause gout attacks and tophi when taken every day. Allopurinol is the first choice; it is also used to prevent uric acid kidney stones and to protect the kidneys from the surge of uric acid released when some cancer treatments destroy large numbers of cells. It takes several weeks to bring uric acid down, and the dose is built up gradually because starting high, or stopping for a few days and restarting at the old dose, raises the risk of a severe skin reaction. Febuxostat is the alternative for people who cannot take allopurinol or do not reach target on a fully adjusted dose; in the United States it carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death and is restricted to those situations.
xanthine-oxidase-inhibitors.mechanism: Xanthine oxidase converts hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid at the end of purine breakdown. Blocking it drops blood urate below its saturation point, so no new crystals form and existing deposits slowly dissolve. Attacks can increase for the first months as crystals mobilise, so an NSAID or colchicine is given as cover, and the dose is raised until the urate target is reached. Allopurinol itself is cleared from the blood within hours, but the liver rapidly oxidises it to oxypurinol, an active metabolite that also blocks xanthine oxidase and persists for most of a day, which is why once-daily dosing works and why the drug accumulates when kidney function is poor. A second, smaller contribution comes from the incorporation of hypoxanthine and xanthine into nucleic acids, which feeds back to suppress new purine synthesis. Oxypurinol is also central to the class's most feared harm: in people carrying the HLA-B*58:01 allele, which is most common in those of Korean, Han Chinese or Thai descent, it is thought to bind the HLA molecule and alter its shape so that CD8 T cells attack the skin, producing Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis or the broader allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (fever, rash, eosinophilia and organ involvement), which carries a substantial mortality. Reduced kidney clearance lets oxypurinol accumulate, which is why the starting dose is cut in kidney disease and increased slowly. Febuxostat is a non-purine inhibitor of the same enzyme; a large cardiovascular outcome trial in people with gout and established cardiovascular disease found more cardiovascular deaths, most often sudden cardiac death, than with allopurinol, which led the US FDA to add a boxed warning, require a patient medication guide and limit its use to people with an inadequate response to a maximally adjusted allopurinol dose, intolerance to allopurinol, or in whom allopurinol is not advisable.

bisphosphonates.name: Bisphosphonates
bisphosphonates.summary: Medicines that slow bone loss by disabling the cells that dissolve bone, cutting hip and spine fractures in osteoporosis and treating Paget's disease and cancer in bone.
bisphosphonates.mechanism: Bisphosphonates bind bone mineral; when osteoclasts resorb that surface they absorb the drug, which disables their metabolism and triggers their death. Resorption falls while bone-building continues for a time, so density rises a few per cent and the bone's fine architecture is preserved. Weekly alendronate and risedronate, monthly ibandronate and yearly zoledronic acid infusions are the main forms.

macrolides.name: Macrolides
macrolides.summary: Antibiotics that stop bacteria making proteins by binding the bacterial ribosome, used for chest, ear, skin and sexually transmitted infections and as the main alternative in penicillin allergy. Azithromycin, clarithromycin and erythromycin differ mainly in how long they last and how much they interact with other medicines.
macrolides.mechanism: Macrolides bind the 23S ribosomal RNA in the exit tunnel of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and block the growing peptide chain, halting protein synthesis; the effect is bacteriostatic against most organisms. They concentrate inside cells, including the white cells that travel to infected tissue, so they work against intracellular pathogens such as Mycoplasma, Chlamydia and Legionella that penicillins cannot reach. Erythromycin and clarithromycin are strong inhibitors of the liver enzyme CYP3A4 and of P-glycoprotein and so raise the levels of statins, calcium channel blockers, warfarin, some anticoagulants and many other drugs; azithromycin barely inhibits CYP3A4 and interacts less. All macrolides can prolong the QT interval. Long-term low-dose azithromycin has anti-inflammatory effects used in COPD and bronchiectasis.
macrolides.target: 23S rRNA of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit
classEffects: Nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain (most with erythromycin, which stimulates gut motility)
QT prolongation and arrhythmia, particularly with other QT-prolonging drugs or low potassium
Liver enzyme rise and cholestatic jaundice
Taste disturbance (clarithromycin), hearing loss with high or prolonged doses
cautions: Heart rhythm disorders, long QT, electrolyte disturbance
Liver disease
Myasthenia gravis
Clarithromycin and erythromycin: many interactions through CYP3A4 (statins, some anticoagulants, calcium channel blockers, colchicine, warfarin)

classWarnings.text: All macrolides can prolong the QT interval and have been associated with torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death; risk is greatest with other QT-prolonging drugs, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, bradycardia and existing heart disease.

Clarithromycin and erythromycin are potent CYP3A4 inhibitors: simvastatin and some other statins, colchicine, ticagrelor and several other drugs are contraindicated or need dose reduction while they are taken. Azithromycin lacks most of these interactions.

classInteractions.with: Statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin) with clarithromycin or erythromycin
classInteractions.effect: Greatly increased statin levels and rhabdomyolysis risk; simvastatin is contraindicated with clarithromycin and paused during erythromycin.
Raised INR with any macrolide; extra INR checks.

classInteractions.with: Other QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, sotalol, some antipsychotics and antidepressants, quinolones)
classInteractions.effect: Additive QT prolongation and arrhythmia risk.

classInteractions.with: Colchicine, digoxin, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, some DOACs (with clarithromycin or erythromycin)
classInteractions.effect: Raised levels through CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibition; colchicine with clarithromycin is contraindicated in kidney or liver impairment.

duplicationRule.text: Two macrolides together add QT prolongation and gut side effects without benefit.

vaccines-influenza.name: Influenza vaccines
vaccines-influenza.summary: Seasonal vaccines against influenza A and B, reformulated every year: inactivated injected vaccines for most people and a live attenuated nasal spray for children. In the UK programme the nasal spray is the preferred vaccine for children of nursery and school age and for children with long-term conditions such as asthma needing a steroid inhaler or tablets, cystic fibrosis, serious heart disease, kidney or liver disease, diabetes or a weakened immune system; babies and toddlers below the spray's age range, and children for whom the spray is unsuitable, receive an injected vaccine instead. Vaccinating children protects not only them but the babies and older people around them. Protection takes about two weeks to develop and a new vaccine is needed every year because the circulating strains change. Side effects are mild and short-lived, serious reactions are rare, and every vaccinator is trained to recognise and treat an allergic reaction immediately.
vaccines-influenza.mechanism: Each formulation presents the immune system with haemagglutinin from the strains expected that season, either as inactivated virus fragments or, in the nasal spray, as weakened live viruses that replicate only in the cooler nose. Antibodies and memory cells form over about two weeks; the antibodies neutralise the virus at the airway surface and the memory cells speed the response if infection occurs. Because circulating strains drift, the strains are reselected annually and immunity from one season fades. The live attenuated viruses in the nasal spray are cold-adapted, so they multiply in the nose but not in the warmer lower airway, producing immunity in a similar way to natural infection but without the illness; they can also be shed for a short period, which is why children who have had the spray are advised to avoid close contact with very severely immunosuppressed people for about two weeks, and why staff who are themselves very severely immunosuppressed do not administer it. Because the spray relies on viral replication, anything that prevents it blunts the response: heavy nasal congestion from infection or allergy can impede delivery, and influenza antiviral drugs inactivate the vaccine viruses, so the spray is deferred until the antiviral course has been finished for a couple of days or an inactivated vaccine is given when protection is needed immediately. Aspirin and related salicylates are avoided in children after the live vaccine because of the association with Reye's syndrome. Most inactivated vaccines are grown in eggs, but the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation has concluded that egg allergy is no longer a contraindication to any influenza vaccine used in the UK and that there is no need to ask about it before vaccinating. The spray contains a highly processed porcine gelatine as a stabiliser; families who object on those grounds are offered an inactivated alternative.
classEffects: Sore arm, mild fever and aches for a day or two
Nasal congestion after the live nasal spray
Nasal spray: runny or blocked nose, headache, tiredness and loss of appetite
Injected vaccines: sore arm, slight fever or aching muscles for a day or two
Rashes and other non-anaphylactic allergic reactions occur occasionally and are not a reason to avoid future doses
Anaphylaxis is rare; vaccinators are trained to treat it on the spot
cautions: Previous severe allergic reaction to the vaccine
The live nasal spray is avoided in significant immunosuppression, pregnancy and severe asthma
Postponed during a feverish illness

A confirmed anaphylactic reaction to a previous dose of influenza vaccine or to any vaccine component is a contraindication to all influenza vaccines, and the person is referred for specialist allergy assessment
Egg allergy is no longer a contraindication to any UK influenza vaccine, and vaccinators need not ask about it

The live nasal spray is not given to children with clinically severe immunodeficiency or on high-dose corticosteroids; topical, standard-dose inhaled and low-dose systemic steroids are not a bar, and HIV-positive children on effective antiretroviral treatment can receive it
Children and adolescents on salicylate (aspirin) therapy are offered an inactivated vaccine rather than the spray because of the link with Reye's syndrome
A child wheezy at the time, or needing extra bronchodilator in the previous few days, receives an inactivated vaccine rather than the spray
Inactivated vaccines are preferred in pregnancy

Minor illness without fever or systemic upset is not a reason to postpone; vaccination is deferred only when someone is acutely unwell, or when heavy nasal congestion would stop the spray reaching the nasal lining
The spray is delayed after influenza antiviral treatment, or an inactivated vaccine used instead if protection is needed at once
Children given the spray avoid close contact with very severely immunosuppressed people for about two weeks
Young children having influenza vaccine for the first time may need two doses a few weeks apart

contrast-agents.name: Contrast agents
contrast-agents.summary: Substances given to make blood vessels, organs, the gut or joints stand out on imaging: iodinated agents for X-ray and CT, gadolinium agents for MRI, microbubbles for ultrasound and barium for the gut. Modern intravascular iodinated agents are non-ionic and of low or iso-osmolality, which is why severe reactions are now uncommon; gadolinium agents are chelates whose structure (macrocyclic versus linear) governs how much gadolinium is left behind in the body. Because the kidneys clear both iodinated and gadolinium agents, kidney function and risk factors such as diabetes, heart disease, asthma and previous reactions are checked on a safety questionnaire before the injection, and the benefit of the information gained is weighed against a small risk for each person.
contrast-agents.mechanism: Each agent changes how the tissue it fills interacts with the imaging energy. Iodine and barium absorb X-rays, so filled vessels and cavities appear bright on X-ray and CT; gadolinium shortens the relaxation time of nearby water protons, brightening perfused tissue on MRI; microbubbles reflect ultrasound strongly and outline blood flow. Timing the scan to when the agent is in arteries, veins or tissue shows different structures. Iodinated agents are given into a vein, an artery, a joint or a body cavity and are eliminated by the kidneys, so a person with normal kidneys clears them quickly; a blood test may be used beforehand to confirm this. Gadolinium is itself toxic, so it is bound in a chelate: macrocyclic agents (gadoterate, gadobutrol, gadoteridol, gadopiclenol) hold it most tightly and leave the least residue, while linear agents release more and are associated with greater retention in bone, brain, skin, kidney, liver and spleen. The US regulator concluded that this retention has not been linked to harm in people with normal kidney function but required class warnings, patient medication guides and advice to avoid closely repeated studies where possible; the established serious hazard of gadolinium is nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in people whose kidneys cannot eliminate it. Immediate reactions to iodinated agents are mostly mild (nausea, vomiting, hives, itch, cough); moderate and severe reactions are much rarer, and the idea of an 'iodine allergy' is not supported by evidence and can lead to contrast being withheld unnecessarily. Kidney injury after contrast is a sudden fall in function within a day or two of exposure; large matched studies suggest it is far less frequent than once believed, and the diagnostic benefit of a well-chosen contrast study is judged to outweigh the risk for almost everyone.
contrast-agents.target: The imaging signal of the tissue the agent occupies (X-ray attenuation, MRI relaxation, ultrasound reflection)
classEffects: A warm flush, metallic taste and nausea during injection
Allergic-type reactions, rarely severe
Kidney injury with iodinated agents in people at risk; gadolinium retention concerns in repeated MRI
A sensation of passing urine during the injection that is not real, and occasional brief nausea
Immediate allergic-type reactions are mostly mild (hives, itching, cough); moderate and severe reactions are much rarer
Gadolinium is retained for months to years, most in bone, with no proven harm in people with normal kidneys; nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is the serious hazard when kidney elimination is impaired
cautions: Kidney function checked before iodinated and gadolinium agents in people at risk
Previous contrast reactions and severe allergy declared beforehand
Pregnancy: used only when the imaging is essential
A safety questionnaire covering diabetes, heart problems, asthma, kidney problems and past reactions is completed before the injection
People taking metformin tell the department in advance
Gadolinium agents are used sparingly, and repeat studies spaced out, in people who may need many lifetime doses, in pregnancy, in children and in inflammatory conditions
Breastfeeding can continue as normal after a contrast scan

UCLH (NHS): Contrast agents for X-ray, fluoroscopy, CT and angiography examinations

radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.name: Diagnostic radiopharmaceuticals
radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.summary: Radioactive medicines given in tiny amounts so that a gamma camera or PET scanner can show where they accumulate: bone turnover, blood flow to the heart, thyroid activity, glucose use by tumours. Two technologies dominate. Technetium-99m, a pure gamma emitter with a short half-life, is the workhorse of gamma-camera and SPECT imaging of the brain, bones, lungs, kidneys, thyroid and heart and labels the great majority of tracers in routine use. Fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a positron emitter, is the standard PET tracer: cancer cells take up more glucose than normal cells, so FDG accumulates in them, which makes PET-CT particularly useful for finding how far a confirmed cancer has spread and how it is responding to treatment, and for mapping the brain's glucose metabolism in suspected neurodegenerative disease. The injected tracer itself has no known side effects in most cases and allergic reactions are extremely rare; the main consideration is a small radiation dose.
radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.mechanism: A radioactive isotope is attached to a molecule the body handles in a known way: a phosphate analogue that binds forming bone, a glucose analogue trapped in metabolically active cells, iodine taken up by the thyroid, or a compound retained by well-perfused heart muscle. The radiation the isotope emits is detected from outside and mapped, so the image shows function rather than anatomy; combining it with CT adds the anatomy. The radiation dose is kept low by using short-lived isotopes and small amounts. Technetium-99m is useful because of its physics: a short half-life and a single gamma photon of an energy well suited to gamma cameras, so good images are obtained at low radiation exposure, and it has little or no therapeutic effect. Any technetium that comes free of its carrier molecule (pertechnetate) collects in the salivary glands, thyroid and stomach, which can complicate interpretation, so quality control of each preparation matters. FDG behaves like glucose: it is taken into cells by the same transporters and, once phosphorylated, is trapped, so the PET signal maps glucose use. Tissues with naturally low metabolic activity, such as the liver and prostate, give little contrast and limit FDG's usefulness there, whereas a fall in uptake in particular brain regions is the pattern seen in neurodegenerative disorders. Because FDG competes with the body's own glucose, blood glucose is checked before injection; a high glucose or insulin level reduces uptake into the target tissue and degrades the scan. After the injection the person sits or lies quietly in a waiting area for an hour or more before the scan. The scanner detects where the tracer does and does not gather, and the CT acquired in the same session supplies the anatomical map on which those functional findings are placed; the whole PET-CT visit typically takes a few hours.
radiopharmaceuticals-diagnostic.target: Physiological processes (bone turnover, perfusion, glucose metabolism, receptor binding) imaged through the tracer's distribution
classEffects: A small radiation dose; reactions to the tracer itself are rare
No known side effects from the injected FDG itself in most people; allergic reactions to radiopharmaceuticals are extremely rare and usually mild
Pain, bruising or leakage (extravasation) at the cannula site, as with any injection
Headache, fatigue, nausea or injection-site irritation have been reported with some newer PET tracers
cautions: Pregnancy and breastfeeding declared before the injection
Radiation-safety advice for the hours after the scan (fluids, bladder emptying, distance from pregnant women and young children)
Preparation specific to the tracer: fasting for FDG, medicine timing for perfusion studies

Blood glucose is checked before an FDG scan; a high glucose or insulin level reduces tracer uptake and spoils the images, so people with diabetes receive specific instructions about meals and medicines
After the FDG injection the person sits or lies quietly until the scan, because activity changes where the tracer goes
Previous reactions to a nuclear medicine test and any allergies are reported to the department beforehand
Free technetium collecting in the thyroid, salivary glands and stomach can mimic or hide disease, so unexpected uptake in these organs is interpreted with care

androgens.name: Androgens
androgens.summary: Steroid hormones that act on the androgen receptor. Testosterone in its various forms replaces the testes' output in hypogonadism and masculinises the body in gender-affirming therapy for trans men and non-binary people; the same molecules misused at high doses for muscle building are the anabolic steroids.
androgens.mechanism: Androgens enter cells and bind the androgen receptor, a nuclear receptor that changes gene expression. In prostate, skin and hair follicles 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, and in fat, bone and brain aromatase converts some to oestradiol. UK practice uses testosterone itself in different forms: gel or patch, injected oil-based esters, implants and capsules. Anti-androgens block the receptor (spironolactone and cyproterone acetate in feminising therapy, bicalutamide in prostate cancer); finasteride and other 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors cut dihydrotestosterone.
androgens.target: The androgen receptor in prostate, testes, muscle, bone, skin, hair follicles, bone marrow and brain, in some tissues after conversion to dihydrotestosterone by 5-alpha-reductase
classEffects: Virilisation: deeper voice, facial and body hair, clitoral enlargement and cessation of periods in people assigned female at birth, wanted in masculinising therapy and in part irreversible
Acne and oily skin, scalp hair loss in those predisposed, fluid retention, weight gain and mood change
Erythrocytosis (raised haemoglobin and haematocrit), more marked with injections
Prostate enlargement and a rise in PSA in men; suppression of sperm production and testicular shrinkage
cautions: Contraindicated in prostate cancer and male breast cancer, and in pregnancy and breastfeeding
Haematocrit is monitored: erythrocytosis thickens the blood and raises clot risk, and the dose or interval is reduced if it climbs
Used with care in heart failure, hypertension, sleep apnoea and kidney or liver disease because of fluid retention; older oral (17-alkylated) androgens damage the liver
Gel can transfer to partners and children through skin contact
Testosterone is not contraception in trans men and non-binary people, and anyone with a cervix still needs cervical screening
Anabolic steroid misuse for muscle building harms the heart, liver, fertility and mood, and in women causes irreversible virilisation

references.title: Endocrine Society: Endocrine treatment of gender-dysphoric/gender-incongruent persons

classWarnings.text: Androgens raise the red cell mass; haemoglobin and haematocrit are checked before treatment and at intervals, and the dose or dosing interval is reduced if erythrocytosis develops.
Testosterone is contraindicated in men with prostate cancer or breast cancer; prostate examination and PSA are part of assessment and follow-up in older men.

classInteractions.effect: Androgens enhance the anticoagulant effect; INR is monitored more closely.
Androgens can lower blood glucose, so requirements may fall.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

oestrogens.name: Oestrogens
oestrogens.summary: Steroid hormones that act on the oestrogen receptor. Estradiol and related oestrogens replace the ovaries' output after the menopause, treat genitourinary symptoms locally and feminise the body in gender-affirming care.
oestrogens.mechanism: Oestrogens diffuse into cells and bind nuclear oestrogen receptors, which switch genes on or off. Estradiol, the ovaries' own hormone, is used for replacement; estriol is a weaker oestrogen in vaginal creams; conjugated oestrogens are an oral mixture; ethinylestradiol resists liver breakdown, which suits the combined pill but makes it more thrombogenic, so it is not used in HRT or feminising therapy. Oestrogen makes the endometrium proliferate, so anyone with a uterus takes a progestogen with systemic oestrogen. Oral routes raise clotting factors in the liver, unlike patches, gel and spray.
oestrogens.target: Oestrogen receptors (ERα and ERβ) in the uterus, breast, bone, blood vessels, brain and liver
classEffects: Breast tenderness, nausea, bloating, headache, leg cramps and fluid retention, especially in the first months
Irregular bleeding in the first months of combined HRT; endometrial thickening if oestrogen is taken unopposed with a uterus
Raised clotting factors and venous thromboembolism risk with oral routes, and a small rise in stroke risk with oral HRT
Relief of hot flushes, improved vaginal and urinary symptoms, preserved bone density and, in feminising therapy, breast growth and fat redistribution
cautions: Previous or current breast cancer or other oestrogen-dependent cancer, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, untreated endometrial hyperplasia, active or recent venous thromboembolism and active liver disease
Systemic oestrogen without a progestogen when the uterus is present raises the risk of endometrial cancer
A transdermal route is chosen where clot risk is raised: previous clots, obesity, smoking, migraine with aura, older age or immobility; oestrogen is usually paused around major surgery
Combined HRT carries a small, duration-dependent increase in breast cancer risk that falls after stopping; breast awareness and screening continue
Enzyme-inducing medicines reduce oestrogen levels, and oestrogens can increase levothyroxine requirements

classWarnings.text: Oestrogens raise the risk of venous thromboembolism, most with oral preparations and least with transdermal ones; they are avoided in active or recent thromboembolism and a transdermal route is preferred where risk factors are present.

Systemic oestrogen taken without a progestogen by anyone who has a uterus increases the risk of endometrial cancer; combined HRT carries a small increase in breast cancer risk related to duration of use.

classInteractions.with: Enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin, St John's wort)
classInteractions.effect: Increase oestrogen metabolism and lower its effect.
Oestrogens raise thyroxine-binding globulin, so the levothyroxine dose may need to rise; TSH is checked.

triptans.name: Triptans
triptans.summary: Triptans are medicines for treating migraine attacks, and sumatriptan is the triptan covered on this site. The NHS says sumatriptan relieves symptoms of migraine but does not prevent migraines from starting.
triptans.mechanism: The NHS says migraines may be linked to temporarily widened blood vessels in the brain, and that sumatriptan narrows these blood vessels.
cautions: Heart problems, a past stroke or transient ischaemic attack, circulation problems in the legs and liver disease are listed by the NHS as reasons sumatriptan may not be suitable.
Combining sumatriptan with some antidepressants or St John's wort can raise the risk of serotonin syndrome, according to the NHS and UK leaflets.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

5-ht3-receptor-antagonists.name: 5-HT3 receptor antagonists
5-ht3-receptor-antagonists.summary: Anti-sickness medicines that block 5-HT3 receptors; ondansetron is the member covered on this site. Ondansetron is used to prevent nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery.
5-ht3-receptor-antagonists.mechanism: They interfere with serotonin, a natural substance that can cause nausea and vomiting, by acting on 5-HT3 receptors.
cautions: It may be given by mouth as a tablet, melt or syrup, or as an injection into a vein, according to Great Ormond Street Hospital.
The MHRA has warned of a small increased risk of cleft lip or palate after use of ondansetron in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
A UK leaflet says ondansetron must not be used with apomorphine.
An NHS prescribing sheet says ondansetron lengthens the QT interval in a dose-related way and is avoided in congenital long QT syndrome.

references.title: emc: Ondansetron 4 mg film-coated tablets package leaflet

dopamine-antagonist-antiemetics.name: Dopamine antagonist anti-sickness medicines
dopamine-antagonist-antiemetics.summary: Dopamine antagonist anti-sickness medicines are used to treat nausea and vomiting, and metoclopramide is the member covered on this site. The MHRA has restricted metoclopramide to short-term use because of the risk of serious neurological side effects.
dopamine-antagonist-antiemetics.mechanism: Metoclopramide is grouped with domperidone in NHS formularies, and the sources used here do not describe the group's mechanism in more detail.
cautions: The MHRA says the risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults, and that in children aged 1 to 18 it is only a second-line option.
Epilepsy and Parkinson's disease are listed by the NHS as conditions where metoclopramide may not suit someone.
The NHS asks people taking Parkinson's disease medicines, drowsiness-causing medicines or other anti-sickness medicines to speak to a doctor or pharmacist first.
The NHS says uncontrollable movements such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms are the most common serious side effect of metoclopramide.

references.title: MHRA: Metoclopramide: risk of neurological adverse effects

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

antimotility-agents.name: Antimotility agents
antimotility-agents.summary: Antimotility agents are medicines that slow the bowel to treat diarrhoea, and loperamide is the member covered on this site. Product information for UK loperamide medicines says it slows the bowel and increases absorption of water and electrolytes, so stools firm up.
antimotility-agents.mechanism: UK and US product information describes loperamide as an opioid (mu) receptor agonist that acts on the gut wall to reduce propulsive movement of the bowel.
cautions: The NHS lists severe diarrhoea after antibiotics, a flare-up of ulcerative colitis, constipation or a swollen stomach, and blood in the stool with a high temperature as situations where loperamide is not suitable.
The NHS says loperamide is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough evidence about it.
The NHS says some medicines can affect how loperamide works, including clozapine, ritonavir, quinidine, itraconazole, gemfibrozil and desmopressin.
MedlinePlus says taking more than the recommended amount of loperamide can cause serious heart problems that may be fatal.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

osmotic-laxatives.name: Osmotic laxatives
osmotic-laxatives.summary: Osmotic laxatives draw water into the bowel to soften poo; lactulose is the one covered on this site. The NHS says osmotic laxatives such as lactulose and macrogol draw water into the bowel to soften poo and make it easier to pass.
osmotic-laxatives.mechanism: The NHS says lactulose draws water into the bowel, which makes poo softer.
cautions: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to lactulose and galactosaemia as reasons it may not be suitable.
Irritable bowel syndrome, diverticular disease, Crohn's disease and a bowel blockage not caused by constipation are conditions where the NHS advises checking first.
The NHS says long-term high amounts of lactulose may affect blood sugar in people with diabetes.
Diarrhoea, bloating and wind are common with lactulose, according to the NHS.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

benzodiazepines.name: Benzodiazepines
benzodiazepines.summary: Benzodiazepines are depressant medicines that slow the central nervous system, and diazepam is the member covered on this site. The MHRA says dependence can occur with therapeutic doses and can become established within weeks.
benzodiazepines.mechanism: NHS Inform describes benzodiazepines as drugs that slow down the central nervous system.
cautions: The NHS advises against alcohol and grapefruit juice while taking diazepam because they can increase the risk of side effects.

The NHS says diazepam should not be taken in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it. The manufacturer's patient leaflet says that regular use during pregnancy may cause withdrawal symptoms in the baby.
NHS Inform says combining benzodiazepines with alcohol, gabapentinoids or opioids raises the risk of overdose.
NHS Inform says stopping benzodiazepines suddenly can cause withdrawal effects that could be life-threatening.
Licensed benzodiazepines such as diazepam, lorazepam and clonazepam are Class C drugs listed in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

z-drugs.name: Z-drugs
z-drugs.summary: Z-drugs are sleeping medicines used for insomnia, and zopiclone is the member covered on this site. NICE technology appraisal TA77 covers zaleplon, zolpidem and zopiclone for short-term insomnia.
z-drugs.mechanism: The NHS says zopiclone boosts the effect of GABA, a calming chemical in the brain.
cautions: The NHS says alcohol with zopiclone can cause very deep sleep, so that breathing is not normal and waking is very difficult.
The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery for 12 hours after taking zopiclone.
The NHS says the body gets used to zopiclone quickly, which is why it is usually prescribed for only 2 to 4 weeks.
The summary of product characteristics for zopiclone says treatment should stop immediately if a complex sleep behaviour such as sleepwalking occurs.
Zopiclone is a Class C drug in Schedule 4 Part 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations.

references.title: NICE TA77: zaleplon, zolpidem and zopiclone for insomnia

tetracyclines.name: Tetracyclines
tetracyclines.summary: Tetracyclines are a group of antibiotics that stop bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive. Doxycycline is the member described here, and the NHS lists it for chest, dental and skin infections, rosacea and some sexually transmitted infections.
tetracyclines.mechanism: The NHS explains that doxycycline, a tetracycline antibiotic, stops bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive. For rosacea, the NHS says it mainly reduces inflammation in the skin.
cautions: Not usually used during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or in younger children, because doxycycline can affect how teeth and bones develop, according to the NHS.

A hospital leaflet advises against taking indigestion remedies, or supplements containing iron, calcium, magnesium, aluminium or zinc, at the same time as doxycycline, because they can interfere with absorption.
The NHS says alcohol is best avoided, as it can stop doxycycline working properly.
The NHS says doxycycline can be taken by people allergic to penicillin, because the two are different types of antibiotic.
Some people get thrush after antibiotics, and the NHS suggests asking a pharmacist or doctor if this happens.
classEffects: Headaches, feeling sick and being sick are common side effects of doxycycline.
Skin that is more sensitive to the sun, which can cause a rash, itching and redness.

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

nitroimidazoles.name: Nitroimidazoles
nitroimidazoles.summary: Antibiotic and antiparasitic medicines, including metronidazole and tinidazole, that act on bacteria and parasites.
nitroimidazoles.mechanism: Microbial enzymes inside susceptible bacteria and parasites activate nitroimidazoles. The activated form then damages proteins and DNA. A study in Giardia found that metronidazole and tinidazole bind to the same subset of proteins.
cautions: For metronidazole, the NHS advises avoiding alcohol during treatment and for 2 days afterwards. Reactions listed include feeling or being sick, stomach pain, hot flushes, a pounding heartbeat and a headache.
NCBI LiverTox describes tinidazole as a nitroimidazole similar to metronidazole, with a likely similar range and frequency of side effects.
Tinidazole is broken down largely in the liver by an enzyme called CYP 3A4, which can lead to significant interactions with other medicines, according to LiverTox.
classEffects: LiverTox says tinidazole causes a low rate of raised liver enzymes during treatment, and rare cases of clinically apparent acute liver injury.

references.title: PMC: Nitroimidazole drugs vary in their mode of action in the human parasite Giardia lamblia

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

urinary-antibacterials.name: Urinary antibacterials
urinary-antibacterials.summary: Antibiotics used for urinary tract infections. The NHS describes nitrofurantoin as a medicine to treat urinary tract infections such as cystitis, and trimethoprim is also an NHS-described antibiotic for urinary tract infections.
urinary-antibacterials.mechanism: Nitrofurantoin reaches useful concentrations only in urine, so it is used for lower urinary tract infections such as cystitis and is unsuitable for upper infections of the kidneys.
cautions: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction, a lung condition, severe kidney problems, diabetes, anaemia or vitamin B deficiency, and porphyria among the reasons nitrofurantoin may not be suitable.
The NHS says nitrofurantoin can usually be taken in earlier pregnancy, but a doctor may not recommend it later because it can affect the baby's red blood cells.
For trimethoprim, the NHS lists an allergic reaction, liver or kidney problems and blood disorders such as porphyria among the reasons it may not be suitable.
The NHS says trimethoprim can lower folic acid levels and is not usually recommended in early pregnancy.
classEffects: Nausea, diarrhoea, loss of appetite, headaches and dark yellow or brown urine are common side effects of nitrofurantoin, and usually go away when it is stopped.
Itching or a skin rash may occur with trimethoprim, and these effects are usually mild and short-lived, according to the NHS.
Serious reactions to nitrofurantoin, such as swelling of the throat or tongue or difficulty breathing, are rare; the NHS lists these as symptoms of anaphylaxis, which needs a 999 call.

NHS: Who can and cannot take trimethoprim

alpha-blockers.name: Alpha blockers
alpha-blockers.summary: Alpha blockers, also called alpha-adrenoreceptor antagonists, are medicines that relax muscle; tamsulosin is used to relax the muscle around the bladder and prostate in an enlarged prostate.
alpha-blockers.mechanism: In an enlarged prostate, tamsulosin relaxes the muscle around the bladder and prostate gland, which makes it easier to pee.
cautions: The NHS says other alpha blockers, such as doxazosin, alfuzosin, prazosin or terazosin, may lower blood pressure, and some blood pressure medicines may not mix well with tamsulosin.
Orthostatic hypotension, low blood pressure causing dizziness on standing, is listed by the NHS as a reason tamsulosin is not suitable.
The NHS also lists severe liver or kidney problems, planned cataract or glaucoma eye surgery and having fainted while urinating or just afterwards among the reasons tamsulosin may not be suitable.
classEffects: Dizziness or light-headedness, which a hospital leaflet notes may occur when first starting tamsulosin.
An allergic reaction to one alpha blocker, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin or terazosin, is a reason the NHS lists against tamsulosin.

references.title: NHS: Tamsulosin
references.section: Who can and cannot take tamsulosin

provenance.source_name: Anatomy Nexus editorial content written from the references cited on the page

5-alpha-reductase-inhibitors.name: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors
5-alpha-reductase-inhibitors.summary: A group of medicines that stop testosterone turning into the hormone DHT; finasteride, described by the NHS for an enlarged prostate and male pattern hair loss, is one of them. The MHRA has issued safety warnings about psychiatric side effects and sexual dysfunction for finasteride and dutasteride.
5-alpha-reductase-inhibitors.mechanism: These medicines work by stopping testosterone, a sex hormone, turning into another hormone called dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
classEffects: Sexual side effects such as losing interest in sex and difficulty getting an erection are the main side effects the NHS lists for finasteride, and some men report them continuing after stopping.
The MHRA says finasteride is associated with depression, suicidal thoughts and sexual dysfunction, and has added a precautionary warning for dutasteride.
cautions: Finasteride can affect PSA blood test results, so the NHS advises telling the doctor about it if a PSA test is due.
For depression or suicidal thoughts, MHRA guidance for finasteride is to contact a healthcare professional urgently; if someone is in immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E.

references.title: MHRA Drug Safety Update: Finasteride and dutasteride, updated safety warnings
MHRA: MHRA strengthens safety warnings for finasteride and dutasteride

gabapentinoids.name: Gabapentinoids
gabapentinoids.summary: Gabapentinoids are the group that contains pregabalin and gabapentin, which are used for epilepsy and nerve pain.
gabapentinoids.mechanism: For epilepsy, these medicines are thought to reduce abnormal electrical activity in the brain. For nerve pain, they are thought to block pain by affecting pain messages travelling through the brain and down the spine.
cautions: The NHS lists drowsiness and dizziness among the common side effects of both medicines.
The NHS says some people can become addicted to either medicine.
The NHS says that when stopping either medicine the dose is reduced gradually to avoid withdrawal symptoms.

classInteractions.with: Opioids, alcohol and other medicines that cause sleepiness
classInteractions.effect: The MHRA says gabapentin and pregabalin can cause potentially fatal respiratory depression, particularly when used with opioid medicines and alcohol.

source.title: MHRA Drug Safety Update: Pregabalin (Lyrica), gabapentin (Neurontin) and risk of abuse and dependence

classWarnings.text: Pregabalin and gabapentin became Class C controlled drugs, and Schedule 3 under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, on 1 April 2019.

source.title: GOV.UK: Reclassification of pregabalin and gabapentin to Schedule 3 drugs from 1 April 2019

classWarnings.text: The MHRA reports severe breathing difficulty with pregabalin, and a separate update covers gabapentin.

source.title: MHRA Drug Safety Update: Pregabalin (Lyrica) reports of severe respiratory depression

references.title: GOV.UK: Reclassification of pregabalin and gabapentin to Schedule 3 drugs from 1 April 2019

tricyclic-antidepressants.name: Tricyclic antidepressants
tricyclic-antidepressants.summary: Tricyclic antidepressants are a group of medicines that includes amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine and clomipramine. They are used to treat depression, and amitriptyline is also used for pain relief at lower doses than for depression. StatPearls says they cause more significant side effects than SSRIs because of their anticholinergic activity and their lower threshold for overdose.
tricyclic-antidepressants.mechanism: StatPearls says these medicines work by blocking the reuptake of neurotransmitters such as serotonin and noradrenaline. The NHS says amitriptyline is thought to work by increasing levels of serotonin in the brain. StatPearls links many of their side effects to anticholinergic activity, which for imipramine comes from blocking muscarinic receptors.
cautions: A 2024 review concluded that, with one exception, all tricyclics are toxic and dangerous when taken in overdose.

The exception named in that review is lofepramine, a tricyclic used in the UK, which had the lowest risk of death in overdose; the same review noted a greater risk of heart events with lofepramine at clinical exposure, and that the evidence is affected by confounding.

Anyone who has taken more than the prescribed amount of amitriptyline and has a fast or irregular heartbeat, a seizure, drowsiness or passing out, difficulty breathing or sudden confusion needs a 999 call, according to the NHS.
Some local NHS prescribing guidance advises considering limiting the amount prescribed each time because of the risk of toxicity in overdose.

MedlinePlus says a small number of children, teenagers and young adults up to 24 years of age who took antidepressants such as clomipramine in clinical studies became suicidal, especially at the start of treatment and when the dose changes.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E now for thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life; NHS 111 is open 24 hours every day and Samaritans is a free line on 116 123.

classWarnings.text: The NHS pain page says taking more than the prescribed amount of amitriptyline can cause serious effects such as a change in heartbeat and seizures (fits) and advises contacting NHS 111 for advice; the NHS depression page says to call 999 now if a fast or irregular heartbeat, a seizure, drowsiness or passing out, difficulty breathing or sudden confusion follows.

source.title: NHS: How and when to take amitriptyline for depression

snris.name: SNRIs
snris.summary: SNRIs are a group of antidepressants whose NHS examples are duloxetine and venlafaxine. They act on both serotonin and noradrenaline. The NHS says venlafaxine is used to treat depression and sometimes anxiety and panic attacks, and duloxetine is used for depression, anxiety and nerve pain. NHS formulary guidance says venlafaxine and duloxetine can also increase heart rate and blood pressure.
snris.mechanism: SNRIs are thought to work by increasing the amount of the mood-enhancing chemicals serotonin and noradrenaline in the brain.
cautions: The NHS says antidepressants are not addictive, but withdrawal symptoms can occur if they are stopped suddenly or a dose is missed.
A Scottish NHS guide says venlafaxine carries a higher risk of withdrawal effects than other antidepressants.

NHS formulary guidance says venlafaxine and duloxetine can increase heart rate and blood pressure, and the NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service says they can cause dose-related rises in blood pressure and abnormal heart rhythms.
The routes to help for suicidal thoughts are 999 if in immediate danger, NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123.

classInteractions.with: St John's wort, MAOI antidepressants, tramadol
classInteractions.effect: The NHS lists these among the herbal remedies and medicines that can raise the chance of side effects with duloxetine.

source.title: NHS: Taking duloxetine with other medicines and herbal supplements

classInteractions.effect: The NHS lists these among the medicines to take care with alongside duloxetine.

source.title: NHS: Taking duloxetine with other medicines and herbal supplements

classWarnings.text: Stopping an SNRI suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, so the dose is usually lowered gradually.

references.title: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service: Choosing an antidepressant for people with coronary heart disease

noradrenergic-and-specific-serotonergic-.name: NaSSA antidepressants
noradrenergic-and-specific-serotonergic-.summary: The NHS groups antidepressants into types such as SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics and MAOIs, and lists mirtazapine as a noradrenaline and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NaSSA). Mirtazapine is the NaSSA covered on this site.
noradrenergic-and-specific-serotonergic-.mechanism: Pharmacology reviews describe mirtazapine as blocking alpha-2 receptors on nerve cells in the brain, which increases the release of noradrenaline and serotonin, and as also blocking 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 serotonin receptors. Unlike many other antidepressants, it is described as not inhibiting the reuptake of noradrenaline or serotonin. Blocking histamine H1 receptors is linked to its sedating effect.
cautions: The NHS says mirtazapine is not usually recommended for anyone under 18.
The NHS says stopping an antidepressant suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, and the dose is usually reduced gradually.
The NHS says mirtazapine can be taken while breastfeeding if the baby is healthy.

classInteractions.effect: The NHS says it should not be taken during mirtazapine treatment because it increases the risk of side effects.

source.title: NHS: Taking mirtazapine with other medicines and herbal supplements

classInteractions.effect: The NHS says mirtazapine can affect warfarin, so the dose of warfarin may need to change.

source.title: NHS: Taking mirtazapine with other medicines and herbal supplements

classWarnings.text: The NHS side effects page says to call 999 or go to A&E now if a person has thoughts of harming themselves or ending their life, while the main NHS mirtazapine page says to call NHS 111. Samaritans can be reached free on 116 123 at any time.

cholesterol-absorption-inhibitors.name: Cholesterol absorption inhibitors
cholesterol-absorption-inhibitors.summary: Cholesterol absorption inhibitors are medicines that lower cholesterol by partly blocking its absorption in the small intestine. They are used on their own when a statin cannot be taken or has not worked, or alongside a statin.
cholesterol-absorption-inhibitors.mechanism: Heart UK says ezetimibe partly blocks the absorption of cholesterol in the small intestine. Research reviews describe it as acting on a protein called NPC1L1 in the lining of the small intestine, which helps move cholesterol from the gut into the body. Heart UK says ezetimibe works in a different way from statins, and that the two are often combined because their effects add up.
cholesterol-absorption-inhibitors.target: Cholesterol absorption in the small intestine.
classEffects: Stomach pain, diarrhoea, extra wind and tiredness.
With a statin: muscle pain, headaches and moderately raised liver enzymes.
cautions: Unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, or yellowing of the skin or eyes, needs a doctor or NHS 111 straight away, according to the NHS.
The NHS asks people to tell their doctor about pregnancy, planning a pregnancy, breastfeeding and liver problems.
The NHS lists other cholesterol-lowering medicines such as bezafibrate and colestyramine as medicines to mention to a doctor, and UK product information advises caution with ciclosporin.

references.title: NICE TA385: Ezetimibe for treating primary heterozygous-familial and non-familial hypercholesterolaemia
NHS: Who can and cannot take ezetimibe

glp-1-receptor-agonists.name: GLP-1 receptor agonists
glp-1-receptor-agonists.summary: GLP-1 receptor agonists are medicines that imitate GLP-1, a hormone the body releases after eating. Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) is one; tirzepatide (Mounjaro) is described on the NHS website as acting on both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. In the UK they are used to manage type 2 diabetes and to treat obesity.
glp-1-receptor-agonists.mechanism: Semaglutide imitates GLP-1, helps people feel fuller for longer and reduces hunger, according to GOV.UK. Tirzepatide is described by the NHS as reducing appetite so that people feel fuller for longer, and it delays stomach emptying.
classEffects: Feeling sick, being sick, diarrhoea and constipation are common with semaglutide, and tirzepatide is described as commonly causing feeling sick, indigestion, constipation and diarrhoea

Pancreatitis is listed by the NHS as a rare but serious effect of semaglutide, and UK prescribing information says acute pancreatitis has been reported with tirzepatide, including necrotising and fatal cases
Severe stomach pain that does not go away needs urgent advice from NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and a 999 call if it is severe or the person is collapsing
cautions: The MHRA advises against GLP-1 receptor agonists in pregnancy because of a lack of human safety data, and advises effective contraception during treatment

The MHRA has highlighted a potential risk of stomach contents entering the lungs during general anaesthesia or deep sedation, because these medicines delay stomach emptying and food can remain despite fasting
With semaglutide, low blood sugar is more likely when it is taken with other diabetes medicines such as insulin or a sulfonylurea

classWarnings.text: The MHRA advises effective contraception during GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment because human safety data in pregnancy are limited.

references.title: NHS SPS: Considerations and interactions with GLP-1 receptor agonists
GOV.UK: GLP-1 and dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists, potential risk of pulmonary aspiration (MHRA Drug Safety Update)

mineralocorticoid-receptor-antagonists.name: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists
mineralocorticoid-receptor-antagonists.summary: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, also called aldosterone antagonists, are medicines that act against the hormone aldosterone. Spironolactone and eplerenone are the two members covered here, and a Northern Care Alliance heart failure leaflet covers both.
mineralocorticoid-receptor-antagonists.mechanism: A review of spironolactone and eplerenone says they increase the amount of sodium lost in the urine and cause the kidneys to hold on to potassium when aldosterone levels are high, which is why they are described as facultative diuretics. Eplerenone is more selective for the mineralocorticoid receptor, whereas StatPearls says spironolactone also binds progesterone and androgen receptors, which underlies its anti-androgen effects such as breast enlargement in men. A 2024 meta-analysis in people with heart failure found lower rates of gynaecomastia with eplerenone than with spironolactone.
classEffects: Hyperkalaemia (high blood potassium) and acute kidney injury are described as the predominant safety concerns across the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists in pharmacovigilance data
Gynaecomastia (breast enlargement in men) is reported more often with spironolactone than with eplerenone in a 2024 heart failure meta-analysis
cautions: US prescribing information for spironolactone says that potassium supplements, potassium-containing salt substitutes, and medicines that can raise potassium, such as ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs and heparin, may lead to severe hyperkalaemia
Potassium and kidney function are checked before treatment and monitored during treatment, according to NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance for spironolactone and a review of eplerenone

references.title: Northern Care Alliance NHS: Cardiology - Spironolactone or Eplerenone
NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service: Spironolactone monitoring
PMC: Comparative effectiveness and safety of eplerenone and spironolactone in patients with heart failure
PubMed: The aldosterone antagonist and facultative diuretic eplerenone: a critical review

sglt2-inhibitors.name: SGLT2 inhibitors
sglt2-inhibitors.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors are tablets used for type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease. They lower blood sugar by acting on the kidneys, as the NHS describes for dapagliflozin.
sglt2-inhibitors.mechanism: SGLT2 stands for sodium-glucose cotransporter-2. The NHS says dapagliflozin, a medicine of this type, makes the kidneys remove extra sugar in the urine, which lowers blood sugar. Cambridge University Hospitals says the kidney and heart benefits of these medicines apply beyond people with diabetes.
classEffects: Leeds Teaching Hospitals lists genital fungal infections such as thrush as a common side effect of these medicines

Leeds Teaching Hospitals says these medicines may cause acids called ketones to build up in the blood (diabetic ketoacidosis), with warning symptoms including stomach pain, feeling sick and vomiting, rapid breathing and dehydration, which need urgent medical help (a doctor or NHS 111 promptly, or 999 in an emergency)
cautions: NHS leaflets describe sick day rules, in which the medicine is stopped temporarily during illness such as infection, diarrhoea and vomiting or flu

Severe pain, tenderness, swelling or redness around the genitals or the area between them and the anus, with fever or feeling unwell, can be a rare infection called Fournier gangrene and needs emergency help (call 999)

references.title: Leeds Teaching Hospitals: Information for people on SGLT-2 inhibitors
Cambridge University Hospitals: SGLT-2 inhibitors in type 2 diabetes

sulfonylureas.name: Sulfonylureas
sulfonylureas.summary: Sulfonylureas are tablets for type 2 diabetes that prompt the pancreas to make more insulin. Low blood sugar (a hypo) is one of their most common side effects, and some people gain weight. NHS diabetes guidance says to call 999 if a person with a hypo is unconscious, does not regain consciousness or has a seizure.
sulfonylureas.mechanism: Sulfonylureas work by prompting the pancreas to release more insulin, which lowers blood glucose. Diabetes UK says low blood sugar is one of the most common side effects.
classEffects: Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia), which Diabetes UK calls one of the most common side effects
Weight gain: Diabetes UK says some people gain weight while taking a sulphonylurea
Stomach upset such as tummy ache, sickness and diarrhoea
Rarer effects include liver damage and low blood cell counts, according to Diabetes UK
cautions: A hypo that leaves a person unconscious, not regaining consciousness or having a seizure is a 999 emergency, according to NHS diabetes guidance; the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 if sugary food or drink does not help or hypo symptoms return
Driving: Diabetes UK says sulphonylureas can increase the risk of hypos while driving; DVLA guidance says severe hypoglycaemia while driving means stopping driving and notifying the DVLA
NICE lists a sulfonylurea among options to add when further treatment is needed in type 2 diabetes, and describes sulfonylureas as possibly increasing hypoglycaemic events and weight gain
The NHS says gliclazide is not usually used in pregnancy and lists severe kidney or liver disease among the reasons it may not be suitable

references.title: GOV.UK: Diabetes mellitus: assessing fitness to drive
NICE NG28: Type 2 diabetes in adults: management
NHS Scotland, My Diabetes My Way: Hypoglycaemia

pde5-inhibitors.name: PDE5 inhibitors
pde5-inhibitors.summary: PDE5 inhibitors are medicines that include sildenafil and tadalafil, used mainly for erection problems. Some are also used for pulmonary hypertension. The NHS warns against combining them with nitrates and poppers because blood pressure can fall sharply.
pde5-inhibitors.mechanism: StatPearls says these drugs stop the PDE5 enzyme from breaking down cGMP, a chemical messenger. StatPearls also says nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors both cause blood vessels to widen, so using them together can cause severe low blood pressure.
classEffects: Headache, indigestion and a blocked nose are among the side effects the NHS lists for sildenafil and tadalafil.
A painful or prolonged erection and sudden changes in sight or hearing are listed as serious.
cautions: StatPearls says combining PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates is contraindicated because of the risk of profound and potentially life-threatening low blood pressure.
The NHS lists poppers and some illegal drugs as raising the risk of serious side effects.
A recent heart attack or stroke is among the reasons the NHS lists against use of sildenafil and tadalafil.
A review says alpha-blockers call for caution with PDE5 inhibitors.

classWarnings.text: Combining a PDE5 inhibitor with nitrates can cause a dangerous fall in blood pressure.

source.title: NHS: Taking sildenafil with other medicines and herbal supplements

classWarnings.text: Sudden loss of vision or hearing needs a call to a doctor right away.

classInteractions.effect: A dangerous fall in blood pressure; the NHS says sildenafil is not usually prescribed with nitrates, and the same warning applies to tadalafil.

source.title: NHS: Taking sildenafil with other medicines and herbal supplements

classInteractions.effect: A higher risk of serious side effects.

classInteractions.with: Illegal drugs such as amphetamines, ecstasy and cocaine
classInteractions.effect: The NHS says these can increase the risk of serious side effects.

combined-hormonal-contraceptives.name: Combined hormonal contraceptives
combined-hormonal-contraceptives.summary: Combined hormonal contraceptives contain both an oestrogen and a progestogen, and include the combined pill, a skin patch and a vaginal ring.
combined-hormonal-contraceptives.mechanism: They work mainly by stopping ovulation, the release of an egg from the ovaries. For the combined pill, NHS sources add that the mucus made by the cervix becomes thicker.
cautions: They carry a risk of blood clots in the leg or lung, heart attack and stroke, which the NHS describes as very small.
The UK medicines regulator found a higher relative risk of clots with drospirenone, gestodene and desogestrel products than with levonorgestrel, norethisterone or norgestimate products.
A history of blood clots, migraine with aura, breast cancer, liver cancer or severe cirrhosis, heart problems or complications of diabetes can make the combined pill unsuitable.
Some medicines, including some for TB, epilepsy or HIV and the herbal remedy St John's wort, can make the combined pill less effective.
The NHS notes that some hormonal contraceptives can change the effect of other medicines, such as the epilepsy treatment lamotrigine.

classWarnings.text: Blood clots: for a possible clot in the lung, sudden difficulty breathing, chest or upper back pain, a very fast heartbeat or fainting needs a 999 call or A&E; for a possible clot in the leg, the NHS advises getting medical help as soon as possible, for example an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.
The combined pill does not protect against sexually transmitted infections.

references.title: NHS: Side effects and risks of the combined pill
NHS: Which medicines affect my contraception?
GOV.UK (MHRA): Combined hormonal contraceptives and venous thromboembolism

nucleoside-antivirals.name: Nucleoside antivirals
nucleoside-antivirals.summary: Antiviral medicines used for herpes virus infections such as cold sores, shingles, chickenpox and genital herpes. Aciclovir is described on this site, and valaciclovir is a related medicine.
nucleoside-antivirals.mechanism: MedlinePlus describes aciclovir as a synthetic nucleoside analogue antiviral that works by stopping the spread of the herpes virus in the body. The NHS says aciclovir stops the herpes virus growing and spreading, which helps the immune system deal with the infection. The NHS says no medicine or treatment removes the herpes virus from the body completely. NIH LiverTox describes valaciclovir as a nucleoside analogue antiviral and a prodrug of aciclovir.
cautions: UK product information lists allergy to aciclovir or valaciclovir as a reason the medicine is not used.
UK product information says aciclovir is cleared through the kidneys, so treatment may be adjusted in kidney problems.

classInteractions.effect: UK product information says these can raise aciclovir levels in the blood.

source.title: emc: Aciclovir 400 mg Tablets summary of product characteristics

classInteractions.effect: UK product information says aciclovir may raise theophylline levels.

source.title: emc: Aciclovir 400 mg Tablets summary of product characteristics

classWarnings.text: A serious allergic reaction, with signs such as sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or struggling to breathe, needs a 999 call, according to the NHS.

Liver problems, kidney problems and changes to blood cells are also listed as serious side effects; the NHS advises calling NHS 111 if someone using or recently using aciclovir thinks they may be having these.

references.title: NHS: Aciclovir
references.section: Common questions about aciclovir; Side effects of aciclovir
