dhsc-under-18-sales-ban-vapes-nicotine-p.name: Under-18 ban on vapes and nicotine in force
dhsc-under-18-sales-ban-vapes-nicotine-p.summary: New rules took effect on 29 October 2026 making it illegal to sell any vape or non-medicinal nicotine product to anyone under 18, according to a Department of Health and Social Care explainer.
keyPoints: The Department of Health and Social Care published its explainer on 29 October 2026, the day the rules took effect.
Selling any vaping product or non-medicinal nicotine product to under-18s is illegal, online or in shop.
Adults who buy these products for under-18s now commit an offence.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The Department of Health and Social Care says it is illegal to sell any vaping product or non-medicinal nicotine product to anyone under 18, whether online or in a shop. The ban now covers nicotine-free vapes, which were not covered before, and tobacco-free nicotine pouches.

Buying these products for someone under 18, known as proxy purchasing, is now an offence.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The rules restrict free giveaways and substantial discounts used to promote sales and ban most vending-machine sales. Enforcement authorities in England and Wales can issue £200 fixed penalty notices. Legal vaping products remain available to adults.

Separate tobacco rules are due later: from 1 January 2027 it will be illegal to sell tobacco to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009. See the site's smoking page for health information.

diabetes-foot-care-daily-checks-and-annu.name: Looking after your feet with diabetes
diabetes-foot-care-daily-checks-and-annu.headline: Looking after your feet with diabetes: daily checks, footwear and the annual foot check
diabetes-foot-care-daily-checks-and-annu.summary: Diabetes can reduce feeling in the feet and slow healing, so UK sources describe daily checks and an annual foot check.
keyPoints: Diabetes can damage nerves in the feet, so they may not give a warning when something is wrong.
Diabetes UK advises looking at the feet each morning and again at bedtime.
A trained professional checks bare feet as part of the annual diabetes health check, which is free on the NHS.
Sources advise prompt contact with a GP, podiatrist or diabetic foot team about a hot, red or swollen foot or any new wound.

body.heading: Why do feet need extra care with diabetes?
body.body: Diabetes can damage the nerves in the feet, which reduces feeling; this is called neuropathy. Diabetes can also affect the circulation to the feet. Diabetes UK says that if feeling has been lost, a person may not notice an injury to the foot. Sources note that smoking reduces blood flow to the feet.

body.heading: What does a daily check involve?
body.body: Diabetes UK advises looking at the feet before putting socks on in the morning and again before bed. NHS sources describe looking at the tops, soles, heels and between the toes, using a mirror or asking someone for help if the feet cannot be seen. The signs listed include redness, swelling, blisters, cracks, broken skin and colour changes. NHS sources also describe washing the feet daily, drying them well between the toes, and moisturising dry skin. NHS sources describe moisturising dry skin but avoiding the gaps between the toes.

body.heading: What do shoes and socks have to do with it?
body.body: Diabetes UK says shoes and socks that are too tight, too loose or that rub can cause problems. It advises checking inside and outside footwear before putting it on. UK sources describe changing socks daily and choosing natural fibres such as cotton or wool, without holes or thick seams. NHS sources say people at high risk should not cut their own toenails unless a podiatrist advises it.

body.heading: What is the annual foot check?
body.body: Diabetes UK says a trained professional should check bare feet as part of the annual diabetes health check, and that the check is free on the NHS. The check looks at sensation and at blood flow in the feet. The result places a person in a low, moderate or high risk category for foot problems. Diabetes UK says that people at low risk may move to a check every other year, while those at moderate risk usually keep having yearly checks. NICE has a guideline on preventing and managing diabetic foot problems.

body.heading: When should foot changes be reported, and to whom?
body.body: Sources advise prompt contact with a GP, podiatrist or diabetic foot team about a hot, red, swollen foot, new damage to the skin, a change in foot shape, new pain, or a cut that is slow to heal. NHS sources describe seeking help the same day for signs of infection such as redness, swelling, oozing or a bad smell, and NHS Inform says to call NHS 111 for new foot problems with fever, shivering or feeling generally unwell. A foot that is changing colour or going very pale or blue, especially with new numbness or pain, is described as an emergency: call 999 or go to A&E. When the GP practice or podiatrist is closed, the route is NHS 111.

dizziness-and-vertigo-causes-and-warning.name: Dizziness and vertigo: causes and warning signs
dizziness-and-vertigo-causes-and-warning.headline: Dizziness and vertigo: common causes and the signs that need urgent help
dizziness-and-vertigo-causes-and-warning.summary: Dizziness is common and has many causes, from inner ear problems to low blood pressure. The NHS advises calling 999 when it comes with signs of a stroke.
keyPoints: Vertigo is the feeling that you or the room is spinning, and the NHS says inner ear problems are its most common causes.
The NHS says to call 999 for vertigo with double vision, trouble speaking or weakness or numbness in an arm or leg.
A severe headache or feeling very sick with vertigo calls for an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.
Dizziness that keeps coming back, or comes with hearing, eyesight or pulse changes or fainting, is a reason to contact a GP.

body.heading: Is dizziness the same as vertigo?
body.body: Dizziness is a broad word that people use for several sensations, including light-headedness and a feeling of spinning. Vertigo is a particular kind of dizziness in which it feels as if you or the room is spinning, even when nothing is moving. The NHS says inner ear problems, which affect balance, are the most common causes of vertigo.

body.heading: What causes light-headedness?
body.body: NHS inform lists labyrinthitis, migraine, low blood sugar and dehydration among the causes of dizziness. A sudden drop in blood pressure on standing up is another listed cause. Less often, an irregular heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation, or carbon monoxide poisoning, is on the list.

body.heading: What helps while dizzy?
body.body: NHS inform says dizziness usually goes away on its own. Its self-care advice describes lying down until the feeling passes and then getting up slowly. NHS inform also says not to do anything that could be dangerous while dizzy, such as driving, climbing a ladder or using heavy machinery. Most vertigo improves without treatment, and when treatment is needed it depends on the cause. BPPV usually goes away on its own after several weeks or months, and repositioning manoeuvres are used to treat it. For light-headedness on standing, a GP can measure blood pressure lying down and standing up and may arrange blood tests to check thyroid and sugar levels.

body.heading: What are the common causes of vertigo?
body.body: The NHS vertigo page lists benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis, Ménière’s disease and migraine among the causes. In BPPV, certain head movements trigger short spells of spinning. Rolling over in bed or tilting the head back to look up are typical triggers. Labyrinthitis is usually caused by a viral infection such as a cold or flu, so antibiotics will not help, and the vertigo usually lasts a few days. Hearing loss and ringing in the ears (tinnitus) can come with labyrinthitis. Ménière’s disease is a rarer cause, with attacks that can include vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: NHS inform advises contacting a GP if dizziness will not go away or keeps coming back. Changes in hearing, eyesight or pulse, or fainting, are further reasons to make contact. For vertigo, the NHS suggests seeing a GP if it comes on suddenly, does not go away, keeps returning or affects daily life.

body.heading: When is it urgent?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 if vertigo comes with a severe headache, being sick or feeling very sick, or a very high temperature. It says to call 999 or go to A&E if vertigo comes with double vision or loss of vision, hearing loss, trouble speaking, or weakness, numbness or tingling in an arm or a leg. The NHS also advises not to drive yourself to A&E. Dizziness is among the symptoms the NHS lists for stroke, and any sign of stroke is treated as an emergency: the NHS FAST test stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999.

dxa-bone-density-scan-explained.name: DXA bone density scan: what it shows
dxa-bone-density-scan-explained.summary: A DXA scan measures bone density, usually at the hip and spine, using low-dose X-rays. This guide covers who may be referred and what the T-score decides.
keyPoints: A DXA scan is painless: the person lies on a flat table while a scanning arm passes over the hip and lower spine.
The radiation dose is low: the NHS says a DEXA scan uses a much lower level of radiation than a standard X-ray.
The T-score compares bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex.
Treatment decisions use an assessment of the overall chance of breaking a bone, not the scan result alone.

body.heading: What is a DXA scan?
body.body: DXA, also written DEXA, stands for dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, a scan that measures bone density. The scan is used to help diagnose osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker. The NHS describes a DEXA scan as a test that uses low-dose X-rays.

body.heading: Who is offered one?
body.body: NHS trust pages say a doctor can refer a person for a DEXA scan if they may be at risk of osteoporosis, and the criteria differ between services. One NHS trust referral form lists being a current smoker and having had a previous low-trauma fracture among the risk factors it asks about. A doctor usually makes the referral. Results are combined with a fracture risk assessment rather than used alone.

body.heading: Why might a doctor suggest it?
body.body: A bone density scan measures bone density and helps to judge the risk of a fracture. Unlike an ordinary X-ray, it can detect small reductions in bone density, so osteoporosis can be found before a bone breaks. The NHS lists reasons for a scan that include breaking bones easily, long-term use of steroid medicines, and early menopause.

body.heading: What happens during the scan?
body.body: The person lies on their back on a flat table. A scanning arm passes slowly over the body, usually the hip and lower spine. NHS pages describe the scan as quick and painless, and the time it takes varies between services.

body.heading: How much radiation is involved?
body.body: The dose is low. The NHS says a DEXA scan uses a much lower level of radiation than a standard X-ray, similar to what a person is exposed to naturally over about three days.

body.heading: Who should not have one?
body.body: The NHS says the scan uses a low dose of radiation and the risks are much lower than with standard X-rays. Pregnancy is the main caution: the NHS says bone density scans and X-rays are not recommended in pregnancy. The person lies on their back on a flat, open X-ray table while a scanning arm passes slowly over them. An NHS trust page says no special preparation is needed, although metal fasteners on clothing may need to be removed.

body.heading: What do the T-score and Z-score mean?
body.body: The T-score compares a person's bone density with that of a healthy young adult of the same sex. Scores are grouped into bands described as normal, low bone density (osteopenia) and osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is diagnosed using the lowest T-score across the lumbar spine, the neck of the thigh bone and the total hip. The Z-score compares a person with others of the same age, and it is used mainly for premenopausal women, men under 50 and children.

body.heading: Does the result decide treatment?
body.body: A T-score does not decide treatment alone. UK osteoporosis guidance uses a fracture risk tool such as FRAX, which estimates the chance of a broken bone over ten years from bone density and other risk factors, so bone density alone does not decide treatment.

early-pregnancy-symptoms-and-contacting-.name: Early pregnancy signs and contacting a midwife
early-pregnancy-symptoms-and-contacting-.summary: The NHS says a missed period is the earliest sign of pregnancy, and many areas let people refer themselves to a midwife.
keyPoints: The NHS says a missed period is the earliest and most reliable sign of pregnancy for someone with a regular monthly cycle.
Most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first day of a missed period, according to the NHS.
In England, people can usually refer themselves for NHS pregnancy care online without seeing a GP first.
The NHS says the first midwife appointment should happen by about 10 weeks of pregnancy where possible.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad, severe tummy pain or shoulder pain with feeling faint.
For lighter bleeding or milder pain, the NHS points to the maternity unit, a GP or NHS 111.

body.heading: What are the early signs of pregnancy?
body.body: The NHS says the earliest and most reliable sign of pregnancy is a missed period, for someone with a regular monthly cycle. NHS inform notes that an irregular cycle can make a missed period harder to notice. Sometimes a person who is pregnant has a shorter or lighter period than normal. The NHS lists other signs, including feeling or being sick, unusual tiredness and breasts that become larger and tender. A strange taste in the mouth, which many women describe as metallic, is also on the list. Tiredness can be marked, especially during the first 12 weeks or so. Sickness is often called morning sickness, but it can happen at any time of the day or night. Symptoms like these usually start when a person is around 4 to 6 weeks pregnant. They overlap with premenstrual changes and other conditions, so a pregnancy test is the way to find out.

body.heading: How soon can a test confirm it?
body.body: The NHS says most home pregnancy tests can be used from the first day of a missed period. Tests carried out earlier than this are not always accurate. Someone who does not know when the next period is due can test at least 21 days after unprotected sex. NHS inform advises checking the expiry date on the packaging and says an out-of-date test should not be used. Some sources recommend using the first urine of the morning, because it is more concentrated. Fertility medicines based on the hormone hCG may cause a false positive result, according to a hospital guide and MedlinePlus. After a negative result, NHS inform suggests waiting two to three days and testing again. The NHS says a GP can be contacted if a second test is negative but the period has not arrived.

body.heading: Who should someone contact after a positive test?
body.body: In England, the NHS website lets people refer themselves for pregnancy care online, by entering a postcode, town or city to find local trusts with maternity services. A person can choose which trust to refer themselves to. Some trusts ask people to call their community midwifery team instead, and others point to a GP referral, so practice varies. The first midwife appointment is called the booking appointment, and the NHS says it should happen by about 10 weeks of pregnancy where possible. For anyone already past 10 weeks, the NHS says to refer themselves as soon as possible to start pregnancy care. NHS inform says the midwife gives information about screening tests in pregnancy at this appointment, and blood tests are offered to those who would like them. Someone with a long-term condition or who takes medicine still needs to see a GP or specialist about any changes to their care.

body.heading: What happens when someone refers themselves?
body.body: Many NHS trusts let people refer themselves for pregnancy care without seeing a GP first. NHS England has described this route as a way to get a first midwife appointment faster. Some trusts use an online form, and others use a phone number, so the process differs from area to area. One trust says its form gives the team time to arrange a first appointment for between 8 and 10 weeks of pregnancy. Checking the local trust's website is the way to find the route used in a particular area.

body.heading: Which symptoms need urgent help?
body.body: The NHS separates problems that need an ambulance from those that need advice the same day. It says to call 999 or go to A&E for heavy bleeding that soaks a pad soon after it is put on. Severe tummy pain, shoulder pain, or feeling faint or dizzy in pregnancy are also signs of needing immediate treatment. The NHS gives the example of pain so severe that it stops a person doing everyday things such as watching television or reading. Sudden, intense tummy pain with feeling very dizzy, fainting or looking very pale can mean an ectopic pregnancy has ruptured, which the NHS treats as very serious. For a possible pregnancy with a combination of a missed period, tummy pain low down on one side, vaginal bleeding or brown watery discharge, or discomfort when peeing or pooing, the NHS says to contact a GP or call NHS 111. This applies even without a positive pregnancy test.

body.heading: What about bleeding, miscarriage and early pregnancy units?
body.body: The NHS says symptoms of an ectopic pregnancy usually start around weeks 4 to 12, and that an ectopic pregnancy does not always cause symptoms. Vaginal bleeding is the main sign of miscarriage, but bleeding can also have other causes, so the NHS advises getting it checked. For light bleeding or spotting, the NHS says to contact a GP or maternity team, or call NHS 111. For bleeding with mild or no pain, the NHS says to call the maternity unit if there is a number. An early pregnancy unit may help if a person is under 20 weeks pregnant, and its contact details are on the local trust website or in the maternity notes. The Miscarriage Association says some units accept self-referral and others need a GP referral, so local rules vary. The NHS says a person who is unsure can call NHS 111 or the maternity unit.

eating-well-with-type-2-diabetes.name: Eating well with type 2 diabetes
eating-well-with-type-2-diabetes.headline: Eating well with type 2 diabetes: what Diabetes UK, NICE and the NHS say
eating-well-with-type-2-diabetes.summary: Diabetes UK says there is no special diet only for type 2 diabetes, and NICE advises the same healthy balanced eating as for everyone.
keyPoints: Diabetes UK says there is no special diet exclusively for people with type 2 diabetes.
Diabetes UK says the total amount of carbohydrate eaten has the biggest effect on glucose levels after eating.
NICE sets an initial weight-loss goal of 5 to 10 per cent of body weight for adults with type 2 diabetes who are overweight.
NICE says nutrition advice should be individual and ongoing, from a healthcare professional with expertise in nutrition.

body.heading: Is there a special diet for type 2 diabetes?
body.body:
Diabetes UK says there is no such thing as a special diet exclusively for people with type 2 diabetes. Its advice is to choose healthier foods more often and to keep treats occasional. NICE tells clinicians to emphasise healthy balanced eating advice that applies to the general population when advising adults with type 2 diabetes. The NHS says changes to diet and activity can help control blood sugar.

Diabetes UK advises avoiding foods labelled 'diabetic' or 'suitable for diabetics'. NICE also discourages the use of foods marketed specifically for people with diabetes.

body.heading: How do carbohydrates affect blood glucose?
body.body: Diabetes UK says that even low-carb eating shouldn't be no-carb eating. It says the total amount of carbohydrate eaten has the biggest effect on glucose levels after eating. Its guidance favours higher-fibre wholegrain foods over refined carbohydrates such as white bread. NICE also says a limited amount of sucrose-containing food can replace other carbohydrate in the meal plan, provided total energy intake is not excessive.

body.heading: What about fruit, vegetables and protein?
body.body:
Diabetes UK says whole fruit is good for everyone, and that with diabetes it is no different. Diabetes UK's type 2 meal plan includes at least five portions of fruit and vegetables a day. Diabetes UK lists pulses such as kidney beans, chickpeas and lentils as protein sources, and suggests using beans and pulses to replace some or all of the meat in a dish. It recommends at least two portions of oily fish each week.

One NHS trust leaflet (North Bristol) describes, in its weight-loss section, a plate with half vegetables or salad, a quarter starchy carbohydrate foods, and a quarter meat, fish, cheese, eggs or pulses.

body.heading: Where do weight and activity come in?
body.body: For adults with type 2 diabetes who are overweight, NICE sets an initial body weight loss target of 5 to 10 per cent. NICE adds that smaller losses may still help and that larger losses over the longer term have an advantageous effect on metabolism. The NHS page on food and keeping active suggests at least two and a half hours of activity a week, with brisk walking, climbing stairs and more vigorous housework or gardening as examples. The same page describes a short-term low-calorie diet as linked to weight loss and lower blood sugar in some people, and says it is not safe or suitable for everyone with type 2 diabetes.

body.heading: Who gives personal advice?
body.body: NICE says people should get individual and ongoing nutrition advice from a healthcare professional with specific expertise in nutrition, adapted to their needs and culture. The NHS notes that people taking medicines that can cause hypos are advised not to miss meals.

eatwell-guide-healthy-eating.name: The Eatwell Guide: a balanced diet explained
eatwell-guide-healthy-eating.summary: The Eatwell Guide shows the proportions of food groups in a balanced UK diet, with fruit, vegetables and starchy foods making up just over a third each.
keyPoints: The NHS Eatwell Guide divides food into groups and shows how much of each makes up a balanced diet.
Fruit and vegetables and starchy foods each make up just over a third of the guide, with higher-fibre starchy choices preferred.
NHS advice is at least five portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables a day, and at least two portions of fish a week, one of them oily.
Foods high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the main groups and are meant to be eaten less often and in small amounts.

body.heading: What is the Eatwell Guide?
body.body: The Eatwell Guide is the UK government's picture of a balanced diet, and the NHS explains it on its Live Well pages. It divides the foods people eat into groups and shows roughly what share of the diet each should make up. Foods and drinks high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the main groups, and the guide says they should be eaten less often and in small amounts.

body.heading: How much fruit, vegetables and starchy food?
body.body: Fruit and vegetables make up just over a third of the food in the guide. The NHS advises at least five portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables a day. A portion of fresh, canned or frozen fruit or vegetables is 80 grams. Starchy foods also make up just over a third of the guide, and the NHS recommends choosing wholegrain or higher-fibre versions where possible.

body.heading: What about protein, dairy and oils?
body.body: The NHS lists beans, pulses, fish, eggs and meat among good sources of protein. The NHS advises at least two portions of fish a week, including at least one portion of oily fish. For dairy and alternatives the guide points to lower-fat and lower-sugar choices where possible. Unsaturated oils and spreads are the choice for oils, eaten in small amounts.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about fat, sugar and salt?
body.body: NHS healthy eating advice includes cutting down on saturated fat and sugar and eating less salt. Fruit juice and smoothies are limited to a total of 150 millilitres a day, because they are high in sugar. The NHS says sugary drinks can be swapped for diet, sugar-free or no-added-sugar versions.

body.heading: Where do drinks, breakfast and weight fit in?
body.body: The NHS tips say that a healthy, balanced diet can help maintain a healthy weight, and that regular exercise may help reduce the risk of serious health conditions. They describe a breakfast high in fibre and low in fat, sugar and salt as one way to be part of a balanced diet.

body.heading: How do salt and saturated fat fit in?
body.body: The NHS advises adults and children aged 11 and over to have no more than 6 grams of salt a day, and younger children less. The NHS says around three quarters of the salt people eat comes from packaged and everyday foods. Salt is linked to high blood pressure, which can lead to heart disease or stroke. Too much saturated fat can increase cholesterol in the blood and so the risk of heart disease, and the NHS suggests swapping towards unsaturated fats such as vegetable oils, oily fish and avocados.

body.heading: What do food labels show?
body.body: UK nutrition labels show energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt. Front-of-pack labels use red, amber and green colours to show whether a food is high, medium or low in fat, saturated fat, sugars and salt. The NHS lists sweets, sugary drinks, cakes, biscuits, pastries and breakfast cereals among common sources of added sugar, and says the label and ingredients list can show how much sugar a food contains.

ecg-what-it-records-and-shows.name: ECG: what it records and what it can show
ecg-what-it-records-and-shows.summary: An ECG records the heart's electrical activity through patches on the skin. This guide covers the test, longer recordings, what it shows and its limits.
keyPoints: An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart, including its rate and rhythm.
A standard ECG is quick and painless, and patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest.
A standard ECG can miss an abnormal rhythm that is not happening during the recording, which is why longer monitoring is sometimes used.
An ECG can help doctors tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past.

body.heading: What does an ECG record?
body.body: An electrocardiogram, or ECG, records the electrical activity of the heart. The British Heart Foundation describes it as a simple test that records the heart's rhythm, its rate and its electrical activity. Each heartbeat is triggered by an electrical signal, and the machine picks these signals up through sensors on the skin. The result is a graph of the signals.

body.heading: What happens during a standard ECG?
body.body: Sticky patches called electrodes are placed on the arms, legs and chest and connected to the machine. The British Heart Foundation describes the test as quick and painless. The NHS puts a standard ECG at about 5 minutes. People are asked to lie still because movement can affect the recording.

body.heading: What can an ECG show?
body.body: The British Heart Foundation says an ECG can help doctors to tell whether someone is having a heart attack or has had one in the past. The NHS says an ECG is usually done when a doctor suspects symptoms of a heart attack, coronary heart disease or an abnormal heart rhythm (arrhythmia).

body.heading: What are the limits of a standard ECG?
body.body: A standard ECG captures only what happens while it is recording. A standard ECG can miss an abnormal rhythm that is not happening during the recording. That is why longer recordings or other heart tests are sometimes arranged.

body.heading: What are longer and exercise ECGs?
body.body: An ambulatory ECG, sometimes called Holter monitoring, records the heart's electrical activity continuously while the person goes about daily life. The NHS says people are usually asked to wear it for 24 to 48 hours, but it can be up to 7 days. It is used to look for heart rhythm problems that a short recording may miss. An exercise ECG monitors the heart while the person exercises and the heart is working harder. The British Heart Foundation describes an exercise ECG as an ECG recorded while the person walks on a treadmill or cycles, used to see how the heart behaves under exertion and to look for coronary heart disease. Doctors may suggest it for symptoms such as dizzy spells or blackouts. It is also used after procedures such as angioplasty, and to help set exercise levels for cardiac rehabilitation. The person walks or cycles at a gentle pace that gradually gets harder, and staff watch closely.

body.heading: How do the results reach the person?
body.body: The NHS says people may need a follow-up appointment to talk about their ECG results. The NHS says ECG results may be available on the same day, but can take a few weeks depending on the type of ECG. The British Heart Foundation says to call 999 immediately for signs of a heart attack, such as sudden chest pain that does not ease after a few minutes of rest.

echocardiogram-types-and-what-it-shows.name: Echocardiogram: types, what happens and results
echocardiogram-types-and-what-it-shows.summary: An echocardiogram uses ultrasound to picture the heart. This guide explains the standard, stress and throat versions and what each involves.
keyPoints: The most common type is a transthoracic echocardiogram, in which a probe is placed over the chest.
A stress echocardiogram is done during exercise or after a medicine that has a similar effect on the heart.
A transoesophageal echocardiogram passes a probe down the throat and gives more detailed pictures than the standard test.
Most people need no preparation for a standard echocardiogram, but may need to avoid eating for several hours before the throat version.

body.heading: What is an echocardiogram?
body.body: An echocardiogram is a scan that uses ultrasound, high-frequency sound waves, to produce moving pictures of the heart. An ultrasound probe covered in gel is placed on the chest in the standard test.

body.heading: What are the types of echocardiogram?
body.body: The most common type is the transthoracic echocardiogram, in which the probe is placed over the chest. A transoesophageal echocardiogram uses a probe that passes down the throat and gives more detailed pictures of the heart than the standard test. Doctors may use it when the standard test has not shown enough detail. A stress echocardiogram is a transthoracic scan done during exercise on a treadmill or exercise bike, or after a medicine that has a similar effect on the heart. For some echocardiograms, saline or a special dye is injected into a vein to help show the heart more clearly. A stress echocardiogram may be recommended if a heart problem is triggered by physical activity.

body.heading: What happens in the throat version?
body.body: For the transoesophageal test, the back of the throat is numbed with an anaesthetic spray. A sedative may be given to help the person relax. Avoiding food for several hours beforehand may be needed for this version. Afterwards the throat may be sore, and this should pass within one or two days.

body.heading: What can an echocardiogram show?
body.body: An NHS trust says a transoesophageal echocardiogram can look at the heart valves and heart muscle, and check for blood clots and tears in the aorta. An NHS trust says it can help guide surgeons during some heart procedures.

body.heading: What does it check, and how long does it take?
body.body: The British Heart Foundation says an echocardiogram uses sound waves to build up a picture of the heart and its structures, such as the valves. It describes the test as an important investigation for anyone with suspected heart failure, heart valve problems or cardiomyopathy, a disease of the heart muscle. Like other ultrasound scans, which the NHS says do not use radiation, an echocardiogram uses sound waves.

body.heading: Is any preparation needed?
body.body: For a standard echocardiogram people usually need to do nothing to prepare. The exception is the throat version, which may require avoiding eating for several hours.

body.heading: What happens in a standard scan?
body.body: For a standard echocardiogram no preparation is needed, and NHS trust leaflets say people can eat and drink as normal before and afterwards. The person lies on their left side while a cardiac physiologist, a specially trained technician, scans the chest after putting gel on it. The physiologist may ask the person to change position or to hold their breath briefly so that the pictures are clearer. One trust leaflet describes a standard echocardiogram as painless, with no side effects and no radiation.

body.heading: What is a stress echocardiogram like?
body.body: A stress echocardiogram checks how the heart copes with a greater workload, by taking pictures at rest and again under stress. The stress usually comes from walking on a treadmill or, in a dobutamine stress echocardiogram, from a medicine called dobutamine that raises the heart rate. A cardiologist or a specially trained cardiac physiologist supervises the test. Some trust leaflets ask people to avoid certain heart medicines, such as beta blockers, before a dobutamine stress echocardiogram unless the doctor advises otherwise, and each hospital gives its own instructions. Leaflets describe rare complications such as an abnormal heart rhythm and quote different figures, for example around 1 in 1,000 patients in one leaflet and around 1 in 500 in another.

body.heading: How are the results given?
body.body: A cardiac physiologist analyses the recorded images and writes a report for the doctor who requested the test. The doctor who requested the test then receives the report and passes on the results, for example at a clinic appointment or by letter, depending on the trust. One trust leaflet says the letter about stress echocardiogram results, sent to the GP with a copy to the patient, can take about two to four weeks.

egfr-and-creatinine-kidney-blood-tests.name: eGFR and creatinine: kidney test results
egfr-and-creatinine-kidney-blood-tests.summary: Creatinine and eGFR show how well the kidneys filter blood, and kidney disease is confirmed only when abnormal results persist.
keyPoints: Creatinine is a waste product measured in the blood, and eGFR is an estimate of kidney filtering worked out from it.
As kidney function declines, the eGFR may fall over time.
One abnormal result is not enough to diagnose chronic kidney disease, which is confirmed when eGFR stays low over about three months.
A urine test, the albumin to creatinine ratio, is used alongside eGFR because it can show kidney damage.

body.heading: What are creatinine and eGFR?
body.body: Creatinine is a waste product, and the blood test measures how much of it is in the blood. The eGFR, or estimated glomerular filtration rate, is calculated from the creatinine result. The calculation also takes account of age and sex. Lab Tests Online UK explains that the eGFR may fall over time as kidney function declines. Because eGFR comes from a routine blood test, it lets clinicians spot kidney problems before symptoms appear. People with more muscle naturally make more creatinine, which can give a lower eGFR than their kidney function really is. Cystatin C is another marker filtered by the kidneys and is less affected by muscle mass than creatinine.

body.heading: What does a low eGFR mean?
body.body: A low eGFR may be a sign of kidney disease, though a single result is not enough to say. NICE says testing for chronic kidney disease uses both an eGFR and a urine ACR. A slightly raised urine ACR, which checks for the protein albumin, may indicate early-stage kidney disease. eGFR falls naturally with age, which does not always mean kidney disease. The estimate is unreliable when kidney function is changing quickly, as in acute kidney injury.

body.heading: How is chronic kidney disease confirmed?
body.body: One abnormal result is not enough. A diagnosis is usually confirmed only if repeated eGFR tests are consistently lower than normal over about three months. NICE says a low first eGFR should be repeated soon, to check whether sudden kidney injury is the cause. The urine albumin to creatinine ratio, or ACR, compares albumin with creatinine in a urine sample. Alongside the eGFR, urine tests give a more accurate picture of how well the kidneys are working. Results are classed by eGFR category and by ACR category, which together show the stage. Lab Tests Online UK says a very high urine ACR shows that kidney disease is present in a more severe form.

body.heading: Who is tested?
body.body: Testing is recommended for people with risk factors such as diabetes, high blood pressure, past acute kidney injury or cardiovascular disease. Early chronic kidney disease often causes no symptoms, so it is commonly found through routine blood or urine tests. Later symptoms can include tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands, shortness of breath, blood in the urine and passing urine more often at night. The NHS advises seeing a GP about symptoms that persist.

body.heading: What are the limits of the test?
body.body: Creatinine-based eGFR may be less reliable in older adults. In that situation another marker, cystatin C, can help. Creatinine can also be influenced by factors other than the kidneys, such as how much muscle a person has. NICE advises that the urine ACR is ideally measured on an early morning sample.

body.heading: What happens after a diagnosis?
body.body: Chronic kidney disease is most often caused by damage from other conditions, most commonly diabetes and high blood pressure. There is no cure, but care can slow progression. Kidney function is monitored with regular blood and urine tests. Care centres on blood pressure control, managing diabetes, prescribed medicines, diet advice and not smoking. The NHS says medicines can help control related problems and keep the kidneys working for longer. The NHS says most people with chronic kidney disease can control the condition with medicine and regular check-ups. Glomerulonephritis, inflammation of the filters inside the kidneys, is another cause of kidney disease.

body.heading: How often are kidney tests repeated?
body.body: NICE guideline NG203 says the monitoring frequency it recommends is a minimum, and that more frequent monitoring may suit some people. NICE sets a minimum number of checks each year, which depends on the eGFR and ACR categories. It also reflects how quickly the eGFR or ACR is changing and other conditions such as diabetes. NICE says ACR monitoring should be individualised, for example more often when the ACR is higher. NICE lists diabetes among the risk factors for which eGFR and ACR testing is advised.

erectile-dysfunction-causes-and-when-to-.name: Erection problems and seeing a GP
erectile-dysfunction-causes-and-when-to-.summary: Erection problems are common and can have physical causes, and the NHS advises seeing a GP if they keep happening.
keyPoints: Erectile dysfunction means trouble getting or keeping an erection, and occasional problems are common.
The NHS links occasional problems to stress, tiredness, anxiety and drinking too much alcohol.
Diabetes, some operations, low testosterone and some medicines are named physical causes.
NICE says erectile dysfunction shares risk factors with cardiovascular disease, and MedlinePlus calls it an early warning sign of atherosclerosis.
The NHS advises seeing a GP or sexual health clinic if erection problems keep happening.
The MHRA warns that erection pills from unregulated online sellers may contain no active ingredient or toxic ingredients.

body.heading: What counts as an erection problem?
body.body:
Erectile dysfunction, also called impotence, means having trouble getting or keeping an erection. Many men have occasional difficulty, and the NHS describes this as common. It also says occasional problems are often harmless and can resolve by themselves.

What matters is whether the problem keeps happening. The NHS advises seeing a GP or going to a sexual health clinic if erection problems keep happening, rather than simply waiting for them to pass. The sections below describe the usual causes, the links with other conditions, what a GP may offer and how to avoid risky online products.

body.heading: What causes erection problems?
body.body:
The NHS links occasional erection problems to stress, tiredness, anxiety and drinking too much alcohol. These tend to come and go, and they are different from a problem that persists.

Physical causes are also described. NHS sources name diabetes, operations on the bowel, bladder or prostate, and a lack of testosterone, which is a male hormone. One NHS page says hormone problems may be treated with hormone replacement, for example testosterone. Erection problems can also be a side effect of some medicines, including some of those used to treat high blood pressure or depression. Prostate surgery can also cause retrograde ejaculation, which is a separate problem from erectile dysfunction.

The NHS advises talking to a GP before stopping any prescribed medicine, so a suspected medicine side effect is something to raise at an appointment.

body.heading: Is there a link with heart disease and diabetes?
body.body:
NICE says erectile dysfunction shares risk factors with cardiovascular disease, which is disease of the heart and blood vessels. Examples it gives include lack of exercise, obesity, smoking, high cholesterol and metabolic syndrome.

MedlinePlus says erectile dysfunction is an early warning sign that a man may be at higher risk of atherosclerosis, which is a build-up of fatty plaque in the arteries, and its complications. The British Heart Foundation explains that the arteries supplying the penis are narrow, so erection problems can be one of the first warning signs. A large Australian cohort study of 95,038 men found that more severe erectile dysfunction was linked with a higher risk of cardiovascular disease.

An NHS diabetes resource says erectile dysfunction is more common in people with diabetes, especially when diabetes is poorly controlled. It adds that diabetes can damage the blood supply and nerves to the penis. High blood pressure is another link, because the British Heart Foundation notes that high blood pressure and some of its treatments, including beta-blockers and diuretics, can cause erection problems.

body.heading: When should I see a GP?
body.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP or a sexual health clinic if erection problems keep happening. NHS inform Scotland gives more detail, suggesting that people seek help when the symptoms have lasted for more than a few months, things they can do themselves have not helped and they are bothered by the symptoms.

NHS sources describe the GP as the usual first point of contact. The GP can discuss treatment options, may start treatment and can refer on to a hospital or sexual function service if tablets are not suitable. Because erectile dysfunction can sometimes be an early sign of cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure or diabetes, getting it checked is more useful than waiting it out. One NHS trust guideline lists blood tests such as HbA1c and cholesterol among the checks that may be done before a referral.

The British Heart Foundation says erection tablets such as Viagra cannot be used with nitrates or nicorandil, which are medicines used to treat angina. This is one reason clinicians ask about heart medicines before treating erection problems.

body.heading: What treatments are there?
body.body:
NHS trusts describe tablets as the usual first treatment for most men. These include sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and avanafil, and the GP usually prescribes them first. One trust leaflet says medicines of this kind work for up to 70% of men, and the same leaflet notes that most men with erectile dysfunction have an underlying physical cause.

Lifestyle changes are also listed as ways to improve erections, including weight loss, more exercise, stopping smoking and cutting back on alcohol and drugs. Some sources note that these changes can also reduce cardiovascular risk factors.

Psychosexual counselling is one of the offered treatments in primary care guidance, and sexual function clinics can support individuals and couples. Psychological causes are described as more common in younger men.

Vacuum devices are another option, and in some cases the NHS can supply them. Injections into the penis, urethral alprostadil and penile implants are used if tablets fail or are not suitable. A GP or specialist can explain which of these apply in a particular case.

body.heading: What about buying erection medicines online?
body.body:
The MHRA, which regulates medicines in the UK, warns against buying erection pills from unlicensed online sellers. It says such products are unauthorised, so their contents are unknown, and they may contain no active ingredient, too much of it or toxic ingredients.

The MHRA says its enforcement unit seized about 19.5 million doses of erectile dysfunction medicines between 2021 and 2025, and that many of these were sold illegally online. They contained active ingredients such as sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and avanafil.

It adds that unlicensed erection medicines can be especially dangerous for people with heart disease or high blood pressure, or who take other medicines, and can raise the risk of heart attack, stroke and dangerously low blood pressure. The MHRA says these medicines can only be supplied through a UK-registered pharmacy. Suspected fake products can be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.

eye-tests-who-gets-a-free-nhs-sight-test.name: Eye tests: who gets a free NHS sight test
eye-tests-who-gets-a-free-nhs-sight-test.headline: Eye tests: what happens and who is entitled to a free NHS sight test in England
eye-tests-who-gets-a-free-nhs-sight-test.summary: The NHS says everyone should have regular eye tests, at least every 2 years, and lists who can have a free NHS sight test in England.
keyPoints: An optometrist checks vision and the health of the eyes, and can spot conditions such as glaucoma and cataracts.
The NHS says glaucoma develops slowly and is usually picked up at routine eye tests.
People aged 60 or over, people with diabetes or glaucoma, and under-16s are among those who qualify for a free NHS sight test in England.
The NHS lists sudden intense eye pain with a red eye, nausea and blurred vision as needing emergency care: call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: What happens at an eye test?
body.body:
An optometrist or ophthalmic practitioner examines the inside and outside of the eyes. The aim is to check vision and eye health and to spot conditions such as glaucoma, macular degeneration and cataracts. An ophthalmic practitioner can prescribe glasses or contact lenses, and a dispensing optician fits them. If necessary, the optician refers the person to a GP or a hospital eye clinic for further tests.

When glaucoma is suspected, the NHS says the first checks are quick and painless and include vision tests and measurements of the pressure inside the eye. If glaucoma is suspected, referral to an eye specialist called an ophthalmologist follows for further tests.

body.heading: Why have tests when vision seems fine?
body.body: The NHS says glaucoma develops slowly over many years and is usually picked up during routine eye tests. It says everyone should have regular eye tests, at least every 2 years. People at higher risk of glaucoma, for example those with a parent, brother or sister who has it, may be advised to have tests more often.

body.heading: Who can have a free NHS sight test in England?
body.body: The NHS lists people aged 60 or over, under-16s, and 16 to 18 year olds in full-time education among those who can have a free sight test. People registered as partially sighted or blind, and people diagnosed with diabetes or glaucoma, also qualify. The list also covers some people at risk of glaucoma, including some with a close relative who has been diagnosed; the age and other conditions are set out on the NHS page. The list also covers some people receiving certain benefits; the NHS page gives the details. Everyone else pays for a private test; the full list is on the NHS page. In Scotland the rules differ, and NHS inform says all NHS eye examinations are free for people who usually live in the UK.

body.heading: How often does the NHS pay for a test?
body.body: The standard entitlement is a test every 2 years. An earlier NHS test can be arranged if the optometrist considers it clinically necessary. A person who wants tests more often than the optometrist considers necessary pays for a private test. Optical vouchers, which help with the cost of glasses or contact lenses, have their own eligibility rules separate from free sight tests; the NHS page sets out who qualifies.

body.heading: Which eye symptoms need urgent help?
body.body: NHS trust information advises seeing an optician or GP about vision worries that are not sudden. Glaucoma can sometimes come on suddenly, with intense eye pain, a red eye, rainbow-coloured circles around lights, blurred vision, nausea or vomiting, and a headache. The NHS says these symptoms need emergency care, and directs people to call 999 or go to A&E.

falls-in-older-people-reducing-risk.name: Falls in older people and reducing the risk
falls-in-older-people-reducing-risk.summary: Strength and balance exercises and simple changes at home can lower the risk of falls in older people, according to the NHS. NICE recommends offering falls prevention exercise programmes.
keyPoints: The NHS says the risk of falling can be lowered by exercises for strength and balance and by simple changes at home.
NICE guideline NG249 recommends offering a falls prevention exercise programme.
Clearing clutter and trailing wires, using non-slip mats, keeping rooms and stairs well lit and wearing well-fitting footwear with good grip are among the home-safety suggestions.
Regular sight tests are recommended, and in England the NHS provides free sight tests for people aged 60 or over.

body.heading: Why do falls happen?
body.body: Causes of falls include muscle weakness and balance changes with age, conditions that affect mobility or balance (such as arthritis, stroke or Parkinson's), low blood pressure, problems with eyesight or hearing, and dementia. Anyone can have a fall, but it is more likely in older people or those with mobility problems. Some medicines can affect balance and increase the chance of a fall. The NHS advises speaking to a GP or pharmacist if medicines might be affecting balance. Postural hypotension is a drop in blood pressure on standing up from lying or sitting, which can cause dizziness and may lead to a fall.

body.heading: What exercise helps?
body.body: The NHS says regular exercises for strength and balance can improve strength and balance and reduce the risk of falls. The NHS notes there is evidence that regular tai chi can reduce the risk of falls. Programmes are described as best when tailored to the individual and overseen by a trained professional.

body.heading: What can be changed at home?
body.body: Suggestions include clearing clutter and trailing wires, using non-slip mats, keeping stairs well lit and wearing well-fitting footwear with good grip. Regular sight tests are recommended, and free NHS sight tests are available to people aged 60 or over in England.

body.heading: What does NICE recommend?
body.body: NICE guideline NG249 covers falls assessment and prevention in older people and in people aged 50 and over at higher risk, and recommends offering a falls prevention exercise programme.

body.heading: What can a GP or falls team do?
body.body: A GP can check balance with simple tests, review medicines and refer to local falls services. Some areas have a falls team that offers a full assessment to older people who have fallen or are at high risk, and a GP surgery can say what is available locally.

body.heading: What does the NHS advise after a fall?
body.body: Advice after a fall includes calling for help, using a lifeline alarm if there is one, and keeping warm by covering up with a rug, blanket or towel. Advice for someone who is not hurt includes getting up slowly, and changing position regularly while waiting for help if they cannot get up. The NHS says to call 999 if someone has fallen and may have injured their head, back, neck or hip, cannot get up, is confused, drowsy or vomiting, or has severe bleeding; NHS 111 can help if they may be in pain, injured or unwell, and a GP can be seen after any fall.

fda-atezolizumab-stage-iii-colon-cancer.name: FDA approves atezolizumab for colon cancer
fda-atezolizumab-stage-iii-colon-cancer.summary: The US FDA approved atezolizumab (Tecentriq) with chemotherapy on 8 October 2026 as adjuvant treatment for stage III mismatch repair deficient colon cancer.
keyPoints: The US FDA approved atezolizumab (Tecentriq) on 8 October 2026 for stage III dMMR colon cancer.
It is given with a fluoropyrimidine and oxaliplatin as adjuvant treatment.
The approval rests on a randomised, open-label trial called ATOMIC.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 8 October 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved atezolizumab (Tecentriq, Genentech) with a fluoropyrimidine and oxaliplatin for adjuvant treatment of stage III mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) colon cancer.

The approval covers adults and children aged two years and older.

A subcutaneous form, Tecentriq Hybreza, is approved with the same chemotherapy for patients aged 12 years and older who weigh at least 40 kg.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The FDA notes that ATOMIC enrolled 711 adults and one paediatric patient.

Adjuvant treatment is given after surgery to lower the chance of the cancer returning.

The FDA says the approval rests on the ATOMIC trial, a randomised, open-label, active-controlled study in people with stage III dMMR colon cancer after complete removal of the primary tumour.

This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

fda-camzyos-children-obstructive-hcm.name: FDA approves Camzyos for children
fda-camzyos-children-obstructive-hcm.summary: The US FDA approved Camzyos (mavacamten) for children weighing at least 30 kg with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, on 30 September 2026.
keyPoints: The US FDA approved Camzyos (mavacamten) for children weighing at least 30 kg with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on 30 September 2026.
The FDA says it is the first treatment to improve functional capacity and symptoms in children with this condition.
Camzyos carries a boxed warning for the risk of heart failure and is available only through a restricted programme.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 30 September 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Camzyos (mavacamten) for children weighing at least 30 kg with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

The FDA describes this as the first treatment to improve functional capacity and symptoms in children with the condition.

It describes the condition as inherited and causing a thickened heart muscle, with symptoms that can include shortness of breath, fatigue and an abnormal heart rhythm that can be life-threatening.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
In the paediatric study, patients were randomly assigned to Camzyos or placebo, and Camzyos reduced the Valsalva left ventricular outflow tract gradient compared with placebo.

The FDA says adult data showed a similar reduction, and that it expects the drug to help paediatric patients weighing at least 30 kg.

Camzyos carries a boxed warning for the risk of heart failure and is available only through a restricted programme called the Camzyos Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS).

This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

It is approved for adults with stage II or III locally advanced rectal cancer whose tumours are mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) or microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H).

The FDA says the approval relied on interim results from AZUR-1, a single-arm, open-label study in patients with previously untreated dMMR or MSI-H locally advanced rectal cancer.

Because the approval is accelerated, the sponsor must keep following patients to confirm lasting benefit.

This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

keyPoints: The US FDA approved gedatolisib (Revtorpyk, Celcuity) on 14 July 2026.
It is used with fulvestrant, with or without palbociclib, in adults with HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer without a detectable PIK3CA mutation.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 14 July 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved gedatolisib (Revtorpyk, Celcuity) in combination with fulvestrant, with or without palbociclib.

It is approved for adults with HR-positive, HER2-negative locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer that has no detectable PIK3CA mutation and has progressed after at least one line of endocrine therapy.

The FDA says efficacy was evaluated in VIKTORIA-1, an open-label study in which patients were randomly assigned to gedatolisib with fulvestrant and palbociclib, gedatolisib with fulvestrant, or fulvestrant alone.

The approval letter requires a further randomised trial to characterise known serious risks, including severe stomatitis and mucosal inflammation.

This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

fda-hibsago-chronic-hepatitis-b.summary: The US FDA approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) on 20 October 2026, the first antisense oligonucleotide approved for chronic hepatitis B in certain adults.
keyPoints: The US FDA approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) on 20 October 2026.
The FDA calls it the first antisense oligonucleotide approved to treat chronic hepatitis B.
It is for certain adults without cirrhosis and is used alongside existing antiviral therapy.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 20 October 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) for chronic hepatitis B.

The FDA says it is the first approved antisense oligonucleotide for chronic hepatitis B.

It is approved for certain adults without cirrhosis, as an addition to existing antiviral therapy.

The FDA says eligible patients have taken antiviral therapy for at least six months, have suppressed virus levels, and have a hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) level below a set threshold measured with an FDA-authorised test.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The FDA reports that 24 weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of the patients who had received Hibsago still had the virus under control.

The FDA granted the medicine Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations, and its application received Priority Review.

This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

fda-injectafer-boxed-warning-low-phospha.summary: The US FDA said on 1 September 2026 that it added a boxed warning to Injectafer (ferric carboxymaltose) about the risk of low blood phosphate.
keyPoints: The US FDA added a boxed warning to Injectafer (ferric carboxymaltose) in a safety communication dated 1 September 2026.
The warning describes the risk of symptomatic hypophosphataemia, meaning low blood phosphate.
The FDA says reports continued despite earlier labelling changes in 2020 and 2023.
This is a US decision; UK availability and labelling are decided separately.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 1 September 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) published a drug safety communication about ferric carboxymaltose injection, marketed as Injectafer.

The FDA says it approved label revisions that add a boxed warning, its most prominent safety warning.

The warning describes the risk of symptomatic hypophosphataemia, which is low phosphate in the blood.

It recommends phosphate monitoring in patients at risk and in any patient who receives a repeat course of treatment within three months of the previous course.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The FDA says symptomatic hypophosphataemia continued to be reported despite labelling changes in February 2020 and May 2023.

It also reports that, in data from its Sentinel System, serum phosphate testing took place in fewer than 20% of administration episodes.

Ferric carboxymaltose is an iron replacement given by injection into a vein.

This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

fda-thyroid-tablets-lot-recall-vitruvias.summary: Vitruvias Therapeutics announced a US recall of one lot of Thyroid Tablets, USP 30 mg on 21 August 2026 because of possible superpotency.
keyPoints: Vitruvias Therapeutics announced the recall on 21 August 2026 and the US FDA posted it on 24 August 2026.
It covers one lot, number 504950, of Thyroid Tablets, USP 30 mg, because of possible superpotency.
The notice says too much thyroid hormone can cause symptoms of an overactive thyroid.
This is a US recall; UK medicines alerts come from the MHRA.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
Vitruvias Therapeutics announced on 21 August 2026 a nationwide recall in the US of one lot of Thyroid Tablets, USP 30 mg, and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) published the notice on 24 August 2026.

The recalled lot is number 504950, and the recall is to consumer level.

The reason given is that testing confirmed the product could be superpotent.

The notice says the company has received no reports of adverse events linked to the recall.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The notice says superpotent thyroid tablets can cause symptoms of an overactive thyroid, such as weight loss and changes in heart rate.

It describes older adults, pregnant women and infants as more vulnerable, especially with long-term use.

The notice says people currently using this lot should not stop without first talking to their healthcare provider, who can advise on next steps or a replacement prescription.

The FDA has said that animal-derived (desiccated) thyroid medicines are unapproved, meaning the agency has not reviewed them for safety, effectiveness or quality.

This is a US recall notice; any UK action on medicines is decided separately by the MHRA.

keyPoints: The US FDA granted accelerated approval to Trutakna (atacicept-vymj) on 7 July 2026.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 7 July 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted accelerated approval to Trutakna (atacicept-vymj), an injection given under the skin.

It is approved for adults with primary IgA nephropathy, a kidney disease, who are at risk of the disease getting worse.

The FDA describes it as the first approved medicine that targets both BAFF and APRIL, two signalling proteins involved in the survival and maturation of certain immune cells.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
Accelerated approval here rests on a reduction in proteinuria, which means protein in the urine.

The FDA states that it has not been established whether Trutakna slows the decline in kidney function over the long term, and that an ongoing trial must be completed to confirm this.

The efficacy and safety data come from a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in adults with biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy.

This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

feeling-sick-and-vomiting-in-adults.name: Feeling sick and vomiting in adults
feeling-sick-and-vomiting-in-adults.summary: NHS inform says vomiting in adults usually lasts only 1 or 2 days, but blood in vomit means calling 999 or going to A&E, and vomiting for more than 2 days is a reason to call NHS 111.
keyPoints: The NHS says feeling sick is common and usually goes away on its own.
NHS inform lists signs of severe dehydration, including confusion, a rapid heartbeat, sunken eyes and passing little or no urine, among the reasons to call NHS 111.
NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee granules, or for green or yellow-green vomit.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if the sickness has not improved after a few days or keeps coming back, and calling NHS 111 for advice if a GP cannot be seen.

body.heading: What causes nausea and vomiting?
body.body: The NHS says feeling sick is common and usually goes away on its own. Diarrhoea or vomiting can point to norovirus or food poisoning, and a headache with a high temperature can suggest an infection such as flu. Other causes include morning sickness in pregnancy, motion sickness, anxiety, alcohol, medicines and recent surgery. NHS inform calls gastroenteritis one of the most common causes of vomiting in adults, and also lists migraine, labyrinthitis, appendicitis and medicines such as antibiotics and opioid painkillers. NHS inform says norovirus usually clears up by itself within a few days, and that there is no specific treatment, so the illness has to run its course. NHS inform says antibiotics will not help norovirus because it is caused by a virus, and that small sips of water help to prevent dehydration.

body.heading: What can help at home?
body.body: The NHS describes getting fresh air, sipping cold drinks, trying ginger or peppermint tea, and eating smaller, more frequent meals. It also lists hot, fried or greasy food, eating too quickly and lying down soon after eating as things to avoid. NHS inform advises resting at home and taking small sips of water or squash often so that dehydration does not develop.

body.heading: What are the signs of dehydration?
body.body: NHS inform lists signs of severe dehydration, including confusion, a rapid heartbeat, sunken eyes and passing little or no urine, among the reasons to call NHS 111. NHS inform advises people with diabetes who have been vomiting a lot to call NHS 111, especially if they take insulin, because vomiting can affect blood sugar levels.

body.heading: Which symptoms need urgent help?
body.body: NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee granules, or for green or yellow-green vomit. NHS inform advises calling NHS 111 for a person who keeps being sick and cannot keep fluids down, has been vomiting for more than 2 days, or has lost a lot of weight since becoming ill; its gastroenteritis page lists fever and bloody diarrhoea as reasons to contact NHS 111 or the GP practice urgently. The NHS says to call 999 if sudden sickness comes with tight or heavy chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, back, neck or jaw, or shortness of breath, because these could be signs of a heart attack.

body.heading: When should a GP be involved?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if the sickness has not improved after a few days or keeps coming back, and calling NHS 111 for advice if a GP cannot be seen. The GP can look for the cause and may prescribe anti-sickness medicine. The NHS says a pregnant person who is being sick often and cannot keep food down should tell their midwife or doctor, or contact the hospital, as soon as possible.

feeling-sick-and-vomiting-in-adults.metaDescription: NHS inform says vomiting in adults usually lasts only 1 or 2 days, but blood in vomit means calling 999 or going to A&E.

fever-in-adults-causes-and-when-to-get-h.name: Fever in adults: causes and when to get help
fever-in-adults-causes-and-when-to-get-h.headline: High temperature in adults: what usually causes it and when to get help
fever-in-adults-causes-and-when-to-get-h.summary: A high temperature in adults is usually a sign of infection and often settles at home. The NHS advises urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP if it does not improve, and 999 for some warning signs.
keyPoints: The NHS says a high temperature is usually a symptom of an infection.
Home care in the NHS advice includes resting, drinking fluids and, if needed, taking paracetamol or ibuprofen.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if a high temperature is not improving after home treatment or is getting worse.
The NHS meningitis page says to call 999 or go to A&E for a very painful headache, confusion, a stiff neck with sensitivity to bright lights, or a rash that does not fade when pressed.

body.heading: What causes a high temperature?
body.body: The NHS says a high temperature is usually a symptom of an infection. Infections such as flu and glandular fever can cause a high temperature.

body.heading: What helps at home?
body.body: NHS advice for a high temperature is to rest and drink plenty of fluids. The NHS also says paracetamol or ibuprofen can be taken to help feel more comfortable, following the instructions on the packet or leaflet. NHS inform also suggests wearing loose, comfortable clothing and avoiding alcohol. Staying away from other people while you have a temperature is also advised, to avoid passing on an infection.

body.heading: When is it worth speaking to a GP or NHS 111?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 if a high temperature is not improving after treating it at home, or is getting worse. NHS 111 is free and open every day of the year, day and night.

body.heading: Which signs mean 999 or A&E?
body.body: The NHS meningitis page lists a rash that does not fade when pressed, a very painful headache, confusion, and a stiff neck with sensitivity to bright lights among the signs that need immediate action. For a rash, the NHS describes the glass test: pressing a clear glass firmly against the skin to see whether the spots fade. Spots that stay visible through the glass are called a non-blanching rash, and rashes can be harder to see on darker skin, so the palms, soles and tummy are worth checking.

fever-in-adults-causes-and-when-to-get-h.metaDescription: A high temperature in adults is usually a sign of infection and often settles at home.

fever-in-children-when-to-get-help.name: Fever and rashes in children: when to get help
fever-in-children-when-to-get-help.summary: Most fevers in children can be looked after at home. The NHS says call 999 for signs such as a stiff neck or a rash that does not fade, and NHS 111 or a GP for a baby under 3 months.
keyPoints: The NHS says a child with a fever can usually be looked after at home, with plenty of fluids and regular checks, including overnight.
Call 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under a glass, blue, grey or pale skin, being hard to wake, or difficulty breathing.
For a baby under 3 months with a high temperature, the NHS says to call NHS 111 or contact a GP.
A GP or NHS 111 should be contacted if a fever lasts 5 days or more.

body.heading: Can a fever be looked after at home?
body.body: The NHS says a child with a fever can usually be looked after at home. It recommends giving plenty of fluids and checking on the child regularly, including overnight.

body.heading: When does a fever need 999?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, or a first seizure caused by fever. The same list includes cold hands and feet, blue, grey or pale skin, lips or tongue, being drowsy and hard to wake, extreme agitation or confusion, and difficulty breathing. A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it is described as non-blanching, and the NHS treats it as an emergency.

body.heading: When should NHS 111 or the GP be contacted?
body.body: For a baby under 3 months with a high temperature, the NHS says to call NHS 111 or contact a GP. For babies aged 3 to 6 months, the NHS also advises calling NHS 111 or contacting a GP when the temperature is high. For older children, the NHS advises calling NHS 111 or contacting a GP when a fever has lasted 5 days or more. Signs of dehydration, such as fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes and no tears when crying, also call for advice from NHS 111 or a GP.

body.heading: What about rashes in babies?
body.body: Healthier Together pages say that most baby rashes are harmless and go away on their own, and that dry or peeling skin in the first week or two is normal. Tiny white or yellow spots on the nose or face (milia) usually clear within a few weeks without treatment. Healthier Together lists signs that need urgent help from a health professional: a rash that does not fade under the glass test, redness around the belly button, and a baby who is pale, very sleepy or breathing hard.

fever-in-children-when-to-get-help.metaDescription: Most childhood fevers can be managed at home; the NHS sets out signs that need 999 or NHS 111.

body.heading: What was announced

flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.name: Flu or a cold: how they differ
flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.headline: Flu or a cold: how to tell them apart, how long each lasts and when to get help
flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.summary: Flu tends to start faster and feel worse than a cold, with fever, aches and exhaustion; a cold mostly stays in the nose and throat.
keyPoints: Cold and flu symptoms overlap, but flu tends to be more severe and often comes on within hours.
A cold mainly affects the nose and throat and builds up gradually.
Antibiotics do not work against colds or flu, because both are caused by viruses.
Sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness or coughing up blood needs 999 or A&E.
NHS 111 or a GP can advise if symptoms get worse or last longer than expected.

body.heading: How do flu and a cold differ?
body.body:
Colds and flu are both viral infections that affect the nose and throat, and their symptoms overlap. Flu and colds differ in how severe they are and in how quickly they start.

Flu tends to be more severe than a cold. A cold mostly affects the nose and throat, while flu can also bring a fever, aches and exhaustion.

Because the symptoms overlap, it can be hard to tell flu and a cold apart from symptoms alone. With a cold a person usually feels unwell but can manage usual activities, while flu can leave a person exhausted and too unwell to carry on as normal.

body.heading: How quickly do the symptoms start?
body.body:
Speed of onset is another difference the NHS pages point to. Flu tends to come on suddenly, often within hours.

A cold usually builds more gradually. The main signs of a cold are a blocked or runny nose, sneezing, a sore throat, a hoarse voice, a cough, and feeling tired and unwell.

body.heading: How long do they last?
body.body:
Most people start to feel better from a cold within about one to two weeks. Flu usually improves within about a week.

Tiredness can linger for longer after flu, even when the other symptoms have settled.

body.heading: What treatment is there?
body.body:
A cold is caused by a virus and usually gets better by itself. The NHS says the usual approach is to rest and drink fluids while the body clears the infection.

For a cold, a pharmacist can recommend suitable medicines and check which ones are suitable for the person. Antibiotics do not help, because both illnesses are caused by viruses rather than bacteria.

A flu vaccine protects against flu, but it does not protect against colds.

A pharmacist can recommend suitable cold medicines and check which ones are suitable for the person, and some are not suitable for children, pregnant women or people taking certain other medicines.

body.heading: When should someone get medical help?
body.body:
The NHS separates emergencies from problems that can wait for a call or an appointment.

Sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood is an emergency, and the route is 999 or A&E.

For less urgent worries, NHS 111 or the GP can advise. The NHS says to get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for flu symptoms with feeling very unwell, shortness of breath or no improvement.

The NHS says people aged 65 or over, people who are pregnant, and people with a long-term condition or a weakened immune system should get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if they have flu symptoms.

The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood, with someone else driving or an ambulance rather than the person driving themselves.

body.heading: Is it flu, a cold or something else?
body.body:
Other infections can look like flu or a cold. The UKHSA publishes a guide to the signs and symptoms of flu, COVID-19 and colds, and the NHS pages for each illness set out what to look for.

Symptoms overlap, so the only way to know for sure whether a person has flu or COVID-19 is a test.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Flu symptoms can include a sudden high temperature, an aching body and feeling exhausted. A cold usually causes a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, watery eyes and a sore throat, and does not usually bring a fever or body aches. The NHS offers the flu vaccine every year, in autumn or winter, to people at higher risk of becoming seriously ill from flu.

references.title: UKHSA: Do I have flu, COVID-19 or a cold? Know the signs and symptoms
