gastroscopy-what-happens-and-what-to-exp.name: Gastroscopy: what happens and what to expect
gastroscopy-what-happens-and-what-to-exp.summary: A gastroscopy uses a thin camera to look at the gullet and stomach. This guide covers fasting, throat spray or sedation, risks and results.
keyPoints: A gastroscopy passes a thin, flexible tube with a camera through the mouth and down to the stomach.
The stomach needs to be empty, and trusts ask for a fast of several hours beforehand.
People can have a throat spray and stay awake, or sedation that leaves them relaxed and drowsy.
Serious complications are rare, but vomiting blood after a gastroscopy is among the reasons the NHS lists for calling 999 or going to A&E.

body.heading: What is a gastroscopy?
body.body: A gastroscopy is a test in which a thin, flexible tube with a small camera goes into the mouth and down into the stomach. The doctor or nurse watches the lining of the gullet, stomach and the first part of the small bowel on a screen. Tiny tissue samples, called biopsies, may be taken, and this is painless.

body.heading: How do people prepare?
body.body: The stomach must be empty, so trusts ask people to stop eating for about six hours beforehand. Many trusts allow sips of clear fluid until about two hours before the test, though some stop earlier.

body.heading: Throat spray or sedation: what is the difference?
body.body: People can usually have a throat spray, sedation, or both, depending on the trust. The throat spray is a local anaesthetic that numbs the back of the throat, and the person stays awake while a nurse talks them through the test. For sedation, a small tube called a cannula is placed in a vein, usually in the back of the hand. The medicine makes the person relaxed and sometimes drowsy, but not fully asleep.

body.heading: What happens during the test?
body.body: Air is passed in to inflate the stomach, which can cause bloating and burping. Trust leaflets give different times for the test itself, and the NHS page gives 15 to 45 minutes. Common effects include a sore throat and bloating, which usually pass within 24 hours, according to trust leaflets.

body.heading: What happens afterwards?
body.body: After a throat spray alone, people may be able to make their own way home, and can drink once swallowing returns to normal, which one leaflet puts at about 20 to 60 minutes. After sedation, people rest in the endoscopy department for an hour or two, according to a trust leaflet. After sedation, an escort is needed to take the person home, and one trust says the sedative can stay in the body for up to 24 hours. One trust says that after sedation, clear thinking and decision-making may be affected for up to 24 hours.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body: Serious complications are rare, and trust leaflets give differing figures for a tear in the gut wall, from about 1 in 2,000 to less than 1 in 10,000. Possible problems include a tear in the gut wall that may need surgery, bleeding, and an allergic reaction to the sedation or throat spray. Sedation can occasionally cause short-term problems with breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. Rare complications include damage to loose teeth, crowns or bridgework. The NHS lists vomiting blood after a gastroscopy among the reasons to call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: When do the results arrive?
body.body: A doctor or nurse will usually go through the main findings before the person leaves. Biopsy results from the laboratory are not available on the day. Biopsy results go to the referring doctor and the GP, and trust leaflets give waits that range from a couple of weeks to several weeks.

general-anaesthetic-before-during-and-af.name: General anaesthetic: before, during, after
general-anaesthetic-before-during-and-af.summary: A general anaesthetic puts a person into controlled unconsciousness for surgery. Preparation includes fasting, and common effects afterwards are sickness, shivering and a sore throat.
keyPoints: A general anaesthetic produces a state of controlled unconsciousness.
Fasting beforehand matters because food or liquid in the stomach could be breathed into the lungs.
Common effects afterwards include sickness, feeling cold or shivering, a sore throat and drowsiness.
Every general anaesthetic carries some risk, and a person's medical history can change the picture.

body.heading: What is a general anaesthetic?
body.body:
A general anaesthetic puts a person into a state of controlled unconsciousness, so they are asleep and feel nothing during the procedure.

A breathing tube is sometimes used, and it can cause a sore throat afterwards.

body.heading: How do I prepare?
body.body:
Hospitals ask people to follow fasting instructions before a general anaesthetic. Trusts give different timings, so the instructions from the hospital's own team apply.

Fasting matters because food or liquid left in the stomach could come back up to the back of the throat and be breathed into the lungs, causing injury. Trusts also give advice about dentures and alcohol beforehand, so the hospital's own instructions apply. Smoking makes a chest infection after an anaesthetic more likely.

One trust leaflet says that an operation will be cancelled on the day if the fasting rules were broken.

body.heading: What happens afterwards?
body.body:
After the anaesthetic wears off, common effects include sickness, feeling cold or shivering, and a sore throat. Medication may leave a person drowsy.

The effects of a general anaesthetic can last for around a day, and hospitals give aftercare advice.

body.heading: What are the risks?
body.body:
Anyone having a general anaesthetic is at some risk. Possible complications include a chest infection, particularly in people who smoke or have lung problems, and confusion, which is more common in older people and usually temporary.

Allergic reactions can be serious but are rare, and awareness during surgery is also rare. The anaesthetist discusses this before the operation.

references.title: Royal College of Anaesthetists: Anaesthesia explained
Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust: On the day of your operation

grief-and-bereavement-what-to-expect.name: Grief and bereavement: what to expect
grief-and-bereavement-what-to-expect.summary: Grief is a natural response to loss, and the NHS says feelings usually ease gradually. A GP or bereavement service can help when grief is very strong or does not ease.
keyPoints: Grief is a normal response to loss, and the NHS says feelings of sadness should ease gradually over time.
NHS Inform says there is no time limit on grief.
The NHS says to see a GP if someone is struggling to cope, or their own efforts are not helping.
In an emergency, with immediate danger to life, the NHS says to use 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 are routes to urgent support.

body.heading: What does grief feel like?
body.body: Grief can bring shock, numbness, sadness, exhaustion and anger. NHS inform says there is no deadline on feeling better or recovering after a bereavement. NHS inform describes delayed grief, when grief is not fully felt at the time, and says it is never too late to grieve. The NHS lists shock, sadness, tiredness, anger and guilt among common reactions to loss.

body.heading: What can help?
body.body: The NHS suggests talking to someone trusted, joining peer support, taking regular exercise and eating regular meals. The NHS advises against relying on alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to cope with grief. Bereavement support organisations such as Cruse can help, and talking to others can bring comfort.

body.heading: When is it worth getting help?
body.body: The NHS says sadness should ease gradually with time, but medical help may be needed if someone feels increasingly depressed or anxious. It advises seeing a GP when someone is struggling to cope, has had low mood for more than two weeks, or finds their own efforts are not helping. People in England can refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service without seeing a GP first.

body.heading: Where can bereaved people and children find support?
body.body: The NHS has a page on grief after bereavement or loss and a separate page on children and bereavement. Cruse Bereavement Support offers a helpline and information on dealing with grief, and Child Bereavement UK and Winston's Wish support bereaved children and families.

body.heading: What is prolonged grief?
body.body: For some people, painful feelings do not ease as months go by, and the NHS says this may be prolonged grief disorder, which may need a clinician's assessment. Signs the NHS lists include difficulty accepting the death and suicidal thoughts, and it says to seek help from a GP, or urgent help if there are suicidal thoughts.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If grief brings thoughts of suicide, urgent help is available; NHS inform in Scotland points to NHS 111 for people in distress or despair. In an emergency, when someone is in immediate danger or has been physically harmed, the NHS says to use 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

references.title: NHS: Get help with grief after bereavement or loss
NHS inform: Advice and support on coping with grief

hba1c-test-what-it-shows.name: HbA1c test: what it shows and why it matters
hba1c-test-what-it-shows.summary: The HbA1c test shows average blood glucose over the past two to three months and is used to diagnose and monitor diabetes.
keyPoints: HbA1c reflects the average blood glucose level over roughly the previous two to three months.
The test is used to diagnose diabetes, to check how well diabetes is managed and to follow people with prediabetes.
Targets are personal, and a diabetes team may set a higher one for someone with frequent low blood glucose or an older person.
Conditions that affect red blood cells can make HbA1c unreliable, and another test may suit better.

body.heading: What does an HbA1c test show?
body.body: The HbA1c blood test reflects the average level of glucose in the blood over the past two to three months. That is why it differs from a finger-prick reading, which captures one moment. Glucose attaches to a part of the red blood cell, and the more glucose there is in the blood, the more HbA1c is present. Red blood cells live for about two to three months before new ones replace them, which sets the window the test covers. Because it covers a longer window, the test does not show short-term rises or dips in glucose. Hospital guidelines say HbA1c may be unsuitable for diagnosis when diabetes symptoms have been present for less than about two to three months, and local protocols differ.

body.heading: What is the test used for?
body.body: Doctors use it to diagnose diabetes. They also use it to keep an eye on levels in people at risk of developing diabetes, a state called prediabetes. In people who already have diabetes, it shows how well blood sugar has been controlled. MedlinePlus says the test is not used to diagnose type 1 diabetes. Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed with blood tests, and HbA1c is the usual first test. HbA1c is not used to diagnose diabetes during pregnancy.

body.heading: How are the results given and what are the targets?
body.body: UK laboratories give HbA1c in millimoles per mole, while some countries use a percentage. NICE-based guidance says an individual HbA1c target should be agreed with each person. A higher target may suit someone who has had many problems with low blood glucose. As people age, the diabetes team may raise the target, because the risks of tight control can outweigh the benefits.

body.heading: How often is it done?
body.body: NICE patient information advises that HbA1c is usually tested every three to six months. It may be done more often if blood glucose levels are changing quickly. Once blood glucose is stable, NICE patient information says the test is usually every six months.

body.heading: What can make the result less reliable?
body.body: Conditions that affect red blood cells can make the result less accurate, such as anaemia or an uncommon form of haemoglobin. Where HbA1c is unreliable, glucose-based blood tests are used for diagnosis instead. Pregnancy, heavy bleeding and recent blood transfusion can also make HbA1c unreliable. An NHS Scotland resource says the HbA1c may change if diet, physical activity, weight or medication have changed. An estimated average glucose converts HbA1c into meter units, but it is an average and not an exact match for readings. Heavy bleeding or haemolytic anaemia can make HbA1c falsely low, while iron deficiency may raise it. Lab Tests Online UK says the accuracy of an HbA1c result depends on the method used to measure it, and some haemoglobin variants can interfere with the measurement.

body.heading: What happens after a result in the prediabetes range?
body.body: The usual response to an intermediate result is lifestyle advice on eating, activity and weight. A GP can refer eligible people to the free NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme, and some areas allow self-referral. People with an intermediate result are usually monitored at least once a year. A GP appointment is the route to discuss any result. A raised result in someone without symptoms is usually repeated, and a second result in the diabetes range confirms the diagnosis.

body.heading: Why does a prediabetes result matter?
body.body: Prediabetes means blood sugar is higher than normal but not high enough for a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. It also means a high risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Prediabetes usually causes no symptoms, so it is found through blood tests. Feeling very thirsty, passing urine more often, feeling more tired than usual and losing weight without trying are symptoms of diabetes itself. The NHS notes that not everyone with diabetes has symptoms, which is why getting checked matters. The programme is free, lasts nine months and gives support with healthy eating, physical activity and weight.

head-injury-and-concussion-when-to-get-h.name: Head injury and concussion: when to get help
head-injury-and-concussion-when-to-get-h.headline: What happens after a head injury, which signs need 999 or A&E, and how concussion usually settles
head-injury-and-concussion-when-to-get-h.summary: Most head injuries are not serious, but the NHS says being knocked out and not waking, a fit or being unable to stay awake need a 999 call.
keyPoints: The NHS says to call 999 if a person was knocked out and has not woken up, cannot stay awake or keep their eyes open, or has a fit (seizure).

NHS inform says to go to A&E or call 999 for repeated vomiting, a severe or worsening headache, increasing drowsiness or confusion; the NHS says to get help from NHS 111 if the person is being sick or feels dizzy.
NICE sets out when a CT head scan is advised in hospital, with separate rules for adults and for children under 16.
The NHS says someone should stay with the injured person for the first 24 hours; NHS inform describes a responsible adult watching for 72 hours when concussion is suspected.
Headway says fewer than one in ten concussions involve loss of consciousness, and that going back to sport too early risks a second blow before the brain has recovered.

body.heading: What counts as a head injury, and what is concussion?
body.body:
The NHS says most head injuries are not serious, but it advises getting medical help for any symptoms. Concussion is a temporary brain injury, and the NHS says it can last a few weeks.

Headway describes concussion as the brain shaking back and forth inside the skull, causing mild damage. Being knocked out is not required. Headway says fewer than one in ten concussions involve loss of consciousness.

Headway lists confusion, dizziness and forgetfulness after a significant blow to the head as early signs. It says headaches, poor concentration and sleep problems can appear over the following days.

body.heading: Which signs mean calling 999?
body.body:
The NHS head injury page says to call 999 if the person has been knocked out and has not woken up. It gives the same route if the person cannot stay awake or keep their eyes open, or has a fit (seizure).

The NHS also lists a fall from more than 1 metre or five stairs, problems with vision or hearing, clear fluid coming from the ears or nose, and bleeding or bruising behind the ears. NHS 111 Wales adds numbness or weakness in part of the body, and problems with walking, balance, understanding or speaking.

NHS 111 Wales also says that 999 is the route if someone cannot be taken to A&E safely.

body.heading: When is A&E the route, and when NHS 111?
body.body:
NHS inform says to go to A&E or call 999 for repeated vomiting, a worsening or severe headache, increasing drowsiness or confusion. NHS 111 Wales lists A&E for a person who was knocked out but has since woken, has vomited since the injury, has a headache that painkillers do not ease, shows a change in behaviour or has memory problems.

The NHS says to get help from NHS 111 if the person is being sick or feels dizzy. NHS inform says that when concussion is suspected but there are no signs needing urgent A&E care, it advises phoning NHS 111 for advice, even if a hospital visit is not needed.

body.heading: What happens at A&E, and who has a CT scan?
body.body:
In hospital, staff assess the person after a head injury. NICE guidance, written for health professionals, covers assessment and early management and sets out when a CT head scan is advised.

For adults aged 16 and over, NICE advises a scan if the score on a standard alertness scale is still lower than normal two hours after the injury. A scan within eight hours is advised for people who were knocked out or have memory loss since the injury, and for people taking anticoagulant (blood-thinning) medicines.

For children under 16 the rules are separate. NICE also describes observing children for a minimum of four hours when no risk factors are present.

body.heading: What about babies and children?
body.body:
The advice comes from local NHS trust leaflets, which differ a little. Many describe an adult watching the child for 48 hours after a head injury, while some say 24 to 48 hours.

The leaflets list signs for 999 or A&E, including repeated vomiting (more than twice), becoming drowsy or hard to wake, confusion, a fit, difficulty speaking or understanding, weakness in the arms or legs, loss of balance, problems with eyesight, and clear fluid from the nose or ears. For babies they add not waking for feeds, or crying that cannot be soothed.

Some leaflets put a headache that does not go away in the 999 or A&E group, while Alder Hey places it under NHS 111 or an urgent GP review unless it is getting worse.

body.heading: What care at home does the NHS describe?
body.body:
The NHS says someone should stay with the injured person for the first 24 hours. NHS inform describes a responsible adult keeping watch for 72 hours when concussion is suspected, and says the person should not drive, drink alcohol, take recreational drugs or play sport.

NHS 111 Wales says a person who is tired does not need to stay awake. NHS inform describes a staged recovery plan, starting with relative rest for 24 to 48 hours and light activity with little screen time.

Trust leaflets differ on timings, so the advice from the treating team is the one that applies.

body.heading: What if symptoms carry on, and when can sport resume?
body.body:
Headway says to see a GP if symptoms persist. One of its leaflets gives about two weeks and another gives 28 days, and it says symptoms that are severe or getting worse need prompt medical assessment.

Headway advises against returning to play or training until cleared by a medical professional, even if the person feels fine, and describes a staged return to sport. It says another blow to the head before the brain has recovered can worsen the damage and, on rare occasions, can be fatal.

NHS inform's post-concussion syndrome page describes pacing, which means increasing activity gradually, to help with returning to work and leisure.

Alder Hey Children's Hospital: Head injury

head-lice-and-nits-what-the-nhs-says.name: Head lice and nits: what the NHS says
head-lice-and-nits-what-the-nhs-says.summary: Head lice are tiny insects in the hair. The NHS says wet combing is tried first, then a medicated lotion or spray if needed.
keyPoints: The NHS says head lice are small insects up to 3mm long, and finding a live louse is the only sure sign.
The NHS describes wet combing with conditioner and a detection comb as the first treatment to try.
A medicated lotion or spray is the next step if combing has not worked, and a pharmacist can advise.
The NHS says children do not need to stay off school because of head lice.
The NHS lists repellents, electric combs and plant oils such as tea tree as unlikely to work.

body.heading: What are head lice and nits?
body.body:
Head lice are small insects that live in human hair. The NHS says they are up to 3mm long, which makes them hard to spot. Nits are the eggs that the lice lay, and they can be small brown or white specks attached to the hair.

Head lice are a common problem, but they are not a sign of poor hygiene. NHS 111 Wales says they are not caused by dirty hair. NHS inform adds that lice do not prefer any particular type of hair, whether dirty, clean, long or short.

Empty egg cases left on the hair can be hard to tell apart from dandruff, which is one reason careful checking matters. Sources differ a little on how nits are described, with NHS 111 Wales calling them brown or white and a West Yorkshire NHS page calling them the empty egg cases that lice hatch from.

body.heading: What signs do head lice cause?
body.body:
The NHS lists small brown or white eggs in the hair and an itchy scalp as signs of head lice. NHS inform also lists a rash on the back of the neck and a feeling that something is moving in the hair. Some people with head lice have no symptoms at all, although itching is the main symptom for many.

Itching can have other causes, so it does not prove that lice are present. Nits alone do not show that a person has an active infestation. The sources say the only certain sign is finding a live, moving louse.

body.heading: How do head lice spread?
body.body:
The sources describe head lice as spreading through close head-to-head contact. NHS Northern Ireland says they are very unlikely to be spread by objects such as hats, combs and pillows.

The NHS says there is no proven way to prevent head lice, but that regular combing helps to catch them early. Medicated lotions and sprays should not be used to prevent them, because they can irritate the scalp.

Because lice spread easily, the NHS advises checking other family members' hair regularly. They may need to wet comb too.

NHS Northern Ireland describes head lice as spread by direct head-to-head contact. For that reason, checking everyone in the household is part of the advice given by local NHS services.

body.heading: How can someone tell for sure?
body.body:
The NHS says the only way to be sure is to find live lice. This is done by combing the hair with a special fine-toothed comb, called a detection comb.

One NHS source notes that conditioner keeps the lice from moving, which makes wet combing more reliable than dry combing. Lice that have been seen to move confirm an infestation.

Nits on their own do not prove an active infestation, so the NHS advises looking for a live louse before treating. The comb is used on the whole head, working through the hair from the roots to the ends.

body.heading: How does the NHS say head lice are treated?
body.body:
The NHS describes wet combing as the first method to try. Hair is washed with ordinary shampoo, covered in plenty of conditioner, and combed from the roots to the ends with a fine-toothed detection comb, going through the whole head twice.

Combing is repeated on days 1, 5, 9 and 13 to catch newly hatched lice, and everyone is checked again on day 17.

If wet combing has not worked, the NHS says a medicated lotion or spray can be tried, and these can be bought from a pharmacy. Some treatments need to be repeated after a week to kill newly hatched lice.

The NHS says everyone in the household who has head lice should be treated on the same day. Washing bedding and towels on the day treatment starts is optional.

The NHS says the aim of these steps is to catch lice that hatch after the first combing session. For this reason the days are spread across about two weeks, ending with the day 17 check.

body.heading: What does the NHS say does not work, and do children stay off school?
body.body:
The NHS lists several products as unlikely to work. These include head lice repellents and electric combs for head lice.

The NHS says children do not need to stay off school because of head lice. It also says laundry does not need a hot wash.

The NHS guidance lists these as unlikely to work, so wet combing or a medicated lotion or spray from a pharmacy remains the route the NHS describes. Washing bedding and towels on the day treatment starts is optional.

body.heading: When might a pharmacist help?
body.body:
The NHS says a pharmacist can advise on the best lotion or spray when wet combing has not worked.

The NHS advises asking a pharmacist for advice if wet combing has been tried through day 17 and live lice are still present.

Medicated lotions and sprays are described by the NHS as the next step when combing has not worked. A pharmacist is the person the NHS names for advice on the choice of product.

headache-types-causes-and-warning-signs.name: Headaches: types, causes and warning signs
headache-types-causes-and-warning-signs.summary: Tension-type headache is the most common type, and a headache that starts suddenly and is very severe needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: The NHS says the main symptom of a tension headache is pain on both sides of the head, face or neck, which lasts at least 30 minutes and can last much longer.
The NHS describes migraine as a throbbing headache that can be severe, is often on one side of the head and can be worse when moving around.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a headache that comes on suddenly and is extremely painful, or one that follows a serious head injury.
Great Ormond Street Hospital describes medication overuse headache as a headache that develops and gets worse with frequent use of medicines taken for pain.

body.heading: What are the common types of headache?
body.body:
The NHS says the main symptom of a tension headache is pain on both sides of the head, face or neck, which lasts at least 30 minutes and can last much longer. NHS Cheshire and Merseyside describes tension-type headache as the most common headache, usually mild to moderately severe, with a pressing or tightening feel. The NHS says stress is a common cause of tension headaches.

The NHS describes migraine as a throbbing headache that can be severe, is often on one side of the head and can be worse when moving around. Other migraine symptoms include feeling sick and sensitivity to light and sound.

Some people also get an aura, such as seeing zigzag lines or flashing lights. NHS inform says migraine affects around 1 in 5 women and 1 in 15 men. NHS inform describes cluster headaches as rare, coming in bouts of short daily headaches that last a month or two, with pain usually around the eye.

body.heading: Can painkillers cause headaches?
body.body: Great Ormond Street Hospital describes medication overuse headache as a headache that develops and gets worse with frequent use of medicines taken for pain. Great Ormond Street Hospital says medication overuse headache occurs in people who already have tension-type headache or migraine. A Nottinghamshire NHS pathway says headache from overusing painkillers improves or resolves within 3 months of stopping them.

body.heading: Which headaches need a 999 call?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a headache that comes on suddenly and is extremely painful, or one that follows a serious head injury. NHS inform lists other reasons to call 999 or go to A&E, including signs of stroke such as weakness on one side or slurred speech, signs of meningitis or sepsis, and being drowsy or confused.

body.heading: Which headaches need an urgent GP visit?
body.body: NHS inform lists a headache set off by coughing, sneezing, a change in posture or effort as a reason to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed. A headache that wakes someone from sleep, or keeps getting worse despite treatment, is listed under contacting the GP practice. NHS inform lists a sore scalp or jaw pain when chewing in someone over 50 as a reason to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed. NHS inform lists changes in vision, or a new or worsening headache with dizziness, vomiting or weakness, as reasons to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed. An NHS formulary guideline describes giant cell arteritis, also called temporal arteritis, as a medical emergency that needs prompt assessment and immediate steroid treatment to prevent permanent loss of vision.

body.heading: How is migraine treated?
body.body: The NHS describes triptans as a painkiller made specifically for migraine, available as tablets, injections and nasal sprays. NHS inform says a GP may recommend a triptan if over-the-counter medicines are not helping. Anti-sickness medicines can help during a migraine even without nausea, and the NHS says they work better when taken as soon as symptoms begin. The NHS lists stress, tiredness, skipping meals and too much caffeine among common migraine triggers.

body.heading: When is a routine GP visit sensible, and what might the GP do?
body.body: The NHS says tension headaches can be treated with painkillers, but advises seeing a GP for several headaches a week or severe ones. A GP may suggest keeping a migraine diary. There is no specific test for migraine, so the GP looks for a pattern of recurring headaches with the typical symptoms. The NHS says an antidepressant medicine called amitriptyline is sometimes recommended to help prevent tension headaches.

healthy-weight-bmi-explained.name: Healthy weight: what BMI shows and what it misses
healthy-weight-bmi-explained.summary: BMI is an NHS check on whether weight suits height, but it cannot tell muscle from fat, so waist size and a GP discussion add to it.
keyPoints: The NHS BMI calculator checks whether a person is a healthy weight for their height.
BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, so very muscular people may be rated overweight and people who lose muscle with age may still fall in the healthy range.
The NHS says Black, Asian and some other minority ethnic groups have a higher risk of some long-term conditions at a lower BMI.
NHS treatment for obesity ranges from lifestyle changes and weight management programmes to medicines and surgery.

body.heading: What does BMI measure?
body.body: Body mass index, or BMI, is calculated from height and weight, and the NHS calculator uses it to check whether an adult is a healthy weight for their height. The calculator shows which category a result falls in, and the NHS gives a different healthy range for Black, Asian and some other minority ethnic groups. The reason given is that these groups have a higher risk of developing some long-term conditions, such as type 2 diabetes, at a lower BMI.

body.heading: What are the limits of BMI?
body.body: BMI cannot tell the difference between muscle and fat. Very muscular people and athletes may be rated overweight or obese despite low body fat. Adults who lose muscle as they get older may fall in the healthy weight range even though they may be carrying excess fat.

body.heading: Why does waist size matter?
body.body: The NHS gives a method for measuring the waist: find the bottom of the ribs and the top of the hips, place a tape measure midway between them, and measure after breathing out naturally. The NHS and NICE describe a waist measurement of more than half a person's height as linked with increased health risks. The NHS advises seeing a GP for help with losing weight, or if the waist measurement is more than half of height.

body.heading: What treatment does the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS says a GP can advise on weight loss and on options such as weight management programmes, medicines or surgery. Options include lifestyle changes, weight management programmes, medicines and surgery. Local NHS specialist weight management services, often called tier 3, usually have a team that can include a doctor, dietitians, specialist nurses and psychologists. NHS access to weight-loss injections such as semaglutide and tirzepatide depends on eligibility criteria and varies by area; some are offered through specialist weight management services, and tirzepatide is being introduced through GP practices in phases for people with the highest clinical need.

body.heading: What health risks are linked to excess weight?
body.body: The NHS lists type 2 diabetes, heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure, several cancers, osteoarthritis and fatty liver disease among conditions linked to excess weight.

body.heading: Why does weight change?
body.body: The NHS describes overweight and obesity as having more body fat than the body needs. It can happen when a person eats or drinks more than the body needs or does not do enough physical activity. Other factors listed include genes, some medicines, and some health conditions such as an underactive thyroid.

body.heading: What does a GP check, and what support is free?
body.body: The NHS says a GP looks for possible underlying causes of obesity, for example a medicine the person is taking. The NHS offers a free 12-week weight loss plan as an app. The NHS says that for someone living with obesity, losing about 3 per cent of starting body weight can reduce the risk of obesity-related complications.

hearing-loss-causes-tests-and-help.name: Hearing loss: causes, tests and what helps
hearing-loss-causes-tests-and-help.summary: Gradual hearing loss is common and a GP can arrange hearing tests. Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears needs an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111, according to the NHS.
keyPoints: Gradual hearing loss in both ears is usually linked to ageing or long-term exposure to loud noise.
A GP can look in the ears and may refer to an audiologist for a hearing test.
Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears needs an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.
NHS hearing aids are free.

body.heading: What causes hearing loss?
body.body: Gradual hearing loss in both ears is usually linked to ageing or to damage from loud noise over many years. Earwax, ear infections and a perforated eardrum are other common causes. Sensorineural hearing loss involves damage to the inner ear or the nerve pathway to the brain, while conductive loss means sound is blocked in the outer or middle ear, for example by earwax, fluid or infection.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP, and what happens?
body.body: Some pharmacies and opticians also offer a free hearing test. A GP can check for problems such as earwax or infection and may refer to an audiologist for further tests. If the GP finds no obvious cause, they should refer the person to an NHS audiologist for a full hearing assessment. In a common hearing test, the person wears headphones, hears sounds at different levels and presses a button each time they hear one. The test shows which pitches are affected and by how much.

body.heading: What if hearing is lost suddenly?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss in one or both ears. If neither is reachable, the nearest accident and emergency department is the route. Sudden hearing loss can be permanent, and treatment given early can reduce that risk. For sudden sensorineural loss the cause is often never found, and the usual treatment is steroids, which are most likely to help when given soon after the loss starts.

body.heading: What helps with permanent hearing loss and tinnitus?
body.body: For tinnitus, the first person to speak to is the GP, who can check the ears for treatable causes and may refer to a specialist. Treatable causes such as earwax or infection can often be dealt with by a GP, while permanent loss is usually managed with hearing aids. Hearing aids do not make hearing perfect, but they make sounds louder and clearer, and NHS hearing aids are free.

heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.name: Heart attack, cardiac arrest and angina
heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.headline: Heart attack, cardiac arrest and angina: the differences and when to call 999
heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.summary: A heart attack is a blocked blood supply to the heart muscle, cardiac arrest is the heart stopping, and angina is chest pain that eases with rest.
keyPoints: A heart attack happens when the blood flow to the heart is blocked.
In a cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively, the person collapses and is not breathing normally.
Angina is chest pain caused by a temporary reduction in the blood supply to the heart.
Angina symptoms usually ease with rest or a nitrate medicine, whereas heart attack symptoms usually do not.
For a suspected heart attack or cardiac arrest the NHS says to call 999 straight away.

body.heading: What is the difference between a heart attack and cardiac arrest?
body.body:
The British Heart Foundation (BHF) explains that a heart attack and a cardiac arrest are different, and that both are emergencies.

A heart attack happens when the blood flow to the heart is blocked. The BHF describes a heart attack as a sudden loss of blood flow to part of the heart muscle, and the NHS says it can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital.

In a cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively. The person collapses, does not respond and is not breathing normally. The BHF says a heart attack can sometimes lead to a cardiac arrest.

If a defibrillator is nearby, the 999 call handler will say where it is and may ask someone to fetch it, and CPR should not be stopped.

A cardiac arrest usually happens suddenly and without warning.

body.heading: What is angina?
body.body:
Angina is chest pain or discomfort that happens when the blood supply to the heart muscle is temporarily reduced. The BHF says the discomfort of angina does not damage the heart muscle in the way a heart attack does.

Angina symptoms usually happen during exercise and pass within a few minutes, and they can be eased by resting or by using a nitrate tablet or spray.

Angina symptoms usually pass in a few minutes, but heart pain that lasts longer may be a heart attack, so call 999.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of a heart attack?
body.body:
The NHS lists chest pain that feels tight or squeezing. The pain can spread to the arms, jaw, neck, back or tummy.

Other signs include feeling sick, sweating, shortness of breath and light-headedness.

A key difference from angina is that heart attack symptoms are not usually relieved by a nitrate tablet or spray.

Some people with a heart attack also look pale or grey.

Women are more likely to notice symptoms such as shortness of breath, feeling sick, and back or jaw pain, and symptoms can be milder than people expect.

body.heading: What are the signs of a cardiac arrest?
body.body:
A person in cardiac arrest loses consciousness. They do not respond, and they are not breathing or their breathing does not look normal.

Without treatment a person in cardiac arrest may die within minutes, which is why speed matters.

body.heading: When should someone call 999?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 straight away if someone may be having a heart attack.

If someone seems to be in cardiac arrest, the NHS advises calling 999 and starting CPR, with the call handler giving instructions.

The NHS says to call 999 for the main warning signs of a heart attack, and to call NHS 111 for less severe symptoms such as a racing or irregular heartbeat. The BHF says heart attack pain is not relieved by rest or a nitrate medicine, and that a heart attack is a 999 emergency.

The NHS advises a person who may be having a heart attack to call 999 rather than drive themselves to A&E.

For less severe symptoms such as a racing or irregular heartbeat, the NHS says to call NHS 111.

body.heading: How are they diagnosed and treated?
body.body:
A heart attack is usually assessed with an ECG, which records the heart's electrical activity, and a blood test for troponin, a protein released when the heart muscle is damaged. The site's pages on these tests give more detail.

Treatment in hospital, with medicine or a procedure, aims to restore the blood supply to the heart.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: An NHS ECG is usually the first test, and it can show whether the heart attack needs urgent treatment to open the blocked artery.

heart-rhythm-monitors-holter-and-loop-re.name: Heart rhythm monitors: Holter and loop recorders
heart-rhythm-monitors-holter-and-loop-re.summary: A Holter monitor records the heart's electrical activity for 24 to 48 hours or longer, to catch rhythm problems that come and go. An implantable loop recorder can record for much longer.
keyPoints: A Holter (ambulatory ECG) monitor records the heart's electrical activity continuously, usually for about 24 to 48 hours and sometimes longer.
It can help find the cause of palpitations or diagnose conditions such as atrial fibrillation, which do not happen all the time.
The wearer keeps a diary of symptoms so that they can be matched against the recording, and returns the recorder to the hospital.
When shorter tests miss the problem, an implantable loop recorder placed under the skin of the chest can monitor for up to three years.

body.heading: Why would I need a heart rhythm monitor?
body.body:
An ordinary ECG records the heart for only a short time. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) describes a Holter monitor, also called an ambulatory ECG, as a way of recording the heart's electrical activity continuously over about 24 to 48 hours, sometimes longer.

It can help diagnose conditions such as atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm, or uncover the cause of palpitations that do not happen all the time.

body.heading: What is it like to wear a Holter monitor?
body.body:
Electrodes are stuck to the chest and their wires are taped down and connected to a small recorder. The person can carry on with most normal activities, but the monitor must be kept dry, so leaflets say not to bath or shower while it is worn.

A diary sheet is given to note the time and details of any symptoms so they can be matched against the recording. When the test is finished, the recorder is returned to the hospital so the results can be read.

body.heading: What if symptoms are rare?
body.body:
Some monitors, such as an event recorder, have a button the wearer presses when they have symptoms. Other devices can be worn for longer than a day or two.

A hospital leaflet describes an implantable loop recorder, which monitors the heart constantly, unlike an ECG or 24-hour monitor. This is a small device placed under the skin of the upper left chest, under local anaesthetic, that continuously monitors heart rate and rhythm and stores abnormal patterns. Recording can continue for up to three years, and the device only records, so it gives no shocks or treatment.

body.heading: How are symptoms recorded with a loop recorder?
body.body: Leaflets say the wearer presses an activator when they feel palpitations or dizziness, so the device saves the rhythm around that moment. Data is often sent to the healthcare team wirelessly through a home transmitter or smartphone app.

body.heading: Are these tests safe, and what about urgent symptoms?
body.body:
The BHF describes the Holter test as painless. An implantable loop recorder only monitors and records; it does not deliver shocks or other treatment.

The NHS advises calling 999 if palpitations come with chest pain, shortness of breath or feeling faint, and seeing a GP if they keep coming back or are worrying.

heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.name: Heartburn, acid reflux and GORD
heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.headline: Heartburn, acid reflux and GORD: what they are and when to see a GP
heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.summary: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest from acid reflux; when it keeps happening it is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).
keyPoints: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat.
When reflux keeps happening it is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.
Lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are the usual first steps, and a pharmacist can advise on options.
Difficulty swallowing, unintentional weight loss or frequent vomiting need prompt advice from a GP or NHS 111.
A GP can prescribe acid-reducing medicine and arrange tests if symptoms continue.

body.heading: What is heartburn, and how does it relate to GORD?
body.body:
Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest. NHS sources describe it as caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat, which is known as acid reflux.

If it keeps happening, the condition is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.

body.heading: What are the symptoms?
body.body:
The main symptoms of acid reflux are heartburn and an unpleasant sour taste in the mouth caused by stomach acid. Some people also have a hoarse voice, bad breath, bloating or feeling sick.

Symptoms tend to get worse after eating, when lying down or when bending over.

body.heading: What can bring it on?
body.body:
NHS sources list several contributors: certain foods and drinks, being overweight, smoking, stress or anxiety, having a hiatus hernia, and pregnancy.

Some medicines, including anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, can also play a part.

Heartburn can also come with bad breath.

body.heading: What helps?
body.body:
Lifestyle changes are usually the first step. NHS advice includes eating smaller, more frequent meals, avoiding foods that trigger symptoms, and not eating within a few hours of going to bed. Not smoking is also advised.

Antacids and alginates, which are available from pharmacies, can ease symptoms, and a pharmacist can talk through the options.

Antacids and alginates are not meant to be taken regularly for long periods, so a pharmacist can advise on them.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body:
A GP appointment is the usual route if lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines do not help, or if heartburn happens most days.

Some symptoms need prompt attention, by contacting the GP or NHS 111. NHS sources list difficulty swallowing, unintentional weight loss, food getting stuck in the throat and frequent vomiting as reasons to contact a GP or NHS 111.

Chest pain can also be a sign of a heart problem. The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, especially with sweating, feeling sick, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it may be a heart attack.

Food getting stuck in the throat is another reason to see a GP.

Vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds, needs emergency medical care.

Severe chest pain can be mistaken for heart-related pain, so treat sudden severe chest pain as an emergency and call 999.

body.heading: What can a GP offer?
body.body:
A GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that reduces the amount of acid the stomach makes. A GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor for a short time, and some people need a long-term prescription, and the NHS advises anyone whose symptoms continue or return to go back to the GP.

If symptoms continue despite treatment, a GP may refer someone for a gastroscopy, a test to look at the lining of the food pipe.

Surgery to strengthen the valve at the bottom of the food pipe exists but is not usually needed.

Long-lasting reflux can sometimes inflame or ulcerate the food pipe.

references.title: Cambridge University Hospitals: Dietary and lifestyle advice for adults with GORD

heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.metaDescription: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest from acid reflux; when it keeps happening it is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).

heat-exhaustion-and-heatstroke-what-to-k.name: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke: what to know
heat-exhaustion-and-heatstroke-what-to-k.headline: Heat exhaustion and heatstroke: the difference, the signs, and when to call 999
heat-exhaustion-and-heatstroke-what-to-k.summary: Heat exhaustion usually eases with cooling and rest, while heatstroke is an emergency for which the NHS says to call 999.
keyPoints: Heat exhaustion can cause tiredness, dizziness, headache, feeling or being sick, heavy sweating, pale clammy skin and cramps.
Heatstroke is the more serious stage, with very hot skin that is not sweating, confusion, fast breathing, a fit or loss of consciousness.
For heat exhaustion the NHS describes moving somewhere cool, removing extra clothing, drinking water and cooling the skin.
The NHS says to call 999 if someone has not started to improve after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, or if heatstroke is suspected.
Older people, babies and young children, and people with long-term conditions are described as most vulnerable in hot weather.

body.heading: What is the difference between heat exhaustion and heatstroke?
body.body:
Heat exhaustion happens when the body struggles to cope with heat. Heatstroke is the more serious form, and the NHS treats it as an emergency.

NHS inform says heat exhaustion can progress to heatstroke if a person cannot cool down. The NHS says heat exhaustion usually improves once the person cools down within 30 minutes, and NHS inform describes it as usually getting better 30 to 60 minutes after cooling. Someone who has heatstroke, NHS inform says, is treated in hospital.

body.heading: What are the signs of heat exhaustion?
body.body:
The NHS lists tiredness, dizziness, headache, feeling sick or being sick, and heavy sweating. The skin can become pale and clammy, and there can be cramps and a high temperature.

For children, the British Red Cross describes dizziness or confusion, headaches or cramps, sweating with cooler skin, a paler colour than usual, nausea, and fast breathing and heart rate. Its advice is to get medical advice even if the child seems to recover, and to call 999 if the child gets worse.

body.heading: What helps heat exhaustion?
body.body:
For heat exhaustion the NHS describes moving the person somewhere cool and taking off unnecessary clothing. It also describes giving plenty of water, or an isotonic sports drink or rehydration powder. The skin can be cooled by spraying or sponging with cool water and fanning. Cold packs wrapped in a cloth, placed under the armpits or on the neck, are also described. The NHS says to stay with the person until they are better.

The British Red Cross notes that babies under 6 months do not need to be offered water and may need to feed more often instead.

body.heading: What are the signs of heatstroke and what happens next?
body.body:
The NHS lists a very high temperature, and hot skin that is not sweating, among the warning signs of heatstroke. Others are fast breathing, a fast heartbeat, confusion, restlessness, a seizure (fit) and loss of consciousness. The NHS notes that redness can be harder to see on brown or black skin.

If heatstroke is suspected, the NHS says to call 999. It also says not to drive to A&E, and that the 999 call handler will advise what to do. The NHS also says to call 999 if someone with heat exhaustion has not begun to improve after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, being cooled down and drinking fluids.

body.heading: What is done while waiting for help?
body.body:
The NHS describes cooling the person while waiting for the ambulance. This can mean wrapping them in a cool, wet sheet, fanning them, or sponging them with cold water. If the person loses consciousness, the NHS describes putting them in the recovery position. It also describes checking breathing and pulse and starting CPR if there is no sign of life.

For children, the British Red Cross likewise describes calling 999 straight away for heatstroke, moving the child somewhere cool and carrying on cooling while waiting for help.

body.heading: Who is at higher risk, and how can people stay cool?
body.body:
GOV.UK describes older people, babies and young children, and people with long-term conditions as more vulnerable in hot weather. Conditions named include heart, breathing and kidney problems and diabetes.

NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance says some medicines may reduce sweating and affect the body's ability to control temperature, which can raise the risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke. For staying cool, GOV.UK describes closing curtains or blinds on rooms facing the sun, and opening windows at night when it is cooler outside. It also describes planning activity for early morning or evening, drinking plenty of fluids, and limiting alcohol. Never leave babies, children, older people or pets alone in a parked car, the guidance says. Checking on vulnerable neighbours, friends and relatives is also advised.

references.title: NHS inform: Heatstroke and heat illness
GOV.UK: Beat the heat: staying safe in hot weather
British Red Cross: Heatstroke and heat exhaustion first aid for children and babies
NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service: Heatwaves and medicines

heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.name: Heavy periods: causes, tests and treatment
heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.headline: Heavy periods: what can cause them, which checks a GP offers and how they are treated
heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.summary: Heavy periods are common and often have no clear cause, but fibroids, endometriosis and other conditions can be behind them. The NHS advises a GP visit when they affect daily life.
keyPoints: Some people naturally have heavier periods than others, and the NHS says help is available when they affect daily life.
Often there is no underlying medical reason, though fibroids, endometriosis and some other conditions can cause heavy periods.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if heavy periods affect life, have lasted some time, come with severe pain, or if there is bleeding between periods or after sex.
Treatment choices include some contraceptives, medicines to reduce bleeding and surgery, and heavy periods do not always need treatment.

body.heading: What counts as a heavy period?
body.body: The NHS describes heavy periods in practical terms, such as needing to change pads or tampons every one to two hours. Some people naturally have heavier periods than others, but the NHS says that when periods are so heavy that they affect life, help is available. Feeling tired or short of breath, or avoiding daily activities because of periods, are other signs that bleeding may be a problem.

body.heading: What causes them?
body.body: Heavy periods often have no underlying cause. Fibroids, which are non-cancerous growths in or around the womb, are one of the identifiable causes. Other conditions that can cause heavy periods include endometriosis, adenomyosis, polycystic ovary syndrome and pelvic inflammatory disease. Some medicines, such as anticoagulants and some chemotherapy medicines, can also be responsible. Rarely, heavy periods can be a sign of womb cancer.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if heavy periods affect your life, have lasted for some time, or come with severe pain. Bleeding between periods or after sex is also a reason to see a GP. For severe period or pelvic pain that is worse than usual and not helped by painkillers, the NHS advises getting urgent advice, from NHS 111 if needed.

body.heading: Which tests might a GP arrange?
body.body: A GP can investigate why bleeding is heavy, which may include a physical examination, blood tests or scans. A blood test to look for iron deficiency anaemia is usually offered to people with heavy periods. A pregnancy test, an ultrasound scan and, less often, a hysteroscopy (a look inside the womb with a small camera) may follow.

body.heading: How are heavy periods treated?
body.body: Heavy periods do not always need to be treated. If they affect daily life, options include a hormone-releasing intrauterine system (IUS) or the combined contraceptive pill. Medicines to reduce the bleeding, such as tranexamic acid, and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as mefenamic acid or naproxen are also used. Surgical options also exist for heavy periods.

high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.name: High blood pressure: what happens next
high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.headline: High blood pressure: how it is found, what causes it and what treatment involves
high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.summary: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms and is found by measuring it; treatment starts with lifestyle changes and may include medicine.
keyPoints: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, and the only way to know is to have it measured.
In most people no single cause is found; age, family history, ethnicity and lifestyle all play a part.
Readings taken at home or by a 24-hour monitor can be used alongside clinic readings to confirm the diagnosis.
Lifestyle changes are the first step, and a GP may prescribe medicine if blood pressure is very high or stays high.
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it could be a heart attack.

body.heading: What does a blood pressure reading mean?
body.body:
Blood pressure is the force of blood against the walls of the arteries. A reading gives two numbers: the pressure when the heart beats and the pressure between beats. The site's page on blood pressure measurement explains how they are taken.

Doctors use different thresholds for readings taken in a clinic and for readings taken at home when deciding whether blood pressure is high.

body.heading: Does high blood pressure cause symptoms?
body.body:
Usually not. The NHS says high blood pressure often has no symptoms, so many people do not know they have it, and the only way to find out is to have it measured. Rarely it can cause headaches, blurred vision or chest pain.

Over time, the NHS says, untreated high blood pressure raises the chance of problems such as stroke and heart disease.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body:
For most people there is no obvious cause, which is called essential hypertension, and it can run in families. In a small number of people there is an underlying cause, such as a kidney or adrenal gland condition.

The NHS says risk rises with age, with Black African or Black Caribbean ethnicity, and with a family history. Smoking, drinking too much alcohol, being overweight and not being active are also linked.

The NHS advises calling NHS 111 for frequent headaches or blurred vision, chest pain that comes and goes, or other symptoms thought to come from high blood pressure.

body.heading: How is the diagnosis confirmed?
body.body:
A single clinic reading is usually followed by other checks. NICE advises confirming raised clinic readings with home monitoring or with a 24-hour ambulatory monitor, which takes readings through the day.

Some people have higher readings in a clinic than at home, sometimes called the white coat effect, which is one reason these extra checks are used. A GP may also arrange blood and urine tests and an ECG, which checks the heart rhythm.

A reading taken in a clinic is less accurate than home or ambulatory readings and is not enough on its own to diagnose high blood pressure.

body.heading: What does treatment involve?
body.body:
Lifestyle changes come first for many people. The NHS lists cutting down on salt and alcohol, being more physically active, losing weight where needed, and stopping smoking.

A GP will usually prescribe medicine if blood pressure is very high, if the person has a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, or if it stays high after lifestyle changes. Several types are used, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers and diuretics, and the choice depends on things such as age and ethnicity.

Some people need to take blood pressure medicine long term, though if blood pressure stays under control for several years it may be possible to cut back or stop treatment.

Most blood pressure medicines are taken as tablets.

Making lifestyle changes early on may mean some people can avoid needing medicine.

Water tablets (diuretics) work by increasing the amount of salt the kidneys remove.

body.heading: When is it an emergency?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it could be a heart attack.

NHS guidance for pharmacy staff says a very high clinic reading together with symptoms such as headache, palpitations, new confusion or chest pain should be referred to A&E, using 999 where necessary.

high-crp-what-it-means.name: High CRP: what it means and what happens next
high-crp-what-it-means.summary: A high CRP means there is inflammation or infection somewhere in the body, but not where or why, so doctors read it with symptoms and other tests.
keyPoints: A high CRP shows that inflammation or infection is likely, but it does not show where it is or what is causing it.
CRP is a protein made by the liver whose level rises when there is inflammation in the body.
Doctors read the result with the wider clinical picture, and the test is often repeated to see whether treatment has worked.
Some raised results are linked to things other than illness, such as obesity or taking the combined contraceptive pill.
Laboratories and sources do not all use the same cut-offs, so a CRP result is read against the range on its own report.

body.heading: What does a CRP test measure?
body.body:
CRP stands for C-reactive protein, a protein that the liver makes. Its level in the blood rises when there is inflammation somewhere in the body. Infection and several other causes of inflammation can push the level up.

Doctors usually request the test when they suspect an infection or inflammation, for example after surgery. It is also used to help assess long-term inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Lab Tests Online UK says no special preparation is needed for the test.

body.heading: What does a high CRP mean?
body.body:
A high or rising CRP suggests that there is an acute infection or inflammation. It does not show where the inflammation is or which condition is causing it. For that reason the test is not diagnostic on its own. Berkshire and Surrey pathology services say a raised CRP is linked with infection, particularly but not only bacterial, and with inflammation.

A small rise is hard to interpret by itself, so doctors consider it alongside the whole clinical picture. In long-term inflammatory conditions the test is often repeated to see whether treatment is working. The cause of a high CRP cannot always be found.

body.heading: Which conditions can raise CRP?
body.body: MedlinePlus lists cancer, heart attack, infection, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and related diseases, and rheumatic fever among the conditions that can raise CRP. Not every cause is an illness. A Danish blood donor study found low-grade inflammation was more common in women using the combined contraceptive pill. Obesity is linked with low-grade inflammation and with higher CRP levels. StatPearls describes smoking, diabetes and other long-term conditions as associated with low-grade inflammation that can raise CRP.

body.heading: What happens after a high CRP result?
body.body:
Lab Tests Online UK says CRP is used to assess how severe inflammation is and how well treatment is working. The doctor may then arrange further tests or treatment.

The test is often repeated to see whether treatment has been effective. NHS laboratories often report CRP results within about a day, though timing depends on where the test is requested. A CRP result does not show urgency; the NHS says chest tightness or pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw needs a 999 call straight away. StatPearls notes that small CRP rises can occur without obvious widespread inflammation.

body.heading: Is hs-CRP the same test?
body.body: High-sensitivity CRP, or hs-CRP, is a separate and more sensitive version of the test. It has been used to estimate the risk of heart disease in people who seem healthy. Lab Tests Online UK notes that current UK guidelines on cardiovascular risk assessment do not recommend hs-CRP testing. A Sheffield NHS laboratory leaflet says hs-CRP should not replace assessment of the usual cardiovascular risk factors. The same leaflet says people with active infection, inflammation or trauma should not have hs-CRP testing until these have resolved.

body.heading: Can medicines or other factors change the result?
body.body: StatPearls states that some medicines, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and statins, can lower CRP. Long-term conditions linked with low-grade inflammation can lift it.

body.heading: Where else is CRP used?
body.body: Regional NHS guidance on suspected giant cell arteritis, an inflammation of blood vessels, asks for a CRP before steroids are started. A Devon formulary page says polymyalgia rheumatica is possible but very rare when inflammatory markers are normal. Scottish referral guidance for suspected rheumatoid arthritis refers to CRP and ESR results alongside anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor tests. It advises referral for persistent symptoms even when CRP is normal and antibodies are negative. A Scottish NHS guideline on giant cell arteritis says it is rare to see the condition with normal inflammatory markers, and that CRP, plasma viscosity or both should be raised.

high-white-blood-cell-count-causes.name: High white blood cell count: what it means
high-white-blood-cell-count-causes.summary: A high white blood cell count is a non-specific sign, most often from infection, and doctors read it with the type of cell raised.
keyPoints: A high white cell count can be caused by infection, inflammation, some medicines, stress or smoking, and less often by a blood disorder.
The differential count shows which type of white cell is raised, which helps narrow down the cause.
A mild, lasting rise is often linked to chronic inflammation, infection or smoking, while an unexplained very high count leads to urgent referral to haematology.
A single high count does not diagnose anything, and doctors may repeat the test.

body.heading: What does the full blood count measure?
body.body: A full blood count measures the number and type of cells in the blood, including red cells, white cells and platelets. The test gives a total white cell count and a differential that splits white cells into types. Those types include neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Neutrophils are the main defence against bacterial infection.

body.heading: What does a high white cell count mean?
body.body: A raised count is a non-specific signal, which means it does not point to one cause. A high count can indicate infection, inflammation, or leukaemia and other blood disorders. Infection, most often bacterial infection, is the most common cause. Results vary with age and time of day, and older people sometimes do not show a raised count even when they have an infection.

body.heading: What else can raise it?
body.body: Inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis can raise the count, and so can allergies. Some medicines, for example corticosteroids, can raise it. Physical or emotional stress can affect the white cell count. Smoking and pregnancy can also raise the count. Corticosteroids raise the white cell count by releasing neutrophils from the bone marrow into the circulation. A review says the white cell count can double within hours after stressors such as surgery, exercise, trauma or emotional stress, because of large neutrophil stores in the bone marrow and blood vessels.

body.heading: What does the differential add?
body.body: A high neutrophil count usually suggests bacterial infection, inflammation or physical stress on the body. A high lymphocyte count can occur with viral infections or with conditions such as chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. Leukaemia and Hodgkin disease are among the conditions that can cause a high white cell count. Smoking commonly causes a mild rise in neutrophils, lymphocytes or both.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: A hospital guideline from Hampshire says a mild, lasting rise is likely to come from a chronic inflammatory or infective process, or from smoking. The same guideline says an unexplained, very high count prompts an urgent referral to haematology. Doctors read the count with symptoms, the differential and sometimes a repeat test or a blood film. Reference ranges differ with age, sex and laboratory, so the report shows the range used. The NHS says severe breathing difficulty, or someone who has passed out and is not responding normally, needs a 999 call. MedlinePlus says some medicines, such as corticosteroids, can raise the white cell count, while others can lower it.

body.heading: When might a blood disorder be considered?
body.body: A GP may arrange a blood test if leukaemia is suspected, and a very high white cell count could be a sign of it. In that case the person is referred urgently to a specialist in blood conditions, called a haematologist. UK sources list tiredness, bleeding or bruising easily, night sweats, weight loss and frequent infections among leukaemia symptoms. Cancer Research UK says leukaemia symptoms can be vague, and that minor conditions are common while leukaemia is rare. For chronic myeloid leukaemia the NHS advises a non-urgent GP visit if symptoms appear.

how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.name: How long antidepressants take to work
how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.headline: How long antidepressants take to work, and what the NHS says about side effects and stopping
how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.summary: The NHS says antidepressants usually start to help after 1 to 2 weeks and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
keyPoints: The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
For sertraline and citalopram the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, with some people feeling better after 1 to 2 weeks.
Early side effects such as feeling sick, headaches and trouble sleeping are common, and the NHS says they usually ease after a couple of weeks.
The NHS and NICE both say that stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, so changes to the dose are decided with the prescriber.
If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 (free, any time) are other routes.

body.heading: How long do antidepressants take to work?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect. They can take up to 8 weeks to work fully. For sertraline, the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, although some people start to feel better after 1 to 2 weeks. For citalopram, the NHS gives the same pattern, with a usual 4 to 6 weeks before the full benefit and some improvement possible after 1 to 2 weeks.

Both medicines belong to a group called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. For citalopram, the NHS advises against stopping after only 1 or 2 weeks just because it seems not to be helping, since the full benefit takes longer to appear.

body.heading: What can happen in the first weeks?
body.body:
The NHS lists nausea, headaches and diarrhoea among the common side effects of sertraline. It also lists dizziness or drowsiness, dry mouth and sleep problems. For citalopram, common effects include tiredness, feeling nervous, dry mouth and sweating. The NHS says common side effects like these are usually mild and go away after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine.

The NHS lists sexual problems, such as a lower sex drive, among the common side effects of citalopram. Sertraline can make a person feel more or less hungry than usual, so weight may go down or up at the start, the NHS says. The NHS suggests avoiding alcohol with sertraline because it can stop the medicine working properly. It also says grapefruit juice can increase the amount of sertraline in the body and the risk of side effects.

If side effects last beyond 1 or 2 weeks, the NHS suggests asking a pharmacist or doctor about them.

body.heading: What if nothing seems to change?
body.body: The NHS says a GP may recommend trying a different antidepressant if the first one is not helping. People respond differently to different antidepressants, so a change of medicine can sometimes help. Anyone worried about their progress can raise it with a GP or pharmacist.

body.heading: Why is stopping suddenly a question for the prescriber?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants should not be stopped suddenly, because this may cause withdrawal symptoms. For citalopram, the NHS says the doctor will usually recommend reducing the dose gradually over several weeks, or longer after a long course. For sertraline, the NHS says stopping is usually done by reducing the dose gradually.

NICE says reducing the dose in stages, known as tapering, helps to lessen withdrawal effects, and that the taper is agreed with the person's healthcare professional. NICE guidance for adults with depression also says people who want to stop should talk to the person who prescribed the medicine. Tapering is typically needed, and most people manage to stop successfully. The NHS adds that stopping too early can make depression come back.

body.heading: How long does treatment usually last?
body.body: The NHS says a course of antidepressants usually lasts for at least 6 months after a person starts to feel better. For citalopram, the NHS says most doctors recommend taking antidepressants for 6 months to a year. For sertraline, the NHS says most doctors recommend treatment for 6 months to a year after a person no longer feels depressed. The decision to stop or continue depends on symptoms and how well the medicine is working, and is made with the prescriber.

body.heading: Where can someone get help in a crisis?
body.body: If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time of the day or night. In England, adults aged 18 or over can refer themselves directly to NHS talking therapies without a GP referral. These services are for anxiety and depression and are not for urgent crisis help.

how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.name: How to read food labels: traffic lights
how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.headline: How to read food labels: traffic light colours, per 100g figures and salt
how-to-read-food-labels-traffic-lights-a.summary: Red, amber and green traffic light labels show whether a food is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt, and per 100g figures allow comparison.
keyPoints: Front-of-pack labels show whether a product is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt.
Red means high, amber medium and green low; energy is not colour-coded.
The colours are mainly based on 100g or 100ml, which makes comparing similar products easier than portion figures do.
When a label lists sodium, multiplying by 2.5 gives the salt content, according to the NHS.

body.heading: What do the traffic light colours mean?
body.body: Front-of-pack labels show whether a product is high, medium or low in fat, saturates, sugars and salt. Red means a high level of that nutrient, amber means medium and green means low. Guidance suggests choosing products with more green and amber and fewer red. Energy, shown in kilojoules and kilocalories, is not colour-coded.

body.heading: Should products be compared per 100g or per portion?
body.body: The colours are mainly based on the amount in 100g or 100ml of the food. Using the per 100g column makes it easier to compare the nutrient content of similar foods. Portion sizes are chosen by manufacturers and can differ, so per portion figures may not be comparable between products. A serving can be as small as one biscuit, so eating two means doubling the figures.

body.heading: What are reference intakes?
body.body: The percentages on front-of-pack labels are based on guidelines for how much of each nutrient and how much energy an average adult needs in a day. They show how much of that daily amount one portion supplies. Where a label has no colour coding, comparing the percentage of the reference intake in a portion is another way to compare foods.

body.heading: How is salt shown on a label?
body.body: Some labels give sodium rather than salt, and the NHS says multiplying the sodium figure by 2.5 gives the amount of salt. The NHS describes a food as high in salt when it has more than 1.5g of salt per 100g, and low when it has 0.3g or less per 100g. The NHS advises adults to have no more than 6g of salt a day.

body.heading: Are these labels compulsory?
body.body: Government guidance describes front-of-pack nutrition labelling in the UK as voluntary. The nutrition table on the back of the pack is mandatory. Labels therefore differ between products, and the per 100g figures are the common point of comparison.
